0.title: Through the Wilderness: The Book of Numbers
0.overview:
The message. Numbers is the story of a people saved but not yet home. God has brought Israel out of Egypt, given them his law and come to live in a tent at the centre of their camp, and the land he promised lies only eleven days’ walk away. Yet they grumble, rebel and, at the very border, refuse to go in, and a whole generation dies in the desert. Through it all God does not let them go: he feeds them every morning, answers rebellion with judgment and with pardon, and brings their children to the edge of the land. Its question to every believer between rescue and home is simple: will you trust the God who saved you?

Background: the name. The English title comes from the two counts of the people (chapters 1 and 26). The Hebrew title, Bemidbar, “in the wilderness”, taken from the first verse, fits the book better. Almost all of it happens where no one can live unless God provides.

The writer. Numbers is the fourth of the five books of Moses. It says that Moses wrote down Israel’s journey stage by stage “by command of the LORD” (33:2), and the Lord Jesus spoke of these books as “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44). A few lines read like a later inspired touch, such as “the man Moses was very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth” (12:3). Many modern scholars think the book was compiled from sources centuries later. This commentary holds, as in Genesis and Exodus, that its substance comes from Moses, with some later inspired notes, though Christians still debate the details.

When and where. The book opens at Sinai in the second year after the exodus (1:1) and ends nearly forty years later “in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho” (36:13). If the exodus was about 1446 BC, as Scripture’s own figures suggest (1 Kings 6:1), these years ran from about 1445 to 1406 BC; others place them about two centuries later. As in Exodus, this commentary leaves the date open. The story has three settings: the camp at Sinai; the oasis of Kadesh on the southern edge of Canaan, where Israel refused to go in; and the plains of Moab across the Jordan from Jericho. Around them lie Edom, which refuses them passage, the Amorite kings Sihon and Og, and Moab and Midian, who try first to curse Israel and then to seduce it.

The kind of writing. Numbers mixes story with law, lists, a travel record and the poetry of Balaam’s oracles, and the mixture is deliberate. Laws for offerings “when you come into the land you are to inhabit” (15:2) are given straight after the generation that refused it has been sentenced: the promise still stands. The rules for the camp, the holy things and the unclean all teach that a holy God lives among this people, which is both their glory and their danger. Read the stories as true history and the laws as God’s instructions for living near him.

Were there really so many? The first count gives 603,550 fighting men (1:46), perhaps two million people in all, and readers rightly ask how so many lived in the desert. Some faithful scholars note that the Hebrew word for “thousand” can also mean a clan or a military unit, which would make the company far smaller. Others answer that the totals add up only as thousands, and that the census silver of Exodus 38:25–26 matches 603,550 men exactly. This commentary takes the numbers as written, while granting that the difficulty is real and that Christians who fully trust Scripture differ. On either reading, it was God, not the desert, that fed them for forty years.

How the book makes its case. The two counts frame the book, and between them a generation dies. In the first part (1:1–10:10) the redeemed people are counted, camped around the tabernacle with God at the centre, and blessed, and they set out “at the command of the LORD” (9:18). The second part (10:11–25:18) tells of the journey and its failure: complaints (chapter 11), revolt by Moses’ own brother and sister, Aaron and Miriam (chapter 12), and at Kadesh the great refusal, when ten spies frighten the people and only Caleb and Joshua urge them to trust God (chapters 13–14). That generation is sentenced to forty years in the wilderness, and more rebellions follow: Korah challenges the priesthood (chapters 16–17), even Moses fails at the rock and forfeits the land (chapter 20), and the people are bitten by serpents and healed by looking (chapter 21). Then the seer Balaam is hired to curse them and can only bless (chapters 22–24); yet at Peor they fall into idolatry and immorality (chapter 25). The third part (chapters 26–36) begins with a new count and a new generation; not one of the first list was left, “except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun” (26:65). Joshua is commissioned, the offerings of the year are renewed, and the land is divided before it is entered, down to five daughters and their father’s portion. The shape is the message: unbelief cannot enter, but God’s promise outlives the unbelievers.

The God of Numbers. After Kadesh, Moses pleads with God in God’s own words: “The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity and transgression, but he will by no means clear the guilty” (14:18). God pardons, and the faithless generation still dies in the desert. The book will not let us choose between the two. The God who judges is the God who gave the blessing “The LORD bless you and keep you” (6:24), and who declared through Balaam, “God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind” (23:19).

Where it leads: to Christ. The New Testament reads Numbers above all by pattern, and once by promise. Jesus himself chose the bronze serpent: “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15). The manna points to the one who said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35); the water from the rock to him, for “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4); and the manslayer freed by the death of the high priest (35:25) to the High Priest whose death sets us free. Balaam, against his will, saw a coming king: “a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel” (24:17), and Jesus calls himself “the bright morning star” (Revelation 22:16). The book also exposes a need. Even Moses, “faithful in all my house” (12:7), could not bring the people in, and Hebrews answers: “Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant … but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son” (Hebrews 3:5–6). Where Israel grumbled for forty years in the wilderness, Jesus, tempted there for forty days, answered with the lesson of the manna (Matthew 4:4; Deuteronomy 8:3). He is the faithful Israelite who did not fail, and the leader who brings his people home. In Greek, Joshua and Jesus are the same name.

For us. The church is a wilderness people too: redeemed at the cross, not yet home. Paul says of Israel’s desert story, “these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction” (1 Corinthians 10:11). Numbers warns that being counted among God’s people is not the same as arriving, and that grumbling and unbelief are not small sins: “they were unable to enter because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:19). But it also shows a God who knows his people by name, feeds them day by day and keeps every promise. Our Joshua has already gone in ahead of us. So look to the one who was lifted up and keep walking: the God who brought Israel’s children to the border will bring all his people home.

1.overview:
Where we are. Numbers opens at Sinai, just over a year after the exodus and one month after the tabernacle was set up (Exodus 40:17). The law has been given, God has come to live in a tent among his people, and the land he promised lies ahead. Before they march, God orders a count.

The message. God knows his people, every one of them, and he has made them what he promised Abraham: a nation, and an army. What looks like a table of figures is a roll of names, taken “head by head” (v. 2), by a God who does not deal with his people in bulk. At the centre is his own dwelling, guarded by a tribe set apart, for the holy God among sinners is both their glory and their danger.

Why it was said. Israel was about to set out for a land held by strong nations (see the introduction). They needed to know they were not a crowd of escaped slaves but the LORD’s host, counted, ordered and led. Both the generation that would die in the desert and the children who would enter needed to see what obedience looked like.

How the chapter makes its case. God speaks from the tent and orders a census of every man of twenty and over able to go to war (vv. 1–3). Twelve chiefs are named to help, their names full of God (vv. 4–16), and the count is done “as the LORD commanded Moses” (vv. 17–19). Tribe by tribe the same careful formula records 603,550 men, the promise to Abraham made visible (vv. 20–46). Then the pattern breaks: Levi is not counted but set around the tabernacle to carry and guard it, “so that there may be no wrath on the congregation” (vv. 47–53). Israel does all that the LORD commanded (v. 54).

Where it leads. By promise, by pattern and by the need it exposes. The promise: the count shows God keeping his word to Abraham, and one name on the list, Nahshon of Judah, stands in the family line of David and of Jesus (Matthew 1:4). The pattern: the God who numbers his people head by head is the Good Shepherd who “calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3). The need: of all these counted men only two would enter the land (14:30), for being counted is not the same as believing. Only Jesus did all the Father commanded, all the way home.

For us. If you belong to Christ, you are not lost in a crowd: God knows your name. But being on the roll of a church is not the same as trusting the Lord who saved you. Take your place among his people, keep him at the centre, and keep walking.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God begins the journey by counting his people, one by one, as an army. He speaks no longer from the mountain but from the tent pitched among them, a year after the exodus and a month after the tabernacle was raised (v. 1). The count is to be by clans and families, “according to the number of names, every male, head by head” (v. 2): a roll of persons, not an estimate. And it is a muster of every man able to go to war (v. 3), for Israel has been redeemed to march, and the land ahead will have to be taken. From the first verse the book shows God as both Shepherd, who knows each one, and Commander, who leads them out.
verseByVerse.theology: God now speaks from the tent of meeting, the place of atonement, and the census is his way of saying that these people are his own.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a redeemed people were mustered as an army. Now: every Christian is enlisted by grace into a people on the move, and none is merely a spectator.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the tent of meeting, on the first day of the second month, in the second year after they had come out of the land of Egypt, saying, "Take a census of all the congregation of the people of Israel, by clans, by fathers' houses, according to the number of names, every male, head by head. From twenty years old and upward, all in Israel who are able to go to war, you and Aaron shall list them, company by company.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A year after the exodus, God speaks from the tent in the middle of the camp and orders a count of every man fit for war: his redeemed people are to be known by name and mustered for the march.

In the tent of meeting. Israel has not moved: this is the same mountain where the law was given, and the tent has been standing exactly one month (Exodus 40:17). What has changed is that God now speaks from inside it. From here to the end of the five books of Moses he speaks from the tent in the middle of the camp, where the blood of sacrifice is offered.

Head by head. That phrase governs the whole chapter. This is not a population estimate but a roll of names, taken one head at a time, and the tedium of the next fifty verses is the direct result of God refusing to deal with his people in bulk. “He calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3) is not a New Testament novelty. It starts in the dust at Sinai.

All in Israel who are able to go to war. A muster, a roll-call of soldiers. These men were redeemed out of Egypt for something, and the something involves a fight. Nobody was brought out of slavery to sit down.
verseByVerse.note: Numbers covers the nearly forty years from Sinai to the plains of Moab, opposite Jericho.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his promise to Abraham, and he keeps it one name at a time. Twelve chiefs, one from each tribe, are appointed to help (vv. 4–16); their names, many built on God, the Almighty or the Rock, read like a confession of faith, and one of them, Nahshon of Judah, is an ancestor of David and of Christ. The whole congregation registers on a single day, exactly as the LORD commanded (vv. 17–19). Then, tribe by tribe, the same unhurried formula records each total, small tribes and great alike (vv. 20–43), until the grand total of 603,550 shows that the seventy who went down to Egypt have become a nation (vv. 44–46).
verseByVerse.theology: God works through appointed leaders and an ordered community, and the great total shows him keeping his promise to Abraham.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: each tribe was represented and none overlooked. Now: in the body of Christ no believer is too small to be noticed or counted.

verseByVerse.quote: And there shall be with you a man from each tribe, each man being the head of the house of his fathers. And these are the names of the men who shall assist you. From Reuben, Elizur the son of Shedeur; from Simeon, Shelumiel the son of Zurishaddai; from Judah, Nahshon the son of Amminadab; from Issachar, Nethanel the son of Zuar; from Zebulun, Eliab the son of Helon; from the sons of Joseph, from Ephraim, Elishama the son of Ammihud, and from Manasseh, Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur; from Benjamin, Abidan the son of Gideoni; from Dan, Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai; from Asher, Pagiel the son of Ochran; from Gad, Eliasaph the son of Deuel; from Naphtali, Ahira the son of Enan." These were the ones chosen from the congregation, the chiefs of their ancestral tribes, the heads of the clans of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God appoints a chief from every tribe to help with the count, and their names, one of them in the family line of Christ, confess the God who made them a people.

The men who shall assist you. God, who knows every one of the six hundred thousand without being told, appoints a dozen men to do the counting. He characteristically works through named, accountable people rather than by decree, a pattern that runs on to the apostles and elders he gives the church.

Names that preach. More than half of these names have El (God), Shaddai (the Almighty) or Zur (Rock) built into them, so that a clerk reading the roll aloud at Sinai confessed the name of God again and again before he reached the end.

From Judah, Nahshon the son of Amminadab. One name reaches far beyond the list. On the first page of the New Testament we read, “Amminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon” (Matthew 1:4). A clan chief on a wilderness muster roll is the great-great-great-grandfather of David (Ruth 4:20–22) and an ancestor of Jesus Christ. He never knew: the line to Bethlehem was running through an administrative task on an ordinary morning. God still weaves his purposes through ordinary faithfulness whose end we will never see.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses and Aaron took these men who had been named, and on the first day of the second month, they assembled the whole congregation together, who registered themselves by clans, by fathers' houses, according to the number of names from twenty years old and upward, head by head, as the LORD commanded Moses. So he listed them in the wilderness of Sinai.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The count is carried out on the day and in the way God commanded, and the book sets that obedience at its front because what follows is a story of disobedience.

Who registered themselves. Each man came forward and declared his descent, by clan and father’s house (v. 18). To belong to Israel was to be able to say whose you were.

As the LORD commanded Moses. Three verses of procedure end with the phrase that becomes the refrain of these opening chapters, repeated almost to monotony. The monotony is deliberate, because of what is coming. This is the book of the rebellion: within a few chapters the same people will demand meat, refuse the land, follow Korah and talk of stoning the two faithful spies. The writer establishes at the front what the alternative looked like: a nation doing what it was told, on the day it was told, in order.

A quiet dignity. Former brick-makers stand in ranks, and nobody is whipping them. They do it not because they must but because God said so and they still want to. Numbers tells how a people who began like this ended up buried in a desert, and the first answer is simply that they stopped obeying.

Of the people of Simeon, their generations, by their clans, by their fathers' houses, those of them who were listed, according to the number of names, head by head, every male from twenty years old and upward, all who were able to go to war: those listed of the tribe of Simeon were 59,300. Of the people of Manasseh, their generations, by their clans, by their fathers' houses, according to the number of names, from twenty years old and upward, every man able to go to war: those listed of the tribe of Manasseh were 32,200. Of the people of Benjamin, their generations, by their clans, by their fathers' houses, according to the number of names, from twenty years old and upward, every man able to go to war: those listed of the tribe of Benjamin were 35,400. Of the people of Dan, their generations, by their clans, by their fathers' houses, according to the number of names, from twenty years old and upward, every man able to go to war: those listed of the tribe of Dan were 62,700. Of the people of Asher, their generations, by their clans, by their fathers' houses, according to the number of names, from twenty years old and upward, every man able to go to war: those listed of the tribe of Asher were 41,500. Of the people of Naphtali, their generations, by their clans, by their fathers' houses, according to the number of names, from twenty years old and upward, every man able to go to war: those listed of the tribe of Naphtali were 53,400. These are those who were listed, whom Moses and Aaron listed with the help of the chiefs of Israel, twelve men, each representing his fathers' house. So all those listed of the people of Israel, by their fathers' houses, from twenty years old and upward, every man able to go to war in Israel— all those listed were 603,550.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tribe by tribe, with the same care for each, the count reaches 603,550: God has made the seventy who went down to Egypt into the nation he promised Abraham, though most of these men will never reach the land.

According to the number of names. Twenty-four verses of the same sentence, twelve times over, and nobody is summarised. God does not compress the small tribes to save space or give Judah extra room for being important. Each gets the identical formula and care: his attention does not thin out as the list gets long.

Judah and Dan. Two figures will matter later. Judah is the largest at 74,600, and Jacob had said, “The scepter shall not depart from Judah” (Genesis 49:10): the royal tribe is already the strongest, centuries before there is a king. Dan is second at 62,700, a sobering thing to know, because Dan will become a byword for idolatry (Judges 18:30–31) and is missing from the sealed tribes of Revelation 7. A large membership roll has never been the same thing as a faithful church.

The total. 603,550. Set that against the promise made to a childless man outside his tent one night, “Look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them … So shall your offspring be” (Genesis 15:5), and against the seventy people who went down into Egypt (Genesis 46:27). The number is the proof that God kept his word: he promised a nation, and here is a nation.

A shadow across it. Of these 603,550 men, only two will enter the land (14:30). “With most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness. Now these things took place as examples for us” (1 Corinthians 10:5–6). Every man in this list was redeemed, counted, armed and enrolled. Being on the register of the people of God is not the same as arriving; what they lacked was faith in the God who had brought them out (Hebrews 3:19). The only roll that guarantees arrival is “the Lamb’s book of life” (Revelation 21:27), because it rests on his faithfulness, not ours.

Where Christians differ: are the numbers literal? Over 600,000 fighting men implies a people of perhaps two million, and readers rightly ask how so many lived in the Sinai desert. The Hebrew word translated “thousand”, eleph, usually means a thousand but can also mean a clan or a military unit (Gideon calls his clan an eleph in Judges 6:15). So some faithful scholars read each tribe’s figure as so many units and so many hundreds, giving an army of perhaps five or six thousand. That would explain why there were only 22,273 firstborn sons (3:43), and why Moses calls Israel “the fewest of all peoples” (Deuteronomy 7:7). Others answer that the totals add up only as thousands (603,550), and that the census silver of Exodus 38:25–26 matches 603,550 men at half a shekel each exactly.

This commentary’s view. This commentary takes the numbers as written, while granting that the difficulty is real and that Christians who fully trust Scripture differ here. Either way the point stands: God made a nation out of seventy people, and it was God, with manna for forty years, not the desert, that fed them.
verseByVerse.note: Levi is not counted here; its men are numbered separately in chapter 3.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the centre of the counted army stands the holy God, and one tribe is set apart to guard his dwelling. Levi is left off the war roll (vv. 47–49), not as a lesser tribe but as a tribe given to God: the Levites carry the tabernacle, take it down and set it up, and camp around it (vv. 50–51). Their ring of tents stands between the holy presence and the camp, “so that there may be no wrath on the congregation of the people of Israel” (vv. 52–53), and any outsider who comes near must die. The chapter closes on a sentence this book will rarely write again: Israel did all that the LORD commanded (v. 54).
verseByVerse.theology: Worship came before warfare: God would rather go into battle short-handed than leave his dwelling unguarded.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a tribe was set apart to guard holy things. Now: all believers are a kingdom of priests, called to serve and to guard the gospel entrusted to them.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Levites were not listed along with them by their ancestral tribe. For the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Only the tribe of Levi you shall not list, and you shall not take a census of them among the people of Israel. But appoint the Levites over the tabernacle of the testimony, and over all its furnishings, and over all that belongs to it. They are to carry the tabernacle and all its furnishings, and they shall take care of it and shall camp around the tabernacle. When the tabernacle is to set out, the Levites shall take it down, and when the tabernacle is to be pitched, the Levites shall set it up. And if any outsider comes near, he shall be put to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Levi is taken off the war roll, not to be left out but to be given the highest charge in the camp: to carry, care for and surround the dwelling of God.

Only the tribe of Levi you shall not list. The pattern breaks: one tribe is taken off the war roll. It reads at first like exclusion and it is the opposite. The Levites have three jobs: carry the tabernacle, care for it, and surround it. When Israel marches they are the removal men; when Israel stops they are the fence.

Worship before war. Before Israel could fight, Israel had to worship, and God took a whole tribe out of the fighting strength to make sure of it. He was content to go into the conquest short-handed rather than have Israel’s worship run by whoever was free that week.

Any outsider. Here “outsider” means not the enemy but any Israelite who was not a Levite. The fence exists because God’s holy presence inside it is deadly to anyone who approaches in the wrong way. Hold that beside the moment the curtain of the temple was torn “from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51). The rule was not simply dropped. God himself opened the way from the inside, at the cost of the life of the one Man who could stand in his presence.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel shall pitch their tents by their companies, each man in his own camp and each man by his own standard. But the Levites shall camp around the tabernacle of the testimony, so that there may be no wrath on the congregation of the people of Israel. And the Levites shall keep guard over the tabernacle of the testimony." Thus did the people of Israel; they did according to all that the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites camp as a living buffer between the holy God and a sinful people, so that his wrath does not break out, and the chapter ends with Israel doing all that God commanded.

So that there may be no wrath. The reason for the ring of Levites is given without euphemism: it is a buffer. God is in the middle of a sinful camp, and between his holiness and their sin he places a tribe.

The Levites shall keep guard. The verb is the one used when God put the first man in Eden “to work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Adam was set to guard a garden where God walked, and he let the serpent in. Levi is set to guard a tent where God dwells. Many readers hear an echo here: the task Adam failed in is taken up by a tribe with no land of its own.

Thus did the people of Israel. The chapter ends saying twice that Israel did, as though the writer could hardly believe he was able to write it.

One last look. Take one last look at that camp before the book takes it apart: a nation in order, every family in its place, every name recorded, the tent of God at the centre, a guard of Levites around the glory, and the whole camp doing exactly what it was told. It is the nearest thing to Eden since the gate was shut, and it lasts about ten chapters. Only one man has ever gone the whole distance and been able to say, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), and it is his obedience, not Israel’s and not ours, that God’s people finally rest on.

1.theology:
God Knows His People by Name. The same God who numbers the stars (Ps 147:4) numbers his people, and writes the redeemed in the Lamb’s book of life. To be known by God is the foundation of all assurance.

Redemption Unto Warfare. Israel is saved from Egypt not for ease but for battle; the census is a muster of the LORD’s host. So the church is enlisted to fight the good fight of faith, with spiritual weapons, not worldly ones. Salvation is the beginning, not the end, of conflict.

Holiness Guarded by Mediation. The Levites encircle the tabernacle “so that there may be no wrath.” The holy God cannot be approached carelessly. This tribe standing between God and the people foreshadows Christ, our great High Priest, who alone brings us near and bears away the wrath we deserve.
1.examples:
Then: A redeemed people stood in ordered ranks at Sinai, every man counted and the holy tent guarded at the center.

Now: in Christ you are known by God, counted by name, and brought near to the holy God who once kept outsiders at a distance on pain of death. Live, then, as one written in heaven’s register, by the Spirit who dwells in you: serve, guard the gospel, and do what the Lord commands.

keyVerse.quote: Take a census of all the congregation of the people of Israel, by clans, by fathers’ houses, according to the number of names, every male, head by head.
keyVerse.note: God’s first word from the tent is a command to count, and the way he counts shows what he is like: by families, “according to the number of names”, “head by head”. The census is a roll of persons, not an estimate, and it proves the promise to Abraham kept. Everything else in the chapter, from the twelve chiefs to the guard of Levites, orders a people God knows one by one.

1.reflection:
God counts Israel “according to the number of names” and “head by head” (v. 2). How does it change the way you see yourself, and the people in your church, to know that God does not deal with his people in bulk?

Nahshon could not have known that his family line would lead to David and to Jesus (v. 7; Matthew 1:4). What ordinary task or quiet faithfulness in your life might God be using in ways you will never see?

Every man on this list was redeemed and counted, yet almost none of them entered the land (1 Corinthians 10:5–6). What is the difference between being on the roll of a church and trusting Christ, and how can we help one another not to confuse the two?

God took a whole tribe out of the army so that his dwelling and Israel’s worship would be guarded (vv. 47–53). What does that say about the place of worship in a busy Christian life, and what tends to crowd it out for you?

2.title: The Camp Arrangement: God at the Center
2.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying,<sup>2</sup>"The people of Israel shall camp each by his own standard, with the banners of their fathers' houses. They shall camp facing the tent of meeting on every side.<sup>3</sup>Those to camp on the east side toward the sunrise shall be of the standard of the camp of Judah by their companies, the chief of the people of Judah being Nahshon the son of Amminadab,<sup>4</sup>his company as listed being 74,600.<sup>5</sup>Those to camp next to him shall be the tribe of Issachar, the chief of the people of Issachar being Nethanel the son of Zuar,<sup>6</sup>his company as listed being 54,400.<sup>7</sup>Then the tribe of Zebulun, the chief of the people of Zebulun being Eliab the son of Helon,<sup>8</sup>his company as listed being 57,400.<sup>9</sup>All those listed of the camp of Judah, by their companies, were 186,400. They shall set out first on the march.<sup>10</sup>"On the south side shall be the standard of the camp of Reuben by their companies, the chief of the people of Reuben being Elizur the son of Shedeur,<sup>11</sup>his company as listed being 46,500.<sup>12</sup>And those to camp next to him shall be the tribe of Simeon, the chief of the people of Simeon being Shelumiel the son of Zurishaddai,<sup>13</sup>his company as listed being 59,300.<sup>14</sup>Then the tribe of Gad, the chief of the people of Gad being Eliasaph the son of Reuel,<sup>15</sup>his company as listed being 45,650.<sup>16</sup>All those listed of the camp of Reuben, by their companies, were 151,450. They shall set out second.<sup>17</sup>"Then the tent of meeting shall set out, with the camp of the Levites in the midst of the camps; as they camp, so shall they set out, each in position, standard by standard.<sup>18</sup>"On the west side shall be the standard of the camp of Ephraim by their companies, the chief of the people of Ephraim being Elishama the son of Ammihud,<sup>19</sup>his company as listed being 40,500.<sup>20</sup>And next to him shall be the tribe of Manasseh, the chief of the people of Manasseh being Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur,<sup>21</sup>his company as listed being 32,200.<sup>22</sup>Then the tribe of Benjamin, the chief of the people of Benjamin being Abidan the son of Gideoni,<sup>23</sup>his company as listed being 35,400.<sup>24</sup>All those listed of the camp of Ephraim, by their companies, were 108,100. They shall set out third on the march.<sup>25</sup>"On the north side shall be the standard of the camp of Dan by their companies, the chief of the people of Dan being Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai,<sup>26</sup>his company as listed being 62,700.<sup>27</sup>And those to camp next to him shall be the tribe of Asher, the chief of the people of Asher being Pagiel the son of Ochran,<sup>28</sup>his company as listed being 41,500.<sup>29</sup>Then the tribe of Naphtali, the chief of the people of Naphtali being Ahira the son of Enan,<sup>30</sup>his company as listed being 53,400.<sup>31</sup>All those listed of the camp of Dan were 157,600. They shall set out last, standard by standard."<sup>32</sup>These are the people of Israel as listed by their fathers' houses. All those listed in the camps by their companies were 603,550.<sup>33</sup>But the Levites were not listed among the people of Israel, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>34</sup>Thus did the people of Israel. According to all that the LORD commanded Moses, so they camped by their standards, and so they set out, each one in his clan, according to his fathers' house.
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 counted Israel’s fighting men; now God tells them where to stand. Still at Sinai, the counted army is arranged into a camp, ready for the march that begins in chapter 10.

The message. God lives in the middle of his people, and their whole life is arranged around him. The twelve tribes keep their own banners, but every one of them faces the same tent, and when they march, God’s dwelling travels at the centre. His people are held together not by being the same but by facing the same way.

Why it was said. A mass of former slaves (see the introduction) needed order to cross a desert, but more than order they needed to know what they were: not a refugee column with a shrine in the baggage but the camp of the living God. Later generations, scattered and divided, could look back at this square and see what Israel was meant to be.

How the chapter makes its case. The principle comes first: each tribe by its standard, all facing the tent of meeting (vv. 1–2). Then four divisions of three tribes take their sides: Judah to the east, at the entrance and first on the march (vv. 3–9); Reuben, the demoted firstborn, to the south (vv. 10–16); the tent with the Levites in the middle (v. 17); Ephraim to the west, and Dan to the north as rear guard (vv. 18–31). The total matches the census exactly, and the people do all that the LORD commanded (vv. 32–34).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. The pattern: God pitching his tent in the middle of his people is fulfilled when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and completed in the city where “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3). The promise: Judah, the tribe of the sceptre (Genesis 49:10), marches first, and in Christ, “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5), the royal tribe still leads God’s people home.

For us. The church is a camp with Christ at its centre. Our differences are real and need not be erased, but every life should face him. Ask what your days are actually arranged around, and turn them toward him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The Principle: God at the Center
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole design of Israel’s life is given in two clauses. Each tribe is to camp “by his own standard, with the banners of their fathers’ houses” (v. 2): God keeps the tribes distinct and does not melt them into one mass. Yet all of them are to camp “facing the tent of meeting on every side”: whatever their differences, every family is turned toward the same centre. The camp is organised not around a leader, a road or a water supply, but around the place where God had promised to meet them. These two verses are the key to the rest of the chapter, and a picture of the people of God in every age.
verseByVerse.theology: The heart of the chapter is that God lives in the middle of his people, not at a distance from them.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel pitched its tents facing the tabernacle; Christians order their lives around Christ, in whom God has come to dwell with us.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying, "The people of Israel shall camp each by his own standard, with the banners of their fathers' houses. They shall camp facing the tent of meeting on every side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every tribe keeps its own banner, yet every tribe faces the tent of meeting: God’s people are held together not by sameness but by facing the same way, toward him.

Each by his own standard. God does not melt the twelve into one mass; Reuben stays Reuben and Dan stays Dan. The people of God are not uniform.

Facing the tent of meeting on every side. Twelve different banners, and every one turned inward toward the same point. The camp is organised not around a leader, a border, a water source or a road, but around an address: the place where God had said he would meet them.

The shape of a church. Picture it from above at dusk: a vast square of firelight with a single tent at the centre. That is the shape of a church, and the shape of the Bible’s closing chapters, where the city lies foursquare and has no temple, “for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22).

Uncertain wording. The “banners” are literally “signs”, probably a mark for each family, and Scripture never describes what any of the flags looked like. “Facing” translates a phrase that can also mean “opposite” or “at a distance” (older versions have “far off about”): the tribes were turned toward the tent but did not crowd it, for the Levites camped between (1:53).
verseByVerse.note: Two words for flags appear in v. 2: the “standard” of each three-tribe division and the smaller “banners” of the families within it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives every tribe its place, and the places themselves preach. Judah, with the largest division, camps at the entrance on the east and sets out first, as Jacob’s blessing of the royal tribe foretold (vv. 3–9). Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, who lost his first place through sin, leads the south and marches second (vv. 10–16). Then the tent of meeting moves off with the Levites in the middle of the camps, on the march as at rest (v. 17). Ephraim, the younger son set over the elder, leads the west (vv. 18–24), and Dan, the second strongest, guards the north and brings up the rear (vv. 25–31). The strong are at the edges, and God is at the heart.
verseByVerse.theology: The whole host is ordered for both rest and march, and the order already hints at God’s purposes for Judah (see vv. 3–9).
verseByVerse.examples: Israel was arrayed like a disciplined army; the church is likewise meant to be set in order under her King, each member in his place.

verseByVerse.quote: Those to camp on the east side toward the sunrise shall be of the standard of the camp of Judah by their companies, the chief of the people of Judah being Nahshon the son of Amminadab, his company as listed being 74,600. Those to camp next to him shall be the tribe of Issachar, the chief of the people of Issachar being Nethanel the son of Zuar, his company as listed being 54,400. Then the tribe of Zebulun, the chief of the people of Zebulun being Eliab the son of Helon, his company as listed being 57,400. All those listed of the camp of Judah, by their companies, were 186,400. They shall set out first on the march.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah, the royal tribe and the largest division, camps at the entrance and leads the march, a placement that quietly points to the king God had promised from Judah.

On the east side toward the sunrise. Judah is given two honours, both of placement. The tabernacle’s entrance faced east, so Judah camps at the door, and when the trumpet sounds Judah goes first. No reason is given; it is simply where God puts them.

Jacob’s blessing. Jacob had given the reason on his deathbed: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you … The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet” (Genesis 49:8–10). Israel will have no king for centuries, yet already, in the marching order of a refugee column, the royal tribe heads the line with the largest division in the camp.

The Lion goes first. God builds his plans into practical arrangements long before anyone sees where they lead. The tribe that led the march out of Sinai is the tribe of David and of David’s greater Son, and the road ends with a scroll in heaven that nobody can open until someone says, “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered” (Revelation 5:5). He has been going first since Sinai.
verseByVerse.note: Judah’s division, at 186,400, was the largest of the four (v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: "On the south side shall be the standard of the camp of Reuben by their companies, the chief of the people of Reuben being Elizur the son of Shedeur, his company as listed being 46,500. And those to camp next to him shall be the tribe of Simeon, the chief of the people of Simeon being Shelumiel the son of Zurishaddai, his company as listed being 59,300. Then the tribe of Gad, the chief of the people of Gad being Eliasaph the son of Reuel, his company as listed being 45,650. All those listed of the camp of Reuben, by their companies, were 151,450. They shall set out second.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, leads only the second division: his sin cost him first place, yet God still gives him a standard, a place and a chief in the camp.

On the south side. Reuben is Jacob’s firstborn. By ancient custom the firstborn led the family and received a double share, so Reuben should head the column, yet he is in second place on the southern flank. His father had told him why to his face: “Unstable as water, you shall not have preeminence, because you went up to your father’s bed” (Genesis 49:4). One night, decades earlier, and the birthright went elsewhere for good. Sin has a long reach.

The standard of the camp of Reuben. Yet Reuben is not expelled or unnamed. He has a standard of his own, a division under it, a place in the square and a chief. God took away his first place but did not stop treating him as a son. The arrangement quietly says what the New Testament says outright, that in the people of God position never rested on birth order: “So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy” (Romans 9:16). Every one of us lost a firstborn’s standing in Adam, and the only way back is by belonging to the true Firstborn (Colossians 1:15).

Textual note. Gad’s chief is Deuel’s son in 1:14 and Reuel’s here (v. 14). In Hebrew the letters d and r look almost alike, and some Hebrew manuscripts, the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Latin Vulgate read Deuel here too: one man, two spellings.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the tent of meeting shall set out, with the camp of the Levites in the midst of the camps; as they camp, so shall they set out, each in position, standard by standard. "On the west side shall be the standard of the camp of Ephraim by their companies, the chief of the people of Ephraim being Elishama the son of Ammihud, his company as listed being 40,500. And next to him shall be the tribe of Manasseh, the chief of the people of Manasseh being Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur, his company as listed being 32,200. Then the tribe of Benjamin, the chief of the people of Benjamin being Abidan the son of Gideoni, his company as listed being 35,400. All those listed of the camp of Ephraim, by their companies, were 108,100. They shall set out third on the march. "On the north side shall be the standard of the camp of Dan by their companies, the chief of the people of Dan being Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai, his company as listed being 62,700. And those to camp next to him shall be the tribe of Asher, the chief of the people of Asher being Pagiel the son of Ochran, his company as listed being 41,500. Then the tribe of Naphtali, the chief of the people of Naphtali being Ahira the son of Enan, his company as listed being 53,400. All those listed of the camp of Dan were 157,600. They shall set out last, standard by standard."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tent of meeting travels in the very middle of the camp, with the strongest divisions at front and rear: God is at the centre of his people, on the move as at rest.

In the midst of the camps. Verse 17 is the pivot of the chapter. The tent sets out not at the front, like a general, nor behind, like a supply train, but in the middle, so that whatever the nation was doing, God was at its centre. Six hundred thousand men could look inward from any point on the perimeter and see the same tent.

A God who comes down. That is what sets the Bible apart from every religion of climbing up to God: not a people climbing toward a distant God but a God who has come down and pitched his tent in the middle of the camp. In the end “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), where John’s verb means to pitch a tent.

On the west side. Ephraim goes west, leading Manasseh: as when Jacob crossed his hands to bless them, the younger is set over the elder (Genesis 48:17–19). Dan goes north with the second largest division and marches last as rear guard. The two strongest bodies are at the head and the tail, with the tabernacle between them.

How God keeps his people. That is a picture of how God keeps his people: the strength on the outside, what is most precious in the middle. “The LORD will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rear guard” (Isaiah 52:12).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–34 — The Total and the Obedience
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The camp is complete, and for the second chapter running it ends in obedience. The total matches the census exactly, 603,550, with the Levites counted apart because they belong to the tabernacle (vv. 32–33). Then comes the summary: “Thus did the people of Israel” (v. 34). They camped by their standards and set out in their order, each in his clan, just as the LORD commanded Moses. It is a beautiful sight and a fragile one, for the same camp will soon be a mob. The order was real, but it could not give Israel a new heart.
verseByVerse.theology: The closing refrain of obedience seals the chapter: the well-ordered people do all that God commands.
verseByVerse.examples: Here Israel obeyed in every detail. A church redeemed and indwelt by the Spirit is meant to follow her Lord’s word as gladly.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the people of Israel as listed by their fathers' houses. All those listed in the camps by their companies were 603,550. But the Levites were not listed among the people of Israel, as the LORD commanded Moses. Thus did the people of Israel. According to all that the LORD commanded Moses, so they camped by their standards, and so they set out, each one in his clan, according to his fathers' house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The camp is complete and Israel obeys: a picture of what God’s people were made to be, and a reminder that outward order cannot change the heart.

All those listed in the camps by their companies. The totals match chapter 1 exactly, 603,550, with the Levites again counted separately. (On how so large a host could live in the wilderness, and whether the Hebrew word for “thousand” may mean a clan or unit, see the note at 1:20–46.) For the second chapter running, the chapter ends on obedience: they camped and set out just as the LORD said.

Not enough. Before long, nothing like this can be said of them. From chapter 11 this same camp is a mob, and most of the men counted here will die in the sand. The order was real and it was not enough. Israel needed a new heart, and the rest of Numbers proves it, until there came one Man in the middle of his people who could say without qualification, “I do as the Father has commanded me” (John 14:31). His obedience, not ours, is what the people of God finally stand in.

2.theology:
God Dwells in the Midst. Resting or marching, the tabernacle stands at the centre of the camp: God has come down to dwell among his people.

Order Reflecting Glory. The God of salvation is the God of order; he arranges his people that they may reflect his glory and march as one.

The Primacy of Judah. Reuben forfeited the firstborn’s place, the birthright passing to Joseph and the leadership to Judah (1 Chronicles 5:1–2), and Jacob’s prophecy of a ruler from Judah takes visible shape, pointing to Christ, who leads his people to the inheritance.
2.examples:
Then: Twelve tribes pitched their tents in order, every banner facing the glory at the centre, and moved out at his word.

Now: God has come to dwell among us in Christ before we ever turned toward him, and by his Spirit he lives in his people now. So turn the face of your whole life toward him: keep your God-given identity, yet orient everything around his glory, and march under the Lion of Judah toward the inheritance he secured.

keyVerse.quote: The people of Israel shall camp each by his own standard, with the banners of their fathers’ houses. They shall camp facing the tent of meeting on every side.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter unfolds from this verse. Each tribe keeps its own standard, so God’s people are not made uniform; but every tribe faces the tent of meeting, so they are made one. A people of real differences, held together by a shared centre where God lives among them, is the pattern of the church and of the city to come.

2.reflection:
Each tribe keeps its own standard, yet all face the tent of meeting (v. 2). What differences in your church should be welcomed rather than erased, and what keeps a varied church facing the same way?

If someone could map your week from above, as this chapter maps the camp, what would they find at the centre? What would it take to turn more of it toward Christ?

Reuben lost first place through sin, but kept his standard and his place among God’s people (vv. 10–16; Genesis 49:4). How might this help someone who lives with the consequences of past sin to believe they still belong?

God travelled in the middle of the camp, and in Jesus he “dwelt among us” (John 1:14). How does knowing that God has come to live among his people change the way you think about your church meeting together?

3.title: The Levites as Substitutes: Standing in Place of the Firstborn
3.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the generations of Aaron and Moses at the time when the LORD spoke with Moses on Mount Sinai.<sup>2</sup>These are the names of the sons of Aaron: Nadab the firstborn, and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.<sup>3</sup>These are the names of the sons of Aaron, the anointed priests, whom he ordained to serve as priests.<sup>4</sup>But Nadab and Abihu died before the LORD when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD in the wilderness of Sinai, and they had no children. So Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests in the lifetime of Aaron their father.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>6</sup>"Bring the tribe of Levi near, and set them before Aaron the priest, that they may minister to him.<sup>7</sup>They shall keep guard over him and over the whole congregation before the tent of meeting, as they minister at the tabernacle.<sup>8</sup>They shall guard all the furnishings of the tent of meeting, and keep guard over the people of Israel as they minister at the tabernacle.<sup>9</sup>And you shall give the Levites to Aaron and his sons; they are wholly given to him from among the people of Israel.<sup>10</sup>And you shall appoint Aaron and his sons, and they shall guard their priesthood. But if any outsider comes near, he shall be put to death."<sup>11</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>12</sup>"Behold, I have taken the Levites from among the people of Israel instead of every firstborn who opens the womb among the people of Israel. The Levites shall be mine,<sup>13</sup>for all the firstborn are mine. On the day that I struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, I consecrated for my own all the firstborn in Israel, both of man and of beast. They shall be mine: I am the LORD."<sup>14</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, saying,<sup>15</sup>"List the sons of Levi, by fathers' houses and by clans; every male from a month old and upward you shall list."<sup>16</sup>So Moses listed them according to the word of the LORD, as he was commanded.<sup>17</sup>And these were the sons of Levi by their names: Gershon and Kohath and Merari.<sup>18</sup>And these are the names of the sons of Gershon by their clans: Libni and Shimei.<sup>19</sup>And the sons of Kohath by their clans: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel.<sup>20</sup>And the sons of Merari by their clans: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites, by their fathers' houses.<sup>21</sup>To Gershon belonged the clan of the Libnites and the clan of the Shimeites; these were the clans of the Gershonites.<sup>22</sup>Their listing according to the number of all the males from a month old and upward was 7,500.<sup>23</sup>The clans of the Gershonites were to camp behind the tabernacle on the west,<sup>24</sup>with Eliasaph, the son of Lael as chief of the fathers' house of the Gershonites.<sup>25</sup>And the guard duty of the sons of Gershon in the tent of meeting involved the tabernacle, the tent with its covering, the screen for the entrance of the tent of meeting,<sup>26</sup>the hangings of the court, the screen for the door of the court that is around the tabernacle and the altar, and its cords—all the service connected with these.<sup>27</sup>To Kohath belonged the clan of the Amramites and the clan of the Izharites and the clan of the Hebronites and the clan of the Uzzielites; 3.overview:
Where we are. The camp has been counted and arranged (chapters 1–2), with the Levites left off the war roll and placed around the tabernacle. Now God explains who the Levites are and why they belong to him, beginning with the priests they serve.

The message. God claimed every firstborn son of Israel when he spared them on the night of the Passover, and now he takes the tribe of Levi in their place: one life instead of another, counted exactly, with a ransom paid for every firstborn left over. The holy God can live among sinners only on his own terms, through priests, guards and substitutes he himself provides.

Why it was said. Israel needed to understand why one tribe served at the tabernacle and the others did not (see the introduction). It was not privilege earned but substitution given, and the memory of Nadab and Abihu warned that nearness to God is never to be treated lightly. Korah’s revolt (chapter 16) shows how much the lesson was needed.

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with Aaron’s family and the death of Nadab and Abihu, who offered “unauthorized fire” (vv. 1–4). The Levites are given to Aaron to serve and guard, and any outsider who comes near must die (vv. 5–10). God declares that he takes the Levites “instead of every firstborn”, since all the firstborn have been his from the Passover (vv. 11–13). The Levites are counted from a month old, and each clan is given its side of the tabernacle and its charge, with Moses and Aaron at the entrance (vv. 14–39). Finally Israel’s firstborn are counted, 273 more than the Levites, and five shekels a head are paid for their redemption (vv. 40–51).

Where it leads. By pattern. The chapter’s key ideas, one life “instead of” another, a redemption price, firstborn sons spared by the blood of the Passover, are the vocabulary of the cross. Jesus was himself a firstborn son presented in the temple under the law of the firstborn (Luke 2:22–23), and he came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). So Peter tells believers they were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19).

For us. If Christ has stood in your place, “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). That is not a burden but a freedom: the one who owns you paid everything to have you, and he leaves no debt unanswered.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Priestly Line and Its Peril
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priesthood begins with a grave. These are the generations of Aaron, the family God chose to serve at his altar: four sons, all anointed and ordained (vv. 1–3). But Nadab and Abihu, the two eldest, died before the LORD when they offered “unauthorized fire”, and they left no children, so only Eleazar and Ithamar served with their father (v. 4). The story is told in Leviticus 10, and it is recalled here on purpose. Everything that follows concerns who may come near to God and on whose terms, and before the rules are given, the reader is shown what it costs to treat God’s holiness carelessly.
verseByVerse.theology: The priesthood is holy and perilous; God must be approached on his terms alone.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel’s priests learned at great cost how God may be approached. We draw near through Christ, the one mediator God accepts, and in him we come boldly rather than in dread.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Aaron and Moses at the time when the LORD spoke with Moses on Mount Sinai. These are the names of the sons of Aaron: Nadab the firstborn, and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. These are the names of the sons of Aaron, the anointed priests, whom he ordained to serve as priests. But Nadab and Abihu died before the LORD when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD in the wilderness of Sinai, and they had no children. So Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests in the lifetime of Aaron their father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The record of Aaron’s priestly family begins with a grave: two of his sons died for coming near to God their own way.

These are the generations of Aaron and Moses. The opening words are the ones that mark each new section of Genesis, and here they open a new stage: the founding of a priesthood that will stand between God and Israel. Only Aaron’s sons are listed. Then, in the middle of the family record, verse 4 comes like a door slamming.

Unauthorized fire before the LORD. The story is in Leviticus 10. Two of Aaron’s four sons, newly ordained, men with every right to be in the tabernacle, offered fire God had not commanded. Fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them, on the day their ministry began.

They had no children. The priestly line was nearly cut off in an afternoon, four sons down to two, the dead leaving no heirs. Numbers 3 is full of words like “guard”, “outsider” and “put to death”, and before any of them is used the writer shows us two graves, so that nobody thinks the words are only for show.

A better priest. The High Priest God finally provided has “no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins” (Hebrews 7:27). He came near on the Father’s terms, through his own blood, and brings us with him.

Uncertain wording. “Unauthorized fire” is literally “strange fire”, fire “which he had not commanded them” (Leviticus 10:1). Whether the coals came from somewhere other than the altar (compare Leviticus 16:12), the timing was wrong, or the men had been drinking (compare Leviticus 10:9) is not said. The heart of it is clear: they came near on their own terms.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–39 — The Levites Assigned and Counted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives the Levites to the priests, and he takes them for himself in place of Israel’s firstborn. They are brought near to serve Aaron and to guard the tabernacle, while the priests guard their own office, and any outsider who comes near must die (vv. 5–10). The Levites belong to God “instead of every firstborn”, because he claimed the firstborn on the night he struck Egypt’s (vv. 11–13). They are counted from a month old, owned before they can do anything (vv. 14–20). Each clan receives its side of the tabernacle and its charge: Gershon the fabric, Kohath the holy furniture, Merari the frame, with Moses and Aaron guarding the entrance (vv. 21–39).
verseByVerse.theology: The Levites are a gift to the priesthood and to the whole people, set apart wholly to the LORD.
verseByVerse.examples: One tribe was given over to sacred service; now every believer is called to present himself to God as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Bring the tribe of Levi near, and set them before Aaron the priest, that they may minister to him. They shall keep guard over him and over the whole congregation before the tent of meeting, as they minister at the tabernacle. They shall guard all the furnishings of the tent of meeting, and keep guard over the people of Israel as they minister at the tabernacle. And you shall give the Levites to Aaron and his sons; they are wholly given to him from among the people of Israel. And you shall appoint Aaron and his sons, and they shall guard their priesthood. But if any outsider comes near, he shall be put to death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites are brought near to serve the priests and guard the tabernacle, because a holy God now lives among sinners.

Bring the tribe of Levi near. The Levites are brought near and given to Aaron: nearer to God than the other tribes, but not as near as the priests. The arrangement has steps: the congregation is served by the Levites, the Levites serve the priests, the priests serve at the altar, and God is at the centre. Every step is guarded, and at the bottom stands the fence: “if any outsider comes near, he shall be put to death.”

They shall guard their priesthood. Even the guards are guarded: Aaron and his sons are to “guard their priesthood”, an office to be watched over rather than simply possessed. Korah will try to seize it in chapter 16, and this verse is already warning him off.

Why the fences. A modern reader resents the fences. They exist because of what is inside them: God really present in the middle of a camp. The final answer was not another fence but a way through, “the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:20), made by Jesus, who as both God and man could safely stand on both sides of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Behold, I have taken the Levites from among the people of Israel instead of every firstborn who opens the womb among the people of Israel. The Levites shall be mine, for all the firstborn are mine. On the day that I struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, I consecrated for my own all the firstborn in Israel, both of man and of beast. They shall be mine: I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God takes the Levites in place of Israel’s firstborn, whom he claimed when he spared them at the Passover.

Instead of every firstborn. Here is the sentence the whole chapter exists to say, and it turns on two words: “instead of”. The whole Bible turns on them too: one person standing where another should have stood.

All the firstborn are mine. God’s claim on the firstborn came from Passover night. Every house in Egypt lost its eldest son except the houses with blood on the doorposts, and in those houses a boy woke in the morning who had no business being alive. God had passed over him. From that night, by right of rescue, every firstborn son in Israel belonged to God, not as a figure of speech but as a debt. The spared are owned.

A tribe in their place. Now God stands a whole tribe in the place of all those sons. The Levites are not more deserving; God simply lets his claim fall on them instead. Every firstborn boy in Israel lived as a free man because somebody else was carrying his obligation.

The firstborn Substitute. Centuries later a poor couple carried a baby into the temple “to present him to the Lord” (Luke 2:22). He was a firstborn son under the law of the firstborn, and he had come to be the substitute. Every Christian, spared like those firstborn, is not his own (1 Corinthians 6:19–20), and to belong to the one who spared us is not slavery but safety.
verseByVerse.note: The same claim is restated at 8:16–18, when the Levites are cleansed for their work.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, saying, "List the sons of Levi, by fathers' houses and by clans; every male from a month old and upward you shall list." So Moses listed them according to the word of the LORD, as he was commanded. And these were the sons of Levi by their names: Gershon and Kohath and Merari. And these are the names of the sons of Gershon by their clans: Libni and Shimei. And the sons of Kohath by their clans: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. And the sons of Merari by their clans: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites, by their fathers' houses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites are counted from a month old: they belong to God before they can do anything for him.

From a month old and upward. In chapter 1 the qualification was twenty years old and able to go to war; that census asked what a man could do. This one does not ask. A Levite baby of thirty days, who can contribute nothing and carry nothing, is written on the roll, because the roll is not a list of the useful. It is a list of the owned. He is on the list because of whose he is. (A month is also the age from which a firstborn son was redeemed, 18:16, so the Levites are counted on the same terms as the firstborn they replace, v. 40.)

For those who feel useless. Anyone who wonders whether they are of any use to God can take heart: the month-old babies were as thoroughly the Lord’s as the men carrying the ark. We belong to God by his choice and rescue before we ever serve him.

verseByVerse.quote: To Gershon belonged the clan of the Libnites and the clan of the Shimeites; these were the clans of the Gershonites. Their listing according to the number of all the males from a month old and upward was 7,500. The clans of the Gershonites were to camp behind the tabernacle on the west, with Eliasaph, the son of Lael as chief of the fathers' house of the Gershonites. And the guard duty of the sons of Gershon in the tent of meeting involved the tabernacle, the tent with its covering, the screen for the entrance of the tent of meeting, the hangings of the court, the screen for the door of the court that is around the tabernacle and the altar, and its cords—all the service connected with these. To Kohath belonged the clan of the Amramites and the clan of the Izharites and the clan of the Hebronites and the clan of the Uzzielites; these are the clans of the Kohathites. According to the number of all the males, from a month old and upward, there were 8,600, keeping guard over the sanctuary. The clans of the sons of Kohath were to camp on the south side of the tabernacle, with Elizaphan the son of Uzziel as chief of the fathers' house of the clans of the Kohathites. And their guard duty involved the ark, the table, the lampstand, the altars, the vessels of the sanctuary with which the priests minister, and the screen; all the service connected with these. And Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest was to be chief over the chiefs of the Levites, and to have oversight of those who kept guard over the sanctuary. To Merari belonged the clan of the Mahlites and the clan of the Mushites: these are the clans of Merari. Their listing according to the number of all the males from a month old and upward was 6,200. And the chief of the fathers' house of the clans of Merari was Zuriel the son of Abihail. They were to camp on the north side of the tabernacle. And the appointed guard duty of the sons of Merari involved the frames of the tabernacle, the bars, the pillars, the bases, and all their accessories; all the service connected with these; also the pillars around the court, with their bases and pegs and cords. Those who were to camp before the tabernacle on the east, before the tent of meeting toward the sunrise, were Moses and Aaron and his sons, guarding the sanctuary itself, to protect the people of Israel. And any outsider who came near was to be put to death. All those listed among the Levites, whom Moses and Aaron listed at the commandment of the LORD, by clans, all the males from a month old and upward, were 22,000.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each Levite clan receives its place and its charge, and Moses and Aaron guard the entrance.

The work divided. Gershon camps west, with charge of the curtains, coverings and hangings: 7,500 males. Kohath camps south and has charge of the holy furniture, the ark, table, lampstand and altars: 8,600. Merari camps north and has charge of the structure, down to the pegs and cords: 6,200.

No clan alone. Nobody is left to work out for himself what he is for, and no clan can do without the others: the Kohathites could carry the ark all day and there would be nowhere to put it if Merari had left the bases behind. So it is in the church (1 Corinthians 12:21).

On the east, toward the sunrise. The place at the door belongs to Moses, Aaron and the priests (v. 38), so that anyone approaching met the mediators first: nobody comes to God except past the priest. For us there is one such door: “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved” (John 10:9).

Why 22,000, not 22,300? The three clans as printed add to 22,300, not 22,000 (v. 39). An old Jewish answer is that the extra 300 were themselves firstborn Levites, who could not stand in for anyone else; another is a single copying slip, since in Hebrew “three” and “six” differ by one letter, so that Kohath’s 8,600 may first have been 8,300. The chapter’s arithmetic runs on 22,000.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–51 — The Redemption of the Firstborn
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Substitution is exact, and where it falls short a ransom is paid. The firstborn sons of Israel are counted, and they number 22,273 (vv. 40–43). God takes the 22,000 Levites in their place, life for life, and the Levites’ cattle for Israel’s firstborn cattle (vv. 44–45). But 273 firstborn are left over, with no Levite to stand for them, and God will not let the gap pass. Each is redeemed for five shekels, and the 1,365 shekels are given to Aaron and his sons, exactly as the LORD commanded (vv. 46–51). On a page of bookkeeping God teaches that every claim on a life must be answered, one by one.
verseByVerse.theology: God accounts for every life he has claimed; none is left unanswered for.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel’s surplus firstborn were ransomed with silver; we are ransomed at an infinitely greater cost (see vv. 46–51).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "List all the firstborn males of the people of Israel, from a month old and upward, taking the number of their names. And you shall take the Levites for me—I am the LORD—instead of all the firstborn among the people of Israel, and the cattle of the Levites instead of all the firstborn among the cattle of the people of Israel." So Moses listed all the firstborn among the people of Israel, as the LORD commanded him. And all the firstborn males, according to the number of names, from a month old and upward as listed were 22,273. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Take the Levites instead of all the firstborn among the people of Israel, and the cattle of the Levites instead of their cattle. The Levites shall be mine: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s firstborn are counted and found to outnumber the Levites by 273: God insists that the substitution be exact, life for life.

All the firstborn males. A second count is taken, of the firstborn sons, and the answer is 22,273. Levites: 22,000. The substitution is 273 short.

The shortfall counted. It could easily have been smoothed over; instead God has it counted precisely and will not move on until it is dealt with. He will not have 273 boys in Israel walking about with a claim on them that nothing has answered. That is the character of God in an arithmetic problem. Substitution in Scripture is never approximate: one life for one life, counted to the last head.

Only 22,273 firstborn among 603,550 men? That implies very large families. One common answer is that the count covered only the firstborn born since the Passover, when God claimed them (v. 13). Others think it counted only a mother’s first son, and some see here a sign that the large census figures are better read as clans or units (see the note on the Hebrew eleph at 1:20–46). The text does not say, and faithful readers differ.

verseByVerse.quote: And as the redemption price for the 273 of the firstborn of the people of Israel, over and above the number of the male Levites, you shall take five shekels per head; you shall take them according to the shekel of the sanctuary (the shekel of twenty gerahs), and give the money to Aaron and his sons as the redemption price for those who are over." So Moses took the redemption money from those who were over and above those redeemed by the Levites. From the firstborn of the people of Israel he took the money, 1,365 shekels, by the shekel of the sanctuary. And Moses gave the redemption money to Aaron and his sons, according to the word of the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The 273 left over are redeemed with silver, five shekels each, a price that points to the ransom Christ paid once for all.

Five shekels per head. A price is set for the shortfall, five shekels a head, and the total recorded is 1,365 shekels: 273 times five, exactly.

Ransomed with something better. God had a claim, he provided a substitute, and when the substitute ran out the gap was closed with silver. Then read Peter: “knowing that you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Peter does not cite Numbers 3, but he thinks in its terms: a price set for a life. And he says silver was never going to be enough, not for 273, and not for one.

No shortfall. The tribe of Levi could cover 22,000 and no more. There is a Substitute who covers a number no one can count, with no shortfall and no supplementary payment: “For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). The books balanced at Sinai for 1,365 shekels. They balanced at Calvary for ever, and the price was not silver.
verseByVerse.note: Five shekels was about 2 ounces of silver (a shekel was about 2/5 ounce, or 11 grams).

3.theology:
Substitution. The Levites are taken “instead of” the firstborn, and that pattern is fulfilled when Christ, the true Firstborn, stands in the place of his people and bears the judgment they deserved.

Redemption at a Price. Redemption is never costless: where the substitute fell short, a price had to be paid for every remaining life.

Belonging to God. God’s saving acts establish his ownership. The redeemed are not their own; they belong, body and soul, to the God who claimed them.
3.examples:
Then: One tribe stood in the place of a nation’s firstborn, and silver ransomed the rest.

Now: You belong to God by a greater substitution and a costlier ransom. Christ stood in your place; his blood, not silver, paid your release. You are not your own, and the Spirit he has given you is the power to live as one who belongs wholly to the God who redeemed you, even on the days you do it poorly.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, I have taken the Levites from among the people of Israel instead of every firstborn who opens the womb among the people of Israel. The Levites shall be mine, for all the firstborn are mine. On the day that I struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, I consecrated for my own all the firstborn in Israel, both of man and of beast. They shall be mine: I am the LORD.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter hangs on the words “instead of”. God owns the firstborn because he spared them at the Passover, and he takes the Levites in their place. Rescue, ownership and substitution, set out here in the arrangements of a camp, are fulfilled in the firstborn Son who gave his life as a ransom for many.

3.reflection:
Nadab and Abihu died for coming near to God in a way he had not commanded (v. 4; Leviticus 10:1–3). In what ways are Christians tempted to approach God on their own terms, and why does it matter how we worship?

God says the firstborn are his because he spared them at the Passover (v. 13), and Paul says, “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). How should belonging to the one who rescued you shape your choices this week?

The Levites were listed from a month old, before they could do anything (v. 15). How does it help to know that you belong to God before you are useful to him, especially in seasons when you feel you have little to offer?

God would not leave even 273 firstborn without a ransom (vv. 46–51). What does that exactness show you about the way Christ’s death deals with your sin?

4.title: Levitical Service: The Reverent Transport of Holy Things
4.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Take a census of the sons of Kohath from among the sons of Levi, by their clans and their fathers' houses,<sup>3</sup>from thirty years old up to fifty years old, all who can come on duty, to do the work in the tent of meeting.<sup>4</sup>This is the service of the sons of Kohath in the tent of meeting: the most holy things.<sup>5</sup>When the camp is to set out, Aaron and his sons shall go in and take down the veil of the screen and cover the ark of the testimony with it.<sup>6</sup>Then they shall put on it a covering of goatskin and spread on top of that a cloth all of blue, and shall put in its poles.<sup>7</sup>And over the table of the bread of the Presence they shall spread a cloth of blue and put on it the plates, the dishes for incense, the bowls, and the flagons for the drink offering; the regular showbread also shall be on it.<sup>8</sup>Then they shall spread over them a cloth of scarlet and cover the same with a covering of goatskin, and shall put in its poles.<sup>9</sup>And they shall take a cloth of blue and cover the lampstand for the light, with its lamps, its tongs, its trays, and all the vessels for oil with which it is supplied.<sup>10</sup>And they shall put it with all its utensils in a covering of goatskin and put it on the carrying frame.<sup>11</sup>And over the golden altar they shall spread a cloth of blue and cover it with a covering of goatskin, and shall put in its poles.<sup>12</sup>And they shall take all the vessels of the service that are used in the sanctuary and put them in a cloth of blue and cover them with a covering of goatskin and put them on the carrying frame.<sup>13</sup>And they shall take away the ashes from the altar and spread a purple cloth over it.<sup>14</sup>And they shall put on it all the utensils of the altar, which are used for the service there, the fire pans, the forks, the shovels, and the basins, all the utensils of the altar; and they shall spread on it a covering of goatskin, and shall put in its poles.<sup>15</sup>And when Aaron and his sons have finished covering the sanctuary and all the furnishings of the sanctuary, as the camp sets out, after that the sons of Kohath shall come to carry these, but they must not touch the holy things, lest they die. 4.overview:
