Where we are. Chapter 3 gave each Levite clan its place and charge around the tabernacle. Now God spells out exactly how the holy things are to be carried when the camp moves, and counts the men in their working years who will carry them.

The message. The holy God really lives among his people, and his presence is both their highest privilege and their gravest danger. So he provides a way for sinners to live and work near him: the priests go in first and cover every holy thing, and each carrier is given his own task. Every rule is there, as God says, “that they may live and not die” (v. 19).

Why it was said. Israel was about to set out across the desert with the dwelling of God in the middle of the column (see the introduction). Moving it was not like moving furniture. These instructions guarded the people from presumption, and the death of Uzzah centuries later, when the ark was moved the wrong way (2 Samuel 6:6–7), shows how much they were needed.

How the chapter makes its case. The Kohathites aged thirty to fifty are counted for the most holy things (vv. 1–4). Before they touch anything, Aaron and his sons go in and wrap the ark, the table, the lampstand, the altars and their vessels in layers of cloth and skin (vv. 5–14). Only then may the Kohathites carry them, without touching or even looking, for God does not want them destroyed (vv. 15–20). The Gershonites carry the curtains and the Merarites the frames and pegs, under Ithamar (vv. 21–33). The working Levites are counted, 8,580 in all, “each one with his task of serving or carrying” (vv. 34–49).

Where it leads. By pattern and by the need it exposes. The coverings say: God is here, and you cannot come; only a priest could go in and make the holy things safe to approach. Jesus, our High Priest, has gone in ahead of us as “a forerunner on our behalf” (Hebrews 6:20), and through his flesh he has opened a new and living way for us to draw near (Hebrews 10:19–20). The glory the Kohathites dared not look at we now see “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

For us. Never treat God casually, and never fear that you are kept out: the one who covers us with his own righteousness has made it safe to come near. And whatever your task in his house, glorious or hidden, he assigned it, and he does not overlook it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Kohathites and the Holy Things
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The most holy things are given to the Kohathites, and God takes great care that the privilege does not kill them. Only men in their working prime, thirty to fifty, are counted for the task (vv. 1–4). When the camp moves, Aaron and his sons go in first, wrap each holy object in layers of cloth and skin, and put in its carrying poles (vv. 5–14). Only then do the Kohathites come to lift them, and they must not touch the holy things or even look at them uncovered, lest they die (vv. 15, 20). Eleazar oversees the oil, incense and offerings (v. 16), and God himself states his purpose: “that they may live and not die” (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: God’s glory must be approached through his own provision, or sinful people cannot survive it.
verseByVerse.examples: The ark travelled covered and untouched; we come to the holy God only through Christ, who clothes us in his righteousness so that we may draw near.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying, "Take a census of the sons of Kohath from among the sons of Levi, by their clans and their fathers' houses, from thirty years old up to fifty years old, all who can come on duty, to do the work in the tent of meeting. This is the service of the sons of Kohath in the tent of meeting: the most holy things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Kohathites in their working prime are counted for the highest privilege in the camp: carrying the most holy things.

From thirty years old up to fifty years old. A third census, and a third set of criteria. Chapter 1 counted men who could fight; chapter 3 counted Levites from a month old, because they were owned. This one counts the working years: men strong enough to carry a tabernacle across a desert and mature enough to be trusted with it.

A season for each. A man is claimed as an infant, listed for service in his prime, and released at fifty (8:25–26). Scripture knows a season for heavy work and a season for laying it down, and the God who assigns both values the man no less in the one than in the other.

The most holy things. The Kohathites are given the highest privilege in the camp, and the next sixteen verses are almost entirely about how dangerous it is.

Thirty or twenty-five? The starting age is thirty here but twenty-five in 8:24. The likeliest answer is that Levites entered service at twenty-five and took up the heavy work of carrying the holy things at thirty.

verseByVerse.quote: When the camp is to set out, Aaron and his sons shall go in and take down the veil of the screen and cover the ark of the testimony with it. Then they shall put on it a covering of goatskin and spread on top of that a cloth all of blue, and shall put in its poles. And over the table of the bread of the Presence they shall spread a cloth of blue and put on it the plates, the dishes for incense, the bowls, and the flagons for the drink offering; the regular showbread also shall be on it. Then they shall spread over them a cloth of scarlet and cover the same with a covering of goatskin, and shall put in its poles. And they shall take a cloth of blue and cover the lampstand for the light, with its lamps, its tongs, its trays, and all the vessels for oil with which it is supplied. And they shall put it with all its utensils in a covering of goatskin and put it on the carrying frame. And over the golden altar they shall spread a cloth of blue and cover it with a covering of goatskin, and shall put in its poles. And they shall take all the vessels of the service that are used in the sanctuary and put them in a cloth of blue and cover them with a covering of goatskin and put them on the carrying frame. And they shall take away the ashes from the altar and spread a purple cloth over it. And they shall put on it all the utensils of the altar, which are used for the service there, the fire pans, the forks, the shovels, and the basins, all the utensils of the altar; and they shall spread on it a covering of goatskin, and shall put in its poles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before any Kohathite touches anything, the priests wrap every holy object: only a priest can make the holy things safe to be near.

Cover the ark of the testimony. The priests take down the veil and cover the ark with it, then with goatskin, then with a cloth of blue, then put in the poles so it can be lifted without a hand coming near it. The table, the lampstand, both altars and all the vessels are wrapped the same way, by priestly hands. The Kohathites arrive to find everything already wrapped, and all they lift is the poles or the carrying frame.

The ark in blue. One difference stands out. Every other object travelled with a skin covering outermost; the ark alone had the blue cloth on top. As the column moved, the ark was the one holy thing marked out to every eye.

Protection both ways. The coverings protect the vessels from men who are not permitted, and the men from the glory inside. It is not that the ark was fragile. It is that they were.

A way prepared. Nobody comes to the holy God on his own initiative, and nobody handles what is holy except by a way a priest has prepared. Israel could carry the ark because Aaron had gone in first. The church comes to God at all because “Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf” (Hebrews 6:20).

Uncertain wording. “Goatskin” translates a rare Hebrew word, tachash, whose meaning is uncertain. Older English versions have “badgers’ skins”; others suggest the hide of a sea creature such as the dugong or dolphin, or a fine dyed leather. What is clear is that it was a tough, weatherproof outer covering.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Aaron and his sons have finished covering the sanctuary and all the furnishings of the sanctuary, as the camp sets out, after that the sons of Kohath shall come to carry these, but they must not touch the holy things, lest they die. These are the things of the tent of meeting that the sons of Kohath are to carry. "And Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest shall have charge of the oil for the light, the fragrant incense, the regular grain offering, and the anointing oil, with the oversight of the whole tabernacle and all that is in it, of the sanctuary and its vessels." The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying, "Let not the tribe of the clans of the Kohathites be destroyed from among the Levites, but deal thus with them, that they may live and not die when they come near to the most holy things: Aaron and his sons shall go in and appoint them each to his task and to his burden, but they shall not go in to look on the holy things even for a moment, lest they die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the appointed carriers must not touch or look at the holy things, yet every rule is given so “that they may live and not die”.

They must not touch the holy things. These are the men appointed to the job, doing exactly what God told them, and if a hand slips onto the ark itself they die. Centuries later Uzzah put out his hand to steady the ark when the oxen stumbled, and God “struck him down there because of his error, and he died there beside the ark of God” (2 Samuel 6:7). He was trying to help. It was still death. The ark had been put on a cart instead of carried by Levites as this chapter commands, and David later admitted, “we did not seek him according to the rule” (1 Chronicles 15:13).

Holiness like a live current. Modern readers find that intolerable, but the text does not explain it away. Holiness is not a mood; the Bible treats it as something like a live current, real enough to kill, and the poles and coverings exist so that sinful men can work all day within a few feet of it and go home.

That they may live and not die. God states his motive plainly: “Let not the tribe of the clans of the Kohathites be destroyed” (v. 18). Every prohibition is there for their survival. God is not looking for an excuse to strike a Kohathite. He is going to enormous trouble so that men who cannot survive his presence unprotected can spend their lives carrying his furniture, and he has each man appointed “to his task and to his burden”, so that nobody blunders into what was never his to handle.

Uncertain wording. “Even for a moment” (v. 20) is literally “as a swallowing”, most likely an idiom for an instant, the time it takes to gulp. Some Jewish translators take it instead to mean while the holy things are being “swallowed up”, that is, wrapped and packed away. Either way, the Kohathites were not to look on the holy things uncovered, as the men of Beth-shemesh later did, to their cost (1 Samuel 6:19). On the glory we may now look on, see the note on vv. 46–49.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every part of God’s dwelling matters, and every load is assigned. The Gershonites aged thirty to fifty are to carry the fabric of the tabernacle: its curtains, coverings, screens and hangings, with their cords (vv. 21–26). The Merarites carry its skeleton: the frames, bars, pillars and bases, down to the pegs and cords of the courtyard, and their loads are listed by name (vv. 29–32). Both clans work at the command of the priests, under the direction of Ithamar, Aaron’s son (vv. 27–28, 33). Their burdens were heavier and less glorious than the Kohathites’, but without them the house of God could not stand.
verseByVerse.theology: Every servant has an appointed task; the body of God’s servants is ordered and complete.
verseByVerse.examples: As every clan had its assigned burden, so every believer is gifted and placed in the body of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Take a census of the sons of Gershon also, by their fathers' houses and by their clans. From thirty years old up to fifty years old, you shall list them, all who can come to do duty, to do service in the tent of meeting. This is the service of the clans of the Gershonites, in serving and bearing burdens: they shall carry the curtains of the tabernacle and the tent of meeting with its covering and the covering of goatskin that is on top of it and the screen for the entrance of the tent of meeting and the hangings of the court and the screen for the entrance of the gate of the court that is around the tabernacle and the altar, and their cords and all the equipment for their service. And they shall do all that needs to be done with regard to them. All the service of the sons of the Gershonites shall be at the command of Aaron and his sons, in all that they are to carry and in all that they have to do. And you shall assign to their charge all that they are to carry. This is the service of the clans of the sons of the Gershonites in the tent of meeting, and their guard duty is to be under the direction of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest. "As for the sons of Merari, you shall list them by their clans and their fathers' houses. From thirty years old up to fifty years old, you shall list them, everyone who can come on duty, to do the service of the tent of meeting. And this is what they are charged to carry, as the whole of their service in the tent of meeting: the frames of the tabernacle, with its bars, pillars, and bases, and the pillars around the court with their bases, pegs, and cords, with all their equipment and all their accessories. And you shall list by name the objects that they are required to carry. This is the service of the clans of the sons of Merari, the whole of their service in the tent of meeting, under the direction of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Gershonites carry the fabric of God’s dwelling and the Merarites its frame, each load assigned: work that is necessary, if not glorious.

Under the direction of Ithamar. Gershon takes the fabric of the dwelling, Merari its skeleton, both “under the direction of Ithamar”. The Merarites’ loads are even listed by name (v. 32), down to the pegs. Somewhere in that camp was a man whose whole commission from Almighty God was a bundle of tent pegs, assigned to him as carefully as the ark was assigned to Kohath.

Necessary, if not glorious. The tabernacle could not stand without the frames, nor the frames without the bases, and the whole structure would come down in a night wind without the pegs and cords. The Kohathite had the more glorious burden, not the more necessary one, and nobody chose which he had.

Merarites today. Every congregation has its Merarites: people whose unnoticed work holds everything up, and whose absence would be felt within a week. God assigned that work himself. “The parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable” (1 Corinthians 12:22). And the Lord of the house himself “came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45), so no hidden service is beneath his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–49 — The Levites Numbered for Service
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps the register of those who serve him. Moses, Aaron and the chiefs count the Levites of working age clan by clan: 2,750 Kohathites, 2,630 Gershonites and 3,200 Merarites (vv. 34–45). The total is 8,580 (vv. 46–48), a small company beside the army of chapter 1, yet they carried the dwelling place of God through the wilderness. The chapter ends with its refrain, that all was done as the LORD commanded, and with a summary of every Levite’s life: “each one with his task of serving or carrying” (v. 49). No load was self-chosen, and none was overlooked.
verseByVerse.theology: The obedient ordering of God’s servants is sealed once more: all is done as the LORD commanded.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel’s servants were counted and ready for the march; the church too is equipped and sent out for the work of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses and Aaron and the chiefs of the congregation listed the sons of the Kohathites, by their clans and their fathers' houses, from thirty years old up to fifty years old, everyone who could come on duty, for service in the tent of meeting; and those listed by clans were 2,750. This was the list of the clans of the Kohathites, all who served in the tent of meeting, whom Moses and Aaron listed according to the commandment of the LORD by Moses. Those listed of the sons of Gershon, by their clans and their fathers' houses, from thirty years old up to fifty years old, everyone who could come on duty for service in the tent of meeting— those listed by their clans and their fathers' houses were 2,630. This was the list of the clans of the sons of Gershon, all who served in the tent of meeting, whom Moses and Aaron listed according to the commandment of the LORD. Those listed of the clans of the sons of Merari, by their clans and their fathers' houses, from thirty years old up to fifty years old, everyone who could come on duty, for service in the tent of meeting— those listed by clans were 3,200. This was the list of the clans of the sons of Merari, whom Moses and Aaron listed according to the commandment of the LORD by Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fewer than nine thousand working Levites carried the dwelling place of God, and God kept the register of every one.

Small numbers. Kohathites 2,750, Gershonites 2,630, Merarites 3,200. Beside the six hundred thousand of chapter 1 these are small: the men who carried the dwelling place of God through the wilderness were fewer than nine thousand. The visible strength of Israel was the army; what made Israel God’s people, his dwelling among them, was carried by a fraction of one tribe.

Unseen service. That is encouragement for anyone whose service is unseen: God has never once lost track of who is doing the work. He keeps the register himself, and he has been publishing it for more than three thousand years.

verseByVerse.quote: All those who were listed of the Levites, whom Moses and Aaron and the chiefs of Israel listed, by their clans and their fathers' houses, from thirty years old up to fifty years old, everyone who could come to do the service of ministry and the service of bearing burdens in the tent of meeting, those listed were 8,580. According to the commandment of the LORD through Moses they were listed, each one with his task of serving or carrying. Thus they were listed by him, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each Levite had his own task of serving or carrying, assigned by the LORD, and all was done as he commanded.

As the LORD commanded Moses. The chapter closes, twice over, with the seal on every chapter so far: as the LORD commanded. Not one arrangement in four chapters was merely somebody’s good idea.

Each one with his task of serving or carrying. That is not a bad summary of a life, and the difference between drudgery and worship lies not in the weight of the load but in who assigned it.

He is here, and you cannot come. There is a shadow over the whole arrangement. All this careful holiness exists because God had come to live among a people who could not survive him. Every layer of goatskin says: he is here, and you cannot come. Then a man walked into the middle of the camp with no covering over him, touched lepers and they were made clean, and took the poles and the veils and the distance away: “for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Ephesians 2:18). The Kohathites carried the presence of God without daring to look at it. We are invited to look, and it has a human face.

4.theology:
The Peril and Glory of Holiness. God’s holiness is real enough to kill; his nearness is both Israel’s glory and her peril. The coverings are mercy, allowing sinful men to serve and live.

Mediation Before Approach. There is no access to the glory of God except through the mediator God appoints: Christ, who alone can stand before that glory in his own right, and who clothes us to draw near.

Every Servant Assigned. In Israel each clan and each man had a named task; in the body of Christ every member is gifted, placed and precious.
4.examples:
Then: The holy things were wrapped in blue and borne on poles, untouched and unseen; every Levite knew his task, from the ark to the tent pegs.

Now: What the Kohathite could not touch, you behold in the face of Christ and live. Approach the holy God with reverence, clothed in his righteousness, and take up your appointed burden in his house by the Spirit who gifted you for it. No faithful service is overlooked.

keyVerse.quote: but deal thus with them, that they may live and not die when they come near to the most holy things: Aaron and his sons shall go in and appoint them each to his task and to his burden, but they shall not go in to look on the holy things even for a moment, lest they die.
keyVerse.note: These verses hold the chapter’s two truths together. God’s holiness is real enough to kill, so the carriers may not even look at the holy things; yet every rule is given in love, “that they may live and not die”. The priest goes in first and makes a way, which is exactly what Christ has done for us.

4.reflection:
The Kohathites were given the highest privilege in the camp, and the most dangerous (vv. 4, 15). Why is God’s nearness both a gift and a danger, and how does this chapter correct casual attitudes to God?

God says these rules are given “that they may live and not die” (v. 19). Which of God’s commands do you find restrictive, and how might it change things to see them as given for your life?

Somewhere in the camp a man’s whole task was a bundle of tent pegs (vv. 31–32). What unnoticed work holds your church together, and how can you honour those who do it, or do it yourself gladly?

The Kohathites carried the presence of God without daring to look at it, but in Christ we are invited to draw near (Hebrews 10:19–22). What keeps you from drawing near to God with confidence, and what has Christ done about it?

5.title: Laws on Uncleanness and Unfaithfulness
5.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Command the people of Israel that they put out of the camp everyone who is leprous or has a discharge and everyone who is unclean through contact with the dead.<sup>3</sup>You shall put out both male and female, putting them outside the camp, that they may not defile their camp, in the midst of which I dwell."<sup>4</sup>And the people of Israel did so, and put them outside the camp; as the LORD said to Moses, so the people of Israel did.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>6</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, When a man or woman commits any of the sins that people commit by breaking faith with the LORD, and that person realizes his guilt,<sup>7</sup>he shall confess his sin that he has committed. And he shall make full restitution for his wrong, adding a fifth to it and giving it to him to whom he did the wrong.<sup>8</sup>But if the man has no next of kin to whom restitution may be made for the wrong, the restitution for wrong shall go to the LORD for the priest, in addition to the ram of atonement with which atonement is made for him.<sup>9</sup>And every contribution, all the holy donations of the people of Israel, which they bring to the priest, shall be his.<sup>10</sup>Each one shall keep his holy donations: whatever anyone gives to the priest shall be his."<sup>11</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>12</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, If any man's wife goes astray and breaks faith with him,<sup>13</sup>if a man lies with her sexually, and it is hidden from the eyes of her husband, and she is undetected though she has defiled herself, and there is no witness against her, since she was not taken in the act,<sup>14</sup>and if the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife who has defiled herself, or if the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife, though she has not defiled herself,<sup>15</sup>then the man shall bring his wife to the priest and bring the offering required of her, a tenth of an ephah of barley flour. He shall pour no oil on it and put no frankincense on it, for it is a grain offering of jealousy, a grain offering of remembrance, bringing iniquity to remembrance.<sup>16</sup>"And the priest shall bring her near and set her before the LORD.<sup>17</sup>And the priest shall take holy water in an earthenware vessel and take some of the dust that is on the floor of the tabernacle and put it into the water.<sup>18</sup>And the priest shall set the woman before the LORD and unbind the hair of the woman's head and place in her hands the grain offering of remembrance, which is the grain offering of jealousy. And in his hand the priest shall have the water of bitterness that brings the curse.<sup>19</sup>Then the priest shall make her take an oath, saying, 'If no man has lain with you, and if you have not turned aside to uncleanness while you were under your husband's authority, be free from this water of bitterness that brings the curse.<sup>20</sup>But if you have gone astray, though you are under your husband's authority, and if you have defiled yourself, and some man other than your husband has lain with you,<sup>21</sup>then' (let the priest make the woman take the oath of the curse, and say to the woman) 'the LORD make you a curse and an oath among your people, when the LORD makes your thigh fall away and your body swell.<sup>22</sup>May this water that brings the curse pass into your bowels and make your womb swell and your thigh fall away.' And the woman shall say, 'Amen, Amen.'<sup>23</sup>"Then the priest shall write these curses in a book and wash them off into the water of bitterness.<sup>24</sup>And he shall make the woman drink the water of bitterness that brings the curse, and the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain.<sup>25</sup>And the priest shall take the grain offering of jealousy out of the woman's hand and shall wave the grain offering before the LORD and bring it to the altar.<sup>26</sup>And the priest shall take a handful of the grain offering, as its memorial portion, and burn it on the altar, and afterward shall make the woman drink the water.<sup>27</sup>And when he has made her drink the water, then, if she has defiled herself and has broken faith with her husband, the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain, and her womb shall swell, and her thigh shall fall away, and the woman shall become a curse among her people.<sup>28</sup>But if the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, then she shall be free and shall conceive children.<sup>29</sup>"This is the law in cases of jealousy, when a wife, though under her husband's authority, goes astray and defiles herself,<sup>30</sup>or when the spirit of jealousy comes over a man and he is jealous of his wife. Then he shall set the woman before the LORD, and the priest shall carry out for her all this law.<sup>31</sup>The man shall be free from iniquity, but the woman shall bear her iniquity."
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 1–4 counted the tribes, set them in order around the tabernacle and gave the Levites their duties. With the camp arranged around God’s dwelling, chapter 5 asks what kind of life belongs in a camp where the holy God lives.

The message. God lives among his people, so nothing that defiles may stay hidden in the camp: not the marks of death, not a wrong done to a neighbour, not secret unfaithfulness in a marriage. Yet every one of these laws also makes a way through. The unclean can be cleansed and return, the guilty can confess and repay, and a suspected wife is taken out of her husband’s hands and put into the hands of the God who knows the truth.

Why it was said. Israel was about to march through the wilderness as a holy people with God at its centre (see the introduction). A camp that size would know disease, death, fraud and jealousy. These laws taught it that the body, the purse and the marriage bed all lie open before the God who dwells there.

How the chapter makes its case. Three laws move from the visible to the hidden. Bodily uncleanness, which everyone can see, is put outside the camp (vv. 1–4). Wrongs done to a neighbour, which may be known only to the one who did them, must be confessed and repaid with a fifth added, and if the victim has no kin left, the debt is paid to the LORD (vv. 5–10). Last comes the most hidden thing of all, a suspected adultery with no witness. It is brought before God, who alone gives the verdict: guilt exposed, or innocence publicly cleared (vv. 11–31).

Where it leads. Chiefly by pattern and by the need it exposes. The unclean went outside the camp; Jesus touched the leper he should have shunned, and “suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). The cup of the curse awaited only the guilty wife, yet the prophets describe Israel itself as the LORD’s unfaithful wife (Hosea 2), and the faithful Bridegroom drank the cup of judgment for his unfaithful bride, “becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). That last link is drawn from the whole of Scripture rather than stated here, but it fits the chapter’s shape.

For us. Nothing in our lives is hidden from the God who lives among us, and in Christ that is good news before it is frightening, because he has made a way back. Bring your uncleanness to the one who touches lepers, put right the wrongs you can, and leave the suspicions you cannot resolve with the Judge who knows all things.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Putting the Unclean Outside the Camp
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Where God lives, the marks of death may not stay. Three kinds of uncleanness, skin disease, bodily discharge and contact with a corpse, put a man or woman outside the camp for a time (vv. 1–3). None of them is a sin; each is a sign of a world under the curse, and the reason given is God’s presence: “in the midst of which I dwell.” Israel obeys at once (v. 4). Other laws provide the way back (Leviticus 13–15; Numbers 19), so this is a holy quarantine, not a permanent sentence.
verseByVerse.theology: The purity laws are not arbitrary hygiene: they follow from the nearness of the holy God.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel put the unclean outside the camp; Christ went outside the camp himself, bearing our uncleanness, to bring us in.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Command the people of Israel that they put out of the camp everyone who is leprous or has a discharge and everyone who is unclean through contact with the dead. You shall put out both male and female, putting them outside the camp, that they may not defile their camp, in the midst of which I dwell." And the people of Israel did so, and put them outside the camp; as the LORD said to Moses, so the people of Israel did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where the living God dwells, the signs of death are put at a distance. The unclean are not punished but moved outside the camp for a time, for the sake of his presence.

The body coming apart. Skin disease, bodily discharge and contact with a corpse are all forms of decay, leakage and death. They are not sins, and none is anybody’s fault; they are the visible marks of a world under the curse. The reason is given without softening: “that they may not defile their camp, in the midst of which I dwell.”

The people of Israel did so. It was a hard command, and Israel obeyed it: families put out their own relatives. The exclusion was temporary, and the law provided a way to be cleansed and come back (Leviticus 14; Numbers 19); but a man carrying his sick brother’s bedding to the edge of the camp was not much consoled by that on the day.

The touch of Jesus. Under this law uncleanness spreads and holiness does not. Then a leper knelt before Jesus, and “moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him” (Mark 1:41). The contamination did not travel up his arm; the cleansing travelled down it. The camp had to put its unclean outside. He went outside the gate himself (Hebrews 13:12) and brought them in.

What it does not mean. Not that illness marks some special sin (John 9:2–3). These ceremonial laws are fulfilled in Christ, and the church does not put the sick outside; it goes to them (James 5:14).
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew word translated “leprous” covers a range of skin diseases, not only what is now called leprosy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wronging a neighbour is breaking faith with God, and repentance must reach the purse as well as the lips. When a guilty person realises his guilt, he confesses the particular sin and repays it in full with a fifth added (vv. 5–7). If the one he wronged has died with no next of kin, the debt does not vanish: it is paid to the LORD through the priest, alongside the ram of atonement (v. 8). The section closes by confirming that gifts brought to the priests belong to them (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: Repentance is more than feeling sorry: it names the wrong and puts it right.
verseByVerse.examples: The repentance the gospel produces still bears this fruit: honest confession and, where it can be done, things made right with the people we have wronged.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, When a man or woman commits any of the sins that people commit by breaking faith with the LORD, and that person realizes his guilt, he shall confess his sin that he has committed. And he shall make full restitution for his wrong, adding a fifth to it and giving it to him to whom he did the wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cheating a neighbour is unfaithfulness to God, and real repentance names the sin and pays it back with more besides.

Breaking faith with the LORD. The offence is theft or fraud against a neighbour (repeating Leviticus 6:1–7), yet God calls it breaking faith with him. If I cheat a man in business, what has God got to do with it? Everything: every person you deal with belongs to God, and every dealing happens in his presence. David said it of a sin that had ruined two other lives: “Against you, you only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4).

Real repentance in three steps. He “realizes his guilt”: he calls it a sin, not a mistake or a difficult season. He “shall confess” it, naming the particular wrong rather than regretting sin in general. And he “shall make full restitution,” adding a fifth: the money goes back, and more than went missing.

Zacchaeus. When Christ came into his house, Zacchaeus offered four times over (Luke 19:8), the penalty for a stolen sheep (Exodus 22:1), and Jesus did not call it unnecessary. Notice the order: Jesus came to him first, and the restitution followed. Grace has never made restitution unnecessary; it is what finally makes it possible.

Uncertain wording. “Any of the sins that people commit” is literally “any sins of the man,” which can mean sins people commit or sins against another person. The restitution that follows shows that wrongs against a neighbour are meant either way.

verseByVerse.quote: But if the man has no next of kin to whom restitution may be made for the wrong, the restitution for wrong shall go to the LORD for the priest, in addition to the ram of atonement with which atonement is made for him. And every contribution, all the holy donations of the people of Israel, which they bring to the priest, shall be his. Each one shall keep his holy donations: whatever anyone gives to the priest shall be his."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A debt does not die with the one it was owed to: if no relative can receive it, it is paid to the LORD.

If the man has no next of kin. In every human system a debt with no claimant evaporates. God’s law says it is still owed, and he receives it himself through the priest. Neither time nor a funeral discharges a wrong; the accounts of a man cheated forty years ago are still open, and God holds them. And the ram of atonement is still required (Leviticus 6:6–7): restitution puts things right with the neighbour, but only atonement puts things right with God.

Debts we cannot repay. Read alone, that is hard news, because most of us have wronged people we can no longer find. Read in the light of the whole Bible, it is why the cross was necessary and why it is enough. Every debt is owed finally to God, so it had to be settled with God, and at the cross it was.

Uncertain wording. In verse 10, “Each one shall keep his holy donations” is compressed: it may mean that each giver chooses which priest receives his gift, or that each priest keeps what is brought to him. Either way the verse’s point is plain: what is given to God’s servants is theirs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–31 — The Ordeal of Bitter Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A husband who suspects adultery but cannot prove it may not act on his suspicion; he must bring his wife before the LORD and let God give the verdict. The law twice allows that she may be innocent (vv. 11–15). The priest sets her before the LORD, she accepts the oath with “Amen, Amen,” and she drinks holy water mixed with dust from the tabernacle floor and the washed-off words of the curse (vv. 16–26). Nothing in the cup can harm her; only God can. If she is guilty she bears her iniquity; if innocent, she “shall be free and shall conceive children” (vv. 27–31).
verseByVerse.theology: God sees in secret; he defends the wronged and will not let hidden unfaithfulness quietly corrode his people.
verseByVerse.examples: The rite of bitter water has passed away, but its truth remains: every hidden thing will be brought to light before the One who judges righteously, and the innocent will be cleared.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, If any man's wife goes astray and breaks faith with him, if a man lies with her sexually, and it is hidden from the eyes of her husband, and she is undetected though she has defiled herself, and there is no witness against her, since she was not taken in the act, and if the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife who has defiled herself, or if the spirit of jealousy comes over him and he is jealous of his wife, though she has not defiled herself, then the man shall bring his wife to the priest and bring the offering required of her, a tenth of an ephah of barley flour. He shall pour no oil on it and put no frankincense on it, for it is a grain offering of jealousy, a grain offering of remembrance, bringing iniquity to remembrance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A husband who suspects his wife but has no proof may not take matters into his own hands; he must bring her before God.

If the spirit of jealousy comes over him. Deuteronomy 22:22 deals with adultery proved; this law deals with suspicion, with no evidence and no witness. Twice it describes the husband: the “spirit of jealousy” comes over him whether she has defiled herself or “though she has not defiled herself.” That double clause is the key: the law openly allows that she may be entirely innocent and he simply consumed by jealousy.

Out of the husband’s hands. Without this statute, a jealous husband in the ancient world had no procedure and no restraint: she could be divorced, disgraced, put out or worse at his whim. This law says he may not act. He must bring it to the priest, in public, and let God decide. The barley offering, without oil or frankincense, has none of the marks of joy; it only brings the matter before God, “bringing iniquity to remembrance.”

verseByVerse.quote: "And the priest shall bring her near and set her before the LORD. And the priest shall take holy water in an earthenware vessel and take some of the dust that is on the floor of the tabernacle and put it into the water. And the priest shall set the woman before the LORD and unbind the hair of the woman's head and place in her hands the grain offering of remembrance, which is the grain offering of jealousy. And in his hand the priest shall have the water of bitterness that brings the curse. Then the priest shall make her take an oath, saying, 'If no man has lain with you, and if you have not turned aside to uncleanness while you were under your husband's authority, be free from this water of bitterness that brings the curse. But if you have gone astray, though you are under your husband's authority, and if you have defiled yourself, and some man other than your husband has lain with you, then' (let the priest make the woman take the oath of the curse, and say to the woman) 'the LORD make you a curse and an oath among your people, when the LORD makes your thigh fall away and your body swell. May this water that brings the curse pass into your bowels and make your womb swell and your thigh fall away.' And the woman shall say, 'Amen, Amen.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman is set before the LORD and takes an oath that leaves the verdict entirely with him.

Nothing harmful in the cup. Holy water, dust from the tabernacle floor, and (v. 23) the written curse washed into it: nothing that could harm anybody, and that is the design. In other ancient ordeals the accused might be thrown into a river, and the river did the damage. In Israel’s rite, if anything happens to this woman, God did it. The verdict is taken from the priest and above all the husband, and placed with the only one who knows.

Amen, Amen. She is not a passive victim. The oath is stated in both directions, “be free from this water” if she is innocent, and she answers for herself. An innocent woman had every reason to say it loudly, because the only power in the cup was the God who knew she had done nothing.

Why only wives? Adultery by either partner was a capital crime (Leviticus 20:10). This rite dealt with suspicion without evidence and protected a wife from a jealous husband by putting the verdict in God’s hands. It was part of Israel’s ceremonial law and does not apply today.

Uncertain wording. “Unbind the hair” may mean loosen or uncover; either way it was a sign of mourning or disgrace (compare Leviticus 13:45). “Thigh” is probably a modest word for the organs of childbearing, and “your thigh fall away and your body swell” has been read as barrenness, miscarriage or a fallen womb. Verse 28, “she shall be free and shall conceive children,” shows that the curse touches childbearing, but the exact condition is unknown. The NIV’s “miscarry” is an interpretation; the text does not describe an abortion.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the priest shall write these curses in a book and wash them off into the water of bitterness. And he shall make the woman drink the water of bitterness that brings the curse, and the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain. And the priest shall take the grain offering of jealousy out of the woman's hand and shall wave the grain offering before the LORD and bring it to the altar. And the priest shall take a handful of the grain offering, as its memorial portion, and burn it on the altar, and afterward shall make the woman drink the water. And when he has made her drink the water, then, if she has defiled herself and has broken faith with her husband, the water that brings the curse shall enter into her and cause bitter pain, and her womb shall swell, and her thigh shall fall away, and the woman shall become a curse among her people. But if the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, then she shall be free and shall conceive children. "This is the law in cases of jealousy, when a wife, though under her husband's authority, goes astray and defiles herself, or when the spirit of jealousy comes over a man and he is jealous of his wife. Then he shall set the woman before the LORD, and the priest shall carry out for her all this law. The man shall be free from iniquity, but the woman shall bear her iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself gives the verdict: the guilty wife bears her own iniquity, and the innocent one is cleared before everyone and blessed with children.

She shall be free and shall conceive children. The outcome usually forgotten. The innocent woman is publicly vindicated and given what a woman under this suspicion most needed: her good name and children in her arms. The gossip ended the day she walked out of the tabernacle cleared by God himself; no husband could reopen it and no neighbour whisper about it.

The direction of the law. It is a hard law from a world not ours, but it removes a woman from the power of a man who cannot prove anything, forbids him to act on his suspicion, costs him an offering and gives the innocent a public verdict she could get no other way. In its own world, this statute protects.

The man shall be free from iniquity. He does not sin by bringing a genuine suspicion to God rather than acting on it. Suspicion wants to fester or explode; Scripture offers a third way: “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Let God be the judge, because he is, and you are not.

The cup the Bridegroom drank. The prophets call Israel the LORD’s unfaithful wife (Hosea 2), and by this law she would have to drink the cup of the curse. Instead the faithful Bridegroom prayed, “Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36), and drank it, “becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), so that his bride goes free.

What it does not mean. Nothing here licenses a jealous or controlling husband, or any test to make God prove a spouse guilty. Suspicion is not proof, and a spouse who threatens or harms sins gravely. Anyone in that danger should seek safety at once, report violence and tell the church’s elders.

5.theology:
Holiness Because God Dwells. Every purity command flows from the presence of the holy God. Where God lives, the marks of sin and death cannot remain.

Repentance That Restores. Sin against a neighbour is breaking faith with the LORD, and true repentance confesses the specific sin and makes full restitution.

The God Who Sees in Secret. The ordeal shows a God who exposes hidden sin and defends the innocent.
5.examples:
Then: The unclean were put outside, wrongs were restored with a fifth added, and hidden unfaithfulness was brought before God, because the holy God dwelt in Israel’s midst.

Now: Christ went outside the camp bearing your uncleanness, drank the cup you deserved, and was the faithful one in your place, so that your standing rests on his record, not yours. Walk in the light by his Spirit, confess your sins, make things right with those you have wronged, and when you fail, come back to the One who knows every secret and yet declares you clean.

keyVerse.quote: You shall put out both male and female, putting them outside the camp, that they may not defile their camp, in the midst of which I dwell.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter hangs on its last words, “in the midst of which I dwell.” Every law that follows, about the body, the purse and the marriage, comes from the nearness of a holy God. It is both Israel’s glory and its danger, and it explains why the Son of God went outside the camp to bring the unclean near.

5.reflection:
Verses 1–4 put the unclean outside because God dwells in the camp. How does Jesus’ touching of the leper (Mark 1:41) change what holiness looks like, and what does it mean for us to “go to him outside the camp” (Hebrews 13:13)?

Verses 5–7 call a wrong against a neighbour “breaking faith with the LORD” and require confession and restitution with a fifth added. Is there a wrong you have done that you have regretted but never named or put right? What would that take?

The ordeal of verses 11–31 takes a suspicious husband’s case out of his hands and places it before God. Where are you tempted to act as judge over someone on suspicion alone, and what would it look like to leave it with God?

Israel was the LORD’s unfaithful wife, yet Christ drank the cup of the curse for his bride. How does that shape the way you come to God with your own unfaithfulness?

6.title: The Nazirite Vow and the Priestly Blessing
6.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When either a man or a woman makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD,<sup>3</sup>he shall separate himself from wine and strong drink. He shall drink no vinegar made from wine or strong drink and shall not drink any juice of grapes or eat grapes, fresh or dried.<sup>4</sup>All the days of his separation he shall eat nothing that is produced by the grapevine, not even the seeds or the skins.<sup>5</sup>"All the days of his vow of separation, no razor shall touch his head. Until the time is completed for which he separates himself to the LORD, he shall be holy. He shall let the locks of hair of his head grow long.<sup>6</sup>"All the days that he separates himself to the LORD he shall not go near a dead body.<sup>7</sup>Not even for his father or for his mother, for brother or sister, if they die, shall he make himself unclean, because his separation to God is on his head.<sup>8</sup>All the days of his separation he is holy to the LORD.<sup>9</sup>"And if any man dies very suddenly beside him and he defiles his consecrated head, then he shall shave his head on the day of his cleansing; on the seventh day he shall shave it.<sup>10</sup>On the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two pigeons to the priest to the entrance of the tent of meeting,<sup>11</sup>and the priest shall offer one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering, and make atonement for him, because he sinned by reason of the dead body. And he shall consecrate his head that same day<sup>12</sup>and separate himself to the LORD for the days of his separation and bring a male lamb a year old for a guilt offering. But the previous period shall be void, because his separation was defiled.<sup>13</sup>"And this is the law for the Nazirite, when the time of his separation has been completed: he shall be brought to the entrance of the tent of meeting,<sup>14</sup>and he shall bring his gift to the LORD, one male lamb a year old without blemish for a burnt offering, and one ewe lamb a year old without blemish as a sin offering, and one ram without blemish as a peace offering,<sup>15</sup>and a basket of unleavened bread, loaves of fine flour mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers smeared with oil, and their grain offering and their drink offerings.<sup>16</sup>And the priest shall bring them before the LORD and offer his sin offering and his burnt offering,<sup>17</sup>and he shall offer the ram as a sacrifice of peace offering to the LORD, with the basket of unleavened bread. The priest shall offer also its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>18</sup>And the Nazirite shall shave his consecrated head at the entrance of the tent of meeting and shall take the hair from his consecrated head and put it on the fire that is under the sacrifice of the peace offering.<sup>19</sup>And the priest shall take the shoulder of the ram, when it is boiled, and one unleavened loaf out of the basket and one unleavened wafer, and shall put them on the hands of the Nazirite, after he has shaved the hair of his consecration,<sup>20</sup>and the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before the LORD. They are a holy portion for the priest, together with the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed. And after that the Nazirite may drink wine.<sup>21</sup>"This is the law of the Nazirite. But if he vows an offering to the LORD above his Nazirite vow, as he can afford, in exact accordance with the vow that he takes, then he shall do in addition to the law of the Nazirite."<sup>22</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>23</sup>"Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, Thus you shall bless the people of Israel: you shall say to them,<sup>24</sup>The LORD bless you and keep you;<sup>25</sup>the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you;<sup>26</sup>the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace.<sup>27</sup>"So shall they put my name upon the people of Israel, and I will bless them."
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 5 guarded the purity of the camp around God’s dwelling. Chapter 6 completes these laws for the camp with two provisions: a vow that any Israelite may take, and a blessing that the priests must speak.

The message. God welcomes anyone who wants to belong to him wholeheartedly, and he gives himself freely to all his people. Any man or woman may be set apart to the LORD for a season, and over all Israel, the devoted and the ordinary alike, God has his priests speak his name with blessing, keeping, a shining face and peace. Consecration is what we offer; blessing is what he gives, and it comes last and lasts longest.

Why it was said. In a camp where almost everything was settled by birth, priest, Levite or soldier, Israel needed to know that devotion was open to everyone. And a people about to walk into the desert needed to hear, again and again, what God’s face was towards them (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The vow has three signs: nothing from the vine, no razor, and no contact with the dead, even a parent; if death strikes suddenly beside him, there is cleansing and a fresh start (vv. 1–12). When the vow is complete, the Nazirite brings offerings, a sin offering among them, and burns his hair on the altar; then he may drink wine again (vv. 13–21). Finally God dictates the blessing: three lines, each naming the LORD, by which his name is put on Israel and he himself blesses them (vv. 22–27).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. Jesus was not a Nazirite, but he lived the wholehearted consecration the vow pictured: “for their sake I consecrate myself” (John 17:19). The Nazirite had to keep away from the dead; Jesus touched a bier and raised the dead. And the blessing finds its full meaning in him: the shining face of God is seen “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6), the peace is ours through him (Romans 5:1), and the risen Lord’s last act on earth was to lift up his hands and bless (Luke 24:50–51).

For us. Belonging wholly to God is not for professionals only; it is every Christian’s calling, and it never earns his favour, for even the finished vow needed a sin offering. Live each day under the blessing: because of Christ, the LORD keeps you, his face shines on you, and he gives you peace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Nazirite Vow of Consecration
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Any Israelite, man or woman, may take a vow to be set apart to the LORD for a season, and God gives it three signs. The Nazirite abstains from everything that comes from the vine, down to the seeds and skins (vv. 1–4). He lets his hair grow, carrying his vow on his head, and he must not go near a dead body, not even a parent’s (vv. 5–8). If someone dies suddenly beside him, he is defiled through no fault of his own; he must be cleansed, bring offerings and begin the vow again (vv. 9–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Consecration touches every part of life: what a person eats and drinks, how he looks, and whom he mourns.
verseByVerse.examples: The Nazirite was set apart by visible signs for a season; every believer is called to belong to God wholeheartedly for life.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When either a man or a woman makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD, he shall separate himself from wine and strong drink. He shall drink no vinegar made from wine or strong drink and shall not drink any juice of grapes or eat grapes, fresh or dried. All the days of his separation he shall eat nothing that is produced by the grapevine, not even the seeds or the skins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Any Israelite, man or woman, may choose to belong to God in a special way for a season, and the first sign is giving up a good gift.

The vow of a Nazirite. Nazirite means “one separated” or “one consecrated”, from the same Hebrew root as the word for the holy crown on the high priest’s turban. For a season, the person becomes something like a consecrated object.

Either a man or a woman. Everything else in Numbers so far has been settled by birth: priest, Levite, soldier. This is the first arrangement anybody may enter, and the only qualification is wanting to. A woman, or a shepherd from the smallest clan, could take on a consecration close to a priest’s. Holiness is not rationed to the professionals.

Not even the seeds or the skins. The first sign is abstinence from the vine, to almost comic lengths. Nothing is said against wine itself; Scripture calls it God’s gift to gladden the heart (Psalm 104:15). That is why it is chosen. The Nazirite lays down a legitimate joy, not a sin, so completely that even a raisin is out.

Is the Nazirite vow for today? Samson, Samuel and John the Baptist were set apart for life (Judges 13:5; 1 Samuel 1:11; Luke 1:15). Paul cut his hair because of a vow (Acts 18:18), perhaps a Nazirite one, and later joined four men completing theirs (Acts 21:23–26). The vow belonged to the ceremonial law, fulfilled in Christ, and no Christian is bound to it. Jesus was a “Nazarene”, from Nazareth (Matthew 2:23), not a Nazirite; he drank wine (Luke 7:34). What remains is the call to belong wholly to God (Romans 12:1).

Uncertain wording. The two words translated “seeds” and “skins” occur nowhere else in the Bible, and translations differ over which part of the grape each means. The point is not in doubt: nothing at all from the vine.
verseByVerse.note: Lifelong Nazirites are rare and are dedicated before birth (Judges 13:5; 1 Samuel 1:11); the vow described here is for a set time.

verseByVerse.quote: "All the days of his vow of separation, no razor shall touch his head. Until the time is completed for which he separates himself to the LORD, he shall be holy. He shall let the locks of hair of his head grow long. "All the days that he separates himself to the LORD he shall not go near a dead body. Not even for his father or for his mother, for brother or sister, if they die, shall he make himself unclean, because his separation to God is on his head. All the days of his separation he is holy to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Nazirite wears his vow on his head and keeps away from death, even at a parent’s grave, because he belongs wholly to the God of life.

No razor shall touch his head. The second sign is public: uncut hair. Everyone could see a Nazirite coming; he carried his vow on his head, where neither he nor anybody else could forget it.

Not even for his father or for his mother. The third sign is the hardest thing in the chapter. Word comes that his mother has died, and he may not touch the body or stand at the grave. Ordinary priests could bury their parents (Leviticus 21:2–3); only the high priest was held to this. For the length of his vow, an ordinary Israelite is bound tighter than a priest.

His separation to God is on his head. The reason is not squeamishness. Death is what has gone wrong with the world, and this man has put himself, for a season, on the side of life. One greater than any Nazirite would walk up to a bier, touch it, and say, “Young man, I say to you, arise” (Luke 7:14). He did not have to keep away from death. Death had to keep away from him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if any man dies very suddenly beside him and he defiles his consecrated head, then he shall shave his head on the day of his cleansing; on the seventh day he shall shave it. On the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two pigeons to the priest to the entrance of the tent of meeting, and the priest shall offer one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering, and make atonement for him, because he sinned by reason of the dead body. And he shall consecrate his head that same day and separate himself to the LORD for the days of his separation and bring a male lamb a year old for a guilt offering. But the previous period shall be void, because his separation was defiled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If death touches the Nazirite through no fault of his own, his vow is defiled, but God provides cleansing and a fresh start.

If any man dies very suddenly beside him. The case nobody can plan for. He did nothing wrong and could not have prevented it, and he is defiled. He must shave his head, bring a sin offering, a burnt offering and a lamb for a guilt offering, and begin again from day one: “the previous period shall be void.” Eleven months of a twelve-month vow would be wiped out.

Innocent yet unclean. Defilement is a fact, whatever was intended: a man can be entirely innocent and entirely unclean at once. That is uncomfortable to modern ears, and it is the plain teaching of the passage. The offerings “make atonement for him, because he sinned by reason of the dead body”: here “sinned” means he has incurred an uncleanness that needs atonement, not that he did wrong.

A way back. In the same breath, God provides a way back. He does not say the man is disqualified; he says, here is the sacrifice, start again. Anybody who has had long, good work ruined by something they did not do knows the sick feeling of verse 12. God’s answer is not to pretend the damage did not happen. It is a lamb, and a new first day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Completion of the Vow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The vow ends not with a celebration of the Nazirite but with offerings to God. At the tent of meeting he brings a burnt offering, a sin offering and a peace offering with bread, grain and drink offerings (vv. 13–17). He shaves his consecrated head and puts the hair on the fire under the peace offering, and the priest waves portions before the LORD; then he may drink wine again (vv. 18–20). Anything more he has vowed, he must also keep (v. 21). Even the most devoted life needs atonement, and gives God everything back.
verseByVerse.theology: A consecrated life ends where it began, in God’s hands, given back to him.
verseByVerse.examples: The completed vow was sealed with sacrifice; the Christian offers his whole life to God as a living sacrifice, resting on Christ’s once-for-all offering.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the law for the Nazirite, when the time of his separation has been completed: he shall be brought to the entrance of the tent of meeting, and he shall bring his gift to the LORD, one male lamb a year old without blemish for a burnt offering, and one ewe lamb a year old without blemish as a sin offering, and one ram without blemish as a peace offering, and a basket of unleavened bread, loaves of fine flour mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers smeared with oil, and their grain offering and their drink offerings. And the priest shall bring them before the LORD and offer his sin offering and his burnt offering, and he shall offer the ram as a sacrifice of peace offering to the LORD, with the basket of unleavened bread. The priest shall offer also its grain offering and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The completed vow ends with sacrifices, a sin offering among them, because even the most devoted person needs atonement.

When the time of his separation has been completed. The Nazirite does not simply walk away. He comes to the door of the tent with a procession of offerings: a burnt offering of dedication, a sin offering, and a peace offering shared in fellowship with God, with bread, grain and drink offerings.

A sin offering. A man at the summit of his devotion, who has gone without wine for a year and stayed away from his own family’s funerals, cannot conclude the thing without an animal to atone for his sin.

The trap for serious believers. The more a man gives up for God, the more he begins to think it counts for something. Israel’s law shut that door at the moment it was most likely to open: the ceremony that celebrated a completed consecration required him to confess that he was still a sinner who needed blood. The vow had not made him acceptable. He kept it because he was already the Lord’s, and only Christ, whose consecration was flawless, could offer his life to God for us.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Nazirite shall shave his consecrated head at the entrance of the tent of meeting and shall take the hair from his consecrated head and put it on the fire that is under the sacrifice of the peace offering. And the priest shall take the shoulder of the ram, when it is boiled, and one unleavened loaf out of the basket and one unleavened wafer, and shall put them on the hands of the Nazirite, after he has shaved the hair of his consecration, and the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before the LORD. They are a holy portion for the priest, together with the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed. And after that the Nazirite may drink wine. "This is the law of the Nazirite. But if he vows an offering to the LORD above his Nazirite vow, as he can afford, in exact accordance with the vow that he takes, then he shall do in addition to the law of the Nazirite."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Nazirite gives the very sign of his devotion back to God on the altar, and then returns to ordinary life.

Shave his consecrated head. He shaves at the entrance and puts the hair on the fire under the peace offering. The hair was the sign of the vow, the thing everybody recognised him by, and he burns it. There is no relic, no memento, nothing to show anybody afterwards. He walks home with a shaved head looking like everybody else. That is where genuine consecration ends: not in a trophy but in an offering, not in the man looking holier but in God being given the whole thing back.

The Nazirite may drink wine. There is no suggestion that the abstaining life was superior. The season of separation was real, and it was a season. Most of the Christian life is lived after the hair is burned, in the ordinary run of things, and it is no less consecrated for that.

Above his Nazirite vow. Verse 21 adds that anything more he promised must also be given “in exact accordance with the vow”: a vow made to God is kept in full (compare Ecclesiastes 5:4–5).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives Aaron the very words with which to bless Israel, and says what they do. The priests are not to compose their own blessing (vv. 22–23). Three lines, each beginning with the LORD’s name and each longer than the last, promise his gifts and protection, his shining and gracious face, and his full attention and peace (vv. 24–26). By them, God says, the priests put his name on his people, and he himself will bless them (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: Blessing comes from God himself; the priest is only the mouth through which it is spoken.
verseByVerse.examples: What Aaron spoke over Israel, Christ has made good for his people: in him God’s face is turned toward us.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, Thus you shall bless the people of Israel: you shall say to them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself supplies the words of blessing, so that what the people hear is his declaration over them, not a priest’s wish.

Thus you shall bless the people of Israel. God has spent five chapters ordering this camp; now he gathers it up and blesses it, and he does not leave the wording to the priest. He dictates it.

God’s words, a man’s mouth. Aaron is handed a script. What the people hear at the end of the service is not their priest’s hope for them but God’s declaration over them, in God’s own words, through a man’s mouth. That is why a benediction is not a closing prayer and should not be spoken as one. It is not the minister asking God to be kind; it is God telling the congregation what he is towards them.

Words that outlived everything. A version of this blessing on two tiny silver scrolls, found in a tomb outside Jerusalem and dated to about 600 BC, is older than the Dead Sea Scrolls by centuries (see the note on v. 24). Israelites wore these lines round their necks and were buried with them.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD bless you and keep you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD gives his people good things and then guards what he has given.

Three lines. The blessing has three lines, each beginning with the covenant name, the LORD, so that the name falls on the congregation three times. Each line is longer than the last: in Hebrew three words, then five, then seven. The blessing swells as it goes.

Bless you and keep you. To bless is to give good: the harvest, the child, the rain. To keep is the watchman’s word, to guard what has been given. Blessing without keeping is worth little, for good things are given and then lost: health, a marriage, the years. So the first thing God says over his people is that he gives, and then stands over what he has given (Psalm 121:7).

Jesus kept them. Jesus made the word his own on the last night: “I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost” (John 17:12). In Numbers 6 the keeping was a blessing over a camp in a desert. In his mouth it is a report of work done.
verseByVerse.note: The amulet: a version of the blessing, on two tiny silver scrolls found in Jerusalem and dated to about 600 BC, is the oldest known copy of any biblical text.

verseByVerse.quote: the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s face is turned towards his people and lit up with favour, and his grace is given to those who do not deserve it.

Make his face to shine upon you. The second line rises from what God gives to what God is towards his people. A face lights up when it sees someone it loves, as a father’s does when a child comes into the room, and because it is involuntary we trust it more than words.

A hidden face. Its opposite is the terror of the Old Testament: “How long will you hide your face from me?” (Psalm 13:1); “Hide not your face from me” (Psalm 27:9). A hidden face is worse than anger: the absence of regard, the sense that God has turned away to something else. Here God commands his priests to tell his people, again and again, that his face is turned towards them and lit up.

A test for yourself. Not what you believe about God’s existence, or his power, or even his forgiveness, but this: when God looks at you, what is his face doing? Most people imagine something between disappointment and patience. This verse says otherwise, and the New Testament says where the light comes from: “God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). If you want to know what the face of God looks like when it is turned towards sinners, it is the face of Jesus, which looked at Peter across a courtyard after Peter had denied him three times (Luke 22:61).

Whose face are you living for? Everyone lives under some face: a parent’s, later a coach’s, a lover’s, a boss’s, or the faceless crowd that rates what we post. The sociologist Charles Horton Cooley called it the looking-glass self: we come to see ourselves largely through how we imagine others see us. That is why one frown in a meeting can spoil a week. Whoever’s face we most need becomes, in practice, our god, and human faces are fickle, shining on us only while we perform. The priestly blessing offers a face that does not flicker with our results, because it is turned towards us on account of someone else. Christ went under the hidden face for us, crying, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34), so that God’s face could shine on people who had not earned it. Whoever has seen that face lit up towards them can bear other people’s frowns and does not live on their applause: “Those who look to him are radiant, and their faces shall never be ashamed” (Psalm 34:5).

verseByVerse.quote: the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives his people his full attention and his peace: wholeness, with nothing broken or missing between them and him.

Lift up his countenance upon you. The third line is the summit. To lift up the face is to raise the eyes and hold the look: not a glance but full attention.

Give you peace. The last word is shalom, which English flattens into the absence of trouble. Shalom is wholeness: everything in its place, nothing broken, nothing missing. It is what a room is like when the quarrel is over, what a body feels when the illness has gone, and what a life is when its accounts with God are settled.

Where that peace is found. Gifts, then a face, then peace. Paul tells us where that peace is found: “since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). Aaron pronounced shalom over a people who would be in open rebellion within a few chapters, not knowing how it would be paid for. The peace was real, and it cost the life of the one who “himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14), and who still says, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14:27).

verseByVerse.quote: "So shall they put my name upon the people of Israel, and I will bless them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
By speaking this blessing the priests put God’s own name on his people, and God himself, not the priest, does the blessing.

My name upon the people of Israel. The name spoken three times is what does the work. The priest is not describing a blessing; he is placing the name of God on a people, as a brand on a possession or a signature on a deed. Israel walks away carrying the name of the God who owns them, and in the end his people “will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads” (Revelation 22:4).

I will bless them. It is God, not the priest, who blesses; Aaron supplies the mouth. That is a relief to anybody who has sat under a preacher he did not admire, and a warning to anybody in the pulpit. The words have power because of whose they are.

The triune name. The New Testament blesses the same way: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:14). Three lines, the name three times, and the name now known to be Father, Son and Spirit. What Aaron placed on Israel in a wilderness, the church places on her people every Lord’s Day. And Christ himself, after his last words to his disciples, closed with a blessing: “lifting up his hands he blessed them. While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven” (Luke 24:50–51). He went up with his hands raised over his people, and nothing has happened since to make him put them down.

6.theology:
Consecration for All. Holiness is not reserved for ministers; any believer may give up good things for a time to declare that God is better.

God Is the Source of Blessing. The priest only pronounces; God himself blesses, and his pledge, “I will bless them,” stands behind every word.

Christ the Consecrated High Priest. Jesus is the wholly consecrated One who touched our death and conquered it, and the High Priest in whose face the light of God shines upon us.
6.examples:
Then: Israelites took the Nazirite vow to be wholly the LORD’s, and Aaron put God’s name upon the people.

Now: You live under a greater benediction: the face of God shines upon you in Christ, who has put the Father’s name upon you and given you peace. Out of that, and by his Spirit, hold even good things loosely for the joy of nearness to God.

keyVerse.quote: the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you;
keyVerse.note: The blessing rises from God’s gifts to God himself: not only what he gives but how he looks at his people. A hidden face was Israel’s deepest fear, and here God commands his priests to tell them that his face is turned towards them with favour. The New Testament shows where that face is seen: “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

6.reflection:
The Nazirite vow was open to “either a man or a woman”, not only to priests. What does that say about who may belong wholly to God? What legitimate joys might you lay down for a season, and why?

A Nazirite whose vow was ruined by a sudden death had to begin again, and the completed vow still needed a sin offering (vv. 9–17). How do these details guard us both against despair and against pride in our own devotion?

Verse 25 asks what God’s face is doing when he looks at you. What do you honestly imagine, and how does 2 Corinthians 4:6 answer it? Whose approval do you find yourself living for instead?

God says the blessing puts his name on his people and that he himself blesses them (v. 27). How might it change the way you hear the benediction at the end of a service, or the way you face the week ahead?

7.title: The Offerings of the Chiefs: God Receives Each One
7.text: <sup>1</sup>On the day when Moses had finished setting up the tabernacle and had anointed and consecrated it with all its furnishings and had anointed and consecrated the altar with all its utensils,<sup>2</sup>the chiefs of Israel, heads of their fathers' houses, who were the chiefs of the tribes, who were over those who were listed, approached<sup>3</sup>and brought their offerings before the LORD, six wagons and twelve oxen, a wagon for every two of the chiefs, and for each one an ox. They brought them before the tabernacle.<sup>4</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses,<sup>5</sup>"Accept these from them, that they may be used in the service of the tent of meeting, and give them to the Levites, to each man according to his service."<sup>6</sup>So Moses took the wagons and the oxen and gave them to the Levites.<sup>7</sup>Two wagons and four oxen he gave to the sons of Gershon, according to their service.<sup>8</sup>And four wagons and eight oxen he gave to the sons of Merari, according to their service, under the direction of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest.<sup>9</sup>But to the sons of Kohath he gave none, because they were charged with the service of the holy things that had to be carried on the shoulder.<sup>10</sup>And the chiefs offered offerings for the dedication of the altar on the day it was anointed; and the chiefs offered their offering before the altar.<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "They shall offer their offerings, one chief each day, for the dedication of the altar."<sup>12</sup>He who offered his offering the first day was Nahshon the son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah.<sup>13</sup>And his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;<sup>14</sup>one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense;<sup>15</sup>one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;<sup>16</sup>one male goat for a sin offering;<sup>17</sup>and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old.
