This was the offering of Nahshon the son of Amminadab.<sup>18</sup>On the second day Nethanel the son of Zuar, the chief of Issachar, made an offering.<sup>19</sup>He offered for his offering one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;<sup>20</sup>one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense;<sup>21</sup>one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;<sup>22</sup>one male goat for a sin offering;<sup>23</sup>and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Nethanel the son of Zuar.<sup>24</sup>On the third day Eliab the son of Helon, the chief of the people of Zebulun:<sup>25</sup>his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;<sup>26</sup>one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense;<sup>27</sup>one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;<sup>28</sup>one male goat for a sin offering;<sup>29</sup>and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Eliab the son of Helon.<sup>30</sup>On the fourth day Elizur the son of Shedeur, the chief of the people of Reuben:<sup>31</sup>his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;<sup>32</sup>one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense;<sup>33</sup>one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;<sup>34</sup>one male goat for a sin offering;<sup>35</sup>and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Shelumiel the son of Zurishaddai.<sup>42</sup>On the sixth day Eliasaph the son of Deuel, the chief of the people of Gad:<sup>43</sup>his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;<sup>44</sup>one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense;<sup>45</sup>one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;<sup>46</sup>one male goat for a sin offering;<sup>47</sup>and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur.<sup>60</sup>On the ninth day Abidan the son of Gideoni, the chief of the people of Benjamin:<sup>61</sup>his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;<sup>62</sup>one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense;<sup>63</sup>one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;<sup>64</sup>one male goat for a sin offering;<sup>65</sup>and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Abidan the son of Gideoni.<sup>66</sup>On the tenth day Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai, the chief of the people of Dan:<sup>67</sup>his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;<sup>68</sup>one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense;<sup>69</sup>one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;<sup>70</sup>one male goat for a sin offering;<sup>71</sup>and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai.<sup>72</sup>On the eleventh day Pagiel the son of Ochran, the chief of the people of Asher:<sup>73</sup>his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;<sup>74</sup>one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense;<sup>75</sup>one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;<sup>76</sup>one male goat for a sin offering;<sup>77</sup>and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Pagiel the son of Ochran.<sup>78</sup>On the twelfth day Ahira the son of Enan, the chief of the people of Naphtali:<sup>79</sup>his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;<sup>80</sup>one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense;<sup>81</sup>one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering;<sup>82</sup>one male goat for a sin offering;<sup>83</sup>and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Ahira the son of Enan.<sup>84</sup>This was the dedication offering for the altar on the day when it was anointed, from the chiefs of Israel: twelve silver plates, twelve silver basins, twelve golden dishes,<sup>85</sup>each silver plate weighing 130 shekels and each basin 70, all the silver of the vessels 2,400 shekels according to the shekel of the sanctuary,<sup>86</sup>the twelve golden dishes, full of incense, weighing 10 shekels apiece according to the shekel of the sanctuary, all the gold of the dishes being 120 shekels;<sup>87</sup>all the cattle for the burnt offering twelve bulls, twelve rams, twelve male lambs a year old, with their grain offering; and twelve male goats for a sin offering;<sup>88</sup>and all the cattle for the sacrifice of peace offerings twenty-four bulls, the rams sixty, the male goats sixty, the male lambs a year old sixty. This was the dedication offering for the altar after it was anointed.<sup>89</sup>And when Moses went into the tent of meeting to speak with the LORD, he heard the voice speaking to him from above the mercy seat that was on the ark of the testimony, from between the two cherubim; and it spoke to him.
7.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 1–6 set the camp in order around the tabernacle. Chapter 7 steps back a month, to the day Moses finished setting up the tent (Exodus 40:17), and tells how the leaders of the twelve tribes brought their gifts for it and how God then spoke from within it.

The message. God receives every gift his people bring, and he receives every giver by name. He does not rank them or hurry them; each chief has his own day and his own record in Scripture. And the giving is not the end of the story: the point of the whole dedicated sanctuary is that God might speak to his people from the place of atonement.

Why it was said. A people about to march through the wilderness needed to know that the tent at their centre belonged to all twelve tribes equally, and that the God who lived there had come to speak with them, not merely to be served by them (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First, practical gifts: six wagons and twelve oxen, shared among the Levites according to their loads, though the holiest things are still carried on the shoulder (vv. 1–9). Then, for twelve days, one chief each day brings an identical offering for the dedication of the altar, and each is recorded in full (vv. 10–83). The totals follow, dominated by peace offerings, the sacrifices that were shared as a meal (vv. 84–88). Last, when Moses goes in, he hears God’s voice from above the mercy seat (v. 89).

Where it leads. By pattern. Every bull, ram, lamb and goat brought to this altar pointed to the one offering that would make the altar unnecessary (Hebrews 10:10–14). The mercy seat, the lid of the ark where the blood was sprinkled, is the word the New Testament uses of Christ himself: God “put forward” Jesus “as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25). The God who spoke from between the cherubim “has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2). And the first chief, Nahshon of Judah, is named again in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:4).

For us. No gift brought to God in faith is too ordinary, and no giver is lost in the crowd; he knows each by name. But the greatest thing at the tent is not what we bring but what he says, and he speaks to sinners only from the place where the blood was shed, in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Wagons and Oxen for the Levites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chiefs’ first gift is practical: transport for the tabernacle, and God accepts it. On the day the tent is finished and anointed, the twelve tribal leaders bring six covered wagons and twelve oxen, a wagon for every two chiefs (vv. 1–3). God tells Moses to accept them and give them to the Levites according to their work: two wagons to Gershon for the curtains, four to Merari for the heavy frames and bases (vv. 4–8). Kohath receives none, because the holy things must be carried on the shoulder (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: God provides means for the service he commands; the gifts of the people equip the work of his house.
verseByVerse.examples: The wagons were given for carrying the tabernacle; God still supplies, often through the gifts of his people, what his church needs for its work.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day when Moses had finished setting up the tabernacle and had anointed and consecrated it with all its furnishings and had anointed and consecrated the altar with all its utensils, the chiefs of Israel, heads of their fathers' houses, who were the chiefs of the tribes, who were over those who were listed, approached and brought their offerings before the LORD, six wagons and twelve oxen, a wagon for every two of the chiefs, and for each one an ox. They brought them before the tabernacle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as God’s dwelling was finished, the leaders brought him a gift, and the first one recorded was plain, practical transport.

Moses had finished setting up the tabernacle. This chapter is a flashback. The tent was raised on the first day of the first month of the second year (Exodus 40:17), a month before Numbers 1 opens; the episode is told here because it belongs with the ordering of the camp.

Six wagons and twelve oxen. Nobody asked for a present; no command required it. And it was not gold or incense, nothing that would be seen inside the tent: transport. Somebody had worked out that a tabernacle which has to be dismantled, carried across a wilderness and put up again needs carts.

The gift God took. It is the least glamorous gift in the chapter and the first recorded. There is a kind of giving that looks hard at the actual work and asks what would make it possible, and it rarely produces anything anybody admires. God took the wagons.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Accept these from them, that they may be used in the service of the tent of meeting, and give them to the Levites, to each man according to his service." So Moses took the wagons and the oxen and gave them to the Levites. Two wagons and four oxen he gave to the sons of Gershon, according to their service. And four wagons and eight oxen he gave to the sons of Merari, according to their service, under the direction of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest. But to the sons of Kohath he gave none, because they were charged with the service of the holy things that had to be carried on the shoulder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God accepts the wagons and shares them out according to each group’s load, but the holiest things must still be carried by hand.

To each man according to his service. Gershon, carrying curtains and coverings, gets two wagons; Merari, carrying frames, bars and bases, dead weight in timber and metal, gets four. The provision is matched to the burden.

To the sons of Kohath he gave none. The holy things “had to be carried on the shoulder” (compare 4:15). Kohath had the highest privilege among the Levites and no help at all. The most sacred load in Israel was walked on human shoulders for forty years. There is no shortcut for the holiest work, and the men given the greatest honour had the sorest backs.

David’s new cart. Centuries later a king forgot this verse. David brought the ark up to Jerusalem “on a new cart” (2 Samuel 6:3): new, expensive, respectful, and expressly ruled out here. The oxen stumbled, Uzzah reached out, and a man died on a happy afternoon. It was not open irreverence that killed him. It was a good idea put in place of a plain instruction. God had said shoulders, and when David tried again, the Levites carried the ark as Moses had commanded (1 Chronicles 15:13–15).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–88 — The Twelve Days of Offerings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For twelve days, one chief each day brings the same offering for the dedication of the altar, and every one is recorded in full. God commands the order: one chief each day (vv. 10–11). Nahshon of Judah goes first, bringing silver vessels of flour and oil, a gold dish of incense, and animals for burnt, sin and peace offerings (vv. 12–17). The other eleven chiefs follow, tribe by tribe and day by day, each gift identical and each giver named (vv. 18–83). The totals close the section, with the peace offerings, the shared meals, by far the largest part (vv. 84–88).
verseByVerse.theology: All come to God on the same terms, and none is lost in the crowd.
verseByVerse.examples: Each of the twelve gifts was named and recorded; no act of worship offered through Christ goes unseen by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And the chiefs offered offerings for the dedication of the altar on the day it was anointed; and the chiefs offered their offering before the altar. And the LORD said to Moses, "They shall offer their offerings, one chief each day, for the dedication of the altar."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God spreads the dedication over twelve days so that every chief, and every tribe, has a day of its own before him.

One chief each day. The gifts were identical, and the whole thing could have been done in one magnificent morning, twelve men stepping forward together. That would have been more impressive and far more efficient. God spread it over nearly a fortnight so that every man got a day of his own. Elizur of Reuben had the fourth day to himself, with the whole camp watching him and nobody else. It is a decision about how God receives what people bring him, and the next seventy verses make it unmistakable.

verseByVerse.quote: He who offered his offering the first day was Nahshon the son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah. And his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Nahshon the son of Amminadab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first chief’s gift, repeated by all twelve, holds everything a person can bring to God: his food, his prayers, himself, his guilt and his fellowship.

Nahshon the son of Amminadab. Judah goes first, as at the count and on the march (2:3), and Nahshon brings the gift that all twelve will bring. His sister married Aaron (Exodus 6:23), and he stands in the family line of David, and so of Jesus (Ruth 4:20; Matthew 1:4).

What each gift contained. See it once, because the reader will meet it eleven more times. A silver plate and basin, weighed in shekels, full of fine flour and oil: the grain offering, the produce of a life. A golden dish of incense, a picture of prayer. A bull, a ram and a lamb for a burnt offering, given wholly to God. A goat for a sin offering, because even at a dedication sin has to be answered. And the peace offering, the meal shared with God and one another.

A whole life offered. Everything a person can bring to God is in that list: the food off his table, his prayers, his whole self, his guilt and his company. Nothing is missing. Yet “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4): every animal pointed to the one who would offer himself.

verseByVerse.quote: On the second day Nethanel the son of Zuar, the chief of Issachar, made an offering. He offered for his offering one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Nethanel the son of Zuar. On the third day Eliab the son of Helon, the chief of the people of Zebulun: his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Eliab the son of Helon. On the fourth day Elizur the son of Shedeur, the chief of the people of Reuben: his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Elizur the son of Shedeur. On the fifth day Shelumiel the son of Zurishaddai, the chief of the people of Simeon: his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Shelumiel the son of Zurishaddai. On the sixth day Eliasaph the son of Deuel, the chief of the people of Gad: his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Eliasaph the son of Deuel. On the seventh day Elishama the son of Ammihud, the chief of the people of Ephraim: his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Elishama the son of Ammihud. On the eighth day Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur, the chief of the people of Manasseh: his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur. On the ninth day Abidan the son of Gideoni, the chief of the people of Benjamin: his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Abidan the son of Gideoni. On the tenth day Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai, the chief of the people of Dan: his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai. On the eleventh day Pagiel the son of Ochran, the chief of the people of Asher: his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Pagiel the son of Ochran. On the twelfth day Ahira the son of Enan, the chief of the people of Naphtali: his offering was one silver plate whose weight was 130 shekels, one silver basin of 70 shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, both of them full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; one golden dish of 10 shekels, full of incense; one bull from the herd, one ram, one male lamb a year old, for a burnt offering; one male goat for a sin offering; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. This was the offering of Ahira the son of Enan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same gift is recorded eleven more times in full, because God values each giver by name and lets none outshine the others.

On the second day. Now sixty-six verses in which nothing new is said: day two, Issachar, the same; day three, Zebulun, the same. Twelve times in full, in the longest chapter of the five books of Moses.

Why not summarise? Any editor would say it once, add “the remaining eleven brought the same”, and save four pages. God evidently thought something would be lost. Summarised, eleven of these men would have become “the others.” Instead every one has his name, tribe, father, day and inventory written into the word of God. Nobody is a footnote to the man who went first, just as the Good Shepherd “calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3).

Nobody could outgive anybody. Because every gift was identical, there was no largest offering and no smallest, no chief admired for his generosity and none quietly ashamed on his day. God designed a ceremony in which competition was impossible, which anybody who has watched a collection plate go round will recognise as a mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: This was the dedication offering for the altar on the day when it was anointed, from the chiefs of Israel: twelve silver plates, twelve silver basins, twelve golden dishes, each silver plate weighing 130 shekels and each basin 70, all the silver of the vessels 2,400 shekels according to the shekel of the sanctuary, the twelve golden dishes, full of incense, weighing 10 shekels apiece according to the shekel of the sanctuary, all the gold of the dishes being 120 shekels; all the cattle for the burnt offering twelve bulls, twelve rams, twelve male lambs a year old, with their grain offering; and twelve male goats for a sin offering; and all the cattle for the sacrifice of peace offerings twenty-four bulls, the rams sixty, the male goats sixty, the male lambs a year old sixty. This was the dedication offering for the altar after it was anointed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The totals show that the largest part of the altar’s dedication was the peace offering, a meal shared with God.

The rams sixty. Burnt and sin offerings run to twelve of each kind; the peace offerings run to twenty-four bulls and sixty each of rams, goats and lambs: more than four times the rest put together.

The sacrifice of peace offerings. The burnt offering went up in smoke entirely, and the sin offering dealt with guilt. The peace offering was cooked, shared out and eaten by worshippers and priests together, in God’s presence, as a meal.

A shared feast. So the largest element in the dedication of Israel’s altar was dinner. The place where sin was dealt with was opened with a shared feast, which is the direction the whole Bible runs: from a lamb eaten in Egypt, to a table in an upper room, to “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). God deals with sin so that he can sit down and eat with people.

verseByVerse.ref: v. 89 — God Speaks from the Mercy Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The section is one verse, and it is the climax of the chapter: after twelve days of giving, God speaks. Moses goes into the tent of meeting to speak with the LORD and hears the voice speaking to him from above the mercy seat on the ark, between the two cherubim, just as God had promised at Sinai (Exodus 25:22). The sanctuary was dedicated not only so that Israel could bring God gifts, but so that God could speak to his people from the place of atonement.
verseByVerse.theology: The dedication of the altar opens the way to communion; the gifts of the people lead to the voice of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses heard God’s voice from between the cherubim; God now speaks to us in his Son (Hebrews 1:2), and we may come to the throne of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Moses went into the tent of meeting to speak with the LORD, he heard the voice speaking to him from above the mercy seat that was on the ark of the testimony, from between the two cherubim; and it spoke to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After twelve days of giving, God speaks, and he speaks from the mercy seat, the place of atonement above the broken law.

From above the mercy seat. This is the verse the chapter has been waiting for, and the promise made on the mountain is kept in the finished tent: “There I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you” (Exodus 25:22).

Where God speaks from. The place itself is the message. Inside the ark were the tablets of the law Israel had already broken, silently condemning everybody in the camp. Over the box was a slab of gold called the kapporet, the mercy seat, where once a year the high priest sprinkled blood (Leviticus 16:14–15). At either end were two cherubim, the creatures who had guarded the way back into Eden (Genesis 3:24).

From between the two cherubim. God does not speak from inside the box. He speaks from the lid: above the broken law, out of the place where the blood goes, between the two guardians once posted to keep people out. If the voice had come from the tablets it would have had nothing to say to Israel but the sentence of death. It comes from the covering, where the blood is.

The mercy seat has a name now. The Greek Old Testament translated kapporet with the word Paul uses of Christ, meaning the sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger: “whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith” (Romans 3:25). God still does not speak to sinners over the law they have broken; he speaks from the place where the blood was applied, and that place is a person.

And it spoke to him. The chiefs gave for twelve days, and at the end the tent was not silent. That is what the whole arrangement was for: not so that Israel could give God things, but so that God could talk to Israel. He had come down to live in the middle of the camp, and he wanted to speak, as he still does: “in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2).

Uncertain wording. Kapporet comes from a root meaning to cover or to make atonement, so it may mean “lid” or “place of atonement”. It was probably both; “mercy seat”, Tyndale’s phrase, catches the second sense.

7.theology:
Equal Yet Known. The identical offerings teach that all come to God on the same terms, by the same blood; the separate days and records, that each worshipper is known and welcomed by name.

The Voice from the Mercy Seat. Communion with God comes only over the blood-covered mercy seat, fulfilled in Christ, whose blood turns away God’s just anger, and through whom God now speaks to us.
7.examples:
Then: Twelve chiefs each brought the same gift on his own day, and the dedication opened the way to the voice of God.

Now: You are never a statistic to God. You come to him on the same ground as every other believer, the blood of Christ, and he receives your worship individually and speaks to you in his Son. Give freely as the chiefs did, not to be noticed, and draw near to hear the voice from the mercy seat.

keyVerse.quote: And when Moses went into the tent of meeting to speak with the LORD, he heard the voice speaking to him from above the mercy seat that was on the ark of the testimony, from between the two cherubim; and it spoke to him.
keyVerse.note: Eighty-eight verses of giving end in one verse of hearing. The whole dedicated sanctuary exists so that God may speak with his people, and he speaks from the mercy seat, the place of atoning blood above the broken law. That place now has a name: Christ, “put forward as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25).

7.reflection:
The first gift recorded is six wagons and twelve oxen, plain transport for the tabernacle (vv. 1–9). What “unglamorous” gifts help God’s work go forward in your church, and who brings them?

God gave each chief his own day and recorded each identical gift in full (vv. 10–83). What does that tell you about how God sees each member of his people, and how might it free us from comparing our giving or service with others?

The largest part of the dedication was the peace offering, a meal shared in God’s presence (vv. 84–88). How does the Lord’s Supper, and the promised “marriage supper of the Lamb”, show the same purpose?

God spoke to Moses from above the mercy seat, not from the tablets of the law (v. 89). Why does it matter that God speaks to sinners from the place of atonement, and how does that shape the way you come to him in Christ?

8.title: The Levites Consecrated: Cleansed and Given to God
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to Aaron and say to him, When you set up the lamps, the seven lamps shall give light in front of the lampstand."<sup>3</sup>And Aaron did so: he set up its lamps in front of the lampstand, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>4</sup>And this was the workmanship of the lampstand, hammered work of gold. From its base to its flowers, it was hammered work; according to the pattern that the LORD had shown Moses, so he made the lampstand.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>6</sup>"Take the Levites from among the people of Israel and cleanse them.<sup>7</sup>Thus you shall do to them to cleanse them: sprinkle the water of purification upon them, and let them go with a razor over all their body, and wash their clothes and cleanse themselves.<sup>8</sup>Then let them take a bull from the herd and its grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, and you shall take another bull from the herd for a sin offering.<sup>9</sup>And you shall bring the Levites before the tent of meeting and assemble the whole congregation of the people of Israel.<sup>10</sup>When you bring the Levites before the LORD, the people of Israel shall lay their hands on the Levites,<sup>11</sup>and Aaron shall offer the Levites before the LORD as a wave offering from the people of Israel, that they may do the service of the LORD.<sup>12</sup>Then the Levites shall lay their hands on the heads of the bulls, and you shall offer the one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering to the LORD to make atonement for the Levites.<sup>13</sup>And you shall set the Levites before Aaron and his sons, and shall offer them as a wave offering to the LORD.<sup>14</sup>"Thus you shall separate the Levites from among the people of Israel, and the Levites shall be mine.<sup>15</sup>And after that the Levites shall go in to serve at the tent of meeting, when you have cleansed them and offered them as a wave offering.<sup>16</sup>For they are wholly given to me from among the people of Israel. Instead of all who open the womb, the firstborn of all the people of Israel, I have taken them for myself.<sup>17</sup>For all the firstborn among the people of Israel are mine, both of man and of beast. On the day that I struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt I consecrated them for myself,<sup>18</sup>and I have taken the Levites instead of all the firstborn among the people of Israel.<sup>19</sup>And I have given the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons from among the people of Israel, to do the service for the people of Israel at the tent of meeting and to make atonement for the people of Israel, that there may be no plague among the people of Israel when the people of Israel come near the sanctuary."<sup>20</sup>Thus did Moses and Aaron and all the congregation of the people of Israel to the Levites. According to all that the LORD commanded Moses concerning the Levites, the people of Israel did to them.<sup>21</sup>And the Levites purified themselves from sin and washed their clothes, and Aaron offered them as a wave offering before the LORD, and Aaron made atonement for them to cleanse them.<sup>22</sup>And after that the Levites went in to do their service in the tent of meeting before Aaron and his sons; as the LORD had commanded Moses concerning the Levites, so they did to them.<sup>23</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>24</sup>"This applies to the Levites: from twenty-five years old and upward they shall come to do duty in the service of the tent of meeting.<sup>25</sup>And from the age of fifty years they shall withdraw from the duty of the service and serve no more.<sup>26</sup>They minister to their brothers in the tent of meeting by keeping guard, but they shall do no service. Thus shall you do to the Levites in assigning their duties."
8.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 7 ended inside the tent, with God speaking from above the mercy seat. Chapter 8 stays there for a moment, with the lamps of the holy place, and then completes the arrangements of chapters 3–4 by consecrating the Levites, the tribe God took in place of Israel’s firstborn.

The message. Those who serve God near his presence must first be cleansed and wholly given to him, and they are given for the sake of his people. The Levites do not make themselves clean by serving; they are washed, atoned for and offered to God as a living gift, and God hands them back as a gift to the priests, so that ordinary Israelites can come near the sanctuary and live.

Why it was said. A holy God was living in the middle of a sinful camp, and coming near him carelessly meant death (see the introduction). Israel needed to know who could serve at the tent, how they were made fit, and why: not for their own honour, but to protect and serve the whole people.

How the chapter makes its case. First the lampstand: Aaron sets up its seven lamps to shine forward, and the stand is beaten from one piece of gold to God’s pattern (vv. 1–4). Then the Levites are cleansed with water, razor and washing (vv. 5–7); the people lay hands on them and Aaron presents them to God as a wave offering (vv. 8–11); they lay hands on bulls for their own atonement (vv. 12–14). God explains that they are wholly his in place of the firstborn spared in Egypt, and given to Aaron to guard Israel from plague, and it is all done (vv. 15–22). Last, their years of service are set, with release from heavy work at fifty (vv. 23–26).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. The Levites, substitutes for the firstborn, needed a substitute themselves; the chain of laid-on hands could only end in the one of whom it is written, “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). The firstborn Son was wholly given to the Father for us, and, ascended, he “gave gifts to men” (Ephesians 4:8), servants for his church as the Levites were given to Aaron. And the lamps of the holy place point to the one who said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12).

For us. God does not ask you to make yourself clean in order to serve him; he washes you in Christ and then gives you to his people. Offer yourself to him as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1), and remember that your worth lies in belonging to him, not in how much you can still carry.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Lampstand Lit Before the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the Levites are dedicated, the lamps of the holy place are set to shine. God tells Aaron that when he sets up the seven lamps, they are to give light in front of the lampstand, and Aaron does exactly as commanded (vv. 1–3). The lampstand itself is hammered from gold, base to flowers, made according to the pattern God showed Moses (v. 4). In the windowless holy place, this was the only light, shining on what stood before it in God’s presence.
verseByVerse.theology: The light of the sanctuary shines before God; his servants are called to be light-bearers in his house.
verseByVerse.examples: Seven lamps burned before the LORD in the tabernacle; the church now shines in a dark world with a light that is not her own but Christ’s.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron and say to him, When you set up the lamps, the seven lamps shall give light in front of the lampstand." And Aaron did so: he set up its lamps in front of the lampstand, as the LORD commanded Moses. And this was the workmanship of the lampstand, hammered work of gold. From its base to its flowers, it was hammered work; according to the pattern that the LORD had shown Moses, so he made the lampstand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lamps of the holy place are set to shine forward, on what stands before God, from a lampstand made exactly to his pattern.

When you set up the lamps. The instruction probably stands here because 7:89 has just taken the reader inside the tent, where the lampstand stood, and because Aaron’s own duty in the holy place is set out before the Levites are given to assist him.

In front of the lampstand. The sanctuary had no windows. The lampstand was the only light in the holy place, and Aaron tended its lamps every evening and morning (Exodus 27:21). Its light fell on the table of the bread of the Presence opposite: the lamps did not illuminate themselves but what was in front of them. And the lampstand was not cast or assembled from parts but hammered out of gold, base, branches and blossoms all of a piece.

The light of the world. Jesus, probably at the Feast of Booths, when great lamps were lit in the temple courts, said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). And John sees seven golden lampstands with one like a son of man, robed as a priest, walking among them: “the seven lampstands are the seven churches” (Revelation 1:13, 20). The church’s light is kept burning by the great High Priest, and like the lamps of the holy place it shines on what is in front of it, never on itself.

Uncertain wording. “Set up the lamps” is literally “make the lamps go up.” It may mean lighting them, making the flame rise, or mounting them on the branches; either way, they were to throw their light forward.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–22 — The Cleansing and Dedication of the Levites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levites are cleansed, atoned for and presented to God by the whole congregation, and God explains why. They are sprinkled, shaved and washed (vv. 5–7). The people lay hands on them and Aaron offers them as a wave offering (vv. 8–11). They lay hands on two bulls, a sin offering and a burnt offering, to make atonement for themselves (vv. 12–14). God claims them as wholly his, in place of the firstborn he spared when he struck Egypt, and gives them to Aaron to serve, so that no plague falls on Israel when the people come near (vv. 15–19). Everything is done as the LORD commanded (vv. 20–22).
verseByVerse.theology: God’s servants are first cleansed, and then given to him entirely.
verseByVerse.examples: The Levites were washed and then offered to God; believers, cleansed by Christ, offer themselves in the same order.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Take the Levites from among the people of Israel and cleanse them. Thus you shall do to them to cleanse them: sprinkle the water of purification upon them, and let them go with a razor over all their body, and wash their clothes and cleanse themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the Levites can serve, they are cleansed, and the cleansing is done to them, not by them.

Cleanse them. Three actions move outward from the person. Water sprinkled on them, done to them, not by them. A razor over the whole body: every hair removed, the man as bare as a newborn. Then clothes washed, so that even what he wears into the tent is clean.

Made clean to serve. The order is the point. Israel’s servants did not become clean by serving; they were made clean in order to serve. People constantly reverse that order and try to make themselves fit for God by what they do. God has always done it the other way round: “he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:5). The washing comes first, and it is done to a man, not by him.

Uncertain wording. “The water of purification” is literally “water of sin”, a phrase found only here. It probably means water that removes sin’s defilement, perhaps the water prepared with the ashes of the red heifer (19:9), though that is called by a different name.

verseByVerse.quote: Then let them take a bull from the herd and its grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, and you shall take another bull from the herd for a sin offering. And you shall bring the Levites before the tent of meeting and assemble the whole congregation of the people of Israel. When you bring the Levites before the LORD, the people of Israel shall lay their hands on the Levites, and Aaron shall offer the Levites before the LORD as a wave offering from the people of Israel, that they may do the service of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole nation lays hands on the Levites, and Aaron presents them to God as an offering: they are not the ones who bring the gift; they are the gift.

Lay their hands on the Levites. In the sacrifices, that is what a worshipper does to an animal about to be killed, to say “this one goes in my place” (Leviticus 1:4). Israel does it to a tribe of living men, who stand in for the whole people.

As a wave offering. Aaron “offers” them as a wave offering: the portion presented to God and received back for use. The Levites are not the men who bring the offering; they are the thing on the plate.

A living sacrifice. This is what Paul asks of every Christian, and he grounds it first in what God has done: “I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship” (Romans 12:1). The picture was acted out before the whole nation long before it was written down.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Levites shall lay their hands on the heads of the bulls, and you shall offer the one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering to the LORD to make atonement for the Levites. And you shall set the Levites before Aaron and his sons, and shall offer them as a wave offering to the LORD. "Thus you shall separate the Levites from among the people of Israel, and the Levites shall be mine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites, offered for the people, need atonement themselves, and so point to a substitute who needs none.

Lay their hands on the heads of the bulls. Follow the hands and you see the whole system. The people put their hands on the Levites. The Levites put their hands on the bulls. The bulls die.

To make atonement for the Levites. The men just presented to God as an offering need atonement themselves and cannot supply it. The substitutes need a substitute. Nothing in their washing, shaving or waving made them fit to stand where they stood.

One head, and no further transfer. The chain cannot truly end with a bull: “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). What was needed was one place where the hands could be laid and the chain could stop: someone who did not need a bull because he was the offering, and did not need a priest because he was the priest. “The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). One set of hands, one head, and no further transfer required.

verseByVerse.quote: And after that the Levites shall go in to serve at the tent of meeting, when you have cleansed them and offered them as a wave offering. For they are wholly given to me from among the people of Israel. Instead of all who open the womb, the firstborn of all the people of Israel, I have taken them for myself. For all the firstborn among the people of Israel are mine, both of man and of beast. On the day that I struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt I consecrated them for myself, and I have taken the Levites instead of all the firstborn among the people of Israel. And I have given the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons from among the people of Israel, to do the service for the people of Israel at the tent of meeting and to make atonement for the people of Israel, that there may be no plague among the people of Israel when the people of Israel come near the sanctuary." Thus did Moses and Aaron and all the congregation of the people of Israel to the Levites. According to all that the LORD commanded Moses concerning the Levites, the people of Israel did to them. And the Levites purified themselves from sin and washed their clothes, and Aaron offered them as a wave offering before the LORD, and Aaron made atonement for them to cleanse them. And after that the Levites went in to do their service in the tent of meeting before Aaron and his sons; as the LORD had commanded Moses concerning the Levites, so they did to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites belong wholly to God in place of the firstborn he spared in Egypt, and he gives them to the priests so that his people can come near and live.

They are wholly given to me. The Hebrew doubles the word, “given, given”: not partly, not on certain days, but given. The ground of the claim goes back, as in chapter 3, to a night in Egypt and blood on a doorframe. Every firstborn son in Israel was spared that night and so belonged to God (Exodus 13:1–2), and the Levites take their place.

As a gift to Aaron and his sons. Then God turns it round: what is handed over to God does not disappear into heaven; it comes back into the life of the people as provision for them. So the ascended Christ “gave gifts to men” (Ephesians 4:8), giving his church its ministers to serve it (Ephesians 4:11–12).

That there may be no plague. Five times in one verse God says “the people of Israel”; he has his eye on the congregation. The Levites guarded the holy things so that ordinary Israelites could come near and live, and every ministry God has established since exists for the same kind of reason.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — The Term of Levitical Service
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levites’ working years are set, with a release from the heavy work at fifty. They begin service at twenty-five (vv. 23–24). At fifty they withdraw from the labour of the tent, yet they are not dismissed: they continue to assist their brothers by keeping guard (vv. 25–26). God provides for the limits of his servants’ strength and keeps a place for them when the heavy work is done.
verseByVerse.theology: God appoints seasons of service and of rest, and he provides tenderly for his servants’ later years.
verseByVerse.examples: The Levites served for a fixed term; we serve faithfully in whatever season we are given, trusting the God who appoints our times.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "This applies to the Levites: from twenty-five years old and upward they shall come to do duty in the service of the tent of meeting. And from the age of fifty years they shall withdraw from the duty of the service and serve no more. They minister to their brothers in the tent of meeting by keeping guard, but they shall do no service. Thus shall you do to the Levites in assigning their duties."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sets limits to his servants’ heavy work and keeps a place for them when it ends.

From twenty-five years old and upward. The chapter ends with a retirement policy, which nobody expects in the books of Moses: service from twenty-five, and at fifty a firm stop to the heavy work. Carrying the frames of the tabernacle across a desert is young men’s labour, and God does not ask a man of sixty to do it. Nor does he wait for the man to fail; the release is built into the law before anybody has an awkward conversation.

By keeping guard. But the man is not finished. He stays in the tent, keeping guard alongside the men now doing the lifting. The heavy work stops; his place in God’s house does not. A congregation with an older believer who prays, watches and knows where the dangers are has something the Levites had.

Who am I when the work stops? Our culture hears “What do you do?” as if it meant “Who are you?” So retirement, which ought to be a gift, often arrives as a quiet crisis: a man who was somebody on Friday is nobody on Monday. If your worth was your output, the day the output ends is a kind of death. But before a single frame was lifted, God said of the Levites, “they are wholly given to me” (v. 16). They belonged before they carried, and they still belonged when the carrying stopped. That is the order of the gospel. At the Jordan, before one miracle or sermon, the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and everyone in Christ is spoken to on the same terms. Work then becomes an expression of love, not a defence of your existence, and when it ends you have lost a task, not yourself.

Twenty-five or thirty? The age is twenty-five here and thirty in 4:3. A common explanation is that Levites began service at twenty-five and took on the carrying of the holy things at thirty. David later lowered the age to twenty (1 Chronicles 23:24–27).

8.theology:
Wholly Given to God. The Levites are not only servants but themselves the offering, as every Christian is called to be.

Cleansing Before Service. Only “after that”, once cleansed and atoned for, do the Levites serve. Grace comes first: we work because God has accepted us, not in order to be accepted.

Given Twice, for the People. The Levites are given by the people to God and then by God to the priesthood, so that Israel may draw near and live. So Christ is given by the Father and gives himself, the Mediator whose work lets us approach God and live.
8.examples:
Then: The Levites were cleansed, atoned for and presented to God as a living offering, then sent to serve.

Now: Washed by Christ and made his by the Spirit, present yourself to God as a living sacrifice. Serve not to earn his favour but from grace already received, knowing that where your offering falls short, his did not. You are wholly his, in your seasons of labour and of rest alike.

keyVerse.quote: And I have given the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons from among the people of Israel, to do the service for the people of Israel at the tent of meeting and to make atonement for the people of Israel, that there may be no plague among the people of Israel when the people of Israel come near the sanctuary.
keyVerse.note: Five times in one sentence God names “the people of Israel.” Those wholly given to him are given back as a gift, and their whole purpose is that ordinary people may come near a holy God and live. That is the shape of every true ministry, and supremely of Christ’s, who was given for us so that we might draw near.

8.reflection:
The lamps in the holy place shone on what was in front of them, not on themselves (vv. 1–4). What would it look like for your church’s light to shine on Christ rather than on itself?

The Levites were cleansed before they served, and the washing was done to them (vv. 5–7). Where are you tempted to try to make yourself fit for God by what you do? How does Titus 3:5 answer that?

The people laid hands on the Levites, and the Levites laid hands on the bulls (vv. 10–12). How does this chain of substitutes help you understand what Christ has done as the one on whom the LORD laid “the iniquity of us all”?

God said the Levites were “wholly given to me” before they lifted a single frame, and kept a place for them after fifty (vv. 16, 25–26). How does belonging to God before you work, and after you stop, change the way you think about your work, your limits or your retirement?

9.title: The Passover Kept; the Cloud of Guidance
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the first month of the second year after they had come out of the land of Egypt, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Let the people of Israel keep the Passover at its appointed time.<sup>3</sup>On the fourteenth day of this month, at twilight, you shall keep it at its appointed time; according to all its statutes and all its rules you shall keep it."<sup>4</sup>So Moses told the people of Israel that they should keep the Passover.<sup>5</sup>And they kept the Passover in the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, at twilight, in the wilderness of Sinai; according to all that the LORD commanded Moses, so the people of Israel did.<sup>6</sup>And there were certain men who were unclean through touching a dead body, so that they could not keep the Passover on that day, and they came before Moses and Aaron on that day.<sup>7</sup>And those men said to him, "We are unclean through touching a dead body. Why are we kept from bringing the LORD's offering at its appointed time among the people of Israel?"<sup>8</sup>And Moses said to them, "Wait, that I may hear what the LORD will command concerning you."<sup>9</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If any one of you or of your descendants is unclean through touching a dead body, or is on a long journey, he shall still keep the Passover to the LORD.<sup>11</sup>In the second month on the fourteenth day at twilight they shall keep it. They shall eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.<sup>12</sup>They shall leave none of it until the morning, nor break any of its bones; according to all the statute for the Passover they shall keep it.<sup>13</sup>But if anyone who is clean and is not on a journey fails to keep the Passover, that person shall be cut off from his people because he did not bring the LORD's offering at its appointed time; that man shall bear his sin.<sup>14</sup>And if a stranger sojourns among you and would keep the Passover to the LORD, according to the statute of the Passover and according to its rule, so shall he do. You shall have one statute, both for the sojourner and for the native."<sup>15</sup>On the day that the tabernacle was set up, the cloud covered the tabernacle, the tent of the testimony. And at evening it was over the tabernacle like the appearance of fire until morning.<sup>16</sup>So it was always: the cloud covered it by day and the appearance of fire by night.<sup>17</sup>And whenever the cloud lifted from over the tent, after that the people of Israel set out, and in the place where the cloud settled down, there the people of Israel camped.<sup>18</sup>At the command of the LORD the people of Israel set out, and at the command of the LORD they camped. As long as the cloud rested over the tabernacle, they remained in camp.<sup>19</sup>Even when the cloud continued over the tabernacle many days, the people of Israel kept the charge of the LORD and did not set out.<sup>20</sup>Sometimes the cloud was a few days over the tabernacle, and according to the command of the LORD they remained in camp; then according to the command of the LORD they set out.<sup>21</sup>And sometimes the cloud remained from evening until morning. And when the cloud lifted in the morning, they set out, or if it continued for a day and a night, when the cloud lifted they set out.<sup>22</sup>Whether it was two days, or a month, or a longer time, that the cloud continued over the tabernacle, abiding there, the people of Israel remained in camp and did not set out, but when it lifted they set out.<sup>23</sup>At the command of the LORD they camped, and at the command of the LORD they set out. They kept the charge of the LORD, at the command of the LORD by Moses.
9.overview:
Where we are. The camp at Sinai has been counted, arranged around the tabernacle and cleansed (chapters 1–8), and Israel is about to set out for the promised land. Numbers first looks back to a Passover kept at the mountain, then forward to the cloud that will lead them.

The message. God’s people travel as the redeemed, not in order to be redeemed: they eat the lamb before they march. And the God who saved them goes with them, deciding every move and every halt himself. He makes room at his table for those who long to come and cannot, and he warns those who could come and will not.

Why it was said. Israel was a freed slave nation facing a desert with no map (see the introduction). It needed to remember whose it was, and to learn that its whole life, waiting as much as walking, would be ordered by God’s word.

How the chapter makes its case. First the feast. Israel keeps the Passover as commanded (vv. 1–5); men unclean through burying the dead ask why they must miss it, and Moses waits for God’s answer (vv. 6–8). God provides a full Passover a month later for the unclean or far away (vv. 9–12), cuts off the one who simply neglects it, and welcomes the foreigner on the same terms (vv. 13–14). Then the cloud. It covers the tabernacle day and night (vv. 15–16); when it lifts Israel goes and where it settles Israel stays, for a night or a year (vv. 17–22), all “at the command of the LORD” (v. 23).

Where it leads. By pattern, and here the New Testament draws the line itself. The lamb whose bones were not to be broken (v. 12) is fulfilled at the cross, where John sees the Scripture kept in Jesus’ unbroken legs (John 19:36), and Paul says plainly, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The cloud of God’s presence over the tent finds its fulfilment in the Word who “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and in the Spirit who now leads God’s children from within (Romans 8:14). And God’s second chance for the unclean shows his character, fully revealed in a Saviour who sought those the law had shut out.

For us. We set out as people already bought by the blood of the Lamb, and the Lord’s Table says so again. The God who made a second Passover for the hindered welcomes the weak and the far-off, but he will not be treated with indifference. And because Christ leads us, we can wait without fretting and move without fear, one lift of the cloud at a time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Passover in the Wilderness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before they march, God’s people remember that they were redeemed by the blood of a lamb, and God makes sure no one who longs to come is left out. Israel keeps the Passover at Sinai exactly as commanded (vv. 1–5). Men made unclean by burying the dead ask why they must miss it, and Moses waits for God’s word (vv. 6–8). God answers with a full Passover a month later for the unclean and the traveller, lamb, herbs and unbroken bones included (vv. 9–12). Yet the one who could keep it and does not is cut off, and the foreigner who wants to keep it is welcomed under one statute with the native (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Redemption is remembered before the journey begins, and God makes a way for those who are kept from the feast against their will.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel remembered the Passover lamb in the wilderness; the Christian’s whole journey flows from Christ our Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the first month of the second year after they had come out of the land of Egypt, saying, "Let the people of Israel keep the Passover at its appointed time. On the fourteenth day of this month, at twilight, you shall keep it at its appointed time; according to all its statutes and all its rules you shall keep it." So Moses told the people of Israel that they should keep the Passover. And they kept the Passover in the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, at twilight, in the wilderness of Sinai; according to all that the LORD commanded Moses, so the people of Israel did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Israel takes one step towards the land, God has them sit down and eat the lamb that reminds them they were bought out of slavery by blood. They travel as the redeemed, not to become redeemed.

The first month of the second year. The date puts this a month before the census of chapter 1, which began “on the first day of the second month” (1:1). Numbers places it here for its meaning: a nation about to set out on the hardest journey of its life first eats the Passover and remembers.

The same meal again. It is the second Passover. The first was eaten in haste in Egypt with the destroyer outside; this one by free people a year later, and it is the same meal. Redemption is not something you graduate from. The Christian of forty years comes to the Lord’s Table and eats the same bread as the man converted last Tuesday, because there is nothing further along than the blood of the Lamb: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

The last Passover for forty years. It is also the last Passover on record for nearly forty years; the next is at Gilgal, after the whole generation has died (Joshua 5:10). The reader is given this scene to hold on to before the wilderness starts.

Uncertain wording. “At twilight” (vv. 3, 5, 11) is literally “between the two evenings”. It may mean the time between sunset and full dark, or, as Jewish practice took it by Jesus’ day, the later afternoon. Either way it is the evening of the fourteenth day (Exodus 12:6).

verseByVerse.quote: And there were certain men who were unclean through touching a dead body, so that they could not keep the Passover on that day, and they came before Moses and Aaron on that day. And those men said to him, "We are unclean through touching a dead body. Why are we kept from bringing the LORD's offering at its appointed time among the people of Israel?" And Moses said to them, "Wait, that I may hear what the LORD will command concerning you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men shut out of the feast by no fault of their own ask why, and Moses, instead of guessing, waits to hear from God.

Unclean through touching a dead body. They have done nothing wrong. Somebody had to bury the dead, and whoever did was unclean for seven days (19:11–13). An act of love had shut them out of the most important meal of the year.

Why are we kept from bringing the LORD’s offering? Their question is a lovely sentence. They are grieved at not being able to give God what is his. These men ached, and that ache is itself evidence of a heart God has been at work in: nobody grieves over missing what they never wanted.

Wait, that I may hear. Moses’ answer is as good as their question: “Wait, that I may hear what the LORD will command concerning you.” He neither improvises a merciful ruling nor sends them away with the law as it stands. He says, in effect: I do not know, and I will ask. There is a kind of leader who would rather be wrong than say that.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If any one of you or of your descendants is unclean through touching a dead body, or is on a long journey, he shall still keep the Passover to the LORD. In the second month on the fourteenth day at twilight they shall keep it. They shall eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. They shall leave none of it until the morning, nor break any of its bones; according to all the statute for the Passover they shall keep it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers by opening a second door: a full Passover a month later for anyone unclean or far away. It is the same feast, down to the lamb whose bones must not be broken.

In the second month. God does not merely excuse the hindered; he arranges a second observance so that nobody who wanted to come goes without, and not a reduced version but “according to all the statute for the Passover”: unleavened bread, bitter herbs, the same meal.

Nor break any of its bones. This detail from the original statute (Exodus 12:46) will travel a long way. On a Friday afternoon outside Jerusalem, soldiers broke the legs of the crucified men so the bodies could be taken down before the Sabbath, and finding Jesus already dead, did not break his. John, standing there, writes: “For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘Not one of his bones will be broken’” (John 19:36). He is quoting this law, and perhaps Psalm 34:20. A rule about handling a lamb in the wilderness described what a Roman execution squad would decline to do to the Son of God.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone who is clean and is not on a journey fails to keep the Passover, that person shall be cut off from his people because he did not bring the LORD's offering at its appointed time; that man shall bear his sin. And if a stranger sojourns among you and would keep the Passover to the LORD, according to the statute of the Passover and according to its rule, so shall he do. You shall have one statute, both for the sojourner and for the native."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second Passover was for the hindered, not the indifferent; and the foreigner who longed to come was welcomed on equal terms.

That person shall be cut off. The grace has a hard edge. The men of verse 7 and the man of verse 13 differ most of all in their hearts: those men ached to come and could not; this man could come and did not bother. To despise the meal of redemption was to despise the redemption.

In everyday life. That distinction comforts the right people and warns the rest. The believer kept from church by illness or by nursing somebody is not the one who could have gone and preferred not to, and God knows which is which. Even the careless is not beyond the reach of the feast: the way back is to come, confessing, while the door is still open.

One statute. The last verse widens the door again: “You shall have one statute, both for the sojourner and for the native.” A foreigner who wanted to come was welcomed on identical terms, once his household had joined the covenant by circumcision (Exodus 12:48). There has never been a second-class table in the house of God, and in Christ the nations come in freely (Ephesians 2:19).

Uncertain wording. What “cut off from his people” meant in practice is not certain. Some think of death at God’s own hand, perhaps with the family line ended; others of being put out of the community and its covenant privileges. Either way it is God’s serious judgment: “that man shall bear his sin”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who redeemed Israel now leads it, and his people go and stay at his word alone. From the day the tabernacle was set up, a cloud covered it by day and fire by night, always (vv. 15–16). When the cloud lifted, Israel set out; where it settled, Israel camped (vv. 17–18). The writer lists the possibilities, many days or a few, a night, a month, a year, so that no one could predict a move (vv. 19–22). The chapter closes with “at the command of the LORD” three times in a single verse: waiting and walking are equally obedience (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: The life of faith depends on God’s presence and guidance, in staying as much as in moving.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel was led by cloud and fire; believers are led by the Spirit as they follow Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day that the tabernacle was set up, the cloud covered the tabernacle, the tent of the testimony. And at evening it was over the tabernacle like the appearance of fire until morning. So it was always: the cloud covered it by day and the appearance of fire by night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the day the tabernacle was raised, God’s presence stood visibly over the centre of the camp, cloud by day and fire by night, without a break.

So it was always. Take in the word “always”: not just at the great moments, not only when Israel was behaving. Every day and every night for forty years a visible sign of God’s presence stood over the middle of the camp, and any Israelite who woke frightened in the dark could put his head out of the tent and see fire burning over the tabernacle.

Cloud and fire. The two forms fit the two needs. A cloud by day, in a desert, is shade; fire by night is warmth and light. The same presence takes whatever form the hour requires, and Isaiah promises it for the age to come: “There will be a booth for shade by day from the heat, and for a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain” (Isaiah 4:6).

What we have instead. We have no pillar of fire. But the God who hung a cloud over a tent came to live among us in his Son, who “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and he has said to his people, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). What was visible to Israel from the outside is now true of Christians from the inside: the church is the tabernacle, for God’s Spirit lives in her (1 Corinthians 3:16).

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the cloud lifted from over the tent, after that the people of Israel set out, and in the place where the cloud settled down, there the people of Israel camped. At the command of the LORD the people of Israel set out, and at the command of the LORD they camped. As long as the cloud rested over the tabernacle, they remained in camp. Even when the cloud continued over the tabernacle many days, the people of Israel kept the charge of the LORD and did not set out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel moved when the cloud moved and stayed when it stayed, and staying put, even for many days, was as much obedience as marching.

Whenever the cloud lifted. Here is the rhythm of forty years. Israel had no timetable, no map, no list of stopping places; there was a cloud, and you watched it. When it lifted, everything came down, tents, pens, the sick, convenient or not; when it settled they stopped, even if there was a better valley an hour on.

Even when the cloud continued. Verse 19 makes the harder half explicit: “Even when the cloud continued over the tabernacle many days, the people of Israel kept the charge of the LORD and did not set out.” Most people find staying harder than moving. The waiting seasons, when nothing is happening and every instinct says do something, are as much the will of God as the marching ones, and Israel could spoil its obedience as thoroughly by going early as by refusing to go at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Sometimes the cloud was a few days over the tabernacle, and according to the command of the LORD they remained in camp; then according to the command of the LORD they set out. And sometimes the cloud remained from evening until morning. And when the cloud lifted in the morning, they set out, or if it continued for a day and a night, when the cloud lifted they set out. Whether it was two days, or a month, or a longer time, that the cloud continued over the tabernacle, abiding there, the people of Israel remained in camp and did not set out, but when it lifted they set out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cloud’s timings were deliberately unpredictable, so Israel had to hold everything loosely and stay ready to follow God at any hour.

Whether it was two days, or a month. The text lists the possibilities, a night, a day, two days, a month, longer, so that no reader can work out a rule. Israel could never say, “We have been here three weeks, so we are due to move.”

Living without a timetable. You pitch the tent with no idea whether you will be here one night or half a year. Do you unpack? Do you start something? The only way to live like that is to hold everything loosely and stay ready, and that is the design.

Our condition too. That is the Christian’s condition too. We are not told the timings either: “you do not know what tomorrow will bring… Instead you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that’” (James 4:14–15). It is not the absence of a plan. It is a plan held by God, revealed one lift of the cloud at a time.

verseByVerse.quote: At the command of the LORD they camped, and at the command of the LORD they set out. They kept the charge of the LORD, at the command of the LORD by Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s whole life, its camping and its marching, came from the mouth of God, and at this moment, before the complaining starts, the nation is simply led.

At the command of the LORD. The phrase comes three times in one verse; literally, “at the mouth of the LORD”. Both halves are given equal weight, with camping named first. There is no suggestion that travelling was the obedient part and sitting still was wasted time.

Before the complaining. Nine chapters have been about order, carried out as the LORD commanded. In two chapters’ time the people will be wailing for meat.

They were led. So read this verse while it is still true of them: a nation with no map, going only where God went, stopping only where he stopped. Whatever else they were, they were led. So is everyone who belongs to Christ, not by a cloud outside but by the Spirit within: “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8:14).

9.theology:
Redemption Before Pilgrimage. The Christian journeys not to be saved but because, in Christ our Passover, we already are.

Grace for the Excluded, Judgment for the Despiser. The gospel makes a way for the hungry, the foreigner among them, but it is never licence for the careless.

The Life of Guidance. Israel moved and rested only “at the command of the LORD”, and the believer is led in the same way by the Spirit.
9.examples:
Then: Israel kept the Passover, made room for the longing outsider, and followed the cloud.

Now: Your journey flows from redemption: Christ, your Passover, was sacrificed for you. If you feel excluded or defiled yet long to draw near, know that God makes a way. And live the cloud-led life: hold your plans loosely, watch for the Lord’s leading, and follow wherever the Spirit goes.

keyVerse.quote: At the command of the LORD they camped, and at the command of the LORD they set out. They kept the charge of the LORD, at the command of the LORD by Moses.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s last verse gathers its message into one line: Israel’s staying and going alike came from the mouth of God. Camping is named first, so waiting is as much obedience as marching. It is the life of a people who have been redeemed by the Passover lamb and now follow the God who goes with them.

9.reflection:
Israel kept the Passover before taking a single step towards the land (vv. 1–5). Why does it matter that the Christian life begins and continues with what Christ has already done, and how does the Lord’s Supper keep reminding us of it?

The unclean men grieved that they could not bring the LORD’s offering (v. 7), while the man of verse 13 could come and did not bother. Which of these is closer to your attitude to worship at the moment, and what would help?

Moses said, “Wait, that I may hear what the LORD will command concerning you” (v. 8). Where are you tempted to improvise an answer when you should first go to God’s word?

The cloud sometimes stayed a night and sometimes a year (vv. 20–22). Are you in a season of waiting or of moving? What would it look like to trust Christ’s leading in it?

10.title: The Silver Trumpets; Israel Departs from Sinai
