And the ark of the covenant of the LORD went before them three days' journey, to seek out a resting place for them.<sup>34</sup>And the cloud of the LORD was over them by day, whenever they set out from the camp.<sup>35</sup>And whenever the ark set out, Moses said, "Arise, O LORD, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee before you."<sup>36</sup>And when it rested, he said, "Return, O LORD, to the ten thousand thousands of Israel."
10.overview:
Where we are. Israel has kept the Passover and learned to follow the cloud (chapter 9). Now, after nearly a year at Sinai, God gives the trumpets that will order the march, the cloud lifts, and the people set out. It is the hinge of the book.

The message. God does not send his people into the wilderness alone or in confusion. He gives them a clear voice, keeps them in order, carries his presence in their midst and goes ahead to find them rest. Others are invited to share the good he has promised, and the people’s prayer is simple: arise against your enemies, and come back to dwell with us.

Why it was said. A people of hundreds of thousands was about to leave the mountain where God had spoken and cross a desert towards enemies (see the introduction). They needed to know that God would lead, gather and protect them, and that the promised good was real enough to invite others into.

How the chapter makes its case. Two silver trumpets, blown by the priests, summon, set the camps marching, cry to God in war and celebrate at the feasts (vv. 1–10). On the twentieth day of the second month the cloud lifts, and the tribes set out exactly in the order of chapter 2, the tabernacle carried in their midst (vv. 11–28). Moses urges his Midianite in-law Hobab to come and share Israel’s good (vv. 29–32), the ark goes ahead to seek a resting place (vv. 33–34), and Moses prays as it sets out and as it rests (vv. 35–36).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. The ark going before Israel to find a resting place is the shape of what Christ has done: he has gone ahead as our forerunner (Hebrews 6:20), to prepare a place for us (John 14:2), and he gives the rest Israel was seeking (Matthew 11:28). “Arise, O LORD, and let your enemies be scattered” opens Psalm 68, which Paul hears fulfilled in Christ’s ascension (Ephesians 4:8); and “Return, O LORD” is answered when “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3). And Moses’ offer to Hobab shows God’s heart for outsiders, fully opened in the gospel to the nations.

For us. The Christian life is a journey with God in the middle and Christ out in front. Listen for his voice in his word, keep in step with his people, cry to him in trouble and in joy, and invite others to come with you, for the LORD has promised good.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives his people a clear voice to gather them, move them and bring them before him. Two silver trumpets of hammered work are made: both blown together call the whole congregation, one calls the leaders (vv. 1–4). Short alarms set the camps marching, a long blast assembles them, and only the priests may blow them (vv. 5–8). In war the trumpets cry out to God “that you may be remembered”, and at the feasts they sound over the offerings in gladness (vv. 9–10). The same instruments serve for summons, march, danger and joy, because all of Israel’s life is lived before the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: The trumpet is the voice of God’s summons and a prayer that reaches heaven; God remembers his people when they call.
verseByVerse.examples: The silver trumpets called Israel to gather and march. The gospel call now gathers God’s people, and the last trumpet will announce Christ’s return (1 Corinthians 15:52).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Make two silver trumpets. Of hammered work you shall make them, and you shall use them for summoning the congregation and for breaking camp. And when both are blown, all the congregation shall gather themselves to you at the entrance of the tent of meeting. But if they blow only one, then the chiefs, the heads of the tribes of Israel, shall gather themselves to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives his travelling people a clear signal of his own, so that everyone knows when he is called.

Make two silver trumpets. Two, not twelve; silver, not ram’s horn; hammered out of solid metal like the lampstand. A camp spread over miles cannot be shouted at, so God gives it a sound, and the sound is his, not a general’s.

When both are blown. The signals are precise: both trumpets mean everybody; one means the leaders. God did not leave his people guessing whether they had been called; he gave a signal that even a man who could not read could understand from his tent door half a mile away. Everything in this chapter assumes that God intends to be understood by ordinary people. And the gathering trumpet will sound once more, when “the trumpet of God” summons all his people (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: When you blow an alarm, the camps that are on the east side shall set out. And when you blow an alarm the second time, the camps that are on the south side shall set out. An alarm is to be blown whenever they are to set out. But when the assembly is to be gathered together, you shall blow a long blast, but you shall not sound an alarm. And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall blow the trumpets. The trumpets shall be to you for a perpetual statute throughout your generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The calls must be clear and must come from the sanctuary, because a whole nation moves on them.

When you blow an alarm. An alarm, short and broken, means break camp; a long blast means assemble. A mistake would send a nation the wrong way, so verse 8 matters: the priests blow the trumpets, not the army or the chiefs. Israel’s marching orders came out of the sanctuary.

An uncertain sound. That is why Paul reaches for a trumpet when he talks about speaking in church: “if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?” (1 Corinthians 14:8). A priest who blows an uncertain note leaves a nation standing in a field. Being clear is part of the preacher’s task.

verseByVerse.quote: And when you go to war in your land against the adversary who oppresses you, then you shall sound an alarm with the trumpets, that you may be remembered before the LORD your God, and you shall be saved from your enemies. On the day of your gladness also, and at your appointed feasts and at the beginnings of your months, you shall blow the trumpets over your burnt offerings and over the sacrifices of your peace offerings. They shall be a reminder of you before your God: I am the LORD your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The trumpets also go up to God, crying for rescue in war and rejoicing at the feasts, so that in trouble and joy alike his people are “remembered”.

When you go to war. The first use is war, against “the adversary who oppresses you”, and the blast goes upward: “that you may be remembered before the LORD your God, and you shall be saved from your enemies.” The promised result is not morale but rescue (2 Chronicles 13:12–16).

On the day of your gladness. The second is joy, at the feasts and new moons: the same instrument for the worst day and the best.

That you may be remembered. Not because God forgets; Scripture never means that by the word. When God remembers someone, he acts for them: God remembered Noah and the waters went down (Genesis 8:1); God remembered Hannah and she conceived (1 Samuel 1:19). It means his attention turning into action.

In trouble and in joy. The church has the same invitation in plainer words: “Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise” (James 5:13). In both we reach for the same God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After almost a year at Sinai the cloud lifts, and God’s people set out in the order he gave them. On the twentieth day of the second month Israel leaves the mountain for the wilderness of Paran, for the first time “at the command of the LORD by Moses” (vv. 11–13). The march unfolds exactly as chapter 2 arranged it: Judah first, then the carriers of the tabernacle frame, then Reuben, then the Kohathites with the holy things, then Ephraim, with Dan as rearguard (vv. 14–28). The plan works, and the presence of God travels in the middle of his people.
verseByVerse.theology: At last the redeemed people move toward the promised land, carrying God’s presence in ordered obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: As Israel marched out from Sinai, the church is on pilgrimage, moving toward her inheritance under Christ’s lead.

verseByVerse.quote: In the second year, in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, the cloud lifted from over the tabernacle of the testimony, and the people of Israel set out by stages from the wilderness of Sinai. And the cloud settled down in the wilderness of Paran. They set out for the first time at the command of the LORD by Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After nearly a year the cloud lifts, and Israel leaves the mountain where it was made ready for the journey.

Leaving Sinai. This is a turning point in the five books of Moses. Israel arrived at Sinai in the third month of the first year (Exodus 19:1) and has been there nearly a year: law, covenant, golden calf, tabernacle, priesthood, census. Fifty-nine chapters of the Bible take place at the foot of that mountain, and now, in a single sentence, the cloud moves. It settles in the wilderness of Paran, the desert reaching to the southern edge of Canaan, from which the spies will be sent (13:3).

From the wilderness of Sinai. That needs saying to Christians. The mountain where God spoke was never meant to be the destination. There is a kind of believer who wants to live permanently at the site of his best experience of God, and the cloud will not let him. When it lifts, the mountain is behind you, and the God of the mountain goes with you.
verseByVerse.note: Paran was the wilderness south of Canaan; Kadesh, from which the spies are sent in chapter 13, lay in it.

verseByVerse.quote: The standard of the camp of the people of Judah set out first by their companies, and over their company was Nahshon the son of Amminadab. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Issachar was Nethanel the son of Zuar. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Zebulun was Eliab the son of Helon. And when the tabernacle was taken down, the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari, who carried the tabernacle, set out. And the standard of the camp of Reuben set out by their companies, and over their company was Elizur the son of Shedeur. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Simeon was Shelumiel the son of Zurishaddai. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Gad was Eliasaph the son of Deuel. Then the Kohathites set out, carrying the holy things, and the tabernacle was set up before their arrival. And the standard of the camp of the people of Ephraim set out by their companies, and over their company was Elishama the son of Ammihud. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Manasseh was Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Benjamin was Abidan the son of Gideoni. Then the standard of the camp of the people of Dan, acting as the rear guard of all the camps, set out by their companies, and over their company was Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Asher was Pagiel the son of Ochran. And over the company of the tribe of the people of Naphtali was Ahira the son of Enan. This was the order of march of the people of Israel by their companies, when they set out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The march unfolds exactly as God ordered it, with his presence carried in the middle of his people.

This was the order of march. The point is that the plan worked: the whole people, their livestock and a dismantled tabernacle moved off in the sequence of chapter 2, and nobody got lost or argued.

Carrying the holy things. The holy things travel in the middle, behind Judah and Reuben and in front of Ephraim and Dan, with the strongest divisions at the head and the tail. The frame goes ahead, so that “the tabernacle was set up before their arrival” (v. 21). The tabernacle is not at the front where it could be admired, nor at the back where it could be forgotten, but in the middle, with every tribe arranged around it, walking.

A picture of the church. That was Israel’s life for forty years: a column of people with the presence of God moving in the middle of them. It is also a fair description of a church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–36 — Hobab and the Cry of the Ark
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel sets out with an open invitation to outsiders and with God himself going on ahead. Moses urges Hobab, his Midianite relative, to come and share the good the LORD has promised, and to lend his knowledge of the desert (vv. 29–32). The ark goes three days ahead to seek out a resting place, while the cloud shades the people overhead (vv. 33–34). Moses’ two short prayers, at setting out and at resting, frame each day’s march: “Arise, O LORD” against his enemies, and “Return, O LORD” to dwell among his people (vv. 35–36).
verseByVerse.theology: Even as God leads, the cry of faith rises with the ark; the LORD himself goes before his people to scatter their enemies.
verseByVerse.examples: The ark led Israel’s way; Christ now goes before his people, and no enemy can stand against him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to Hobab the son of Reuel the Midianite, Moses' father-in-law, "We are setting out for the place of which the LORD said, 'I will give it to you.' Come with us, and we will do good to you, for the LORD has promised good to Israel." But he said to him, "I will not go. I will depart to my own land and to my kindred." And he said, "Please do not leave us, for you know where we should camp in the wilderness, and you will serve as eyes for us. And if you do go with us, whatever good the LORD will do to us, the same will we do to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses invites Hobab, a Midianite, to share all the good God has promised Israel, and asks for his desert know-how as well.

Is Moses faltering? Hobab refuses, and Moses presses him: “you will serve as eyes for us.” But he has a pillar of cloud; why does he need a desert guide? Some readers see a lapse of faith, not unreasonably. Yet he does not ask Hobab to choose the route; the cloud does that. He asks for a man who knows the country: where the water is, which wadi floods, where a camp that size can pitch. God’s guidance settled the destination, not which side of a valley the wells were on. His leading has never made ordinary know-how unnecessary, and a man who refuses good advice because he is being led by God has usually confused two different things.

Whatever good the LORD will do to us. Moses offers not payment but partnership: “whatever good the LORD will do to us, the same will we do to you.” A Midianite is invited into Israel’s promises on equal terms, an early glimpse of the gospel’s welcome to the nations. The text does not say whether he came, though his descendants, the Kenites, turn up among Judah after the conquest (Judges 1:16), which suggests somebody in that family changed his mind.

Uncertain wording. It is not clear exactly how Hobab was related to Moses. Exodus calls Moses’ father-in-law Reuel (2:18) and Jethro (3:1). Here “Moses’ father-in-law” may describe Reuel, Hobab’s father, though Judges 4:11 gives Hobab the title. The Hebrew word may cover in-laws more widely, so Hobab was most likely Moses’ brother-in-law.

verseByVerse.quote: So they set out from the mount of the LORD three days' journey. And the ark of the covenant of the LORD went before them three days' journey, to seek out a resting place for them. And the cloud of the LORD was over them by day, whenever they set out from the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God goes ahead of his people to find them rest, while his cloud shelters them overhead.

The ark of the covenant of the LORD went before them. Here the ark goes out in front, three days ahead, “to seek out a resting place for them.”

To seek out a resting place. God is not driving his people from behind, nor merely accompanying them, but out in front looking for the place where they can lie down. Rest runs through the whole Bible (Hebrews 4:9) until it arrives at the invitation of Jesus: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

The cloud of the LORD was over them. Above them the cloud; ahead of them the ark: shade over their heads and a resting place chosen before they arrive. Do you wonder whether God has thought about tomorrow? He was three days ahead of Israel, looking for somewhere for them to sleep, and Christ has gone ahead of us to prepare a place for us (John 14:2–3).

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever the ark set out, Moses said, "Arise, O LORD, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee before you." And when it rested, he said, "Return, O LORD, to the ten thousand thousands of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each day’s march opened and closed with prayer: that the LORD would rise and scatter his enemies, and that he would come back to dwell among his people.

Arise, O LORD. Two lines Israel evidently sang for centuries. “Arise, O LORD, and let your enemies be scattered.” Whose enemies? Not “ours” but “your” enemies: the opposition in front of them was opposition to God. Psalm 68 opens with the same line, and the church has borrowed it ever since.

Return, O LORD. At the end of the day’s march: “Return, O LORD, to the ten thousand thousands of Israel.” It is the prayer of a people who wanted God not only to fight for them but to come home with them and stay.

He arises; he returns. Together they sum up the Christian hope, and both are answered in one Man. Psalm 68 goes on to the LORD ascending on high, which Paul applies to Christ (Ephesians 4:8); on the cross “he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). And at the end it will be said, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people” (Revelation 21:3).

Israel at its best. The cloud is over them, the ark ahead, the trumpets in the priests’ hands, and Moses is praying. Israel has never looked more promising than on the twentieth day of the second month. The next chapter opens with the people complaining.

10.theology:
The Summons of God. The silver trumpets made God’s will audible to his people, and the church still moves at the clear call of his word.

God Goes Before and Abides. The ark leads the march to seek a resting place and returns to dwell in the midst: fulfilled in Christ, who has gone to prepare a place and dwells with us by the Spirit.

Arise, O LORD! The battles of God’s people are the LORD’s; the cry finds its answer in the risen Christ, who has scattered sin, death and the devil.
10.examples:
Then: The cloud lifted, and Israel left the mountain behind.

Now: You are a pilgrim, summoned by the gospel and following the One who goes before you to prepare your rest. When enemies oppress, cry, “Arise, O LORD!”, for the risen Christ has already scattered every foe. Invite others to come with you, for the Lord has promised good.

keyVerse.quote: So they set out from the mount of the LORD three days’ journey. And the ark of the covenant of the LORD went before them three days’ journey, to seek out a resting place for them.
keyVerse.note: This verse shows the kind of God Israel followed out of Sinai: not one who drives his people from behind, but one who goes ahead to find them rest. It gathers the chapter’s order and trumpets into its real purpose, and it points to Christ, who has gone ahead as our forerunner to prepare a place for us.

10.reflection:
God gave trumpets with signals clear enough for anyone in the camp to understand (vv. 1–8). Why does clarity matter in the way God speaks and in the way the church passes on his word? Where do we make it unclear?

The same trumpets sounded in war and on “the day of your gladness” (vv. 9–10). Do you turn to God as readily when things go well as when they go badly? What might help you do both?

Moses invited Hobab: “Come with us, and we will do good to you, for the LORD has promised good to Israel” (v. 29). Who could you invite to share the good God has promised, and what holds you back?

The ark went ahead “to seek out a resting place for them” (v. 33). How does knowing that Christ has gone ahead of you change the way you face tomorrow?

11.title: Grumbling and the Seventy Elders

And the people of Israel also wept again and said, "Oh that we had meat to eat!<sup>5</sup>We remember the fish we ate in Egypt that cost nothing, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, and the garlic.<sup>6</sup>But now our strength is dried up, and there is nothing at all but this manna to look at."<sup>7</sup>Now the manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance like that of bdellium.<sup>8</sup>The people went about and gathered it and ground it in handmills or beat it in mortars and boiled it in pots and made cakes of it. And the taste of it was like the taste of cakes baked with oil.<sup>9</sup>When the dew fell upon the camp in the night, the manna fell with it.<sup>10</sup>Moses heard the people weeping throughout their clans, everyone at the door of his tent. And why have I not found favor in your sight, that you lay the burden of all this people on me?<sup>12</sup>Did I conceive all this people? For they weep before me and say, 'Give us meat, that we may eat.'<sup>14</sup>I am not able to carry all this people alone; the burden is too heavy for me.<sup>15</sup>If you will treat me like this, kill me at once, if I find favor in your sight, that I may not see my wretchedness."<sup>16</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Gather for me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people and officers over them, and bring them to the tent of meeting, and let them take their stand there with you.<sup>17</sup>And I will come down and talk with you there. And I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them, and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, so that you may not bear it yourself alone.<sup>18</sup>And say to the people, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat meat, for you have wept in the hearing of the LORD, saying, "Who will give us meat to eat? For it was better for us in Egypt." Therefore the LORD will give you meat, and you shall eat.<sup>19</sup>You shall not eat just one day, or two days, or five days, or ten days, or twenty days,<sup>20</sup>but a whole month, until it comes out at your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you, because you have rejected the LORD who is among you and have wept before him, saying, "Why did we come out of Egypt?"'"<sup>21</sup>But Moses said, "The people among whom I am number six hundred thousand on foot, and you have said, 'I will give them meat, that they may eat a whole month!'<sup>22</sup>Shall flocks and herds be slaughtered for them, and be enough for them? Or shall all the fish of the sea be gathered together for them, and be enough for them?"<sup>23</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Is the LORD's hand shortened? Would that all the LORD's people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!"<sup>30</sup>And Moses and the elders of Israel returned to the camp.<sup>31</sup>Then a wind from the LORD sprang up, and it brought quail from the sea and let them fall beside the camp, about a day's journey on this side and a day's journey on the other side, around the camp, and about two cubits above the ground.<sup>32</sup>And the people rose all that day and all night and all the next day, and gathered the quail. Those who gathered least gathered ten homers. And they spread them out for themselves all around the camp.<sup>33</sup>While the meat was yet between their teeth, before it was consumed, the anger of the LORD was kindled against the people, and the LORD struck down the people with a very great plague.<sup>34</sup>Therefore the name of that place was called Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people who had the craving.<sup>35</sup>From Kibroth-hattaavah the people journeyed to Hazeroth, and they remained at Hazeroth.
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 10 ended with Israel at its best. Three days later the complaining begins, and the journey’s long story of failure sets its pattern here.

The message. Grumbling is never only about the food: it is a verdict on the God who is among us, and it can turn his good gifts into “nothing at all”. God takes it seriously, sometimes by giving people exactly what they crave until it sickens them. Yet he hears the honest cry of his worn-out servant with nothing but kindness, shares his load by giving his Spirit to others, and shows that his hand is never too short to keep his word.

Why it was said. The generation that left Sinai would not reach the land, and here we first see why (see the introduction). Later generations, and the church, were to read these graves as a warning: “these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did” (1 Corinthians 10:6).

How the chapter makes its case. A vague complaint brings fire on the edge of the camp, stopped by Moses’ prayer (vv. 1–3). Then craving spreads: the people weep for Egypt’s fish and despise the manna, whose goodness the narrator quietly describes (vv. 4–9). Moses, crushed, pours out his despair to God (vv. 10–15). God answers him with seventy elders to share his Spirit and burden, and the people with meat until they loathe it; to Moses’ doubt he says, “Is the LORD’s hand shortened?” (vv. 16–23). The Spirit rests on the seventy and two more, and Moses longs for all the LORD’s people to be prophets (vv. 24–30). The quail come, and with them the plague, and the place is named the graves of craving (vv. 31–35).

Where it leads. By pattern, by promise and by the need it exposes. The manna Israel despised points to the one who said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:48), and where Israel failed in the wilderness, Jesus, hungry there for forty days, trusted his Father’s word (Matthew 4:4). Moses could not carry the people “as a nurse carries a nursing child” (v. 12), but the LORD carries his flock “in his bosom” (Isaiah 40:11), and Christ is that shepherd. And Moses’ wish that the Spirit would rest on all God’s people became a promise through Joel and was fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:17).

For us. Watch for the quiet slide from gratitude to grumbling, and for the gifts that have moved into the “nothing at all” column. Bring your exhaustion honestly to God, and accept the help he sends. Aim your desires at Christ, the bread who alone satisfies, rather than at what can fill the mouth and empty the soul.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Complaining against God’s care is a serious sin, but prayer can turn his judgment aside. Only three days after leaving Sinai, the people complain about their misfortunes, though no hardship is named. The LORD hears, and fire burns the edges of the camp (v. 1). The people cry to Moses, Moses prays, and the fire dies down (v. 2). The place is named Taberah, “burning”, the first of the names this book leaves across the desert to mark the people’s unbelief (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: Grumbling against God’s providence kindles his anger; complaint is a serious sin against the goodness of God.
verseByVerse.examples: The fire at Taberah still warns against a grumbling heart, which is quietly accusing God of providing badly.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people complained in the hearing of the LORD about their misfortunes, and when the LORD heard it, his anger was kindled, and the fire of the LORD burned among them and consumed some outlying parts of the camp. Then the people cried out to Moses, and Moses prayed to the LORD, and the fire died down. So the name of that place was called Taberah, because the fire of the LORD burned among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God treats a people’s aimless discontent as a serious sin, yet stops his judgment when Moses prays.

About their misfortunes. No famine, enemy or hardship is named. The vagueness is the point: this is not a crisis but a mood. And it happened inside the very three days in which the ark went ahead to find them a resting place (10:33).

Taberah. Fire falls on the edge of the camp, Moses prays, and it stops. Taberah, “Burning”, is the first of the place-names this book leaves across a desert, each marking a moment when God’s people decided the God carrying them was not doing it well enough.

Written for us. Paul says these things were written for our instruction (1 Corinthians 10:10–11). His own call, “Do all things without grumbling or disputing” (Philippians 2:14), rests on what he has just set out: Christ’s humble obedience to the point of death, and the God who “works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).
verseByVerse.note: Taberah does not appear in the list of camps in chapter 33, which suggests it was a name for part of the area rather than a separate stopping place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–15 — Craving Meat and the Weight of Leadership
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ingratitude rewrites the past and despises the present, and its weight can crush even a faithful leader. A craving that starts among the rabble spreads to all Israel: they remember Egypt’s free food and see “nothing at all but this manna” (vv. 4–6). The narrator answers with a quiet description of how good the manna was (vv. 7–9). As the whole camp weeps, Moses breaks and tells God the truth: he cannot carry this people alone, and would rather die than go on (vv. 10–15). God does not rebuke him for it.
verseByVerse.theology: The weight of leading God’s people is too heavy for one man alone, and God does not pretend otherwise.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel wept for the food of Egypt; we too can despise God’s daily gifts, and we too need others to share our heaviest burdens.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rabble that was among them had a strong craving. And the people of Israel also wept again and said, "Oh that we had meat to eat! We remember the fish we ate in Egypt that cost nothing, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, and the garlic. But now our strength is dried up, and there is nothing at all but this manna to look at."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Craving spreads through the camp, rewriting slavery in Egypt as a free banquet and dismissing God’s daily miracle as “nothing at all”.

The rabble that was among them. Discontent is contagious, and it does not usually start at the centre.

We remember the fish. Here is one of the great pieces of self-deception in Scripture: a mouth-watering menu. Notice what is missing: the whips, the quota of bricks, the baby boys thrown into the Nile, a nation groaning so loudly that “God heard their groaning” (Exodus 2:24). None of that survives in the memory. What survives is the garlic.

That cost nothing. They were slaves; the fish came with the whip. Memory under present discomfort edits out precisely what God rescued us from.

Nothing at all but this manna. Bread from the sky, six mornings a week, free, has become nothing at all. The surest test of a grumbling season is to ask what has quietly moved from the miracle column to the nothing column.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “rabble” occurs only here in the Old Testament. It seems to mean a gathered mob, and most take it to be the “mixed multitude” who left Egypt with Israel (Exodus 12:38), though the text does not say so.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance like that of bdellium. The people went about and gathered it and ground it in handmills or beat it in mortars and boiled it in pots and made cakes of it. And the taste of it was like the taste of cakes baked with oil. When the dew fell upon the camp in the night, the manna fell with it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator answers the complaint simply by describing how good the manna was.

Its appearance like that of bdellium. Israel said there was nothing to look at; the writer says it looked like bdellium, a pale precious resin. Israel implied monotony; the writer lists four ways of preparing it and says it tasted like cakes baked with oil. Israel despised it; the writer says it came down with the dew in the night while they slept. It is the gentlest rebuke in the book.

The bread of life. A Man later took this bread and made a claim about himself with it: “I am the bread of life… I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John 6:48, 51). The generation that called the manna worthless gathered a picture of Christ every morning and complained about the taste.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses heard the people weeping throughout their clans, everyone at the door of his tent. And the anger of the LORD blazed hotly, and Moses was displeased. Moses said to the LORD, "Why have you dealt ill with your servant? And why have I not found favor in your sight, that you lay the burden of all this people on me? Did I conceive all this people? Did I give them birth, that you should say to me, 'Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a nursing child,' to the land that you swore to give their fathers? Where am I to get meat to give to all this people? For they weep before me and say, 'Give us meat, that we may eat.' I am not able to carry all this people alone; the burden is too heavy for me. If you will treat me like this, kill me at once, if I find favor in your sight, that I may not see my wretchedness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Crushed, Moses pours out his despair to God, even asking to die, and God answers his honest prayer not with rebuke but with help.

Why have you dealt ill with your servant? One of the rawest prayers in the Bible, and it should never be tidied up. The meekest man on earth (12:3) tells God he has been badly treated, asks whether the whole arrangement was fair, and finally asks to be killed rather than go on. His image is a mother’s: he is asked to carry a nation “as a nurse carries a nursing child”, a nation that will not stop crying, and he did not give birth to it.

Told to the right person. Moses took his despair to God, not to others behind the people’s backs. Every syllable of it is prayer, and that is why it could be answered.

The one who carries. What Moses could not do, God does: “he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom” (Isaiah 40:11). Jesus is that Good Shepherd, who carries the weight Moses could not.

Telling God the truth. Anyone in ministry, or caring for a parent, or holding a family together, should notice that verse 15 is in the Bible: God can be told the truth. Peter’s “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7) comes with no list of anxieties too ugly to bring. And if you have prayed something like verse 15 and the wish to die has not lifted, tell a pastor, a doctor or a trusted friend today, and if you are in danger of acting on it, get help at once through emergency services. God answered Moses by sending him people, and he often still does.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–30 — The Seventy Elders and the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers his servant’s despair with shared help and the people’s rebellion with a fearful gift, and his Spirit cannot be confined. God tells Moses to gather seventy elders, on whom he will put some of the Spirit that is on Moses, so that they bear the burden with him (vv. 16–17). The people will have meat until it sickens them, for they have rejected the LORD; when Moses doubts it can be done, God asks, “Is the LORD’s hand shortened?” (vv. 18–23). The Spirit rests on the seventy and on Eldad and Medad in the camp, and Moses longs for all God’s people to have the Spirit (vv. 24–30).
verseByVerse.theology: God gives his Spirit to share the burden of leadership, and Moses rejoices rather than guarding his own place.
verseByVerse.examples: The Spirit came on seventy elders; since Pentecost he has been given to all God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Gather for me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people and officers over them, and bring them to the tent of meeting, and let them take their stand there with you. And I will come down and talk with you there. And I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them, and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, so that you may not bear it yourself alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers Moses’ despair by sharing the load among seventy elders who receive the same Spirit.

Too heavy for one man. God puts “some of the Spirit that is on you” on seventy elders, “so that you may not bear it yourself alone.” He does not tell Moses to pray harder or trust more. He agrees that the load is too big for one man and divides it, as Jethro had said: “You are not able to do it alone” (Exodus 18:18). Admitting the work is too heavy is not here a failure of faith: the load was wrong, not Moses’ faith. Some burdens need not more grace for one person but more shoulders.

Not a lesser Spirit. It is the same Spirit, extended, not a lesser one. Moses loses nothing when seventy others receive it, for God never has less to give because he has given. What made Moses able to lead is what will make them able to help.

verseByVerse.quote: And say to the people, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat meat, for you have wept in the hearing of the LORD, saying, "Who will give us meat to eat? For it was better for us in Egypt." Therefore the LORD will give you meat, and you shall eat. You shall not eat just one day, or two days, or five days, or ten days, or twenty days, but a whole month, until it comes out at your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you, because you have rejected the LORD who is among you and have wept before him, saying, "Why did we come out of Egypt?"'" But Moses said, "The people among whom I am number six hundred thousand on foot, and you have said, 'I will give them meat, that they may eat a whole month!' Shall flocks and herds be slaughtered for them, and be enough for them? Or shall all the fish of the sea be gathered together for them, and be enough for them?" And the LORD said to Moses, "Is the LORD's hand shortened? Now you shall see whether my word will come true for you or not."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will give the people meat until they loathe it, for their weeping rejects the LORD among them; and to Moses’ doubts he answers that his hand is never too short.

Until it comes out at your nostrils. God’s answer to the people is frightening: “until it comes out at your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you.” It is a terrible form of judgment the Bible names in one line: “he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them” (Psalm 106:15). There are prayers it is a mercy that God does not grant.

You have rejected the LORD who is among you. They thought they were complaining about food. Grumbling is never really about the circumstance; it is a verdict passed on the God who arranged it.

Is the LORD’s hand shortened? Moses cannot see how six hundred thousand men could be fed for a month. A shortened hand cannot reach far enough, and Isaiah insists the problem has never been at God’s end: “Behold, the LORD’s hand is not shortened, that it cannot save” (Isaiah 59:1).

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses went out and told the people the words of the LORD. And he gathered seventy men of the elders of the people and placed them around the tent. Then the LORD came down in the cloud and spoke to him, and took some of the Spirit that was on him and put it on the seventy elders. And as soon as the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied. But they did not continue doing it. Now two men remained in the camp, one named Eldad, and the other named Medad, and the Spirit rested on them. They were among those registered, but they had not gone out to the tent, and so they prophesied in the camp. And a young man ran and told Moses, "Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp." And Joshua the son of Nun, the assistant of Moses from his youth, said, "My lord Moses, stop them." But Moses said to him, "Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the LORD's people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!" And Moses and the elders of Israel returned to the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit rests on the seventy and on two men in the camp, and when Joshua wants them stopped, Moses wishes that all the LORD’s people had the Spirit.

My lord Moses, stop them. Eldad and Medad, on the list though not at the tent, prophesy in the middle of the camp. Joshua, a loyal assistant, sees unsupervised prophecy as a threat to his master’s standing.

Would that all the LORD’s people were prophets. Moses’ answer is one of the high points of his life: he wishes the opposite of what Joshua wants as hard as he can. There is no trace in him of the instinct that guards its own place, and because he had no interest in being irreplaceable, God could trust him with what he was given.

Fulfilled at Pentecost. His wish was granted. Centuries later the Spirit fell on a hundred and twenty ordinary people at once, and Peter explained it from Joel: “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Acts 2:17). Moses wished it; God said yes, and every believer now has the Spirit (Romans 8:9).

Where Christians differ: does prophecy continue today? Many faithful Christians, continuationists, believe that prophecy in a lesser, tested sense continues, and read Moses’ wish and Pentecost that way.

This commentary’s view: the seventy prophesied once, as a sign that God had given them the Spirit for their task, “But they did not continue doing it” (v. 25). Moses’ wish was fulfilled at Pentecost. But the gift of new revelation belonged to the founding of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and Scripture is now complete; all believers have the Spirit, and all speak God’s completed word to one another. This commentary holds the cessationist view because Ephesians 2:20 places prophets with the apostles in the church’s once-for-all foundation, and it holds that view charitably.

Uncertain wording. “But they did not continue doing it” (v. 25) is literally “they did not add”. Most take it as the ESV does, of a one-time sign; some ancient translations read “they did not cease”. The usual sense of the Hebrew favours the ESV.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–35 — The Quail and the Graves of Craving
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives the people exactly what they craved, and it becomes their judgment. A wind from the LORD brings quail in vast numbers around the camp, and the people gather for a day and a night and another day, hoarding far more than they need (vv. 31–32). While the meat is still in their mouths, the LORD strikes them with a great plague (v. 33). The place is named Kibroth-hattaavah, “graves of craving”, and the people move on to Hazeroth (vv. 34–35).
verseByVerse.theology: Sometimes the severest judgment is to be given what we sinfully insist on.
verseByVerse.examples: These graves are a warning to the church, not a curiosity of ancient history.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a wind from the LORD sprang up, and it brought quail from the sea and let them fall beside the camp, about a day's journey on this side and a day's journey on the other side, around the camp, and about two cubits above the ground. And the people rose all that day and all night and all the next day, and gathered the quail. Those who gathered least gathered ten homers. And they spread them out for themselves all around the camp. While the meat was yet between their teeth, before it was consumed, the anger of the LORD was kindled against the people, and the LORD struck down the people with a very great plague. Therefore the name of that place was called Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people who had the craving. From Kibroth-hattaavah the people journeyed to Hazeroth, and they remained at Hazeroth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends the meat they craved in overwhelming quantity, and judgment falls while it is still in their mouths.

A wind from the LORD. A wind brings quail for a day’s journey in every direction. The people gather for thirty-six hours without sleeping, and the least of them gathers ten homers, an enormous hoard. Quail still migrate across Sinai in spring, and birds exhausted after crossing the sea fly low and can be caught by hand. God used a creature of his own ordering, but the timing, the place and the sheer scale were his doing alone.

While the meat was yet between their teeth. The craving and the judgment arrive in the same mouthful, and the place is named for it: Kibroth-hattaavah, “the graves of craving”. Israel buried its dead at a place named after what killed them.

Written for us. Paul writes it to a church without softening: “Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did” (1 Corinthians 10:6). The Greek Old Testament calls this place the graves of desire, and Paul’s word comes from the same root; he is very probably pointing at these graves.

Isn’t getting what you want the whole point? Much of modern life assumes so: desire is the truest thing about us, and whole industries exist to keep us wanting the next thing. Oscar Wilde, who was no preacher, saw further: “In this world there are only two tragedies. One is not getting what one wants, and the other is getting it.” Kibroth-hattaavah is the second tragedy with a name on it. Israel got exactly what it craved, and the meat did not satisfy; it killed.

Desire aimed too low. The Bible does not tell us to stop desiring. It tells us we have aimed our desire at things too small to bear its weight: “Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy?” (Isaiah 55:2). The manna on the ground every morning was the clue they despised. The God who gave bread from heaven was offering himself, and in the end he gave his Son, the bread that does not leave you hungry again (John 6:35).

How the chapter ends. The chapter that opened three days from the mountain ends in a burial ground. And one prayer in the whole episode God answered with unmixed kindness: the prayer of a man at the end of himself who said so.

Uncertain wording. “About two cubits above the ground” (v. 31), about a metre, may mean that the quail lay piled that deep, or, as many read the Hebrew, that they flew low at about waist height and could be caught by hand, which fits the habits of tired migrating quail.
verseByVerse.note: A homer was about 6 bushels, or some 220 litres, so ten homers is an enormous hoard.

11.theology:
The Sin of Grumbling. To scorn our circumstances is to accuse the God who ordains them; to despise the manna is to despise the Giver.

The Burden of Leadership and the Gift of the Spirit. God shares Moses’ burden by distributing his Spirit. The work of leading God’s people is borne by Spirit-gifted leaders together.

Sin Granted as Judgment. Getting what we sinfully demand can be the severest discipline, and the only answer to a craving heart is a better food: Christ, the bread of life.
11.examples:
Then: Israel despised the bread of heaven, while God answered an exhausted Moses with help.

Now: Where Israel grumbled in the wilderness, Christ, hungry in the wilderness, trusted his Father’s word (Matthew 4:4), and his faithfulness is counted to you who have grumbled too; confess it, and you will find the Father’s welcome, not the graves of craving. Feed on him, the true Bread, and ask the Spirit for a contented heart that sees the daily gifts. And if you lead God’s people, do not carry the burden alone or guard it jealously.

keyVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, “Is the LORD’s hand shortened? Now you shall see whether my word will come true for you or not.”
keyVerse.note: Both the people and Moses doubted in this chapter, the people that God was good and Moses that he was able. God’s question answers both: his hand is never too short to keep his word, in mercy or in judgment. It is the sentence to carry out of the chapter into every hard season.

11.reflection:
The people called God’s daily gift “nothing at all but this manna” (v. 6). What good gifts of God have quietly become ordinary to you, and how could you recover your thankfulness for them?

God said their grumbling meant “you have rejected the LORD who is among you” (v. 20). Why is complaining more serious than it seems, and what is the difference between grumbling and honest lament like Moses’ prayer in verses 11–15?

God answered Moses’ burnout by giving others the Spirit to share his load (vv. 16–17). Is there a burden you are carrying alone that God means you to share? Or someone whose load you could help carry?

Kibroth-hattaavah means “graves of craving” (v. 34). Where do you see people getting what they want and finding it does not satisfy? How does Christ, the bread of life, answer that hunger?

12.title: Miriam and Aaron Oppose Moses
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman whom he had married, for he had married a Cushite woman.<sup>2</sup>And they said, "Has the LORD indeed spoken only through Moses? Has he not spoken through us also?" And the LORD heard it.<sup>3</sup>Now the man Moses was very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth.<sup>4</sup>And suddenly the LORD said to Moses and to Aaron and Miriam, "Come out, you three, to the tent of meeting." And the three of them came out.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD came down in a pillar of cloud and stood at the entrance of the tent and called Aaron and Miriam, and they both came forward.<sup>6</sup>And he said, "Hear my words: If there is a prophet among you, I the LORD make myself known to him in a vision; I speak with him in a dream.<sup>7</sup>Not so with my servant Moses. He is faithful in all my house.<sup>8</sup>With him I speak mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in riddles, and he beholds the form of the LORD. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?"<sup>9</sup>And the anger of the LORD was kindled against them, and he departed.<sup>10</sup>When the cloud removed from over the tent, behold, Miriam was leprous, like snow. And Aaron turned toward Miriam, and behold, she was leprous.<sup>11</sup>And Aaron said to Moses, "Oh, my lord, do not punish us because we have done foolishly and have sinned.<sup>12</sup>Let her not be as one dead, whose flesh is half eaten away when he comes out of his mother's womb."<sup>13</sup>And Moses cried to the LORD, "O God, please heal her—please."<sup>14</sup>But the LORD said to Moses, "If her father had but spit in her face, should she not be shamed seven days? Let her be shut outside the camp seven days, and after that she may be brought in again."<sup>15</sup>So Miriam was shut outside the camp seven days, and the people did not set out on the march till Miriam was brought in again.<sup>16</sup>After that the people set out from Hazeroth, and camped in the wilderness of Paran.
12.overview:
Where we are. The people have complained, craved and been buried at Kibroth-hattaavah (chapter 11), and Israel has moved on to Hazeroth. Now the discontent reaches the top: Moses’ own sister and brother, Miriam the prophetess and Aaron the high priest, speak against him.

The message. God himself defends the servant he has chosen, so the humble do not need to defend themselves. To speak against the one through whom God has chosen to speak is to speak against God. Yet the God who judges also heals and restores, and the man who was wronged becomes the one who prays for those who wronged him.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know that Moses’ authority was not a family arrangement or a personal ambition but God’s appointment (see the introduction). Challenges would come again, most violently from Korah (chapter 16), and this chapter settles where Moses stands.

How the chapter makes its case. Miriam and Aaron criticise Moses’ Cushite wife, but the real complaint is that God has spoken through them too (vv. 1–2). Moses, the meekest of men, says nothing (v. 3). God summons the three of them, comes down in the cloud and declares that Moses is unlike any other prophet: God speaks with him “mouth to mouth” and calls him faithful in all his house (vv. 4–9). The cloud lifts and Miriam is leprous. Aaron begs Moses for mercy, and Moses cries to God for her healing (vv. 10–13). She is healed but shut outside the camp for seven days, and the whole people waits until she is brought back (vv. 14–16).

Where it leads. By pattern, and the New Testament draws it. Moses was “faithful in all God’s house as a servant”, but “Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son” (Hebrews 3:5–6): God spoke to Moses mouth to mouth, but in his Son he has spoken his final word (Hebrews 1:2). Moses’ meekness points to the one who was “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), who “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23). And Moses praying for the sister who opposed him foreshadows the Lord who prayed for those who crucified him: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).

For us. Beware the respectable-sounding grievance that hides envy, and take care how you speak about those God has called to serve you. If you are the one wronged, leave your defence with God and pray for those who hurt you, as Christ did for you. And remember that God’s discipline is not rejection: his people wait for the corrected to come home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The challenge to God’s servant comes from his own family, and it is met with silence. Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses over the Cushite woman he had married, but their real question soon comes out: has the LORD not spoken through them too (vv. 1–2)? Behind the stated grievance lies envy of Moses’ unique calling. And the LORD heard it. The narrator pauses to tell us that Moses was the meekest man on earth (v. 3), which explains why he says nothing and leaves his defence to God.
verseByVerse.theology: Envy of God-given authority is rebellion against God; true greatness is found in meekness, not self-assertion.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses’ own family envied his calling; the warning to us is against jealousy of the callings God gives others.

verseByVerse.quote: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman whom he had married, for he had married a Cushite woman. And they said, "Has the LORD indeed spoken only through Moses? Has he not spoken through us also?" And the LORD heard it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Miriam and Aaron attack Moses over his foreign wife, but their real grievance is his God-given standing.

Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses. The attack comes from inside the family: Miriam, the sister who watched his basket in the reeds, and Aaron, the brother who spoke for him before Pharaoh. She was a prophetess (Exodus 15:20) and he the high priest, the second and third most important people in the nation, and it was not enough.

The Cushite woman. Cush was the region south of Egypt, and a Cushite woman was probably dark-skinned and certainly foreign. But the text shows at once that the wife was not what this was really about.

Has he not spoken through us also? The marriage was the objection they could say aloud; what galled them was Moses’ standing. Such things usually look like this: a principled-sounding grievance, with the energy coming from somewhere else, and a reaction far larger than the stated cause can explain.

And the LORD heard it. They said it privately, in the family. There is no such thing as a private conversation about the servants of God.

Was this racism? God never rebukes the marriage. Moses’ wife was a Cushite, and God sides with Moses; the sin was the jealousy and prejudice of his brother and sister. The law’s bans on marriage concerned idolatry, not ethnicity.

Uncertain wording. Who the Cushite woman was is unknown. She may be Zipporah, the Midianite wife of Exodus 2:21, since Habakkuk 3:7 sets Cushan beside Midian; or a second wife, married after Zipporah’s death. The point does not depend on it.
verseByVerse.note: Miriam was a prophetess and led Israel’s women in song at the Red Sea (Exodus 15:20–21); Micah 6:4 names her with Moses and Aaron as God’s gift to Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the man Moses was very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses was the humblest man on earth, so he says nothing in his own defence and leaves it to God.

Now the man Moses was very meek. The narrator interrupts his story with one of the strangest sentences in Scripture. Readers have puzzled over Moses writing that about himself, and it may well be a note added later under the same inspiration, as the account of his death was (Deuteronomy 34; see the introduction).

Why it stands here. The answer is what Moses does not do next. Slandered by his own brother and sister, his marriage used against him, his call questioned, he says nothing. The silence is not weakness or shock. It is character.

What meekness is. Biblical meekness is not timidity; this is the man who faced down Pharaoh and ground the golden calf to powder. It is strength that has stopped needing to defend itself, because it has handed its defence to God.

Gentle and lowly in heart. The New Testament gives this quality supremely to one person: “learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), and the Greek Old Testament uses the same word for Moses’ meekness here. When Jesus was accused, “he opened not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). Moses’ silence while his family attacks him faintly foreshadows the silence of Christ before Caiaphas.

The exhausting work of defending yourself. Ours is an age of permanent self-defence, where every slight seems to demand a reply and the online world never closes for the night. Underneath it is fear: if I do not defend my name, nobody will. Moses was spared that labour because Someone else had taken charge of his name. That is the freedom the gospel gives: a person whom God has already justified does not have to spend his life justifying himself. Peter describes Christ in exactly these terms: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). Those who are in him may lay down the endless brief for the defence.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself answers for the servant who would not answer for himself. He suddenly summons Moses, Aaron and Miriam to the tent and comes down in the pillar of cloud (vv. 4–5). Other prophets receive visions and dreams, but with his servant Moses, faithful in all his house, God speaks mouth to mouth, plainly, and Moses beholds the form of the LORD (vv. 6–8). So why were they not afraid to speak against him? God’s anger is kindled, and he departs (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: God defends his servants and honours the offices he appoints.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses left his defence to God, and we can do the same when we are wronged.

verseByVerse.quote: And suddenly the LORD said to Moses and to Aaron and Miriam, "Come out, you three, to the tent of meeting." And the three of them came out. And the LORD came down in a pillar of cloud and stood at the entrance of the tent and called Aaron and Miriam, and they both came forward. And he said, "Hear my words: If there is a prophet among you, I the LORD make myself known to him in a vision; I speak with him in a dream.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is silent, so God speaks: he summons all three and comes down to settle the matter himself.

And suddenly the LORD said. Suddenly the three are summoned like children called in from the garden, and the LORD comes down in the cloud to the door of his own house, before the whole camp, to deal with talk behind a brother’s back.

I the LORD make myself known to him. He begins with a general principle: to a prophet he speaks “in a vision” or “in a dream”. That is how he had dealt with Miriam and Aaron, and it is real revelation; God is not taking it away from them. It is simply not the whole of what he does.

verseByVerse.quote: Not so with my servant Moses. He is faithful in all my house. With him I speak mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in riddles, and he beholds the form of the LORD. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?" And the anger of the LORD was kindled against them, and he departed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sets Moses above every other prophet, his trusted servant to whom he speaks face to face, so that to speak against Moses was to speak against God.

Not so with my servant Moses. Every phrase sets Moses higher. Other prophets get visions; with him God speaks “mouth to mouth”. Others get riddles, the image-laden speech of later prophets such as Ezekiel and Zechariah; he gets it plainly. And twice God calls him “my servant Moses”, which in Scripture is almost a title of honour.

He beholds the form of the LORD. Yet no one can see God’s face and live (Exodus 33:20). Moses saw a visible likeness of God’s glory, his back, not his unveiled face (Exodus 33:23). The full sight of God is given in Christ: “No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18).

Why then were you not afraid? God does not ask why they were unkind, but why they were not afraid. Speaking against the man God had set where he set Moses was not a family disagreement; it was reckless.

And he departed. A chilling line: there is no chance to answer. The cloud lifts, and only then do they find out what has happened.

He is faithful in all my house. This phrase travelled a long way: “Now Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant… but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son” (Hebrews 3:5–6). The sentence that set Moses above everybody in Israel is used to say that Moses was, in the end, a servant in the house, and there is a Son over it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — Miriam’s Leprosy and Moses’ Intercession
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God disciplines the one who led the attack, and the one she attacked prays for her healing. As the cloud lifts, Miriam is leprous, and Aaron begs Moses not to let their sin destroy her (vv. 10–12). Moses cries out in a few short words: “O God, please heal her” (v. 13). God answers, but Miriam must still bear seven days of public shame outside the camp (v. 14). The whole people waits for her, and only when she is brought back do they march on (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin bears bitter fruit, but discipline in God’s hands aims at restoration.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses prayed for the sister who had wronged him, and we are called to pray in the same way for those who wrong us.

verseByVerse.quote: When the cloud removed from over the tent, behold, Miriam was leprous, like snow. And Aaron turned toward Miriam, and behold, she was leprous. And Aaron said to Moses, "Oh, my lord, do not punish us because we have done foolishly and have sinned. Let her not be as one dead, whose flesh is half eaten away when he comes out of his mother's womb."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Miriam, who led the attack, is struck with a skin disease, and Aaron confesses their sin and begs the brother they wronged for mercy.

Miriam was leprous, like snow. The judgment is visible, immediate and terrible, and many have seen a grim aptness in it: she had spoken against a foreign woman, and now her own skin is diseased.

Why only Miriam? Her name stands first in verse 1, and the Hebrew verb there is feminine, “she spoke”, marking her as the one who began it. That does not leave Aaron innocent, and it may be that the high priest could not be made unclean without halting the nation’s worship. He is spared and made to watch his sister struck, which is its own punishment.

Oh, my lord, do not punish us. Aaron breaks. He calls Moses “my lord”, the man whose authority he was questioning moments before, and he says “us”, not “her”, which is more than many do when the consequences land on somebody else. He goes to the brother he wronged, because there is nowhere else to go.

As one dead. His picture in verse 12 is of a stillborn child, its flesh already wasting: the disease is a living death.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word translated “leprous” covered a range of skin diseases, not only modern leprosy, and the exact condition is unknown. “Like snow” may describe white skin or flaking skin.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses cried to the LORD, "O God, please heal her—please."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man they wronged prays at once for his sister’s healing, and shows what his meekness really was.

O God, please heal her. Five words in Hebrew, probably the shortest prayer Moses ever prays, with “please” at both ends.

Praying for his accuser. An ordinary man, just vindicated by God, might have let it stand for a day. Moses does not wait an hour. That is what the meekness of verse 3 consists of: given every right to enjoy the outcome, he wanted her well.

Love your enemies. It is the very thing later commanded from a hillside in Galilee: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). Moses had no such command. He had a sister covered in disease who deserved it, and he asked God to take it away. We who have the command keep it poorly, but the One who gave it kept it on the cross, praying for his enemies, and we were among them: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). His Spirit now makes the same prayer possible in us.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD said to Moses, "If her father had but spit in her face, should she not be shamed seven days? Let her be shut outside the camp seven days, and after that she may be brought in again." So Miriam was shut outside the camp seven days, and the people did not set out on the march till Miriam was brought in again. After that the people set out from Hazeroth, and camped in the wilderness of Paran.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God heals Miriam but still requires seven days of public shame outside the camp, and the whole nation waits until she is brought back.

Should she not be shamed seven days? The prayer is answered, though not entirely. A father spitting in his daughter’s face was the sharpest disgrace an ancient household knew, after which she would keep out of sight for a week; God says his displeasure is at least that serious. Miriam is healed and disciplined, and the two are not in conflict.

Forgiveness and consequences. Forgiveness is not always the removal of consequences. Miriam did not die or lose her place in Israel, but she sat seven days outside the camp in full view: the sin was public, and so was the discipline. “The Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6); the discipline is evidence of the love, not a limit on it.

Till Miriam was brought in again. The loveliest detail in the chapter is the waiting. A whole nation with a land to reach sat still for a week for one disgraced woman, and nobody moved on without her. Israel had been stalled by rebellion before; this time it is stalled by mercy.

The God who waits. That tells you what kind of God had been offended. He had every right to be finished with her; instead the cloud did not lift until she could walk back in. It is a picture of how he treats those he has had to correct. When Miriam is next mentioned, she dies at Kadesh and is buried among her people (20:1), still one of them.

12.theology:
Meekness and Self-Forgetfulness. Moses does not defend himself but entrusts his cause to God: a portrait of Christ, who when reviled did not revile in return but entrusted himself to the righteous Judge.

God Vindicates His Servants. To attack God’s appointed servant is to provoke God himself. We need not scramble to justify ourselves; the Judge of all the earth will vindicate his own.

The Mediator Intercedes for his Accuser. The wronged mediator pleads for the guilty: the gospel in miniature, fulfilled in Christ, who ever lives to intercede for sinners.
12.examples:
Then: Miriam and Aaron envied Moses and were rebuked by God, and Moses prayed for his sister.

Now: Christ, the wronged Mediator, has interceded for you and brought you home. Out of that, beware envy of others’ callings, entrust your vindication to God, and when others wrong you, pray for their healing, asking the Spirit for the meekness you do not have by nature.

keyVerse.quote: Not so with my servant Moses. He is faithful in all my house.
keyVerse.note: These words are God’s own defence of the man who would not defend himself, and they answer the question of verse 2. Hebrews takes them up to show that Moses was a faithful servant in God’s house, while Christ is the Son over it. The verse that set Moses above every prophet in Israel points beyond him to the one greater than Moses.

12.reflection:
Miriam and Aaron complained about Moses’ wife, but the real issue was status (vv. 1–2). How can we recognise when a principled-sounding complaint is really covering envy or wounded pride, in ourselves first?

Moses did not defend himself (v. 3), and God did. What makes it so hard to leave our reputation in God’s hands, and how does Christ, who “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23), free us to do it?

Moses prayed at once for the sister who had wronged him (v. 13). Is there someone who has hurt you whom you could pray for this week? What would it mean to ask God for their good?

The whole people waited until Miriam was brought back (v. 15). How should a church treat someone who has been disciplined and is returning, and how does God’s patience with us shape that?

13.title: The Twelve Spies: The Sin of Unbelief
13.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Send men to spy out the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the people of Israel. From each tribe of their fathers you shall send a man, every one a chief among them."<sup>3</sup>So Moses sent them from the wilderness of Paran, according to the command of the LORD, all of them men who were heads of the people of Israel.<sup>4</sup>And these were their names: From the tribe of Reuben, Shammua the son of Zaccur;<sup>5</sup>from the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat the son of Hori;<sup>6</sup>from the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh;<sup>7</sup>from the tribe of Issachar, Igal the son of Joseph;<sup>8</sup>from the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Nun;<sup>9</sup>from the tribe of Benjamin, Palti the son of Raphu;<sup>10</sup>from the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel the son of Sodi;<sup>11</sup>from the tribe of Joseph (that is, from the tribe of Manasseh), Gaddi the son of Susi;<sup>12</sup>from the tribe of Dan, Ammiel the son of Gemalli;<sup>13</sup>from the tribe of Asher, Sethur the son of Michael;<sup>14</sup>from the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi the son of Vophsi;<sup>15</sup>from the tribe of Gad, Geuel the son of Machi.<sup>16</sup>These were the names of the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land. And Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun, Joshua.<sup>17</sup>Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan and said to them, "Go up into the Negeb and go up into the hill country,<sup>18</sup>and see what the land is, and whether the people who dwell in it are strong or weak, whether they are few or many,<sup>19</sup>and whether the land that they dwell in is good or bad, and whether the cities that they dwell in are camps or strongholds,<sup>20</sup>and whether the land is rich or poor, and whether there are trees in it or not. Be of good courage and bring some of the fruit of the land." Now the time was the season of the first ripe grapes.<sup>21</sup>So they went up and spied out the land from the wilderness of Zin to Rehob, near Lebo-hamath.<sup>22</sup>They went up into the Negeb and came to Hebron. Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the descendants of Anak, were there. (Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.)<sup>23</sup>And they came to the Valley of Eshcol and cut down from there a branch with a single cluster of grapes, and they carried it on a pole between two of them; they also brought some pomegranates and figs.<sup>24</sup>That place was called the Valley of Eshcol, because of the cluster that the people of Israel cut down from there.<sup>25</sup>At the end of forty days they returned from spying out the land.<sup>26</sup>And they came to Moses and Aaron and to all the congregation of the people of Israel in the wilderness of Paran, at Kadesh. They brought back word to them and to all the congregation, and showed them the fruit of the land.<sup>27</sup>And they told him, "We came to the land to which you sent us. It flows with milk and honey, and this is its fruit.<sup>28</sup>However, the people who dwell in the land are strong, and the cities are fortified and very large. And besides, we saw the descendants of Anak there.<sup>29</sup>The Amalekites dwell in the land of the Negeb. The Hittites, the Jebusites, and the Amorites dwell in the hill country. And the Canaanites dwell by the sea, and along the Jordan."<sup>30</sup>But Caleb quieted the people before Moses and said, "Let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it."<sup>31</sup>Then the men who had gone up with him said, "We are not able to go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are."<sup>32</sup>So they brought to the people of Israel a bad report of the land that they had spied out, saying, "The land, through which we have gone to spy it out, is a land that devours its inhabitants, and all the people that we saw in it are of great height.<sup>33</sup>And there we saw the Nephilim (the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim), and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them."
13.overview:
Where we are. Israel has left Sinai, complained its way through the wilderness of Paran (chapters 11–12) and reached Kadesh, on the southern edge of Canaan. This chapter brings the people to the threshold of the promise and to the great crisis of the book.

The message. God’s promise does not change with the size of the obstacles; what changes is whether we measure the obstacles against ourselves or against him. Twelve men see the same land, the same fruit and the same giants. Ten see through fear and two through faith, and the difference is not information but trust in the God who said, “which I am giving to the people of Israel” (v. 2).

Why it was said. The generation that first heard Numbers was the generation of the children, standing at the Jordan forty years later with the same promise and the same kind of enemies before them (see the introduction). This chapter told them exactly how their parents had lost the land, so that they would not lose it the same way.

How the chapter makes its case. God sends a leader from each tribe to spy out the land, and Moses gives Hoshea a new name, Joshua (vv. 1–16). Moses asks for a full survey and adds two things facts cannot supply: courage and fruit (vv. 17–20). The spies walk the length of the land for forty days and carry back one enormous cluster of grapes (vv. 21–25). Their report is accurate, and by one word, “However”, it turns the promise into a problem (vv. 26–29). Caleb answers with faith (v. 30); the ten answer with a slander that ends in grasshoppers (vv. 31–33).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need the chapter exposes. Hebrews 3–4 holds this story up as the great warning against unbelief, and says that even Joshua, when he finally led the next generation in, did not give them the rest God promised (Hebrews 4:8). That rest is given by the greater Joshua: the name Moses gives here is the name the angel gave Jesus, “for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Israel’s forty days ended in unbelief; Jesus’ forty days in the wilderness ended in trust, and he goes ahead of his people into the rest they could never take.

For us. Every Christian faces giants between rescue and home: fears, sins, losses, the opinions of others. The question is not how big they are but how big God is. Measure them against Christ, who has already entered the true rest for us, and the sum comes out as Caleb’s did.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends twelve leaders to spy out a land he has already promised, and Moses sends them with a charge to be brave. The land is described as a gift being handed over, “which I am giving” (v. 2), so the spies are to discover how to go in, not whether to. The list of names shows these were the best men of every tribe (vv. 4–15), and one of them, Hoshea, receives a new name: Joshua, “the LORD saves” (v. 16). Moses’ briefing asks for practical facts about the people, cities and soil, but ends with two things facts cannot supply: “Be of good courage and bring some of the fruit of the land” (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: At the very edge of the promise, Israel’s faith is about to be tested.
verseByVerse.examples: Believers often stand where Israel stood, at the edge of an obedience God has made plain, called to trust his promise.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Send men to spy out the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the people of Israel. From each tribe of their fathers you shall send a man, every one a chief among them." So Moses sent them from the wilderness of Paran, according to the command of the LORD, all of them men who were heads of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends spies into a land he is already giving, so the only question is how to go in, not whether.

Whose idea was this? Numbers says God commanded it; Deuteronomy says the people asked (Deuteronomy 1:22). Both are true: the request came from below and God permitted it, a pattern this book shows again with Balaam. God sometimes grants what people ask, and that is often the beginning of trouble.

Which I am giving to the people of Israel. God’s own clause is in the present tense. The land is a gift already being handed over, settled since Abraham. Forty days later ten men will come back and answer a question nobody had asked them.

Was it wrong to send the spies at all? Not in itself. Much disobedience among sincere people starts this way: God has spoken plainly, we go away to gather information, and the plain word quietly becomes one factor among several. But Joshua will send two men into Jericho with God’s blessing and no rebuke (Joshua 2:1). Prudence is not unbelief. The difference lies in what the information is gathered for. Joshua’s spies went out to find the way in. These twelve were sent by a people who had not yet decided to go.
