verseByVerse.quote: And these were their names: From the tribe of Reuben, Shammua the son of Zaccur; from the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat the son of Hori; from the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh; from the tribe of Issachar, Igal the son of Joseph; from the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Nun; from the tribe of Benjamin, Palti the son of Raphu; from the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel the son of Sodi; from the tribe of Joseph (that is, from the tribe of Manasseh), Gaddi the son of Susi; from the tribe of Dan, Ammiel the son of Gemalli; from the tribe of Asher, Sethur the son of Michael; from the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi the son of Vophsi; from the tribe of Gad, Geuel the son of Machi. These were the names of the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land. And Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun, Joshua.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The spies are the best men of every tribe, and one of them receives the name “Joshua”, “the LORD saves”.

These were their names. The list is a roll of the finest men in Israel, every one “a chief” (v. 2). They were not second-rate men, which makes their failure devastating. Two names matter: Caleb of Judah, and Hoshea of Ephraim.

And Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun, Joshua. Hoshea (“salvation”) receives the name of God in his own: Joshua, “the LORD saves”, at the very moment twelve men are about to find out whether they believe God can do what he promised. Ten will come back saying “We are not able”; the man with the new name will say God is. And that name, in Greek, is the one the angel gave a child in Nazareth: “you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Joshua would lead Israel into Canaan; Jesus leads his people into the rest that Canaan only pictured (Hebrews 4:8–10).
verseByVerse.note: “Joshua” means “the LORD saves”.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan and said to them, "Go up into the Negeb and go up into the hill country, and see what the land is, and whether the people who dwell in it are strong or weak, whether they are few or many, and whether the land that they dwell in is good or bad, and whether the cities that they dwell in are camps or strongholds, and whether the land is rich or poor, and whether there are trees in it or not. Be of good courage and bring some of the fruit of the land." Now the time was the season of the first ripe grapes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses asks for a practical survey, and then for two things facts cannot supply: courage, and a taste of the promise.

See what the land is. The briefing is practical: people, cities, soil, timber. It is sensible scouting, with nothing unspiritual in it, and it is midsummer, “the season of the first ripe grapes”, when the land looks its best.

Be of good courage. Facts do not require courage to collect. Moses evidently knew something about the men he was sending, or about human nature.

Bring some of the fruit of the land. He asks them to carry home not a map but fruit: a piece of the promise itself brought back into the wilderness, so that the nation would see evidence of God’s goodness before it heard anything else.

Evidence is not faith. They brought it, and it made no difference. A man can hold the goodness of God in his own hands and still refuse to trust him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–25 — The Survey of the Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The spies find everything God had promised and everything they feared, side by side. They walk the length of the country, from the wilderness of Zin in the south to Lebo-hamath in the far north (v. 21). At Hebron they meet the descendants of Anak, a people of famous size in an ancient city (v. 22). In the Valley of Eshcol they cut a cluster of grapes so heavy that two men carry it on a pole (vv. 23–24). After forty days of safe passage through enemy territory, they come home (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The land proves as good as God said: the fruit is visible evidence of his gift.
verseByVerse.examples: God still gives tangible evidence of his goodness to strengthen faith, though evidence alone never creates it.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went up and spied out the land from the wilderness of Zin to Rehob, near Lebo-hamath. They went up into the Negeb and came to Hebron. Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the descendants of Anak, were there. (Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.) And they came to the Valley of Eshcol and cut down from there a branch with a single cluster of grapes, and they carried it on a pole between two of them; they also brought some pomegranates and figs. That place was called the Valley of Eshcol, because of the cluster that the people of Israel cut down from there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The spies find both the giants and the grapes: everything God promised and everything they fear.

So they went up and spied out the land. They cover the length of the country, several hundred miles on foot through hostile territory. At Hebron they meet the descendants of Anak by name, a people of famous size, in a town the writer dates (“seven years before Zoan in Egypt”) to show it was an old, settled civilisation.

A single cluster of grapes. Eshcol means “cluster”. Picture the walk home: two grown men with a pole across their shoulders and one bunch of grapes between them, carried across the desert to a camp that had eaten manna for over a year. It took two men to carry the fruit of one vine, with pomegranates and figs besides.

Giants and grapes. So two things will be set before Israel at once: three giants and a cluster of grapes, both real and both accurately reported. Everything depends on whether a man measures the giants against himself or against God.
verseByVerse.note: Zoan, also called Tanis, was a city in the Nile delta.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of forty days they returned from spying out the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forty days of safe passage through enemy country end, and the number will measure Israel’s sentence.

At the end of forty days. Forty is one of Scripture’s weighty numbers (the rain in Noah’s day, Moses on the mountain, Elijah’s journey to Horeb), almost always marking a period of testing.

A journey without mishap. No one was caught or killed; God brought all twelve safely home with the fruit. They had just had six weeks of unbroken care in the very land they were about to call impossible to take.

A year for each day. The punishment in the next chapter is measured by this number: “a year for each day” (14:34). Six weeks of looking, four decades of wandering.

One other forty days. There is one other forty days in a wilderness, and it answers this one: “after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry” (Matthew 4:2). Israel was tested with the fruit of the promise in their hands, and failed. Jesus was tested with nothing in his hands, and did not fail. Where the nation looked at what God had given and called it impossible, he looked at what God had not yet given and said, “Man shall not live by bread alone” (Matthew 4:4), and his trust stands in the place of ours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–33 — The Report: Faith and Fear
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The same facts produce two opposite answers, and the difference is faith. The report begins truthfully, in God’s own words, “It flows with milk and honey” (v. 27), then turns on the word “However” to the strength of the people and their cities (vv. 28–29). Caleb silences the crowd and calls for immediate obedience: “we are well able to overcome it” (v. 30). The other ten answer that they are not able, and their report slides from fact into slander and exaggeration: the land devours its inhabitants, everyone there is a giant, and the spies were grasshoppers (vv. 31–33).
verseByVerse.theology: The same evidence produces faith in some and fear in others.
verseByVerse.examples: Every Christian hears both reports in his own heart, and must choose which to believe.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Moses and Aaron and to all the congregation of the people of Israel in the wilderness of Paran, at Kadesh. They brought back word to them and to all the congregation, and showed them the fruit of the land. And they told him, "We came to the land to which you sent us. It flows with milk and honey, and this is its fruit. However, the people who dwell in the land are strong, and the cities are fortified and very large. And besides, we saw the descendants of Anak there. The Amalekites dwell in the land of the Negeb. The Hittites, the Jebusites, and the Amorites dwell in the hill country. And the Canaanites dwell by the sea, and along the Jordan."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The report is true in every detail, but “However” turns the promise into a problem and leaves God out.

It flows with milk and honey. The report begins truthfully, in God’s own words from the burning bush (Exodus 3:8). If it had stopped at verse 27, Israel might have marched that afternoon. They were reporting at Kadesh, an oasis on the southern edge of Canaan, “eleven days’ journey from Horeb” (Deuteronomy 1:2): the land was not a distant hope but a few days’ march away.

However. Then one word, and everything turns on it. Not one word after it is false. The people were strong, the cities fortified, the Anakim there; Caleb will confirm every detail and take Hebron himself (Joshua 14:12–14). It is an accurate report arranged in an order that leads to despair.

How unbelief works. Unbelief rarely needs to invent anything. It only needs to put the facts in a particular order, mention God first and briefly, and spend the rest of the paragraph on the difficulties. By the end of verse 29 the giants, the fortifications and five named nations fill the whole picture, and the God who had said “which I am giving to the people of Israel” has not been mentioned once.

verseByVerse.quote: But Caleb quieted the people before Moses and said, "Let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Caleb has the same facts as the ten but measures the giants against God, and calls for obedience at once.

We are well able to overcome it. Caleb had seen the same walls, met the same giants and carried the same pole. What differs is what he measures them against. The ten measured the giants against Israel and got a true answer: too big. Caleb measured them against God, and the sum came out the other way.

Let us go up at once. He does not propose a committee or a better season. A nation that does not move now will talk itself out of it by morning, which is exactly what happens.

The measure of Caleb. He is one voice against ten, in front of a frightened crowd, and within a day they will be picking up stones to kill him for it (14:10). Forty-five years later, at eighty-five, he walks up to Joshua and asks for the hill country of Hebron, the giants’ own town: “I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me … So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day” (Joshua 14:11–12). He had waited four decades to finish an argument he was right about, and God gave him the ground the giants were standing on.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men who had gone up with him said, "We are not able to go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are." So they brought to the people of Israel a bad report of the land that they had spied out, saying, "The land, through which we have gone to spy it out, is a land that devours its inhabitants, and all the people that we saw in it are of great height. And there we saw the Nephilim (the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim), and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ten slide from fact to slander to exaggeration, until fear shrinks them to grasshoppers.

They are stronger than we are. Their reply is a study in how unbelief talks. It begins with something true and beside the point, because the question was never whether Israel was stronger than Canaan.

A land that devours its inhabitants. Then it slides. In verse 27 the land flowed with milk and honey; now it eats people. The writer calls this “a bad report”, a slander: they have moved from reporting the facts to running down the gift. Then it exaggerates: “all the people” are of great height. That is fear talking, and fear speaks in totals.

We seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them. The first half honestly reports how they saw themselves. The second reports what was in the heads of men they never spoke to. Rahab will tell us how Israel actually appeared to Canaan: “our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you” (Joshua 2:11). The people the spies thought were laughing at them were terrified of them.

In everyday life. A man decides what he is worth, assumes everybody else has reached the same verdict, and lives as though a judgment he passed on himself were a fact about the world. It ruined a nation. The only cure is to stop measuring against the giants and start measuring against God, which is the single difference between Caleb and the ten.

Who were the Nephilim and the sons of Anak? The Anakim were a real people of great stature (Deuteronomy 2:10–11), and Goliath probably came of the same stock (Joshua 11:22 leaves Anakim in Gath). The spies’ claim that they came “from the Nephilim” echoes Genesis 6:4, but this is part of the “bad report” (v. 32). Most take it that the flood had ended that line (Genesis 6:4 itself is much debated), and that these men were simply very tall.

Uncertain wording. The meaning of “Nephilim” is uncertain. Many connect it with the Hebrew verb “to fall”, giving “fallen ones”; the Greek Old Testament rendered it “giants”. On the spies’ lips it was a name meant to frighten.

13.theology:
The Anatomy of Unbelief. Unbelief is rarely a denial of facts; it is a reading of them that leaves God out, so that the obstacle hides the promise.

The Same Evidence, Two Responses. All twelve saw the same things; the difference was in the heart. Faith is a response not to evidence alone but to the trustworthiness of God.

Joshua. The faithful spy who will lead Israel in bears the name that in Greek is Jesus (Heb. 4:8), pointing to the One who brings his people into the true rest.
13.examples:
Then: Ten spies shrank like grasshoppers, but Caleb cried, “Let us go up at once.”

Now: At the edge of every hard obedience, the question is the size of your God, who has already said “which I am giving.” Beware the “however” of unbelief, and measure your giants against the LORD who saves. Where your faith shrinks, Christ’s held firm for you in the wilderness, and his Spirit is given to make you, like Caleb, of “a different spirit” (14:24).

keyVerse.quote: Let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it.
keyVerse.note: Caleb saw exactly what the other ten saw, and this sentence shows the one thing that made the difference: he measured the giants against God rather than against Israel. It is the voice of faith in a chapter otherwise ruled by fear, and it is vindicated forty-five years later when Caleb takes Hebron himself.

13.reflection:
The ten spies said nothing false in verses 28–29, yet their report led to despair. How can a set of true facts, arranged without God in them, lead us into unbelief? Where do you see this in your own thinking?

Caleb and the ten had the same information but measured the giants against different things (vv. 30–31). What are the “giants” you are facing at the moment, and what would it look like to measure them against God?

The spies said, “we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them” (v. 33). How does a low view of ourselves, apart from God, distort how we read other people and our situation?

Joshua’s name means “the LORD saves”, the same name as Jesus. How does knowing that Christ has already entered God’s rest ahead of us (Hebrews 4:8–10, 14) give us courage to keep going where Israel turned back?

14.title: Israel’s Rebellion: The Wilderness Decreed
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Then all the congregation raised a loud cry, and the people wept that night.<sup>2</sup>And all the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron. The whole congregation said to them, "Would that we had died in the land of Egypt! Or would that we had died in this wilderness!<sup>3</sup>Why is the LORD bringing us into this land, to fall by the sword? Our wives and our little ones will become a prey. Would it not be better for us to go back to Egypt?"<sup>4</sup>And they said to one another, "Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt."<sup>5</sup>Then Moses and Aaron fell on their faces before all the assembly of the congregation of the people of Israel.<sup>6</sup>And Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, who were among those who had spied out the land, tore their clothes<sup>7</sup>and said to all the congregation of the people of Israel, "The land, which we passed through to spy it out, is an exceedingly good land.<sup>8</sup>If the LORD delights in us, he will bring us into this land and give it to us, a land that flows with milk and honey.<sup>9</sup>Only do not rebel against the LORD. And do not fear the people of the land, for they are bread for us. Their protection is removed from them, and the LORD is with us; do not fear them."<sup>10</sup>Then all the congregation said to stone them with stones. But the glory of the LORD appeared at the tent of meeting to all the people of Israel.<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "How long will this people despise me? And how long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs that I have done among them?<sup>12</sup>I will strike them with the pestilence and disinherit them, and I will make of you a nation greater and mightier than they."<sup>13</sup>But Moses said to the LORD, "Then the Egyptians will hear of it, for you brought up this people in your might from among them,<sup>14</sup>and they will tell the inhabitants of this land. They have heard that you, O LORD, are in the midst of this people. For you, O LORD, are seen face to face, and your cloud stands over them and you go before them, in a pillar of cloud by day and in a pillar of fire by night.<sup>15</sup>Now if you kill this people as one man, then the nations who have heard your fame will say,<sup>16</sup>'It is because the LORD was not able to bring this people into the land that he swore to give to them that he has killed them in the wilderness.'<sup>17</sup>And now, please let the power of the Lord be great as you have promised, saying,<sup>18</sup>'The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity and transgression, but he will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, to the third and the fourth generation.'<sup>19</sup>Please pardon the iniquity of this people, according to the greatness of your steadfast love, just as you have forgiven this people, from Egypt until now."<sup>20</sup>Then the LORD said, "I have pardoned, according to your word.<sup>21</sup>But truly, as I live, and as all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the LORD,<sup>22</sup>none of the men who have seen my glory and my signs that I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and yet have put me to the test these ten times and have not obeyed my voice,<sup>23</sup>shall see the land that I swore to give to their fathers. And none of those who despised me shall see it.<sup>24</sup>But my servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me fully, I will bring into the land into which he went, and his descendants shall possess it.<sup>25</sup>Now, since the Amalekites and the Canaanites dwell in the valleys, turn tomorrow and set out for the wilderness by the way to the Red Sea."<sup>26</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,<sup>27</sup>"How long shall this wicked congregation grumble against me? I have heard the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against me.<sup>28</sup>Say to them, 'As I live, declares the LORD, what you have said in my hearing I will do to you:<sup>29</sup>your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness, and of all your number, listed in the census from twenty years old and upward, who have grumbled against me,<sup>30</sup>not one shall come into the land where I swore that I would make you dwell, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun.<sup>31</sup>But your little ones, who you said would become a prey, I will bring in, and they shall know the land that you have rejected.<sup>32</sup>But as for you, your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness.<sup>33</sup>And your children shall be shepherds in the wilderness forty years and shall suffer for your faithlessness, until the last of your dead bodies lies in the wilderness.<sup>34</sup>According to the number of the days in which you spied out the land, forty days, a year for each day, you shall bear your iniquity forty years, and you shall know my displeasure.'<sup>35</sup>I, the LORD, have spoken. Surely this will I do to all this wicked congregation who are gathered together against me: in this wilderness they shall come to a full end, and there they shall die."<sup>36</sup>And the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land, who returned and made all the congregation grumble against him by bringing up a bad report about the land—<sup>37</sup>the men who brought up a bad report of the land— died by plague before the LORD.<sup>38</sup>Of those men who went to spy out the land, only Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh remained alive.<sup>39</sup>When Moses told these words to all the people of Israel, the people mourned greatly.<sup>40</sup>And they rose early in the morning and went up to the heights of the hill country, saying, "Here we are. We will go up to the place that the LORD has promised, for we have sinned."<sup>41</sup>But Moses said, "Why now are you transgressing the command of the LORD, when that will not succeed?<sup>42</sup>Do not go up, for the LORD is not among you, lest you be struck down before your enemies.<sup>43</sup>For there the Amalekites and the Canaanites are facing you, and you shall fall by the sword. Because you have turned back from following the LORD, the LORD will not be with you."<sup>44</sup>But they presumed to go up to the heights of the hill country, although neither the ark of the covenant of the LORD nor Moses departed out of the camp.<sup>45</sup>Then the Amalekites and the Canaanites who lived in that hill country came down and defeated them and pursued them, even to Hormah.
14.overview:
Where we are. The twelve spies have come back from Canaan with grapes and with fear, and ten of them have persuaded the people that the land cannot be taken (chapter 13). This chapter is the catastrophe toward which the whole book has been building: at the border of the promise, Israel refuses to go in.

The message. Unbelief is not a lack of evidence but contempt for God, and it shuts people out of what he promised. Yet the same God is “slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love” (v. 18): he pardons in answer to a mediator’s prayer, keeps his promise to the next generation, and still lets the faithless reap what they chose. Forgiveness and consequences stand together in one chapter, from one mouth.

Why it was said. The children of this generation, who heard Numbers on the plains of Moab, had buried their parents in the desert because of this day (see the introduction). They needed to know why, and to know that the promise had been kept for them.

How the chapter makes its case. The people weep, wish they had died and plan to return to Egypt; Caleb and Joshua plead with them and are nearly stoned (vv. 1–10). God threatens to destroy the nation, and Moses intercedes on the ground of God’s name and character (vv. 11–19). God pardons, but none of that generation except Caleb and Joshua will see the land (vv. 20–25). The sentence is spelled out: forty years, a year for each day, and the ten spies die at once (vv. 26–38). The next morning the people try to go up without God and are routed (vv. 39–45).

Where it leads. By pattern, by the need exposed and by God’s character revealed. Moses stands between a guilty people and God’s wrath, pleading God’s own name, and wins a pardon that leaves the rebels outside the land. Christ is the better Mediator: he “always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and his pardon brings his people all the way in. And the God of Exodus 34:6–7, quoted here, is fully seen at the cross, where he is both just and the one who forgives.

For us. Take unbelief seriously: it is not a harmless doubt but a refusal to trust the God who has shown himself again and again. But do not despair if you have failed: plead what Moses pleaded, the greatness of God’s steadfast love, through the Mediator who never fails. And obedience on our own terms is only rebellion in better clothes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Rebellion and the Plea of Caleb and Joshua
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people turn against God and against the only two men who still trust him. They weep all night, wish they had died in Egypt or in the wilderness, accuse the LORD of bringing them to die by the sword, and talk of choosing a leader to take them back to Egypt (vv. 1–4). Moses and Aaron fall on their faces, and Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and plead: the land is exceedingly good, the LORD delights in his people, and he is with them (vv. 5–9). The answer is a call to stone them, and only the sudden appearing of the glory of the LORD stops the first throw (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Unbelief left to itself hardens into open rebellion.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel longed to return to Egypt, and the heart that has been set free can still be drawn back toward its old bondage.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the congregation raised a loud cry, and the people wept that night. And all the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron. The whole congregation said to them, "Would that we had died in the land of Egypt! Or would that we had died in this wilderness! Why is the LORD bringing us into this land, to fall by the sword? Our wives and our little ones will become a prey. Would it not be better for us to go back to Egypt?" And they said to one another, "Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people weep, wish themselves dead, accuse God of planning their slaughter and plan a return to Egypt.

Would that we had died in this wilderness! They cry all night, and in the morning out comes the sentence formed in the dark. God will take those words up in verse 29 and grant them. They could think of nothing worse to say, and God said: very well.

To fall by the sword. Then the accusation, the reverse of the truth: the God who split a sea for them is charged with bringing them here to die, and their wives and little ones to be carried off. That is what unbelief eventually says aloud about the character of God, and it began as a reasonable concern about fortified cities.

Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt. Then the lowest point: a coup and an emigration, back to the brick pits where every family had buried somebody. They would rather have a slavery they understand than a promise that requires them to trust God. People still make that trade, for the same reason.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and Aaron fell on their faces before all the assembly of the congregation of the people of Israel. And Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, who were among those who had spied out the land, tore their clothes and said to all the congregation of the people of Israel, "The land, which we passed through to spy it out, is an exceedingly good land. If the LORD delights in us, he will bring us into this land and give it to us, a land that flows with milk and honey. Only do not rebel against the LORD. And do not fear the people of the land, for they are bread for us. Their protection is removed from them, and the LORD is with us; do not fear them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses and Aaron fall down before the people, and Joshua and Caleb plead with them: the land is good, and the LORD is with us.

Moses and Aaron fell on their faces. Moses and Aaron fall on their faces, and Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes, as a man does at a funeral or in the face of blasphemy.

If the LORD delights in us. Their plea is faith reasoning aloud. They deny not one fact the ten reported, but start from God’s pleasure in his people rather than the height of the walls.

They are bread for us. The ten had said the land devours its inhabitants. Joshua and Caleb say its people are bread for Israel: not because Israel was strong, but because they knew who was doing the eating.

Their protection is removed from them. Here is the whole argument in one sentence: “Their protection is removed from them, and the LORD is with us.” The Hebrew says their shadow has turned aside: whatever sheltered Canaan has moved off it, and the God who shelters Israel stands in the middle of the camp. “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31) is not a new thought. Two men shouted it at a mob about to stone them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the congregation said to stone them with stones. But the glory of the LORD appeared at the tent of meeting to all the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people answer faith with stones, and God himself appears to protect the two men who trusted him.

All the congregation said to stone them. The answer to faith is not argument but rocks. Unbelief, when it has run its course, does not merely disagree with faith; it wants faith silenced, because a man who trusts God is unbearable to a crowd that has decided not to. Stephen made the point to the Sanhedrin, “Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?” (Acts 7:52), and they picked up stones for him too.

But the glory of the LORD appeared. Then, mid-sentence, God arrives, at the tent of meeting, “to all the people of Israel”. The stones never leave their hands. Two defenceless men face a crowd with rocks in its fists, and the glory of God comes between them and the first throw.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God threatens to disinherit his people, and Moses’ prayer turns the threat into pardon. God names the sin at its root: the people despise him and do not believe him despite all his signs, and he offers to make a new nation from Moses (vv. 11–12). Moses refuses, and pleads only God’s honour among the nations and God’s own description of himself, “slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love” (vv. 13–19). God answers, “I have pardoned, according to your word”, and in the same breath swears that the men who tested him will not see the land, except Caleb, who has “a different spirit” (vv. 20–25).
verseByVerse.theology: God pardons for his name’s sake.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses pleaded God’s character back to him; Christ now intercedes for his people, and his prayers are never refused.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "How long will this people despise me? And how long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs that I have done among them? I will strike them with the pestilence and disinherit them, and I will make of you a nation greater and mightier than they."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God names the people’s sin at its root, contempt shown as unbelief, and threatens to destroy them and start again with Moses.

How long will this people despise me? The two charges are one. To despise is the outward act; not to believe is the inward reality; God names them in one breath because he sees no gap between them. That is a hard word for a culture that treats unbelief as an intellectual difficulty and contempt as a moral one. Refusing to trust God after all he has done is not a failure of evidence. It is an insult.

In spite of all the signs. These people had watched a sea open and eaten bread off the ground that morning, under a pillar of fire. More evidence would not have helped, which is the standing answer to anyone who says he would believe if only God did something visible. He did, for more than a year, in front of this congregation.

I will make of you a nation greater and mightier than they. It is the offer God made after the golden calf (Exodus 32:10), a genuine test as well as a genuine threat.

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to the LORD, "Then the Egyptians will hear of it, for you brought up this people in your might from among them, and they will tell the inhabitants of this land. They have heard that you, O LORD, are in the midst of this people. For you, O LORD, are seen face to face, and your cloud stands over them and you go before them, in a pillar of cloud by day and in a pillar of fire by night. Now if you kill this people as one man, then the nations who have heard your fame will say, 'It is because the LORD was not able to bring this people into the land that he swore to give to them that he has killed them in the wilderness.' And now, please let the power of the Lord be great as you have promised, saying, 'The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity and transgression, but he will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, to the third and the fourth generation.' Please pardon the iniquity of this people, according to the greatness of your steadfast love, just as you have forgiven this people, from Egypt until now."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses refuses the offer and pleads for the guilty people on one ground only: God’s own honour and God’s own description of himself.

What Moses does not say. In one of the great intercessions of the Old Testament, Moses does not defend the people, because there is no defence. He does not take the offer or appeal to his long service. Every argument is about God.

Then the Egyptians will hear of it. First, God’s reputation: the nations will conclude that the LORD “was not able to bring this people into the land”. Moses fears God’s name dishonoured in pagan mouths.

The LORD is slow to anger. Then he quotes God back to himself from Exodus 34:6–7. He is not telling God what he ought to be like; he holds up what God said he was and asks him to be it. That is how to pray with confidence: not “I have been good” or “they are worth it”, but “this is who you have said you are”. And Moses quotes the hard half too, “he will by no means clear the guilty”, which is why his prayer is honest, not sentimental. He asks mercy from a God who does not pretend sin is nothing.

What steadfast love is. “Steadfast love” translates the Hebrew hesed: not a feeling, warm while the other person is lovable, but love that has bound itself by promise and goes on loving when the other side has given it every reason to stop. Moses has nothing good to say about Israel, so he appeals to “the greatness of your steadfast love” (v. 19): a love that never rested on them cannot be ended by them. It reaches its height at the cross: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). We are held not because we have stayed faithful but because he has. So when you come to God after a bad week, do not open with your record. Open where Moses did. See also Steadfast love in the Theological Dictionary.

Did Moses change God’s mind? “God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind” (23:19). The threat was real, and God used it to draw out Moses’ prayer, which pleads God’s own name and promise (vv. 17–19). God forgives “according to your word” (v. 20) because the prayer asked for what God had always purposed. He ordains prayer as one of the means by which he does his will.

Is it fair that children suffer for their fathers’ sin? Each person is judged for his own sin (Deuteronomy 24:16; Ezekiel 18:20). The consequences of sin run through families, and children who carry on their fathers’ hatred of God share their judgment (Exodus 20:5, “of those who hate me”). Here the children who were spared entered the land (v. 31).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said, "I have pardoned, according to your word. But truly, as I live, and as all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the LORD, none of the men who have seen my glory and my signs that I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and yet have put me to the test these ten times and have not obeyed my voice, shall see the land that I swore to give to their fathers. And none of those who despised me shall see it. But my servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me fully, I will bring into the land into which he went, and his descendants shall possess it. Now, since the Amalekites and the Canaanites dwell in the valleys, turn tomorrow and set out for the wilderness by the way to the Red Sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God pardons the nation in answer to Moses’ prayer, yet swears that the generation which tested him will never see the land, except Caleb.

I have pardoned, according to your word. The nation is not destroyed and the covenant stands, because one man stood between the people and judgment and prayed.

None of the men who have seen my glory. Yet none of the men who saw his glory and tested him “shall see the land”. Pardoned, and excluded, from the same mouth, and the two do not contradict each other. God forgives, fully and for ever, and forgiveness does not always remove the consequences. David is told “The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die”, and in the same breath what will happen to his household (2 Samuel 12:13–14).

But my servant Caleb. One exception: Caleb, “because he has a different spirit and has followed me fully”. Not better information or a braver temperament: God had put something else in him, and it made him, with Joshua, the only man of his generation to see again the country he had walked through.

Uncertain wording. “These ten times” may be an exact count of Israel’s testings since the Red Sea, as later Jewish teachers reckoned it, or a round figure for “again and again”, as in Genesis 31:7. Either way it was not one bad afternoon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–38 — The Sentence of Forty Years
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sentence is spelled out, and it fits the sin exactly. The people had wished to die in the wilderness, and they will (vv. 26–30, 32). They had said their children would become a prey; those children will inherit the land, though they must first wander for forty years and bear their parents’ faithlessness (vv. 31–33). The forty years match the forty days of spying (vv. 34–35). The ten spies who spread the bad report die by plague at once, and only Joshua and Caleb remain alive (vv. 36–38). The next morning the people go up without God or the ark and are routed (vv. 39–45).
verseByVerse.theology: The inheritance is entered by faith, and unbelief forfeits it.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel spent forty years in the wilderness for unbelief, and Hebrews applies the warning directly to the church (see vv. 39–45).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, "How long shall this wicked congregation grumble against me? I have heard the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against me. Say to them, 'As I live, declares the LORD, what you have said in my hearing I will do to you: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness, and of all your number, listed in the census from twenty years old and upward, who have grumbled against me, not one shall come into the land where I swore that I would make you dwell, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God swears by his own life that the grumblers will get what they asked for: they will die in the wilderness, and only Caleb and Joshua will enter.

How long? God’s word opens with the same “How long” as verse 11 and names the sin plainly: the people grumbled “against me”. Their complaints were spoken against Moses and Aaron (v. 2), but God hears them as said to him. Grumbling runs all through the wilderness story (Exodus 16:7–8), and Paul warns the church not to repeat it (1 Corinthians 10:10).

As I live, declares the LORD. God swears by his own life, because there is no one greater to swear by (Hebrews 6:13), repeating the oath of verse 21. The sentence is now as fixed as the promise. Psalm 95 remembers this oath, and Hebrews quotes it: “As I swore in my wrath, ‘They shall not enter my rest’” (Hebrews 3:11).

Your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness. Now the sentence, in its terrible symmetry. God hands back what they shouted in verse 2. They said they wished to die here. They will.

Listed in the census. It falls on exactly the men counted in chapter 1, “from twenty years old and upward”, the men numbered to fight for the land. The army mustered to take Canaan will be buried short of it. Only Caleb and Joshua, the two who followed the LORD fully, are excepted.

verseByVerse.quote: But your little ones, who you said would become a prey, I will bring in, and they shall know the land that you have rejected. But as for you, your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness. And your children shall be shepherds in the wilderness forty years and shall suffer for your faithlessness, until the last of your dead bodies lies in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The children their parents said would be victims will inherit the land, though first they must share forty years of their parents’ wandering.

But your little ones. This reverses their accusation: “your little ones, who you said would become a prey, I will bring in.” Their unbelief was dressed up as concern for their families, and God answers by taking better care of their families than they would.

Your children shall be shepherds in the wilderness. The children will inherit the land, but first they spend their youth burying their parents in a desert. Nobody sins in a way that stops with himself. Those children are the generation Numbers was first written for. The book ends with them grown up on the plains of Moab, counted again after every man of the first census but Caleb and Joshua had died (26:63–65), and this sentence was kept so that they would not repeat their parents’ refusal at the Jordan.

Shall suffer for your faithlessness. The word translated “faithlessness” is literally “whoredoms”: Israel’s unbelief is the unfaithfulness of a wife who has turned from her husband, as the prophets would later say (Jeremiah 3:6–10; Hosea 1:2). Turning back toward Egypt was not caution but adultery. The children “suffer” it, literally “bear” it: they share the consequence, not the guilt, and the land is still promised to them (v. 31).

verseByVerse.quote: According to the number of the days in which you spied out the land, forty days, a year for each day, you shall bear your iniquity forty years, and you shall know my displeasure.' I, the LORD, have spoken. Surely this will I do to all this wicked congregation who are gathered together against me: in this wilderness they shall come to a full end, and there they shall die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forty days of spying become forty years of wandering, and God himself guarantees that the faithless generation will come to its end in the wilderness.

A year for each day. Forty days of looking at the promise, forty years of walking away from it.

What the forty years were. They were less a punishment from outside than the people’s own choice given room. They said they would rather be in the wilderness than in the land, and God let them have the wilderness. Hell is God’s just sentence on sin, and it is never passed on anyone who wanted him: in the end it grants the sinner what he chose.

I, the LORD, have spoken. The speech ends with God’s own word as its guarantee: “in this wilderness they shall come to a full end.” The forty years are not a delay while God reconsiders. The verdict is settled, and the next verses show it beginning at once with the ten spies (vv. 36–38).

For the troubled believer. Hebrews uses this generation as a warning to Christians (Hebrews 3:16–4:2). A troubled believer who fears he is like them should see the difference: they wanted Egypt and reached for stones, while he grieves that he has not trusted God more. That grief is hearing his voice today, and the throne of grace is open (Hebrews 4:16).

Where Christians differ: can a true believer lose salvation? Arminian Christians, whose love for Christ is not in doubt, read warnings like this as teaching that he can. This commentary’s view: Hebrews also says “we have come to share in Christ, if indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end” (Hebrews 3:14): holding firm shows who truly belongs. The warning is real, and it is one of the means by which God keeps his own (John 10:28–29). Some of this generation, like Moses and Aaron, were true believers who were kept out of Canaan but not away from God. With the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (both chapter 17), this commentary holds that those truly born again will persevere, while recognising that faithful Christians differ.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “displeasure” is rare, and its exact sense is uncertain; it probably means “you shall know what it is to have me against you”, the reverse of Joshua and Caleb’s “the LORD is with us” (v. 9). The people who would not trust God’s presence will learn what his opposition is.
verseByVerse.note: The count of forty years includes the time already spent since the exodus; the actual wandering after Kadesh was about thirty-eight years (Deuteronomy 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: And the men whom Moses sent to spy out the land, who returned and made all the congregation grumble against him by bringing up a bad report about the land— the men who brought up a bad report of the land— died by plague before the LORD. Of those men who went to spy out the land, only Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh remained alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ten spies who spread the bad report die first, and the two who were nearly stoned are the only ones left alive.

A bad report about the land. The writer says it twice in one sentence, so that nobody mistakes the grounds: the ten died for the “bad report”.

Died by plague before the LORD. The whole nation was under sentence, but these ten die first, because they put the words into everyone else’s mouth. God holds more strictly to account those who shape what a community believes: “we who teach will be judged with greater strictness” (James 3:1).

Only Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh remained alive. Of the twelve, only the two threatened with stoning the day before are still standing. The crowd had been entirely wrong about who was in danger.

verseByVerse.quote: When Moses told these words to all the people of Israel, the people mourned greatly. And they rose early in the morning and went up to the heights of the hill country, saying, "Here we are. We will go up to the place that the LORD has promised, for we have sinned." But Moses said, "Why now are you transgressing the command of the LORD, when that will not succeed? Do not go up, for the LORD is not among you, lest you be struck down before your enemies. For there the Amalekites and the Canaanites are facing you, and you shall fall by the sword. Because you have turned back from following the LORD, the LORD will not be with you." But they presumed to go up to the heights of the hill country, although neither the ark of the covenant of the LORD nor Moses departed out of the camp. Then the Amalekites and the Canaanites who lived in that hill country came down and defeated them and pursued them, even to Hormah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people swing from refusing to go to insisting on going, but without God’s command or presence, and they are routed.

For we have sinned. It is the right sentence, and it is not repentance. Yesterday God said go and they would not; today God says do not go and they will. The direction has reversed and the heart has not moved an inch. They are still doing what they have decided, and God’s word is still the thing being overridden.

Two ways to be your own lord. Yesterday rebels, today zealots, armed and saying the right words about “the place that the LORD has promised”: it is the same heart in different clothes. There are two ways to run your own life. One is to break God’s rules; the other is to keep them, or charge up the hill in his name, so that you stay in charge and can present him with the bill. The first is irreligion and the second is religion, and the Bible treats both as the same refusal to be saved by someone else. Jesus told a story with both in it: a younger son who left home, and an elder son who had never disobeyed a command and still would not come in to the feast (Luke 15:29). The gospel is not the respectable middle between them. It is a Father who goes out to both, and a Son who went up the hill of Calvary at his Father’s command, so that rebels and zealots alike may come home on grace.

The LORD will not be with you. Verse 44 is devastating: they went up although “neither the ark of the covenant of the LORD nor Moses departed out of the camp.” They marched off to fight for God’s promises while the ark stayed and watched them go. They are routed “even to Hormah”, a name to keep: Israel returns there in chapter 21, with God, and wins.

A warning to Christians. Hebrews preaches this chapter to Christians without softening: “So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:19). The same promise stands before us, and we can refuse it in the same way. The remedy is the one thing this generation would not do: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion” (Hebrews 3:15). Go in, trusting not our own steadfastness but the High Priest who has passed through the heavens for us (Hebrews 4:14).

14.theology:
Unbelief Forfeits the Inheritance. The promised rest is received by faith alone.

Intercession on the Ground of God’s Glory. Moses refuses his own exaltation and prays God’s own description of himself back to him, and Christ intercedes for us not on our merit but on the ground of his own work and the Father’s love.

Pardon and Discipline Together. Forgiveness does not always remove consequences; mercy and holiness meet in the discipline of a faithful God.
14.examples:
Then: Israel wept for Egypt and reached for stones, and was spared only because one man prayed.

Now: Christ, your Joshua, trusted the Father where this generation would not, and his faithfulness is counted as yours. So take heed lest an unbelieving heart draw you back from grace; hear his voice today, and lean on the Spirit who keeps you trusting. Pray as Moses did, pleading not your worthiness but God’s revealed character, and when you have shrunk back, come to the throne of grace again.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity and transgression, but he will by no means clear the guilty
keyVerse.note: Moses pleads for the people with God’s own words from Exodus 34, and the whole chapter unfolds them: God pardons the nation, yet the guilty generation dies in the wilderness. Both halves are fully true of God, and they meet at the cross, where he forgives sinners without clearing sin.

14.reflection:
The people said, “Would that we had died in this wilderness!” (v. 2), and God gave them what they said (v. 28). Why is grumbling so serious in God’s sight, and what does it reveal about what we really believe about him?

Moses pleaded nothing about the people’s goodness, only God’s name and steadfast love (vv. 13–19). How should that shape the way we pray for ourselves and for others, especially after we have failed?

God pardoned Israel, yet that generation did not enter the land (vv. 20–23). How can forgiveness be complete while some consequences of sin remain? How have you seen that in your own life or others’?

The day after refusing to go, the people insisted on going without God (vv. 40–45). In what ways can “obedience” on our own terms be another form of rebellion, and how does the gospel free us from both?

15.title: Offerings and the Sabbath-Breaker: Grace After Judgment
15.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land you are to inhabit, which I am giving you,<sup>3</sup>and you offer to the LORD from the herd or from the flock a food offering or a burnt offering or a sacrifice, to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering or at your appointed feasts, to make a pleasing aroma to the LORD,<sup>4</sup>then he who brings his offering shall offer to the LORD a grain offering of a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with a quarter of a hin of oil;<sup>5</sup>and you shall offer with the burnt offering, or for the sacrifice, a quarter of a hin of wine for the drink offering for each lamb.<sup>6</sup>Or for a ram, you shall offer for a grain offering two tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a third of a hin of oil.<sup>7</sup>And for the drink offering you shall offer a third of a hin of wine, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>8</sup>And when you offer a bull as a burnt offering or sacrifice, to fulfill a vow or for peace offerings to the LORD,<sup>9</sup>then one shall offer with the bull a grain offering of three tenths of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with half a hin of oil.<sup>10</sup>And you shall offer for the drink offering half a hin of wine, as a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>11</sup>"Thus it shall be done for each bull or ram, or for each lamb or young goat.<sup>12</sup>As many as you offer, so shall you do with each one, as many as there are.<sup>13</sup>Every native Israelite shall do these things in this way, in offering a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>14</sup>And if a stranger is sojourning with you, or anyone is living permanently among you, and he wishes to offer a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD, he shall do as you do.<sup>15</sup>For the assembly, there shall be one statute for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you, a statute forever throughout your generations. You and the sojourner shall be alike before the LORD.<sup>16</sup>One law and one rule shall be for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you."<sup>17</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>18</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land to which I bring you<sup>19</sup>and when you eat of the bread of the land, you shall present a contribution to the LORD.<sup>20</sup>Of the first of your dough you shall present a loaf as a contribution; like a contribution from the threshing floor, so shall you present it.<sup>21</sup>Some of the first of your dough you shall give to the LORD as a contribution throughout your generations.<sup>22</sup>"But if you sin unintentionally, and do not observe all these commandments that the LORD has spoken to Moses,<sup>23</sup>all that the LORD has commanded you by Moses, from the day that the LORD gave commandment, and onward throughout your generations,<sup>24</sup>then if it was done unintentionally without the knowledge of the congregation, all the congregation shall offer one bull from the herd for a burnt offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD, with its grain offering and its drink offering, according to the rule, and one male goat for a sin offering.<sup>25</sup>And the priest shall make atonement for all the congregation of the people of Israel, and they shall be forgiven, because it was a mistake, and they have brought their offering, a food offering to the LORD, and their sin offering before the LORD for their mistake.<sup>26</sup>And all the congregation of the people of Israel shall be forgiven, and the stranger who sojourns among them, because the whole population was involved in the mistake.<sup>27</sup>"If one person sins unintentionally, he shall offer a female goat a year old for a sin offering.<sup>28</sup>And the priest shall make atonement before the LORD for the person who makes a mistake, when he sins unintentionally, to make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>29</sup>You shall have one law for him who does anything unintentionally, for him who is native among the people of Israel and for the stranger who sojourns among them.<sup>30</sup>But the person who does anything with a high hand, whether he is native or a sojourner, reviles the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from among his people.<sup>31</sup>Because he has despised the word of the LORD and has broken his commandment, that person shall be utterly cut off; his iniquity shall be on him."<sup>32</sup>While the people of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath day.<sup>33</sup>And those who found him gathering sticks brought him to Moses and Aaron and to all the congregation.<sup>34</sup>They put him in custody, because it had not been made clear what should be done to him.<sup>35</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "The man shall be put to death; all the congregation shall stone him with stones outside the camp."<sup>36</sup>And all the congregation brought him outside the camp and stoned him to death with stones, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>37</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>38</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, and tell them to make tassels on the corners of their garments throughout their generations, and to put a cord of blue on the tassel of each corner.<sup>39</sup>And it shall be a tassel for you to look at and remember all the commandments of the LORD, to do them, not to follow after your own heart and your own eyes, which you are inclined to whore after.<sup>40</sup>So you shall remember and do all my commandments, and be holy to your God.<sup>41</sup>I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God: I am the LORD your God."
15.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 14 ended with a generation sentenced to die in the wilderness. Chapter 15 opens with a surprising word: “When you come into the land you are to inhabit, which I am giving you” (v. 2).

The message. God’s promise outlives the people who refuse it, and the life he plans for his people in the land is a life of grateful worship, open to outsiders, with full provision for their failures. But there is a sin for which the law offers no sacrifice: open, defiant contempt for his word. God gives his people grace for their weakness and a daily reminder of whose they are, and he will not be mocked.

Why it was said. The children of the condemned generation needed to know that the promise had not died with their parents (see the introduction), and the difference between sins of weakness, which God provides for, and the defiance that had cost their parents the land.

How the chapter makes its case. God gives the amounts of flour, oil and wine to go with each offering in the land, and insists twice that the foreigner who joins Israel worships on exactly the same terms (vv. 1–16). The first of the dough is to be given to the LORD (vv. 17–21). Sins committed unintentionally, by the whole people or by one person, can be atoned for and forgiven (vv. 22–29), but the one who sins “with a high hand” despises the LORD and is cut off (vv. 30–31). A man gathering sticks on the Sabbath shows what that means (vv. 32–36). The chapter ends with tassels of blue to help Israel remember God’s commands and the God who brought them out of Egypt (vv. 37–41).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. God’s faithfulness to the next generation is the faithfulness Paul celebrates: “if we are faithless, he remains faithful” (2 Timothy 2:13). The atonement for unintentional sin points to the one sacrifice that covers all the sins of those who trust him, both those we know and those we do not, and the one law for native and stranger is fulfilled when Gentiles become “fellow citizens with the saints” (Ephesians 2:19). And the man stoned outside the camp is answered by the Lord of the Sabbath, who “suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12) for rebels.

For us. Your failures are not the end of God’s purposes for you. Bring your hidden faults to the sacrifice God has provided, and do not fear that you are beyond forgiveness if you are grieving over your sin. But never treat God’s word with contempt, and give your eyes something better to rest on than whatever the world puts before them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Offerings in the Land; One Law for All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The promise stands, and God lays out the worship of a land the hearers will not see. Straight after the sentence of chapter 14 he says “When you come into the land” (v. 2), and gives the grain, oil and wine to accompany each offering of lamb, ram or bull (vv. 1–10). These are the gifts of a settled, fruitful land, so the law itself is a promise. The same rule applies to every animal, and then God says it twice: the foreigner who lives among Israel and wishes to offer is to do exactly as Israel does. “You and the sojourner shall be alike before the LORD” (vv. 11–16).
verseByVerse.theology: God’s welcome at the altar extends equally to the foreigner.
verseByVerse.examples: The gospel now welcomes all peoples on equal terms in Christ, as Israel’s altar welcomed the sojourner.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land you are to inhabit, which I am giving you, and you offer to the LORD from the herd or from the flock a food offering or a burnt offering or a sacrifice, to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering or at your appointed feasts, to make a pleasing aroma to the LORD, then he who brings his offering shall offer to the LORD a grain offering of a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with a quarter of a hin of oil; and you shall offer with the burnt offering, or for the sacrifice, a quarter of a hin of wine for the drink offering for each lamb. Or for a ram, you shall offer for a grain offering two tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a third of a hin of oil. And for the drink offering you shall offer a third of a hin of wine, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And when you offer a bull as a burnt offering or sacrifice, to fulfill a vow or for peace offerings to the LORD, then one shall offer with the bull a grain offering of three tenths of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with half a hin of oil. And you shall offer for the drink offering half a hin of wine, as a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straight after sentencing a generation to die in the wilderness, God gives instructions for worship in the land: his promise does not depend on them.

When you come into the land. Not “if”. God has just told these people they will never see Canaan, and the next thing he gives is instruction for when they get there: how much flour, oil and wine go with a lamb, a ram, a bull.

Spoken to the children. The men listening will die in the wilderness; the boys beside them are being given the pattern of worship for a country they will inherit. The quantities themselves, measured in ephahs and hins, assume fields of grain, olive groves and vineyards: the law is a promise in disguise.

Judgment is not the end. Judgment is real, and it is not the end of the sentence. Israel’s worst day is followed at once by laws for a future she does not deserve. “If we are faithless, he remains faithful” (2 Timothy 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus it shall be done for each bull or ram, or for each lamb or young goat. As many as you offer, so shall you do with each one, as many as there are. Every native Israelite shall do these things in this way, in offering a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And if a stranger is sojourning with you, or anyone is living permanently among you, and he wishes to offer a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD, he shall do as you do. For the assembly, there shall be one statute for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you, a statute forever throughout your generations. You and the sojourner shall be alike before the LORD. One law and one rule shall be for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The foreigner who joins Israel worships on exactly the same terms as the native Israelite.

You and the sojourner shall be alike. God says it twice in six verses, as though determined it will not be missed.

If a stranger is sojourning with you. The ger is the resident foreigner, with no tribe, land or ancestry in the covenant. He could not inherit a field, but he could inherit everything that mattered: the same offerings and standing at the altar, with no second-class rite and no probation. In an ancient world where a nation’s gods belonged to that nation alone, Israel’s law says: if he will come, he comes on identical terms.

No longer strangers. So Paul can tell Gentiles, “you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). The place made for the outsider in Numbers 15 is now his home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God provides atonement for sins of weakness and draws a sharp line at defiance. Every time Israel eats bread in the land, the first of the dough is to be given to the LORD (vv. 17–21). If the whole congregation, or one person, sins unintentionally, there is a sacrifice, the priest makes atonement, and “they shall be forgiven” (vv. 22–29). The same law covers the native and the stranger. But the person who acts “with a high hand” reviles the LORD and despises his word, and no sacrifice is named for him: he is to be cut off (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology: The law distinguishes the sin of weakness and ignorance from settled defiance of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Grace covers our failings; only the heart that refuses the cross shuts itself out.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you come into the land to which I bring you and when you eat of the bread of the land, you shall present a contribution to the LORD. Of the first of your dough you shall present a loaf as a contribution; like a contribution from the threshing floor, so shall you present it. Some of the first of your dough you shall give to the LORD as a contribution throughout your generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whenever Israel bakes bread in the land, the first of the dough belongs to God, which brings worship into the kitchen.

Of the first of your dough. This is not the firstfruits of the harvest, which are dealt with elsewhere, but a gift made at home. A woman kneading bread takes a piece off the batch before it is baked and gives it away, “like a contribution from the threshing floor”.

Worship on baking day. The harvest offering happened once a year with everybody watching; this one happens on baking day, in front of nobody: the smallest act of worship touching the most ordinary object. And it comes off the top, before the loaf goes in the oven, while it still costs something to give.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word translated “dough” is rare; it may mean dough or coarsely ground meal. Either way the gift comes from the household’s daily bread.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you sin unintentionally, and do not observe all these commandments that the LORD has spoken to Moses, all that the LORD has commanded you by Moses, from the day that the LORD gave commandment, and onward throughout your generations, then if it was done unintentionally without the knowledge of the congregation, all the congregation shall offer one bull from the herd for a burnt offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD, with its grain offering and its drink offering, according to the rule, and one male goat for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for all the congregation of the people of Israel, and they shall be forgiven, because it was a mistake, and they have brought their offering, a food offering to the LORD, and their sin offering before the LORD for their mistake. And all the congregation of the people of Israel shall be forgiven, and the stranger who sojourns among them, because the whole population was involved in the mistake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the whole community sins without realising it, God has already provided a sacrifice and forgiveness.

If you sin unintentionally. The case is a failure to keep what the LORD commanded “by Moses”, through neglect or ignorance rather than defiance (contrast vv. 30–31). “Without the knowledge of the congregation” means the people did not realise what they were doing; once it comes to light, they must deal with it.

Unintentional sin is still sin. It requires blood, a priest and atonement. Israel was not permitted the modern assumption that what a man did not mean does not count. And God provided for it in advance, even where the whole nation is wrong together and nobody notices: a community can be sincerely, collectively mistaken, and Scripture assumes it will happen.

One bull and one male goat. The nation brings two offerings: a male goat as a sin offering, to deal with the guilt, and a bull as a whole burnt offering, “a pleasing aroma to the LORD”, giving the whole people back to God. Forgiveness is not only a debt cancelled but fellowship restored. Leviticus 4:13–21 gives a related rule, with a bull as the sin offering.

And the stranger who sojourns among them. Verse 26 includes the resident foreigner in the nation’s forgiveness, “because the whole population was involved in the mistake.” He shared in the people’s sin, and he shares in their pardon.

verseByVerse.quote: "If one person sins unintentionally, he shall offer a female goat a year old for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement before the LORD for the person who makes a mistake, when he sins unintentionally, to make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven. You shall have one law for him who does anything unintentionally, for him who is native among the people of Israel and for the stranger who sojourns among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The individual who sins unintentionally brings a smaller offering but receives the same atonement and forgiveness.

If one person sins unintentionally. He brings “a female goat a year old”, a smaller animal than the nation’s bull, but the same priest makes the same atonement. No one is too small for the provision, and no one is spared the need of it.

And he shall be forgiven. Not excused: forgiven, which means something was genuinely wrong. So a person can live with knowing that much of the damage he has done was done unawares. “Declare me innocent from hidden faults” (Psalm 19:12) is a prayer with an answer, and its answer is the sacrifice of Christ, which covers the sins of his people that they have never even noticed.

You shall have one law. The same law covers the native Israelite and the stranger: the outsider stands on the same ground at the altar when he has sinned as when he worships (see the note on vv. 11–16).

verseByVerse.quote: But the person who does anything with a high hand, whether he is native or a sojourner, reviles the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from among his people. Because he has despised the word of the LORD and has broken his commandment, that person shall be utterly cut off; his iniquity shall be on him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For open defiance of God’s word, sin with a raised fist, no sacrifice is offered: the sinner is cut off.

With a high hand. The “high hand” is a raised fist: not sin in weakness, or in a moment, or in ignorance, but defiance, knowing what God has said and defying it openly. Such a person “reviles the LORD” and “has despised the word of the LORD”. For that one category the chapter offers no sacrifice. There is no goat listed.

For the fearful conscience. This frightens sensitive Christians. Have I committed it? The text points to the answer: the high-handed man reviles and despises. He is not sorry. A person lying awake afraid he has sinned beyond forgiveness has already shown that he has not, because the high-handed man does not lie awake.

What Peter shows. Peter denied Christ three times with oaths, about as deliberate as sin gets (Matthew 26:74), and was restored on a beach over breakfast (John 21:15–17). What is described here is not the seriousness of a sin but the direction of a life, a settled contempt with no intention of returning. Hebrews says the same: “if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins” (Hebrews 10:26). Not because the blood of Christ is insufficient, but because a man who has decided to despise it will not come and be washed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–41 — The Sabbath-Breaker and the Tassels
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A case of defiant sin is judged, and Israel is given a daily reminder of the commands of the God who saved them. A man is found gathering sticks on the Sabbath; Moses waits for the LORD’s ruling, and the man is stoned outside the camp (vv. 32–36). Then God commands tassels with a cord of blue on the corners of every garment, so that Israel will look at them, remember his commandments and not follow their own hearts and eyes (vv. 37–40). The chapter ends where all Israel’s obedience began: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (v. 41).
verseByVerse.theology: God knows how easily his people forget, and provides for it.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel wore blue to remember; believers too need regular reminders of grace if they are to walk in holiness.

verseByVerse.quote: While the people of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath day. And those who found him gathering sticks brought him to Moses and Aaron and to all the congregation. They put him in custody, because it had not been made clear what should be done to him. And the LORD said to Moses, "The man shall be put to death; all the congregation shall stone him with stones outside the camp." And all the congregation brought him outside the camp and stoned him to death with stones, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man who openly gathers wood on the Sabbath is put to death at God’s command, showing what defiance of his word means.

A man gathering sticks on the Sabbath day. The severity is shocking, and the reader should not be talked out of the shock. But the story comes straight after the definition of high-handed sin, as an example of it. He was gathering fuel in the open, in a camp under the pillar of fire, and the Sabbath had been given at Sinai, with the mountain shaking, as the sign of the covenant itself (Exodus 31:13–17).

They put him in custody. He was held “because it had not been made clear what should be done to him.” Nobody improvised; Moses waited and asked. What was on trial was not firewood but whether God’s word meant anything in that camp, at the moment a nation under sentence was deciding how seriously to take him. The man had raised his fist in public, and the whole congregation had to see what that meant.

The Lord of the Sabbath. Remember who was later accused of breaking this same Sabbath: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27–28). The Lord of the Sabbath took the weight of its broken commandment on himself and was executed outside a city (Hebrews 13:12) for crimes he had not committed.

Should Sabbath-breakers be put to death today? No. The penalty belonged to Israel’s civil law, where the Sabbath was the sign of the covenant itself, and it ended with that theocracy.

Where Christians differ: does the Sabbath bind Christians today? It was the sign of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 31:13), and the New Testament calls Sabbaths “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16–17). Many godly Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, binding by the fourth commandment, and their view deserves respect; Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), so no day binds the conscience (Romans 14:5); rest and gathering for worship on the Lord’s Day remain good gifts. Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy rather than under rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience; faithful believers differ here.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Speak to the people of Israel, and tell them to make tassels on the corners of their garments throughout their generations, and to put a cord of blue on the tassel of each corner. And it shall be a tassel for you to look at and remember all the commandments of the LORD, to do them, not to follow after your own heart and your own eyes, which you are inclined to whore after. So you shall remember and do all my commandments, and be holy to your God. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God: I am the LORD your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tassels with a cord of blue are to remind Israel, at every glance, of God’s commands and of the God who saved them.

A cord of blue. After the stoning, God does something tender: a cord of blue on the tassel of every cloak in Israel. Blue was the colour of the tabernacle curtains and the high priest’s robe, one of the costliest dyes of the ancient world, and now a strand of it was on a shepherd’s coat (see clothing).

To look at and remember. God knows how forgetting works. A man seldom decides to disobey; his eye falls on something and he follows it, and by the time he thinks of God the thing is done. So God puts something at the bottom edge of his vision, where he glances a hundred times a day.

The war for your eyes. The law names the danger exactly: “not to follow after your own heart and your own eyes”. Never have so many clever people been paid so much to capture where we look, because whatever holds the eye begins to steer the heart. We like to think we simply choose our desires; Numbers suggests they are largely trained by what we keep looking at. God’s answer is not merely to look away but to give the eyes something better to rest on: a thread of blue, the colour of the sanctuary, reminding a man whose he is. The New Testament carries the principle to its end. We become like what we behold: “we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18). The cure for a captured eye is not an empty one but a captivated one, fixed on Christ.

Who brought you out of the land of Egypt. The order in the last verse matters: rescue first, commandments second. Israel does not obey in order to be brought out; she was brought out, and the tassel reminds her whose she already is.

The fringe of his garment. These are the tassels a desperate woman reached for, twelve years ill, when she “touched the fringe of his garment” (Matthew 9:20). It was a thread sewn into a hem to recall the commandments, and power went out from the one who had kept them all, and he turned and called her daughter.
