Uncertain wording. The exact shade of “blue” is uncertain: the word names a costly dye made from sea snails, perhaps nearer violet than sky blue.

15.theology:
Grace After Judgment. God’s covenant outlasts his people’s unbelief, and his discipline never cancels his grace.

Weakness and Defiance. Grace abounds for the stumbling believer; settled contempt for God rejects the very mercy God provides.

Reminders of Grace and Holiness. We obey because we have been redeemed, and God gives reminders for forgetful hearts.
15.examples:
Then: A generation barred from the land was given laws for life in it, and tassels of blue to help it remember.

Now: Christ suffered outside the gate, bearing the law-breaker’s curse, and kept the commandments you forget. Rest in that grace, beware the high-handed heart, and use the reminders he gives, the Word, the table, the saints, through which his Spirit turns your wandering eyes back to the Lord who redeemed you.

keyVerse.quote: When you come into the land you are to inhabit, which I am giving you
keyVerse.note: Spoken straight after a whole generation has been sentenced to die in the wilderness, these words show that God’s promise outlives those who refuse it. The laws that follow are instructions for a future that God guarantees, given to the children of the people who said no.

15.reflection:
Straight after the judgment of chapter 14, God says “When you come into the land” (v. 2). How does God’s faithfulness after our failures encourage you? Where do you need to hear that his purposes have not ended?

God provided forgiveness even for sins people did not know they had committed (vv. 22–29). How does Christ’s sacrifice for our hidden faults (Psalm 19:12) bring both humility and peace?

What is the difference between sinning in weakness and sinning “with a high hand” (v. 30)? How would you help a believer who fears that he has committed a sin beyond forgiveness?

The tassels were given so that Israel would not “follow after your own heart and your own eyes” (v. 39). What tends to capture your eyes, and what practical habits help you fix them on Christ?

16.title: Korah’s Rebellion: The One Mediator
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Korah the son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, and Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, and On the son of Peleth, sons of Reuben, took men.<sup>2</sup>And they rose up before Moses, with a number of the people of Israel, 250 chiefs of the congregation, chosen from the assembly, well-known men.<sup>3</sup>They assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron and said to them, "You have gone too far! For all in the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?"<sup>4</sup>When Moses heard it, he fell on his face,<sup>5</sup>and he said to Korah and all his company, "In the morning the LORD will show who is his, and who is holy, and will bring him near to him. The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him.<sup>6</sup>Do this: take censers, Korah and all his company;<sup>7</sup>put fire in them and put incense on them before the LORD tomorrow, and the man whom the LORD chooses shall be the holy one. You have gone too far, sons of Levi!"<sup>8</sup>And Moses said to Korah, "Hear now, you sons of Levi:<sup>9</sup>is it too small a thing for you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation of Israel, to bring you near to himself, to do service in the tabernacle of the LORD and to stand before the congregation to minister to them,<sup>10</sup>and that he has brought you near him, and all your brothers the sons of Levi with you? And would you seek the priesthood also?<sup>11</sup>Therefore it is against the LORD that you and all your company have gathered together. What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"<sup>12</sup>And Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, and they said, "We will not come up.<sup>13</sup>Is it a small thing that you have brought us up out of a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, that you must also make yourself a prince over us?<sup>14</sup>Moreover, you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey, nor given us inheritance of fields and vineyards. Will you put out the eyes of these men? We will not come up."<sup>15</sup>And Moses was very angry and said to the LORD, "Do not respect their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them, and I have not harmed one of them."<sup>16</sup>And Moses said to Korah, "Be present, you and all your company, before the LORD, you and they, and Aaron, tomorrow.<sup>17</sup>And let every one of you take his censer and put incense on it, and every one of you bring before the LORD his censer, 250 censers; you also, and Aaron, each his censer."<sup>18</sup>So every man took his censer and put fire in them and laid incense on them and stood at the entrance of the tent of meeting with Moses and Aaron.<sup>19</sup>Then Korah assembled all the congregation against them at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And the glory of the LORD appeared to all the congregation.<sup>20</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,<sup>21</sup>"Separate yourselves from among this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment."<sup>22</sup>And they fell on their faces and said, "O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?"<sup>23</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>24</sup>"Say to the congregation, Get away from the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram."<sup>25</sup>Then Moses rose and went to Dathan and Abiram, and the elders of Israel followed him.<sup>26</sup>And he spoke to the congregation, saying, "Depart, please, from the tents of these wicked men, and touch nothing of theirs, lest you be swept away with all their sins."<sup>27</sup>So they got away from the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. And Dathan and Abiram came out and stood at the door of their tents, together with their wives, their sons, and their little ones.<sup>28</sup>And Moses said, "Hereby you shall know that the LORD has sent me to do all these works, and that it has not been of my own accord.<sup>29</sup>If these men die as all men die, or if they are visited by the fate of all mankind, then the LORD has not sent me.<sup>30</sup>But if the LORD creates something new, and the ground opens its mouth and swallows them up with all that belongs to them, and they go down alive into Sheol, then you shall know that these men have despised the LORD."<sup>31</sup>And as soon as he had finished speaking all these words, the ground under them split apart.<sup>32</sup>And the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households and all the people who belonged to Korah and all their goods.<sup>33</sup>So they and all that belonged to them went down alive into Sheol, and the earth closed over them, and they perished from the midst of the assembly.<sup>34</sup>And all Israel who were around them fled at their cry, for they said, "Lest the earth swallow us up!"<sup>35</sup>And fire came out from the LORD and consumed the 250 men offering the incense.<sup>36</sup>Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>37</sup>"Tell Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest to take up the censers out of the blaze. Then scatter the fire far and wide, for they have become holy.<sup>38</sup>As for the censers of these men who have sinned at the cost of their lives, let them be made into hammered plates as a covering for the altar, for they offered them before the LORD, and they became holy. Thus they shall be a sign to the people of Israel."<sup>39</sup>So Eleazar the priest took the bronze censers, which those who were burned had offered, and they were hammered out as a covering for the altar,<sup>40</sup>to be a reminder to the people of Israel, so that no outsider, who is not of the descendants of Aaron, should draw near to burn incense before the LORD, lest he become like Korah and his company—as the LORD said to him through Moses.<sup>41</sup>But on the next day all the congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and against Aaron, saying, "You have killed the people of the LORD."<sup>42</sup>And when the congregation had assembled against Moses and against Aaron, they turned toward the tent of meeting. And behold, the cloud covered it, and the glory of the LORD appeared.<sup>43</sup>And Moses and Aaron came to the front of the tent of meeting,<sup>44</sup>and the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>45</sup>"Get away from the midst of this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment." And they fell on their faces.<sup>46</sup>And Moses said to Aaron, "Take your censer, and put fire on it from off the altar and lay incense on it and carry it quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from the LORD; the plague has begun."<sup>47</sup>So Aaron took it as Moses said and ran into the midst of the assembly. And behold, the plague had already begun among the people. And he put on the incense and made atonement for the people.<sup>48</sup>And he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped.<sup>49</sup>Now those who died in the plague were 14,700, besides those who died in the affair of Korah.<sup>50</sup>And Aaron returned to Moses at the entrance of the tent of meeting, when the plague was stopped.
16.overview:
Where we are. Israel is under sentence (chapter 14) and has just been taught the difference between sins of weakness and defiance (chapter 15). Now comes the most serious challenge yet to the order God has set up: Korah, a Levite, joins with Dathan and Abiram of Reuben and 250 chiefs to oppose Moses and Aaron.

The message. No one may come near to God on his own terms, however sincere, respected or numerous; we come only through the mediator God himself appoints. Korah’s slogan sounds almost pious, but it is a demand for access to God without God’s chosen priest. God answers in terrible judgment, and then, when the whole people grumbles, he saves them through the very priest they despised.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know that the priesthood of Aaron was not Moses’ family arrangement but God’s appointment (see the introduction). The bronze plating on the altar kept the lesson before the next generation.

How the chapter makes its case. Korah and his allies accuse Moses and Aaron of exalting themselves over a holy congregation; Moses hands the dispute to God and exposes Korah’s ambition, while Dathan and Abiram refuse even to come (vv. 1–14). God answers at the tent: Moses and Aaron plead for the people, the ground swallows the rebels’ households, and fire consumes the 250 offering incense (vv. 15–35). Their censers are hammered into a covering for the altar as a warning. The next day the whole congregation accuses Moses and Aaron of murder, a plague breaks out, and Aaron runs into the crowd with incense and stands between the dead and the living until it stops (vv. 36–50).

Where it leads. By pattern, and the New Testament draws it out. Korah’s sin was refusing the mediator God appointed; the gospel’s answer is that “there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). Aaron, running with fire from the altar into a dying crowd, is a picture of Christ, the High Priest who “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25). But Aaron carried an offering in his hands; Christ is himself “the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2), standing between the dead and the living by dying in our place.

For us. The way into God’s presence is wider than Korah dreamed and narrower than he would allow: open to every believer, and only through Christ. Beware the discontent that grows in people who already have much, and the arguments that happen to make their makers greater. And when you have grumbled against God, run to the Priest who runs toward the guilty.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A powerful coalition challenges Moses and Aaron, and Moses hands the challenge to God. Korah, a leading Levite, joins with Dathan, Abiram and On of Reuben and 250 well-known chiefs to accuse Moses and Aaron of exalting themselves over a congregation that is all holy (vv. 1–3). Moses falls on his face and proposes a test: tomorrow, with censers and incense, the LORD will show whom he has chosen (vv. 4–7). He exposes the ambition behind the slogan: is it too small a thing for the Levites to serve God, that they want the priesthood too (vv. 8–11)? Dathan and Abiram refuse to come, call Egypt the land of milk and honey and accuse Moses of deceit (vv. 12–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Rebellion against the mediator God appoints, however pious it sounds, is rebellion against God himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Korah despised the priesthood God had appointed; the warning now is against refusing the one Mediator God has given, Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Korah the son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, and Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, and On the son of Peleth, sons of Reuben, took men. And they rose up before Moses, with a number of the people of Israel, 250 chiefs of the congregation, chosen from the assembly, well-known men. They assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron and said to them, "You have gone too far! For all in the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Levites, Reubenites and leading chiefs accuse Moses and Aaron of exalting themselves over a people who are all holy.

Korah the son of Izhar, son of Kohath. The coalition is formidable. Korah is a Kohathite, of the highest-ranking Levitical family, the men who carried the ark (see priests and Levites). Dathan, Abiram and On are Reubenites, from the tribe of Jacob’s firstborn, which had lost the firstborn’s place (Genesis 49:3–4). With them are 250 chiefs, “well-known men”, the most respected in Israel. They were also neighbours, both camped south of the tabernacle (2:10; 3:29).

All in the congregation are holy. The slogan is almost entirely true. God had said at Sinai, “you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6). And the LORD is among them; the cloud is over the tent as they speak.

Why then do you exalt yourselves? The conclusion is a lie. From “we are all holy” Korah infers that no one may be set over us, which does not follow, and which conveniently puts Korah at the head of the movement to abolish leadership.

How dangerous errors are built. Dangerous errors are usually true statements arranged to reach the conclusion someone wants. Watch who ends up better off if the argument wins. Korah wanted the priesthood, and total equality was his way to it. Diotrephes did the same in a New Testament church, and John names the motive: he “likes to put himself first” (3 John 9).

Is this a warning never to question a leader? Moses and Aaron were appointed directly by God and vindicated by miracle; Korah wanted their place. Today’s elders are fallible men, to be honoured (Hebrews 13:17) but also tested by Scripture (Acts 17:11) and corrected when they err (1 Timothy 5:19–20). And “all in the congregation are holy” sounds like the priesthood of all believers (1 Peter 2:9); but that rests on the one Mediator, Christ, not on anyone appointing himself to approach God.

Uncertain wording. Verse 1 says literally “And Korah took”, with no object; the ESV supplies “men”. The sense is clear enough: Korah gathered a party.

verseByVerse.quote: When Moses heard it, he fell on his face, and he said to Korah and all his company, "In the morning the LORD will show who is his, and who is holy, and will bring him near to him. The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him. Do this: take censers, Korah and all his company; put fire in them and put incense on them before the LORD tomorrow, and the man whom the LORD chooses shall be the holy one. You have gone too far, sons of Levi!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses hands his case to God: tomorrow the LORD will show whom he has chosen to come near.

When Moses heard it, he fell on his face. Flat on the ground rather than on his feet arguing: it is the most consistent thing about the man.

In the morning the LORD will show who is his. God himself will show “who is his, and who is holy”. Korah had said that all are holy (v. 3); Moses answers that the question is whom God chooses: “The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him.” To “bring near” is the language of priesthood (Exodus 28:1; Leviticus 10:3), and that is what is really in dispute.

Take censers. The test is the very act in dispute: offering incense, which belonged to the priests alone (see the note on vv. 16–19). Anyone who remembered Nadab and Abihu, who died offering “unauthorized fire” before the LORD (Leviticus 10:1–2), knew how dangerous it was.

You have gone too far, sons of Levi! Moses throws their own words back at them. It is the same Hebrew expression they flung at Moses and Aaron in verse 3: the overreaching is theirs, not his.
verseByVerse.note: In v. 5 the Greek Old Testament reads “The Lord knows those who are his”, words Paul quotes in 2 Timothy 2:19.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to Korah, "Hear now, you sons of Levi: is it too small a thing for you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation of Israel, to bring you near to himself, to do service in the tabernacle of the LORD and to stand before the congregation to minister to them, and that he has brought you near him, and all your brothers the sons of Levi with you? And would you seek the priesthood also? Therefore it is against the LORD that you and all your company have gathered together. What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses exposes the ambition behind the slogan: the Levites already served God, and they wanted the priesthood too.

Hear now, you sons of Levi. Moses lists their privileges one by one: separated from the congregation, brought near to God himself, set to serve in the tabernacle and to “stand before the congregation to minister to them.” The Kohathites carried the most holy things on the march (4:4–15). Their calling was to serve the people, not to rule them, and it was no lesser calling for being a different one.

Is it too small a thing for you? The question goes past the argument to the desire behind it: “And would you seek the priesthood also?” Of all the men in the camp, Korah belonged to the clan entrusted with the holiest object on earth, and it was not enough.

Where discontent grows. Discontent of this kind grows in those who already have much and can see one thing more. Korah was in the presence of God every day, and his eye was on the one door still shut. “Is it too small a thing” is a question to put to yourself when aggrieved about a position, because the honest answer shows how many of God’s gifts we have stopped counting.

It is against the LORD. Moses names the one they are really opposing. Aaron did not appoint himself, and the speech ends with a question that takes him out of the quarrel: “What is Aaron that you grumble against him?” He is a servant under orders, and to grumble at him is to grumble at the God who chose him. Moses had said the same when the manna was given: “Your grumbling is not against us but against the LORD” (Exodus 16:8).

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, and they said, "We will not come up. Is it a small thing that you have brought us up out of a land flowing with milk and honey, to kill us in the wilderness, that you must also make yourself a prince over us? Moreover, you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey, nor given us inheritance of fields and vineyards. Will you put out the eyes of these men? We will not come up."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dathan and Abiram refuse to come, call Egypt the land of milk and honey, and blame Moses for their own unbelief.

We will not come up. The refusal opens and closes their reply.

A land flowing with milk and honey. They apply God’s own phrase for Canaan to Egypt. The place of slavery, infanticide and the lash has become the promised land, and the God who brought them out is charged with murder. It is one of the most shameless reversals of the truth in the Bible.

Nor given us inheritance of fields and vineyards. True, because of the verdict of chapter 14, which fell because they refused to go in. They blame Moses for the consequence of their own rebellion.

Will you put out the eyes of these men? The last line accuses of deception the man who once offered to be blotted out of God’s book for them (Exodus 32:32). There is no arguing with this. It is not a position; it is a mood that has found words.

Uncertain wording. “Put out the eyes” is probably an idiom for hoodwinking people, though it may allude to rulers blinding captives. Either way it accuses Moses of deceit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God settles the dispute himself, and the rebels perish. Moses protests his integrity (v. 15), and the next morning the 250 stand at the tent with their censers while Korah gathers the whole congregation against Moses and Aaron (vv. 16–19). The glory of the LORD appears, and God threatens to consume the whole people; Moses and Aaron plead for them, and the people are told to move away from the rebels’ tents (vv. 20–27). Moses stakes his calling on something only God can do (vv. 28–30), and the ground opens and swallows the rebels’ households alive (vv. 31–34). Fire from the LORD consumes the 250 offering incense (v. 35).
verseByVerse.theology: God vindicates his appointed mediation with terrible judgment; to usurp the priesthood is to perish before the holy God.
verseByVerse.examples: The earth swallowed the rebels, and the scene still shows how serious it is to reject God’s appointed way of approach.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses was very angry and said to the LORD, "Do not respect their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them, and I have not harmed one of them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses, finally angry, protests his integrity to God and asks him to reject the rebels’ offering.

I have not taken one donkey from them. Here is a man defending not his dignity but his integrity, and to God rather than to them. Samuel would later defend himself before the people in almost the same words: “Whose ox have I taken? Or whose donkey have I taken?” (1 Samuel 12:3).

Do not respect their offering. Moses asks God not to accept the “offering” the rebels will bring, probably the incense of the next morning’s test. It is a plea that God will show the truth, not a wish for revenge.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to Korah, "Be present, you and all your company, before the LORD, you and they, and Aaron, tomorrow. And let every one of you take his censer and put incense on it, and every one of you bring before the LORD his censer, 250 censers; you also, and Aaron, each his censer." So every man took his censer and put fire in them and laid incense on them and stood at the entrance of the tent of meeting with Moses and Aaron. Then Korah assembled all the congregation against them at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And the glory of the LORD appeared to all the congregation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The test is the disputed claim acted out: 250 men bring incense to the tent, and the glory of the LORD appears.

Every one of you take his censer. Incense was reserved to the priest alone. Korah claimed there was no such reservation; very well, let him do it. Two hundred and fifty men agreed to find out.

Korah assembled all the congregation against them. By the morning of the test Korah has the whole congregation standing with him at the entrance of the tent of meeting, against Moses and Aaron. The 250 with censers are only the front rank.

And the glory of the LORD appeared. As when the people took up stones against Caleb and Joshua (14:10), God shows himself at the tent before anyone can act. The glory that dwelt among them as a blessing appears now to judge.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, "Separate yourselves from among this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment." And they fell on their faces and said, "O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?" And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Say to the congregation, Get away from the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses and Aaron plead for the very people gathered against them, and win a reprieve for all but the ringleaders.

Shall one man sin? When God says “that I may consume them in a moment”, Moses and Aaron fall on their faces: “shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?” They plead for the people gathered against them.

O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh. The title appears again only in Moses’ prayer for a successor (27:16). God gives every person breath and life and knows each one from within, so he can tell the ringleader from the misled. Moses and Aaron appeal to that knowledge, as Abraham appealed to the Judge of all the earth over Sodom (Genesis 18:23–25).

Get away from the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. The reprieve comes as a command: those who are not to share the judgment must move away from the rebels’ tents (vv. 26–27). The word for “dwelling” is the one normally used for the tabernacle, and it may hint that Korah’s tent had become a rival to the tent of meeting.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses rose and went to Dathan and Abiram, and the elders of Israel followed him. And he spoke to the congregation, saying, "Depart, please, from the tents of these wicked men, and touch nothing of theirs, lest you be swept away with all their sins." So they got away from the dwelling of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. And Dathan and Abiram came out and stood at the door of their tents, together with their wives, their sons, and their little ones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people must separate from the rebels and touch nothing of theirs.

Then Moses rose and went to Dathan and Abiram. They had refused to come up to Moses (vv. 12–14), so Moses goes to them, and the elders of Israel go with him: the whole leadership stands visibly on one side.

Touch nothing of theirs. The congregation must not merely step back but touch nothing that belongs to the rebels, “lest you be swept away with all their sins.” Whoever clings to what is under judgment shares the judgment. The New Testament calls the church to the same separation: “Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins” (Revelation 18:4; compare 2 Corinthians 6:17).

Stood at the door of their tents. Dathan and Abiram come out and stand there with their wives, their sons and their little ones: defiance on show, with their families beside them (on what happened to the households, see the note on vv. 31–33).

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said, "Hereby you shall know that the LORD has sent me to do all these works, and that it has not been of my own accord. If these men die as all men die, or if they are visited by the fate of all mankind, then the LORD has not sent me. But if the LORD creates something new, and the ground opens its mouth and swallows them up with all that belongs to them, and they go down alive into Sheol, then you shall know that these men have despised the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses stakes his calling on something only God can do, announced in advance.

Then the LORD has not sent me. This is the mark of a genuine prophet: he stakes his commission on an event he cannot manufacture (compare Deuteronomy 18:22).

If the LORD creates something new. The verb is the one used in Genesis 1:1, “created”, used in the Old Testament only of God: nothing already in the world would do. The judgment will be as unmistakably God’s work as creation itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And as soon as he had finished speaking all these words, the ground under them split apart. And the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households and all the people who belonged to Korah and all their goods. So they and all that belonged to them went down alive into Sheol, and the earth closed over them, and they perished from the midst of the assembly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The earth swallows the rebels and their households alive, exactly as Moses said.

The ground under them split apart. “As soon as he had finished speaking”: the timing is part of the sign. The earth “opened its mouth”, as Moses had said it would, and closed again over tents, households and goods. Nothing of theirs was left in the camp.

They went down alive into Sheol. Sheol is the Old Testament name for the realm of the dead, pictured as deep beneath the earth. People go there by dying; these went down alive, so that no one could take it for a natural death or a chance disaster.

Korah in the New Testament. Jude puts it among the standing warnings of Scripture: men who “walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion” (Jude 11). Korah has become the name for a kind of person: the man who will not have the mediator God appointed, and appoints himself.

Why did the households die with them? In the Old Testament a family often stood or fell with its head (compare Joshua 7:24), and God as Judge has the right to take any life. It is not a pattern for human justice (Deuteronomy 24:16). And not all perished: “the sons of Korah did not die” (26:11), and their descendants wrote psalms (Psalms 42–49).

verseByVerse.quote: And all Israel who were around them fled at their cry, for they said, "Lest the earth swallow us up!" And fire came out from the LORD and consumed the 250 men offering the incense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fire from the LORD consumes the 250 who came to offer incense on their own terms.

Lest the earth swallow us up! All Israel runs from the cry. It is fear for their own lives, not grief over sin, and the next day shows the difference (see the note on vv. 41–43).

Fire came out from the LORD. The 250 die where they stand with their censers at the entrance of the tent (v. 18). Fire from the presence they had come to approach on their own terms is God’s answer to their incense.

What was being decided. The horror should not be smoothed over. The question was whether a man may approach God on his own terms if he is sincere, respected and part of a majority. These men were not irreligious; they were holding incense, doing the most spiritual thing available to them, and it killed them. There is a way of coming to God worse than not coming at all, as Nadab and Abihu had shown.

Can’t I find God in my own way? It may be the most widely held religious conviction of our time: the spiritual person goes direct, choosing the practices that suit him and answering to no one. Korah said much the same with a censer in his hand, and he grasped a truth: God does want a whole people near him. But the question was never whether we may come close. It is on what ground. A sinner who walks into the presence of a holy God on the strength of his own sincerity is not brave; he is unprotected. The gospel’s answer is wider than Korah dreamed and narrower than he would allow. Every believer, without exception, may now “enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19), and only so, for “there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). The way in is wide open, and it has a name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–50 — Aaron Between the Dead and the Living
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rebellion spreads to the whole people, and the priest they despised saves them. The censers of the dead are hammered into plates for the altar, a permanent warning that only Aaron’s descendants may offer incense (vv. 36–40). The next day the whole congregation accuses Moses and Aaron of killing the LORD’s people, and the glory of the LORD appears again (vv. 41–43). A plague breaks out. At Moses’ word Aaron takes fire from the altar, runs into the assembly, makes atonement, and stands between the dead and the living until the plague is stopped (vv. 44–50).
verseByVerse.theology: The priest puts himself between the wrath of God and the people: the gospel in a single image.
verseByVerse.examples: What Aaron did for a day, Christ has done for ever (see vv. 44–50).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Tell Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest to take up the censers out of the blaze. Then scatter the fire far and wide, for they have become holy. As for the censers of these men who have sinned at the cost of their lives, let them be made into hammered plates as a covering for the altar, for they offered them before the LORD, and they became holy. Thus they shall be a sign to the people of Israel." So Eleazar the priest took the bronze censers, which those who were burned had offered, and they were hammered out as a covering for the altar, to be a reminder to the people of Israel, so that no outsider, who is not of the descendants of Aaron, should draw near to burn incense before the LORD, lest he become like Korah and his company—as the LORD said to him through Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The dead men’s censers become a covering for the altar, a lasting sign that only Aaron’s line may burn incense.

Tell Eleazar. The task goes to Eleazar, Aaron’s son, probably because the high priest had to keep clear of the dead (Leviticus 21:10–12). The censers are taken “out of the blaze” and the fire scattered: the coals had been offered without warrant and must not be used, but the bronze “became holy” because it had been presented before the LORD.

As a covering for the altar. For the rest of that generation, every Israelite approached the place of sacrifice over bronze that had been in the hands of men who died claiming they did not need a priest.

To be a reminder. The plating has a stated purpose: “that no outsider, who is not of the descendants of Aaron, should draw near to burn incense before the LORD.” The answer to Korah’s claim in verse 3 is now fixed in metal on the altar. In this matter even a Levite is an “outsider”.

verseByVerse.quote: But on the next day all the congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and against Aaron, saying, "You have killed the people of the LORD." And when the congregation had assembled against Moses and against Aaron, they turned toward the tent of meeting. And behold, the cloud covered it, and the glory of the LORD appeared. And Moses and Aaron came to the front of the tent of meeting,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The very next day the whole people accuses Moses and Aaron of murder, and the glory of the LORD appears again.

You have killed the people of the LORD. This sentence shows how little had gone in. One day after the earth opened before the entire nation, they had reinterpreted it as a leadership problem.

How the heart handles evidence. The heart does not deny evidence it does not want; it re-explains it. That is why more signs would not have saved this generation, and why the rich man was told his brothers “neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead” (Luke 16:31).

The cloud covered it, and the glory of the LORD appeared. As the crowd gathers against Moses and Aaron, they turn toward the tent and find God already there. Again the glory appears at the moment of rebellion (14:10; 16:19), and the two men go and stand before the tent to wait for his word.

verseByVerse.quote: and the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Get away from the midst of this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment." And they fell on their faces. And Moses said to Aaron, "Take your censer, and put fire on it from off the altar and lay incense on it and carry it quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from the LORD; the plague has begun." So Aaron took it as Moses said and ran into the midst of the assembly. And behold, the plague had already begun among the people. And he put on the incense and made atonement for the people. And he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped. Now those who died in the plague were 14,700, besides those who died in the affair of Korah. And Aaron returned to Moses at the entrance of the tent of meeting, when the plague was stopped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As a plague breaks out, Aaron runs into the dying crowd with incense, makes atonement and stands between the dead and the living.

The plague has begun. People die where they stand. What follows is one of the great scenes of the book.

Take your censer. Moses sends Aaron out because wrath has begun, and every detail counts. He takes a censer, the very object 250 men had died holding the day before. He takes fire “from off the altar”, the place of sacrifice. And an old man past eighty runs, into a plague, toward the people who had spent the morning accusing him of murder, with nothing in his hands but incense.

He stood between the dead and the living. Here is the priesthood the rebels called unnecessary. Fourteen thousand seven hundred were dead, and between the rest and the same end stood one man with a censer: not on a mountain or behind a curtain, but out in the open, holding back the wrath of God with his own body and an offering. That is what a priest is for.

The true Priest. The true Priest did not carry the offering in his hands. “He is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2), the sacrifice that turns God’s wrath away: he stood between the dead and the living by dying himself, and rose, and “he always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). The plague is stopped for ever.

16.theology:
Rebellion Against the Mediator Is Rebellion Against God. Korah’s pious slogan hid a refusal of the mediator God had appointed. To reject the one Mediator God appoints, supremely Christ, is to perish before the holy God.

The Holiness That Consumes. God alone determines how he may be approached. The same glory that blesses can consume; we are spared only because a better Mediator bore the fire in our place.

The Priest Between the Dead and the Living. The mediator puts himself in the way of wrath, and Christ our High Priest does so for ever.
16.examples:
Then: Korah grasped for the priesthood and perished, and the priest he despised saved the people who had sided with him.

Now: Christ, your great High Priest, has run into the midst of your death and stands between you and the wrath of God; because he stands, you live. In that security, and by his Spirit, you need not grasp for what God has withheld or despise the place he has given you, and when envy rises, bring it to the Priest who prays for you.

keyVerse.quote: And he stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stopped.
keyVerse.note: After a chapter about people who claimed they needed no priest, the priest they despised is the one who saves them. Aaron, standing with atoning incense in the middle of a dying crowd, is one of the clearest pictures in the Old Testament of what Christ does for his people as their great High Priest.

16.reflection:
Korah’s slogan, “all in the congregation are holy” (v. 3), was built from true statements but led to a false conclusion. How can we recognise when true ideas are being used to serve someone’s ambition, including our own?

Moses asked the Levites, “is it too small a thing for you” (v. 9) to serve God as they did. Which of God’s gifts to you have you stopped counting, and where might discontent be growing in you?

Many people today believe they can find God in their own way. How would you explain, kindly and clearly, why Christ is the only way to God, and why that way is open to everyone?

Aaron ran with his censer toward the people who had accused him (vv. 46–48). What does this picture show us about Christ, and how should it shape how we treat people who have wronged us?

17.title: Aaron’s Staff Buds: Resurrection and the Confirmed Priesthood
17.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, and get from them staffs, one for each fathers' house, from all their chiefs according to their fathers' houses, twelve staffs. Write each man's name on his staff,<sup>3</sup>and write Aaron's name on the staff of Levi. For there shall be one staff for the head of each fathers' house.<sup>4</sup>Then you shall deposit them in the tent of meeting before the testimony, where I meet with you.<sup>5</sup>And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you."<sup>6</sup>Moses spoke to the people of Israel. And all their chiefs gave him staffs, one for each chief, according to their fathers' houses, twelve staffs. And the staff of Aaron was among their staffs.<sup>7</sup>And Moses deposited the staffs before the LORD in the tent of the testimony.<sup>8</sup>On the next day Moses went into the tent of the testimony, and behold, the staff of Aaron for the house of Levi had sprouted and put forth buds and produced blossoms, and it bore ripe almonds.<sup>9</sup>Then Moses brought out all the staffs from before the LORD to all the people of Israel. And they looked, and each man took his staff.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Put back the staff of Aaron before the testimony, to be kept as a sign for the rebels, that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die."<sup>11</sup>Thus did Moses; as the LORD commanded him, so he did.<sup>12</sup>And the people of Israel said to Moses, "Behold, we perish, we are undone, we are all undone.<sup>13</sup>Everyone who comes near, who comes near to the tabernacle of the LORD, shall die. Are we all to perish?"
17.overview:
Where we are. Korah’s rebellion has just ended in judgment: the earth swallowed the ringleaders, fire consumed the 250 men with censers, and a plague killed 14,700 more before Aaron stood between the dead and the living (chapter 16). The question that started it all is still raw: who may come near to God?

The message. God himself chooses who may stand between him and his people, and he shows it by bringing life out of dead wood. The priesthood is not seized by ambition or settled by a majority; it is given by God and confirmed by life from the dead. And even the sign is mercy: God wants the grumbling to stop so that the people need not die.

Why it was said. Israel, camped in the wilderness after the refusal at Kadesh, had just seen thousands die over a challenge to Aaron’s priesthood (see the introduction). They needed the matter settled for good, in a way no tribe could dispute, before more lives were lost.

How the chapter makes its case. God orders a staff from the chief of each tribe, each with its owner’s name and Aaron’s on Levi’s, laid up overnight before the testimony, with the promise that the chosen man’s staff will sprout (vv. 1–7). In the morning Aaron’s staff alone has sprouted, budded, blossomed and borne ripe almonds (v. 8). Moses shows every staff to the nation, and Aaron’s is put back before the testimony as a lasting sign for rebels, “lest they die” (vv. 9–11). The people, at last convinced of God’s holiness, cry out in terror that anyone who comes near will die (vv. 12–13), and chapter 18 answers them.

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. God settled the true priest by life out of death, and he settles it the same way for Christ, “declared to be the Son of God in power… by his resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:4), a priest “by the power of an indestructible life” (Hebrews 7:16); as with Aaron, “no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God” (Hebrews 5:4). And the people’s cry exposes the need: no sinner can come near the holy God and live without a mediator. Because Christ came near and died and lives, we may “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16).

For us. No one earns a standing before God by ability or by vote; rest in the Priest God has chosen and raised. If you have felt the terror of verse 13, your sin and his holiness, do not stop there: the living Priest is God’s answer to it. And notice how God settles a bitter dispute, not by more force but by a gift of life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Twelve Staffs Laid Up
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the judgments of chapter 16, God settles the priesthood with a quiet, fair test rather than another blow. Each tribal chief hands in his staff, his own name written on it, and Aaron’s name goes on the staff of Levi (vv. 1–3). The twelve dead sticks are laid together before the testimony, where God meets with Moses, and God promises that the staff of the man he chooses will sprout (vv. 4–5). His stated aim is mercy: to end the grumbling that has been killing the people. Moses does exactly as he is told, and Aaron’s staff lies among the rest, unmarked, overnight before the LORD (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: God means to end the grumbling with a sign of his own making rather than with further argument.
verseByVerse.examples: When God’s people quarrel over who has his favour, the answer does not finally come from the loudest voice or the larger party but from what God himself does.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, and get from them staffs, one for each fathers' house, from all their chiefs according to their fathers' houses, twelve staffs. Write each man's name on his staff, and write Aaron's name on the staff of Levi. For there shall be one staff for the head of each fathers' house. Then you shall deposit them in the tent of meeting before the testimony, where I meet with you. And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the judgments of chapter 16, God settles who his priest is by a fair, gentle test: the staff of the man he chooses will come to life.

Twelve staffs. Fourteen thousand seven hundred people have just died, and God’s next move is a sign: one staff per tribe, each with its chief’s name, and Aaron’s on the staff of Levi. The test is scrupulously fair: every tribe is represented, each staff is named so nobody can claim a mix-up, and all lie in the same place overnight with nobody in the room. God is not asking Israel to take Moses’ word for it.

Dead wood. A staff was a shepherd’s rod or a chief’s badge of office: a length of wood cut years before and leaned on daily. Nothing is more thoroughly finished than a staff, and everybody in that tent knew it. So the question is not “which of these men is most capable?” but “on which of these dead sticks will life appear?” The priesthood will not be settled by ability or by the majority who backed Korah, but by a miracle, because nothing else can settle it.

Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings. The stated purpose is mercy. God wants the arguing to stop because the arguing was killing them.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke to the people of Israel. And all their chiefs gave him staffs, one for each chief, according to their fathers' houses, twelve staffs. And the staff of Aaron was among their staffs. And Moses deposited the staffs before the LORD in the tent of the testimony.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aaron’s staff lies unmarked among the others in the dark tent, so that whatever happens next can only be God’s doing.

The staff of Aaron was among their staffs. Not marked out, not placed nearer the ark, but in the pile with the other eleven; anyone walking into that tent at midnight could not have told which was which. And the staffs are left before the LORD overnight, in a dark and empty room.

Nothing but God. That is exactly what God intended. There is no possible human contribution to what comes next: twelve dead sticks in the dark, and the only one who can do anything is God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Budding Staff and the Fear of the People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the question of the priesthood by giving life to dead wood. In the morning Aaron’s staff has sprouted, budded, blossomed and borne ripe almonds, while the other eleven are as dry as before (v. 8). Moses brings them all out, each chief takes back his own, and no argument is left (v. 9). Aaron’s staff is put back before the testimony as a permanent warning, so that rebels need not die (vv. 10–11). But the people swing from defiance to despair: anyone who comes near the tabernacle will die (vv. 12–13). They have learned God’s holiness, and they still need to learn why he gave a priest.
verseByVerse.theology: Life from dead wood is the kind of sign only God can give, and it is the pattern he follows again at the empty tomb.
verseByVerse.examples: The people’s terror at the end of the section is not the last word; the next chapter, and the whole priesthood, is God’s answer to it.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day Moses went into the tent of the testimony, and behold, the staff of Aaron for the house of Levi had sprouted and put forth buds and produced blossoms, and it bore ripe almonds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Overnight Aaron’s dead staff bursts into buds, blossoms and ripe almonds: God marks his chosen priest by making life appear.

Sprouted and put forth buds. Four verbs: sprouted, budded, blossomed, bore ripe almonds. A whole growing season is compressed into one night, on wood long dead, with no soil, root or water.

It bore ripe almonds. In Israel the almond is the first tree to wake in the year, flowering in late winter before anything else has stirred, and its Hebrew name sounds like the Hebrew for “watching”, as the ESV note at Jeremiah 1:11 explains. So God answered Jeremiah: “I see an almond branch.” Then the LORD said to me, “You have seen well, for I am watching over my word to perform it” (Jeremiah 1:11–12). The almond pictures the God who is awake and watching over his word.

God’s chosen priest. Eleven staffs came out as they went in; one came out carrying fruit. God’s chosen priest is not the man with the most support but the one on whom life appeared where there was none.

One empty tomb. The New Testament never mentions the budding staff when it speaks of Jesus’ priesthood, but it argues along the same line. Christ was declared to be the Son of God in power… by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4), and he is a priest not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life (Hebrews 7:16). Twelve dead sticks and one that blossomed; a hillside of graves and one empty tomb. God settles who may stand between him and us in only one way, and he has now done it twice.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses brought out all the staffs from before the LORD to all the people of Israel. And they looked, and each man took his staff. And the LORD said to Moses, "Put back the staff of Aaron before the testimony, to be kept as a sign for the rebels, that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die." Thus did Moses; as the LORD commanded him, so he did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All Israel sees the verdict, and Aaron’s staff is kept before the testimony as a warning, so that no one else need die learning the lesson.

And they looked. Picture that morning. Twelve chiefs collect their staffs before the nation, eleven taking back the same dry stick they handed in, while one man walks away holding a branch in blossom. There was no verdict to announce and no argument to have. They looked, and it was over.

To be kept as a sign for the rebels. Then God makes the sign a permanent fixture before the testimony, and the reason given is kindness: lest they die. The memorial is not a trophy for Aaron; it exists so that nobody else will have to learn this lesson the way Korah did.

What became of the staff? Hebrews 9:4 lists it with the tablets and the jar of manna in the ark, but by Solomon’s day only the tablets were inside (1 Kings 8:9). It was kept with the ark in the wilderness and had probably been lost or removed by Solomon’s time.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel said to Moses, "Behold, we perish, we are undone, we are all undone. Everyone who comes near, who comes near to the tabernacle of the LORD, shall die. Are we all to perish?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At last the people grasp that coming near the holy God means death, but they have learned only half the lesson; chapter 18 gives the other half.

We are all undone. After the earth opening, the fire, the plague and the blossoming staff, the lesson of God’s holiness has landed as despair. They have it half right, and it is the terrifying half. Many who take God seriously stop just here: they know their sin and his holiness, and rightly conclude that they are undone.

What they missed. They have not yet understood that the whole point of the priesthood is that somebody may come near on their behalf. They are standing outside a tent that exists precisely so that they will not perish. That is not the end of the matter. Chapter 18 opens with God telling Aaron what the priest is for: You and your sons… shall bear iniquity connected with the sanctuary (18:1).

The coming near they dreaded. Israel cried that everyone who comes near will die. It was true. So a Priest, Jesus, came near, and did die, and now the invitation reads: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16). The coming near that they dreaded is now the gospel’s welcome.

17.theology:
Resurrection Vindicates the Priest. The question of who may stand between God and his people is settled by life from the dead, not by ability or votes. That is how God settles it again for Christ, whose priesthood rests on the power of an indestructible life.

The Almond, Herald of Life. The first tree to wake in the year marks the true priest as the one God brings to life: the High Priest who, having died, lives forever to make intercession.

The Terror of Holiness and the Need for a Mediator. The people cry, “Are we all to perish?” Apart from a mediator, to approach the holy God is death. Their dread shows why the gospel is needed: through the appointed priest, supremely Christ, we draw near and live.
17.examples: Israel trembled before the holy God and saw only that coming near meant death. If you know your sin well enough to feel the same, you have learned half the lesson. The other half is that your High Priest lives forever to intercede for you, so you may draw near to the holy God not in terror but in confidence.

keyVerse.quote: And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this promise: God, not the people, chooses who may come near him, and he will make the choice plain by bringing life out of dead wood (v. 8). It points to the Priest whom God chose and confirmed by raising him from the dead.

17.reflection:
Korah tried to seize the priesthood; Aaron received it as a gift (vv. 1–5; 18:7). Where are we tempted to grasp at standing, before God or in the church, instead of receiving what he gives?

God settled the question by bringing life out of a dead staff (v. 8). How does Christ’s resurrection settle who may stand between us and God, and why does that give assurance to people who know they are weak?

Aaron’s staff was kept “lest they die” (v. 10). What reminders has God given us of his grace and his holiness, and how do they protect us?

The people cried, “Are we all to perish?” (v. 13). How would you speak to someone who sees God’s holiness and their own sin clearly but cannot yet see a way to come near?

18.title: Duties of Priests and Levites: ‘I Am Your Portion’
18.text: <sup>1</sup>So the LORD said to Aaron, "You and your sons and your father's house with you shall bear iniquity connected with the sanctuary, and you and your sons with you shall bear iniquity connected with your priesthood.<sup>2</sup>And with you bring your brothers also, the tribe of Levi, the tribe of your father, that they may join you and minister to you while you and your sons with you are before the tent of the testimony.<sup>3</sup>They shall keep guard over you and over the whole tent, but shall not come near to the vessels of the sanctuary or to the altar lest they, and you, die.<sup>4</sup>They shall join you and keep guard over the tent of meeting for all the service of the tent, and no outsider shall come near you.<sup>5</sup>And you shall keep guard over the sanctuary and over the altar, that there may never again be wrath on the people of Israel.<sup>6</sup>And behold, I have taken your brothers the Levites from among the people of Israel. They are a gift to you, given to the LORD, to do the service of the tent of meeting.<sup>7</sup>And you and your sons with you shall guard your priesthood for all that concerns the altar and that is within the veil; and you shall serve. I give your priesthood as a gift, and any outsider who comes near shall be put to death."<sup>8</sup>Then the LORD spoke to Aaron, "Behold, I have given you charge of the contributions made to me, all the consecrated things of the people of Israel. I have given them to you as a portion and to your sons as a perpetual due.<sup>9</sup>This shall be yours of the most holy things, reserved from the fire: every offering of theirs, every grain offering of theirs and every sin offering of theirs and every guilt offering of theirs, which they render to me, shall be most holy to you and to your sons.<sup>10</sup>In a most holy place shall you eat it. Every male may eat it; it is holy to you.<sup>11</sup>This also is yours: the contribution of their gift, all the wave offerings of the people of Israel. I have given them to you, and to your sons and daughters with you, as a perpetual due. Everyone who is clean in your house may eat it.<sup>12</sup>All the best of the oil and all the best of the wine and of the grain, the firstfruits of what they give to the LORD, I give to you.<sup>13</sup>The first ripe fruits of all that is in their land, which they bring to the LORD, shall be yours. Everyone who is clean in your house may eat it.<sup>14</sup>Every devoted thing in Israel shall be yours.<sup>15</sup>Everything that opens the womb of all flesh, whether man or beast, which they offer to the LORD, shall be yours. Nevertheless, the firstborn of man you shall redeem, and the firstborn of unclean animals you shall redeem.<sup>16</sup>And their redemption price (at a month old you shall redeem them) you shall fix at five shekels in silver, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, which is twenty gerahs.<sup>17</sup>But the firstborn of a cow, or the firstborn of a sheep, or the firstborn of a goat, you shall not redeem; they are holy. You shall sprinkle their blood on the altar and shall burn their fat as a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>18</sup>But their flesh shall be yours, as the breast that is waved and as the right thigh are yours.<sup>19</sup>All the holy contributions that the people of Israel present to the LORD I give to you, and to your sons and daughters with you, as a perpetual due. It is a covenant of salt forever before the LORD for you and for your offspring with you."<sup>20</sup>And the LORD said to Aaron, "You shall have no inheritance in their land, neither shall you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel.<sup>21</sup>"To the Levites I have given every tithe in Israel for an inheritance, in return for their service that they do, their service in the tent of meeting,<sup>22</sup>so that the people of Israel do not come near the tent of meeting, lest they bear sin and die.<sup>23</sup>But the Levites shall do the service of the tent of meeting, and they shall bear their iniquity. It shall be a perpetual statute throughout your generations, and among the people of Israel they shall have no inheritance.<sup>24</sup>For the tithe of the people of Israel, which they present as a contribution to the LORD, I have given to the Levites for an inheritance. Therefore I have said of them that they shall have no inheritance among the people of Israel."<sup>25</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>26</sup>"Moreover, you shall speak and say to the Levites, 'When you take from the people of Israel the tithe that I have given you from them for your inheritance, then you shall present a contribution from it to the LORD, a tithe of the tithe.<sup>27</sup>And your contribution shall be counted to you as though it were the grain of the threshing floor, and as the fullness of the winepress.<sup>28</sup>So you shall also present a contribution to the LORD from all your tithes, which you receive from the people of Israel. And from it you shall give the LORD's contribution to Aaron the priest.<sup>29</sup>Out of all the gifts to you, you shall present every contribution due to the LORD; from each its best part is to be dedicated.'<sup>30</sup>Therefore you shall say to them, 'When you have offered from it the best of it, then the rest shall be counted to the Levites as produce of the threshing floor, and as produce of the winepress.<sup>31</sup>And you may eat it in any place, you and your households, for it is your reward in return for your service in the tent of meeting.<sup>32</sup>And you shall bear no sin by reason of it, when you have contributed the best of it. But you shall not profane the holy things of the people of Israel, lest you die.'"
18.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 17 ended with the people crying, “Everyone who comes near… shall die. Are we all to perish?” (17:13). After Korah’s revolt, the plague and the budding staff, Israel finally feared God’s holiness, and had no idea how to live beside it. Chapter 18 is God’s reply, spoken directly to Aaron.

The message. God answers the people’s terror with a priesthood: the priests and Levites will stand guard at the sanctuary and carry its danger, so that “there may never again be wrath on the people of Israel” (v. 5). Those who carry this burden own no land; they live on what the people give to God, and God himself is their portion. Coming near God is possible because he appoints someone to bear the risk, and having God is better than having land.

Why it was said. A people who had just buried thousands needed to know whether worship could go on without more death (see the introduction). They also needed to know how the tribe set apart for the tent would live once the land was divided among the others.

How the chapter makes its case. God charges Aaron and his sons to bear iniquity connected with the sanctuary, gives them the Levites as helpers and guards, and calls the priesthood itself a gift (vv. 1–7). He then provides for the priests from the holy offerings, the firstfruits and the firstborn, sealed as “a covenant of salt forever” (vv. 8–19). At the centre he tells Aaron, “I am your portion and your inheritance” (v. 20). The Levites receive Israel’s tithe in return for their service (vv. 21–24), and they in turn must give the best tenth of it to God (vv. 25–32).

Where it leads. By pattern, and the New Testament draws it. Aaron was appointed to “bear iniquity” so that the people might live; Christ “himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). The priesthood was a gift no one could seize, and Christ too “did not exalt himself to be made a high priest” (Hebrews 5:5). Aaron’s line died and was replaced, but Christ “holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:24). And the landless priest points to the Son of Man who had “nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20), and through whom God becomes the portion of all his people.

For us. We may come near to God without fear, because the Priest has carried the danger for us. Those who teach the gospel should be supported by those they serve (1 Corinthians 9:14), and those who are supported should give too. Above all, ask whether God himself is your portion, the one inheritance no loss can take.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Charge of the Priests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the people’s fear of dying at the sanctuary by appointing someone to carry its danger. Aaron and his sons are to bear iniquity connected with the sanctuary and the priesthood, answerable for anything that goes wrong in the holy things (v. 1). Their brothers the Levites are joined to them to guard the tent, but must not touch the holy vessels or the altar (vv. 2–4). The aim is stated plainly: that there may never again be wrath on Israel (v. 5). The Levites are a gift to the priests, and the priesthood itself is a gift from God; any outsider who comes near shall die (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness is still dangerous, but God has placed that danger on appointed shoulders rather than on the whole people.
verseByVerse.examples: The fear of coming near to God is not answered by pretending he is safe, but by a priest he provides.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD said to Aaron, "You and your sons and your father's house with you shall bear iniquity connected with the sanctuary, and you and your sons with you shall bear iniquity connected with your priesthood. And with you bring your brothers also, the tribe of Levi, the tribe of your father, that they may join you and minister to you while you and your sons with you are before the tent of the testimony. They shall keep guard over you and over the whole tent, but shall not come near to the vessels of the sanctuary or to the altar lest they, and you, die. They shall join you and keep guard over the tent of meeting for all the service of the tent, and no outsider shall come near you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers Israel’s terror by appointing Aaron’s family to carry the danger of the sanctuary, so that the people need not die.

So the LORD said to Aaron. Israel has just cried out that anyone who comes near the tabernacle will die (17:13). God’s answer is not reassurance. It is an appointment.

Bear iniquity. To bear iniquity means to carry the liability, to be the one held answerable when something goes wrong. The danger of the holy place is real, and God has assigned it to someone: Aaron will carry it. That is the priesthood in one sentence, and it is not a promotion but a transfer of risk. Every arrangement that follows, with the Levites guarding the tent, exists so that the weight falls on named men instead of on the congregation.

He himself bore our sins. That is why the New Testament can describe Christ’s work in exactly these terms: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). Aaron carried the liability for what went wrong at the sanctuary; there is a Priest who carried it for everything that has ever gone wrong in his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall keep guard over the sanctuary and over the altar, that there may never again be wrath on the people of Israel. And behold, I have taken your brothers the Levites from among the people of Israel. They are a gift to you, given to the LORD, to do the service of the tent of meeting. And you and your sons with you shall guard your priesthood for all that concerns the altar and that is within the veil; and you shall serve. I give your priesthood as a gift, and any outsider who comes near shall be put to death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priesthood exists so that wrath never again breaks out on Israel, and it is God’s gift, which no one may seize.

That there may never again be wrath. Never again points back to the 14,700 graves of chapter 16. This whole arrangement is God’s answer to a disaster.

I give your priesthood as a gift. Then a startling phrase, used twice in three verses: the Levites are a gift to you, and I give your priesthood as a gift. The very thing Korah wanted to seize can only be given. Nobody in Israel could take the priesthood, and nobody had to earn it; Aaron did not qualify for it and was not consulted about it.

Christ did not exalt himself. Hebrews makes exactly this argument: no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was. So also Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest, but was appointed by him who said to him, “You are my Son” (Hebrews 5:4–5). The rule that killed Korah is the rule the Son of God submitted to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–19 — The Provision for the Priests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The family that guards God’s house is fed from God’s table. Because the priests receive no land, God gives them charge of the holy contributions: the most holy portions of grain, sin and guilt offerings, to be eaten in a holy place by the priests (vv. 8–10), and the wave offerings, the best of the oil, wine and grain, the firstfruits and every devoted thing, for their households (vv. 11–14). Every firstborn belongs to the LORD; sons and unclean animals are redeemed for five shekels, while the firstborn of cattle, sheep and goats are sacrificed and their meat given to the priests (vv. 15–18). The whole arrangement is sealed as a covenant of salt forever (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: God provides for those who serve him through the gifts of his people.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation’s giving is one of the ordinary ways God keeps his servants fed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD spoke to Aaron, "Behold, I have given you charge of the contributions made to me, all the consecrated things of the people of Israel. I have given them to you as a portion and to your sons as a perpetual due. This shall be yours of the most holy things, reserved from the fire: every offering of theirs, every grain offering of theirs and every sin offering of theirs and every guilt offering of theirs, which they render to me, shall be most holy to you and to your sons. In a most holy place shall you eat it. Every male may eat it; it is holy to you. This also is yours: the contribution of their gift, all the wave offerings of the people of Israel. I have given them to you, and to your sons and daughters with you, as a perpetual due. Everyone who is clean in your house may eat it. All the best of the oil and all the best of the wine and of the grain, the firstfruits of what they give to the LORD, I give to you. The first ripe fruits of all that is in their land, which they bring to the LORD, shall be yours. Everyone who is clean in your house may eat it. Every devoted thing in Israel shall be yours.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests own no land, so God feeds them from what Israel gives to him.

I have given them to you as a portion. The grain, sin, guilt and wave offerings, the firstfruits, and every devoted thing (whatever had been given over to God irrevocably) all become food on the priest’s table. And the standard is the best of the oil, the wine and the grain: not the surplus, but the top of the harvest.

Fed by others’ worship. A priest ate what had been given to God; his dinner was somebody else’s act of worship. If Israel stopped bringing offerings the priests went hungry, which tied the nation’s spiritual health to the survival of the men who served it.

Paul applies it. Paul applies this arrangement to Christian ministers without embarrassment: Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings? In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:13–14). On the apostle’s reading, a congregation that pays its pastor is making the same provision God made for Aaron.

verseByVerse.quote: Everything that opens the womb of all flesh, whether man or beast, which they offer to the LORD, shall be yours. Nevertheless, the firstborn of man you shall redeem, and the firstborn of unclean animals you shall redeem. And their redemption price (at a month old you shall redeem them) you shall fix at five shekels in silver, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, which is twenty gerahs. But the firstborn of a cow, or the firstborn of a sheep, or the firstborn of a goat, you shall not redeem; they are holy. You shall sprinkle their blood on the altar and shall burn their fat as a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. But their flesh shall be yours, as the breast that is waved and as the right thigh are yours. All the holy contributions that the people of Israel present to the LORD I give to you, and to your sons and daughters with you, as a perpetual due. It is a covenant of salt forever before the LORD for you and for your offspring with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every firstborn belongs to God, and the whole provision for the priests is sealed as a lasting covenant.

The firstborn of man you shall redeem. Israel’s firstborn sons belonged to God because he had spared them on the night of the Passover (Exodus 13:2, 15), so each was bought back for five shekels, and unclean animals were redeemed in the same way. Every family with a firstborn son carried a reminder that its child was alive because a lamb had died.

A covenant of salt forever. Salt keeps things from rotting; it was added to every grain offering (Leviticus 2:13) and used across the ancient Near East to seal agreements meant to last. God is telling a landless family that this arrangement will outlast every harvest.

He continues forever. That “forever” held as long as the Levitical order stood, an order Hebrews says was always waiting for a better one. Its priests died and were replaced, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever (Hebrews 7:24). The covenant of salt kept a mortal family fed at the altar; the Son of God is the Priest whose office never ends at all.

Uncertain wording. “Covenant of salt” is never explained; elsewhere it describes only God’s covenant with David (2 Chronicles 13:5), and Leviticus 2:13 speaks of “the salt of the covenant”. Since salt preserves and was shared at meals that sealed agreements, it most likely means a binding, lasting covenant, but the exact custom behind it is unknown.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–32 — ‘I Am Your Portion’ and the Levites’ Tithe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tribe without land has the LORD himself. Aaron is to have no inheritance among the tribes, because God is his portion (v. 20). The Levites receive Israel’s tithe in return for their service at the tent, so that ordinary Israelites need not come near and die; they bear the risk and have no land (vv. 21–24). Then God tells the Levites to give a tenth of that tithe, taken from its best part, to Aaron the priest (vv. 25–29). Once they have given it, the rest is their honest wage, to be eaten anywhere, but they must not treat the holy things carelessly, or they will die (vv. 30–32).
verseByVerse.theology: The tribe with no fields is given the greatest possession of all.
verseByVerse.examples: Whatever a believer lacks on earth, God himself cannot be taken away.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Aaron, "You shall have no inheritance in their land, neither shall you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel. "To the Levites I have given every tithe in Israel for an inheritance, in return for their service that they do, their service in the tent of meeting, so that the people of Israel do not come near the tent of meeting, lest they bear sin and die. But the Levites shall do the service of the tent of meeting, and they shall bear their iniquity. It shall be a perpetual statute throughout your generations, and among the people of Israel they shall have no inheritance. For the tithe of the people of Israel, which they present as a contribution to the LORD, I have given to the Levites for an inheritance. Therefore I have said of them that they shall have no inheritance among the people of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aaron’s family will own no land in Israel, because the LORD himself is their portion; the Levites live on the tithe.

You shall have no inheritance in their land. Picture the day this came true. Eleven tribes walk away holding a map: this valley, that ridge, the boundary stone with a grandfather’s name on it. Levi is given only towns to live in, scattered among the others (35:1–8), and no field to leave to a son. By every visible measure they got the worst of the settlement, and the text says so twice: no inheritance… no portion.

I am your portion. Then the exchange, the sentence the chapter has been building toward. Everything the other tribes received, God had made. Levi received God.

Would it be heaven? Suppose you were given everything you have ever wanted, health restored, debts cleared, the people you have buried given back, and God himself were not there. Would that be heaven? Asaph reached the right answer after nearly losing his faith over the prosperity of the wicked: Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever (Psalm 73:25–26).

A portion that cannot be taken. Every acre the other tribes received could be taken from them, and eventually was, by drought, debt, Assyria and time. Levi held the only inheritance in Israel that no invading army could reach.

Does the tithe bind Christians today? Israel’s tithes supported the Levites and the worship of a nation under God’s law, and they belonged to that order. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and it calls churches to support those who teach them (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14). Many believers find a tenth a good place to start; it is not a ceiling, and it is not a debt.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Moreover, you shall speak and say to the Levites, 'When you take from the people of Israel the tithe that I have given you from them for your inheritance, then you shall present a contribution from it to the LORD, a tithe of the tithe. And your contribution shall be counted to you as though it were the grain of the threshing floor, and as the fullness of the winepress. So you shall also present a contribution to the LORD from all your tithes, which you receive from the people of Israel. And from it you shall give the LORD's contribution to Aaron the priest. Out of all the gifts to you, you shall present every contribution due to the LORD; from each its best part is to be dedicated.' Therefore you shall say to them, 'When you have offered from it the best of it, then the rest shall be counted to the Levites as produce of the threshing floor, and as produce of the winepress. And you may eat it in any place, you and your households, for it is your reward in return for your service in the tent of meeting. And you shall bear no sin by reason of it, when you have contributed the best of it. But you shall not profane the holy things of the people of Israel, lest you die.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the Levites, who live on the people’s tithe, must give God the best tenth of it, and must never let holy things become common.

A tithe of the tithe. The last provision is the most searching: the Levites must tithe the tithe they live on, from its best part, not a tenth of whatever was hardest to eat.
