The supported must give. A Levite could have concluded that his whole life was already a contribution and the tithe was somebody else’s duty. God does not allow that reasoning. The man who lives off the offerings still brings one, because everything he has was first given to him.

Lest you die. Then the closing warning. A priest could grow so used to holy things that they became merely his supper, and the men closest to the altar are the ones warned about it. No minister guards against that perfectly. The way back for one who has grown cold is the mercy he handles every week, offered by the Priest who never once treated the holy things lightly, and the Spirit who first gave him a heart for them can rekindle it.

The chapter’s answer. Chapter 17 ended with a nation crying Are we all to perish? Chapter 18 answers in two parts: a priest will bear the liability, so that the people may live; and that priest will own nothing on earth, because he has God. That is exactly what the true Priest turned out to be like: Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20).

18.theology:
The Mediators Bear the Danger of Holiness. God does not make himself less holy to calm his people’s fear; he appoints someone to carry the risk for them. That pattern is fulfilled in Christ, who took the full danger of holiness upon himself.

Those Who Serve the Altar Live from the Altar. The landless priests and Levites live on the best of the offerings, and Paul draws the same line for gospel ministry: God’s people support those who serve them spiritually.

God himself the Portion. The landless priests possess the LORD, and so are richer than all the landed tribes. In Christ this becomes the inheritance of every believer: not merely God’s gifts but God himself.
18.examples: Christ has borne the danger of holiness and the weight of your sin, so you may draw near and live. Out of what he has given you, and by the Spirit who makes a stingy heart generous, support those who minister God’s word among you. And treasure your true inheritance: not merely God’s gifts, but God himself, “my portion forever.”

keyVerse.quote: I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter builds to this sentence. The tribe that received no fields received God himself, an inheritance no drought or army could take. The psalmists made the words their own (Psalm 16:5; 73:26), and in Christ every believer may say them.

18.reflection:
Aaron was appointed to “bear iniquity” so the people would not die (vv. 1–5). How does seeing Christ as the one who carried that danger change the way you approach God in prayer and worship?

The priesthood was “a gift” (v. 7), not something to be seized, as Korah tried to do. What does it look like to receive ministry and calling in the church as God’s gift rather than as a right or a prize?

God told Aaron, “I am your portion” (v. 20). If you lost the things you count as your inheritance, what would be left? How can we learn to want God more than his gifts?

Even the Levites, who lived on others’ giving, were to give the best of what they received (vv. 25–32). How does this shape the way we think about our own giving, and about supporting those who teach us?

19.title: The Red Heifer: The Paradox of Purification
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,<sup>2</sup>"This is the statute of the law that the LORD has commanded: Tell the people of Israel to bring you a red heifer without defect, in which there is no blemish, and on which a yoke has never come.<sup>3</sup>And you shall give it to Eleazar the priest, and it shall be taken outside the camp and slaughtered before him.<sup>4</sup>And Eleazar the priest shall take some of its blood with his finger, and sprinkle some of its blood toward the front of the tent of meeting seven times.<sup>5</sup>And the heifer shall be burned in his sight. Its skin, its flesh, and its blood, with its dung, shall be burned.<sup>6</sup>And the priest shall take cedarwood and hyssop and scarlet yarn, and throw them into the fire burning the heifer.<sup>7</sup>Then the priest shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and afterward he may come into the camp. But the priest shall be unclean until evening.<sup>8</sup>The one who burns the heifer shall wash his clothes in water and bathe his body in water and shall be unclean until evening.<sup>9</sup>And a man who is clean shall gather up the ashes of the heifer and deposit them outside the camp in a clean place. And they shall be kept for the water for impurity for the congregation of the people of Israel; it is a sin offering.<sup>10</sup>And the one who gathers the ashes of the heifer shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening. And this shall be a perpetual statute for the people of Israel, and for the stranger who sojourns among them.<sup>11</sup>"Whoever touches the dead body of any person shall be unclean seven days.<sup>12</sup>He shall cleanse himself with the water on the third day and on the seventh day, and so be clean. But if he does not cleanse himself on the third day and on the seventh day, he will not become clean.<sup>13</sup>Whoever touches a dead person, the body of anyone who has died, and does not cleanse himself, defiles the tabernacle of the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from Israel; because the water for impurity was not thrown on him, he shall be unclean. His uncleanness is still on him.<sup>14</sup>"This is the law when someone dies in a tent: everyone who comes into the tent and everyone who is in the tent shall be unclean seven days.<sup>15</sup>And every open vessel that has no cover fastened on it is unclean.<sup>16</sup>Whoever in the open field touches someone who was killed with a sword or who died naturally, or touches a human bone or a grave, shall be unclean seven days.<sup>17</sup>For the unclean they shall take some ashes of the burnt sin offering, and fresh water shall be added in a vessel.<sup>18</sup>Then a clean person shall take hyssop and dip it in the water and sprinkle it on the tent and on all the furnishings and on the persons who were there and on whoever touched the bone, or the slain or the dead or the grave.<sup>19</sup>And the clean person shall sprinkle it on the unclean on the third day and on the seventh day. Thus on the seventh day he shall cleanse him, and he shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water, and at evening he shall be clean.<sup>20</sup>"If the man who is unclean does not cleanse himself, that person shall be cut off from the midst of the assembly, since he has defiled the sanctuary of the LORD. Because the water for impurity has not been thrown on him, he is unclean.<sup>21</sup>And it shall be a statute forever for them. The one who sprinkles the water for impurity shall wash his clothes, and the one who touches the water for impurity shall be unclean until evening.<sup>22</sup>And whatever the unclean person touches shall be unclean, and anyone who touches it shall be unclean until evening."
19.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 16 to 18 have dealt with the danger of coming near the holy God and the priesthood he appointed to carry it. Now, in a wilderness where a whole sentenced generation is dying, God turns to the most common defilement of all: contact with death.

The message. Death defiles, and God provides the cleansing. A red heifer, without blemish and never yoked, is burned outside the camp, and its ashes, mixed with fresh water, are sprinkled on anyone made unclean by a corpse. The remedy is always available, but it must be received: whoever refuses it stays unclean and is cut off. And the remedy carries a riddle: the water that cleanses the unclean makes unclean the clean people who prepare and apply it.

Why it was said. After the sentence at Kadesh (chapter 14) and the plague of chapter 16, Israel was walking through what was in effect a rolling graveyard (see the introduction). Every family would touch death again and again, and needed a way back into the worship of God.

How the chapter makes its case. The heifer is slaughtered outside the camp, its blood sprinkled toward the tent and the whole animal burned with cedarwood, hyssop and scarlet yarn; everyone who handles it becomes unclean (vv. 1–8). Its ashes are kept in a clean place as a standing sin offering for Israel and for the foreigner among them (vv. 9–10). Anyone who touches a dead body is unclean for seven days and must be sprinkled on the third and seventh days, or be cut off (vv. 11–13). The law reaches the tent, the open field, a bone or a grave, and a clean person must sprinkle the unclean (vv. 14–19). It closes with the penalty for refusing and the riddle that the water defiles its handlers (vv. 20–22).

Where it leads. By pattern, and Hebrews draws it. If “the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer” purified the flesh, “how much more will the blood of Christ… purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Hebrews 9:13–14). The heifer died outside the camp, and “Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). The riddle of the clean made unclean so that the unclean may be clean is answered at the cross: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

For us. Death is not natural or neutral; it is the wage of sin, and we cannot wash ourselves clean of it or of the sins we never noticed. But the cleansing Christ provides is never used up, and it is offered to insiders and outsiders alike. The only way to stay unclean is to refuse it.
19.theology:
Death and defilement. The law treats death as the great contaminator, never as something neutral, and provides a way for those it has touched to stay near the living God.

The paradox of substitution. Whoever prepares the cleansing is made unclean by it, a faint picture of Christ, the sinless one who took our sin on himself.

Cleansing of the conscience. The heifer’s ashes made the body outwardly clean; the blood of Christ purifies the conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Heb 9:13–14).
19.examples: If you carry a stain you cannot wash off, whether from what you have done or from what has been done around you, Christ has already gone outside the gate and taken that defilement on himself. You do not have to make yourself clean before you come; come, and be made clean.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God provides, in a wilderness full of graves, a remedy for the defilement of death, and the remedy costs those who prepare it. A red heifer without defect, never yoked, is taken outside the camp and slaughtered before Eleazar the priest, who sprinkles its blood seven times toward the tent of meeting (vv. 1–4). The whole animal is burned, with cedarwood, hyssop and scarlet yarn thrown into the fire (vv. 5–6). The priest and the man who burns it become unclean until evening (vv. 7–8). A clean man gathers the ashes into a clean place outside the camp, where they are kept for the water for impurity, a standing sin offering for Israel and for the stranger among them (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not leave his people helpless in a world full of death: he provides one cleansing, made once and kept in store for all who need it.
verseByVerse.examples: A people surrounded by death had a God-given way back to worship, and so do we.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, "This is the statute of the law that the LORD has commanded: Tell the people of Israel to bring you a red heifer without defect, in which there is no blemish, and on which a yoke has never come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God appoints a spotless, never-yoked red heifer as the source of cleansing: a strange rite that poses a question it cannot answer.

The statute of the law. Jewish tradition has always admitted the strangeness of what follows; the rabbis classed the red heifer as the commandment whose reason God kept to himself, and applied to it Solomon’s confession, I said, “I will be wise,” but it was far from me (Ecclesiastes 7:23).

A red heifer without defect. It is to be red, perhaps because that is the colour of blood, and without defect, as every sacrifice had to be. Then a requirement almost never made: on which a yoke has never come. Scripture asks for an animal that has never worked only at a few of its gravest moments: the heifer killed when a murder is unsolved (Deuteronomy 21:3), and later the cows that carried the ark home (1 Samuel 6:7). It marks something set apart from ordinary use altogether.

On which a yoke has never come. Every other beast in Israel spent its life pulling somebody’s plough; this one had never worn a collar. The law does not explain the detail, and we should not treat it as a secret code. But it is a fitting picture of the One who offered himself without blemish to God (Hebrews 9:14), never harnessed to sin as every other son of Adam has been. Only a pure offering can cleanse.

Is the red heifer still relevant? Its ashes cleansed from contact with death, and Hebrews says it purified only the flesh, while the blood of Christ purifies the conscience (Hebrews 9:13–14). Some who expect a rebuilt temple look for a new red heifer, but the shadow is fulfilled; it is not to be revived.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall give it to Eleazar the priest, and it shall be taken outside the camp and slaughtered before him. And Eleazar the priest shall take some of its blood with his finger, and sprinkle some of its blood toward the front of the tent of meeting seven times. And the heifer shall be burned in his sight. Its skin, its flesh, and its blood, with its dung, shall be burned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heifer dies outside the camp, its blood sprinkled toward the tent: rejected by the camp yet accepted by God, as Christ would be.

You shall give it to Eleazar the priest. The animal is handed not to Aaron but to his son Eleazar, probably because what is about to happen defiles the man who does it, and the high priest must not be defiled.

Taken outside the camp. Not at the altar, but out past the last tent, where the rubbish went and the unclean lived: the place that meant rejection, and the detail the New Testament seizes on. Yet the blood is sprinkled toward the front of the tent of meeting seven times, seven being the number of completeness. The priest stands on waste ground, flicking blood toward a tabernacle he is not entering. The sacrifice is rejected by the camp and accepted by heaven at the same moment.

The heifer shall be burned. The whole animal goes into the fire; nothing is eaten or saved for the priests. Hebrews makes the point from the Day of Atonement, whose sin offerings were also burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27), and the red heifer shares the pattern: the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:11–12). Golgotha was outside the city wall; they put him where they put the heifer. He was not cast out by accident; the law had been drawing the map of that hill for fourteen hundred years.

verseByVerse.quote: And the priest shall take cedarwood and hyssop and scarlet yarn, and throw them into the fire burning the heifer. Then the priest shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and afterward he may come into the camp. But the priest shall be unclean until evening. The one who burns the heifer shall wash his clothes in water and bathe his body in water and shall be unclean until evening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s whole cleansing kit is burned into the ash, and the men who prepare it are left unclean: cleansing costs the one who provides it.

Cedarwood and hyssop and scarlet yarn. These are not decoration but the cleansing kit of the whole law: the same three items cleanse a healed leper (Leviticus 14:4–6), hyssop painted lamb’s blood on the doorposts in Egypt (Exodus 12:22), and the same plant was lifted to Jesus’ lips at the cross (John 19:29). Cedar may stand for what resists decay, and scarlet for blood. Everything Israel had for making foul things clean is burned into this one ash, and every sprinkling for generations will carry the whole of that sacrifice in it.

The priest shall be unclean until evening. Then the sentence that turns the chapter over. So is the man who burned the carcass. They have done exactly what God commanded, and it has left them unclean for the rest of the day.

In everyday life. Think of the last costly thing you did for someone else’s good: the mess you cleaned up that you had not made, the relative you cared for at the end. Some of it stuck to you. Cleansing is never free for the one who provides it. Somebody stands outside the camp until evening so that somebody else may go in.

verseByVerse.quote: And a man who is clean shall gather up the ashes of the heifer and deposit them outside the camp in a clean place. And they shall be kept for the water for impurity for the congregation of the people of Israel; it is a sin offering. And the one who gathers the ashes of the heifer shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening. And this shall be a perpetual statute for the people of Israel, and for the stranger who sojourns among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ashes are stored as a sin offering that never runs out, for Israelite and foreigner alike.

It is a sin offering. Not “it was”. The heifer is dead and burned; the jar of grey ash is the sin offering still, one animal killed once, its value held in reserve for whoever needs it, generation after generation.

A single offering, never used up. No other sacrifice in the law works like that, and it is exactly how the gospel works. Christ was offered once, and that one offering has been applied to sinners every day since, and is not used up. For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14).

Why was the provision needed permanently? Chapter 14 had sentenced a generation to die in the wilderness: six hundred thousand men over thirty-eight years is something like forty funerals a day. Israel was walking through a rolling graveyard.

The stranger who sojourns among them. The foreigner got the same water as the Israelite. God did not make a cleansing for insiders only, and he never has; Israel itself had been a sojourner in Egypt when God took it up (Deuteronomy 10:19).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew for “sin offering” is related to a verb meaning “to cleanse from sin”, and many scholars prefer “purification offering”, since it dealt with defilement as well as guilt. The point stands either way: this rite removes what separates people from God. “Water for impurity” is literally “water of impurity”, water for removing it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Anyone who touches death must be cleansed, and whoever refuses the cleansing stays cut off. Touching a dead body makes a person unclean for seven days; he must be cleansed on the third and seventh days, and if he will not, he defiles the tabernacle and is cut off (vv. 11–13). The law reaches the tent where someone dies, every open vessel in it, and the open field, with its slain, its bones and its graves (vv. 14–16). Ashes and fresh water are mixed, and a clean person sprinkles the unclean with hyssop (vv. 17–19). The chapter ends by repeating the warning against refusing and the riddle that the water defiles those who handle it (vv. 20–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The sprinkled water points to “the sprinkled blood” of Christ (Hebrews 12:24; 1 Pet 1:2), a cleansing freely given that must be personally received by faith.
verseByVerse.examples: The invitation stands: “Let us draw near... with our hearts sprinkled clean” (Hebrews 10:22). A provision made is not yet a pardon received, and the way to receive it is simply to come.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever touches the dead body of any person shall be unclean seven days. He shall cleanse himself with the water on the third day and on the seventh day, and so be clean. But if he does not cleanse himself on the third day and on the seventh day, he will not become clean. Whoever touches a dead person, the body of anyone who has died, and does not cleanse himself, defiles the tabernacle of the LORD, and that person shall be cut off from Israel; because the water for impurity was not thrown on him, he shall be unclean. His uncleanness is still on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Touching the dead defiles for a week, not because burial is sin but because death is sin’s mark; whoever refuses cleansing is cut off.

Whoever touches the dead body. Here is the defilement the chapter was written for: a full week shut out from the worship of God, with cleansing on the third day and the seventh, or no cleansing at all.

Was it a sin to bury your father? It was not, and the distinction matters. Sin is guilt and needs forgiveness; uncleanness is contamination and needs washing. Burying your mother was love, and somebody had to do it. But the law would not let Israel walk away from a graveside as though nothing had happened, because it was teaching one lesson in the body: death is not natural, not neutral, and not fine. It is the wage of sin (Romans 6:23) and the mark of a wrecked world. Every funeral cost a week, so that nobody could quietly get used to burying people.

Defiles the tabernacle of the LORD. The warning in verse 13 is heavier than it looks. The man who will not be cleansed carries his uncleanness to the sanctuary itself, and he is cut off. To refuse the cleansing was sin, and sin is never as private as it feels.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the law when someone dies in a tent: everyone who comes into the tent and everyone who is in the tent shall be unclean seven days. And every open vessel that has no cover fastened on it is unclean. Whoever in the open field touches someone who was killed with a sword or who died naturally, or touches a human bone or a grave, shall be unclean seven days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Death’s defilement spreads to the room and the open field, so that people are defiled by what they never chose or noticed.

Every open vessel. The law works outward from the body, and the detail is strangely tender: even every open vessel in the tent is unclean. Anyone who has cleared out a house after a death knows the half-drunk tea, the reading glasses on the arm of the chair. Death does not stay in the body. It seeps into the room.

A human bone or a grave. Then verse 16 goes out of doors, to the open field: an unmarked grave you walked across without knowing it was there. You could be defiled by something you never chose, never saw, and would never remember.

Sins we cannot list. That is our real condition too. We may know the sins we intended. What we cannot list is what we have walked through: the words absorbed, the habits caught, the damage done to people we never learned about. David prayed the only sane prayer about it: Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults (Psalm 19:12). Israel needed a cleansing that reached further than her memory. So do we.

verseByVerse.quote: For the unclean they shall take some ashes of the burnt sin offering, and fresh water shall be added in a vessel. Then a clean person shall take hyssop and dip it in the water and sprinkle it on the tent and on all the furnishings and on the persons who were there and on whoever touched the bone, or the slain or the dead or the grave. And the clean person shall sprinkle it on the unclean on the third day and on the seventh day. Thus on the seventh day he shall cleanse him, and he shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water, and at evening he shall be clean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cleansing joins a sacrifice’s ashes with living water, and a clean person must apply it, because the unclean cannot cleanse themselves.

Fresh water shall be added. The water is literally “living water”, from a spring, not a cistern. The death of the heifer and the life of the spring are mixed in one bowl. A sacrifice that died and water that is alive: every defiled sinner needs both. Christ gives both, for he is at once the offering made and the one who says the water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life (John 4:14).

The clean person shall sprinkle it on the unclean. Then the point on which the chapter turns. The unclean man may not pick up the hyssop and sprinkle himself. He must wait for a clean person to come and do for him what he cannot do.

We cannot clean ourselves. That sentence rules out every religion that tells us to make ourselves clean. David, who knew the ritual, does not offer to perform it but asks God to do it to him: Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow (Psalm 51:7). It is applied on the third day and again on the seventh, and then at evening he shall be clean. The man is not left to guess whether it worked. The law names the hour when he is clean, and he is.
verseByVerse.note: “Fresh water” is literally “living water” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "If the man who is unclean does not cleanse himself, that person shall be cut off from the midst of the assembly, since he has defiled the sanctuary of the LORD. Because the water for impurity has not been thrown on him, he is unclean. And it shall be a statute forever for them. The one who sprinkles the water for impurity shall wash his clothes, and the one who touches the water for impurity shall be unclean until evening. And whatever the unclean person touches shall be unclean, and anyone who touches it shall be unclean until evening."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who refuses cleansing stays unclean within reach of the cure, and the riddle of the defiling water waits for Christ.

If the man who is unclean does not cleanse himself. The saddest verse in the chapter is about the man who simply will not come. The ashes stood ready, the spring was running, a clean man was willing. There is a way to be lost that involves nothing more dramatic than declining to be washed.

The riddle stated. Then the riddle is stated flatly: the water that makes the unclean clean makes the clean unclean. Everyone who handles it pays for it. No ritual can explain itself, and this one held a question open for fourteen centuries until a Man came who was the answer.

Life ran down his arm. He was the clean One who came to the unclean and touched them. At Nain he laid his hand on the bier of a widow’s only son, where this chapter said death’s defilement would run up his arm; instead life ran down it, and the young man sat up (Luke 7:14–15). He took a dead girl by the hand, and she rose (Mark 5:41–42). And at the last, on a hill outside the gate, the One in whom there was no blemish and who had never worn the yoke was made unclean with a world’s defilement, so that the defiled might be made clean. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). The red heifer asks how the defiled can ever be purified. The cross of Christ is the answer, and there is no other.

keyVerse.quote: And they shall be kept for the water for impurity for the congregation of the people of Israel; it is a sin offering.
keyVerse.note: One heifer, burned once, became a store of cleansing kept ready for anyone who needed it, generation after generation. Hebrews points to this rite to show what Christ’s blood does far better (Hebrews 9:13–14): offered once, it cleanses the conscience and is never used up.

19.reflection:
The law treated contact with death as defiling, even when it was an act of love like burying a parent (vv. 11–16). What does this teach about how God regards death, and how might it shape the way Christians grieve?

Everyone who prepared the cleansing water became unclean (vv. 7–10, 21). Where have you seen that helping others costs the helper something, and how does the cross show this most fully?

The unclean person could not sprinkle himself; a clean person had to do it (vv. 18–19). Why is it so hard for us to accept that we cannot make ourselves clean before God?

The man who refused the water stayed unclean while the remedy stood ready (v. 20). Why might someone today stay away from the cleansing Christ offers, and how could you speak to them about it?

20.title: Water from the Rock; the Death of Aaron: When the Mediator Fails
20.text: <sup>1</sup>And the people of Israel, the whole congregation, came into the wilderness of Zin in the first month, and the people stayed in Kadesh. And Miriam died there and was buried there.<sup>2</sup>Now there was no water for the congregation. And they assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron.<sup>3</sup>And the people quarreled with Moses and said, "Would that we had perished when our brothers perished before the LORD!<sup>4</sup>Why have you brought the assembly of the LORD into this wilderness, that we should die here, both we and our cattle?<sup>5</sup>And why have you made us come up out of Egypt to bring us to this evil place? It is no place for grain or figs or vines or pomegranates, and there is no water to drink."<sup>6</sup>Then Moses and Aaron went from the presence of the assembly to the entrance of the tent of meeting and fell on their faces. And the glory of the LORD appeared to them,<sup>7</sup>and the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>8</sup>"Take the staff, and assemble the congregation, you and Aaron your brother, and tell the rock before their eyes to yield its water. So you shall bring water out of the rock for them and give drink to the congregation and their cattle."<sup>9</sup>And Moses took the staff from before the LORD, as he commanded him.<sup>10</sup>Then Moses and Aaron gathered the assembly together before the rock, and he said to them, "Hear now, you rebels: shall we bring water for you out of this rock?"<sup>11</sup>And Moses lifted up his hand and struck the rock with his staff twice, and water came out abundantly, and the congregation drank, and their livestock.<sup>12</sup>And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Because you did not believe in me, to uphold me as holy in the eyes of the people of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them."<sup>13</sup>These are the waters of Meribah, where the people of Israel quarreled with the LORD, and through them he showed himself holy.<sup>14</sup>Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom: "Thus says your brother Israel: You know all the hardship that we have met:<sup>15</sup>how our fathers went down to Egypt, and we lived in Egypt a long time. And the Egyptians dealt harshly with us and our fathers.<sup>16</sup>And when we cried to the LORD, he heard our voice and sent an angel and brought us out of Egypt. And here we are in Kadesh, a city on the edge of your territory.<sup>17</sup>Please let us pass through your land. We will not pass through field or vineyard, or drink water from a well. We will go along the King's Highway. We will not turn aside to the right hand or to the left until we have passed through your territory."<sup>18</sup>But Edom said to him, "You shall not pass through, lest I come out with the sword against you."<sup>19</sup>And the people of Israel said to him, "We will go up by the highway, and if we drink of your water, I and my livestock, then I will pay for it. Let me only pass through on foot, nothing more."<sup>20</sup>But he said, "You shall not pass through." And Edom came out against them with a large army and with a strong force.<sup>21</sup>Thus Edom refused to give Israel passage through his territory, so Israel turned away from him.<sup>22</sup>And they journeyed from Kadesh, and the people of Israel, the whole congregation, came to Mount Hor.<sup>23</sup>And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron at Mount Hor, on the border of the land of Edom,<sup>24</sup>"Let Aaron be gathered to his people, for he shall not enter the land that I have given to the people of Israel, because you rebelled against my command at the waters of Meribah.<sup>25</sup>Take Aaron and Eleazar his son and bring them up to Mount Hor.<sup>26</sup>And strip Aaron of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son. And Aaron shall be gathered to his people and shall die there."<sup>27</sup>Moses did as the LORD commanded. And they went up Mount Hor in the sight of all the congregation.<sup>28</sup>And Moses stripped Aaron of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son. And Aaron died there on the top of the mountain. Then Moses and Eleazar came down from the mountain.<sup>29</sup>And when all the congregation saw that Aaron had perished, all the house of Israel wept for Aaron thirty days.
20.overview:
Where we are. After the laws of chapters 18 and 19, the story jumps nearly forty years. The generation sentenced at Kadesh (chapter 14) has almost died out, and Israel is back at Kadesh, on the edge of the land. It is the last year of the wandering, and a chapter heavy with loss.

The message. God is faithful to a grumbling people, and he is holy, even toward his greatest servants. He gives the thirsty crowd water in abundance, but when Moses misrepresents him before the nation, God bars him and Aaron from the land, and shows himself holy at Meribah. The best human mediators fail and die; only God’s purposes go on.

Why it was said. The new generation, about to enter the land, needed to learn that their parents’ grumbling was not the way, and that even Moses could not bring them in (see the introduction). They also needed to see that God’s promise did not depend on any one leader.

How the chapter makes its case. Miriam dies at Kadesh (v. 1). The people, short of water, quarrel with Moses in their parents’ words (vv. 2–5). Moses and Aaron fall before the LORD, and he tells them to take the staff and speak to the rock (vv. 6–8). Moses instead calls the people rebels and strikes the rock twice; water gushes out, and God declares that because they did not believe him or uphold him as holy, they will not bring the people into the land (vv. 9–13). Edom, Israel’s brother nation, refuses passage, and Israel turns away rather than fight (vv. 14–21). At Mount Hor Aaron’s garments are put on Eleazar, Aaron dies, and Israel mourns him thirty days (vv. 22–29).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Paul says “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4): struck once at Horeb, he now gives water to those who ask, and Moses’ second blow marred that picture. Moses’ failure shows that no mere man can bring God’s people home; Christ, faithful “over God’s house as a son” (Hebrews 3:6), never once failed to show his Father as holy. And Aaron’s death on the mountain shows the weakness of every earthly priest: “they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:23–24).

For us. Bring your complaints to God as lament, not against him as grumbling. If you speak for God, at home or in church, ask whether your manner shows him as he is. Do not mistake God’s blessing on your work for his approval of your heart. And when leaders fail and loved ones die, look to the Priest who lives forever and will bring his people home.
20.theology:
The smitten Rock. The rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4), struck once for sin. Moses’ second striking marred the gospel picture, though the reason God gives is Moses’ unbelief.

The holiness of God in leadership. Those who speak for God carry a weighty responsibility, because people learn what God is like from them; and even a great servant who fails is not thrown away.

The mortal priesthood. Aaron dies outside the land, his office passed on. Priests who die show by contrast the greatness of Christ, the Priest who never dies.
20.examples: The Rock has been struck once for you. Drink freely of the living water that flows from the smitten Savior, and follow the Priest who never fails and never dies.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A new generation repeats the old grumbling, and God answers with grace to the people and holiness toward his servant. Miriam dies at Kadesh (v. 1). With no water, the people quarrel with Moses and wish they had died with their brothers (vv. 2–5). Moses and Aaron go to the tent, the glory of the LORD appears, and God tells them to take the staff and speak to the rock (vv. 6–8). Moses instead rebukes the people, claims the miracle for himself and Aaron, and strikes the rock twice (vv. 9–11). Water flows in abundance, but because they did not believe God or uphold him as holy, neither brother will lead Israel into the land (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: God’s holiness matters more than any servant’s reputation, even Moses’. Yet his kindness to the thirsty does not wait on his servant’s obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: We come to our Rock not by striking but by asking, and the living water flows (John 7:37-38).

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel, the whole congregation, came into the wilderness of Zin in the first month, and the people stayed in Kadesh. And Miriam died there and was buried there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After nearly forty silent years Israel is back at Kadesh, where it refused the land, and Miriam dies.

Thirty-eight silent years. Between chapter 19 and this verse probably lie some thirty-eight years, and the Bible gives them a paragraph break. A generation grew old and died, and Scripture does not narrate it, because nothing was going anywhere.

The people stayed in Kadesh. This is where the spies came back (13:26) and the nation wept all night. Nearly four decades and several hundred miles later, Israel is camped where it started. Unbelief does not take you backwards. It takes you in a circle, and then hands you the bill.

Miriam died there. The last time we saw Miriam in a good light she was on the far shore of the Red Sea with a tambourine, leading the song: Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously (Exodus 15:20–21). Now, a grave in the wilderness of Zin. Within a year Miriam, Aaron and Moses will all be dead, and none of the three will cross the Jordan.

Uncertain wording. The verse gives the month but not the year. Since Aaron dies later in the chapter, in the fortieth year (33:38), most take this to be the fortieth year after the exodus.
verseByVerse.note: Kadesh lay on the southern edge of Canaan. This is the last year of the wilderness wanderings.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was no water for the congregation. And they assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron. And the people quarreled with Moses and said, "Would that we had perished when our brothers perished before the LORD! Why have you brought the assembly of the LORD into this wilderness, that we should die here, both we and our cattle? And why have you made us come up out of Egypt to bring us to this evil place? It is no place for grain or figs or vines or pomegranates, and there is no water to drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirsty, the new generation quarrels with Moses in their parents’ very words, turning a real need into a charge against God.

Now there was no water. The oldest crisis in the book produces the oldest reaction. They assembled themselves together against Moses, the language of a mob forming, and their words echo their parents’ at Rephidim (Exodus 17:2–3). A new generation, and an old script.

No place for grain or figs. Look at what they complain about: no place for grain or figs or vines or pomegranates. Those are the fruits the spies carried back to Kadesh (13:23). They are complaining that the wilderness is not Canaan, the land their parents refused at this very spot. They want the fruit without the crossing.

How complaint remembers. And Egypt, the place of the lash, has become in their telling a land of pomegranates. Complaint has a memory, and the memory edits. The first symptom is always the same: we start to speak of what God rescued us from as though it were what we lost.

Lament or grumbling? Their thirst was real, and God does not scold them for saying so; in a moment he will give them everything they asked for. Many of the Psalms tell God the situation is unbearable. The difference is one small word. They assembled against Moses instead of crying to the LORD. Lament carries the trouble to God and stays with him; grumbling carries it to everyone else and puts God on trial. Both can say the same true sentence, there is no water, and only one of them is worship. A Christian who has grumbled can still turn it into lament: the God who redeemed him still listens, and the Spirit helps us in our weakness (Romans 8:26).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and Aaron went from the presence of the assembly to the entrance of the tent of meeting and fell on their faces. And the glory of the LORD appeared to them, and the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Take the staff, and assemble the congregation, you and Aaron your brother, and tell the rock before their eyes to yield its water. So you shall bring water out of the rock for them and give drink to the congregation and their cattle."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses and Aaron rightly take the complaint to God, who answers with glory and grace: bring the staff, but speak to the rock.

And fell on their faces. What Moses and Aaron do first is exactly right. They walk away from the shouting to the tent of meeting; they do not argue or defend their record, but take the crowd’s complaint to God. And God answers not with a rebuke but with splendour: the glory of the LORD appeared.

Take the staff. Then the instruction, with two commands pulling in different directions. The staff recalls the rod that struck the rock at Horeb nearly forty years before (Exodus 17:5–6); it is an instrument of striking. Moses is told to carry it in front of the nation and not use it. He is to tell the rock.

Why does that matter so much? Because the rock at Horeb was struck once, and God is now teaching Israel that it is never to be struck again. Water for the thirsty is not obtained by hitting the rock a second time but by asking. The staff in Moses’ hand is a memorial of a blow already struck; the word in his mouth is all that is needed now. Hold on to that, because in three verses a good man is going to spoil the lesson.

The water was promised first. And notice the comfort in the order: the water was promised before the rock was struck. God had decided to give this mutinous crowd everything they were shouting for before his servant lost his temper. The grace was settled at the tent door. What happened at the rock could spoil the picture of that grace; nothing could stop its flow.

Uncertain wording. Which staff is not stated. Moses takes it “from before the LORD” (v. 9), where Aaron’s budded staff was kept (17:10), so it is very probably Aaron’s; but verse 11 says “his staff”, and some think of Moses’ own rod from Horeb. The lesson does not depend on which.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses took the staff from before the LORD, as he commanded him. Then Moses and Aaron gathered the assembly together before the rock, and he said to them, "Hear now, you rebels: shall we bring water for you out of this rock?" And Moses lifted up his hand and struck the rock with his staff twice, and water came out abundantly, and the congregation drank, and their livestock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses speaks in anger, claims the miracle and strikes the rock twice, yet God still gives water in abundance.

And Moses took the staff. So far, so obedient. Then the whole thing collapses in a single sentence.

Hear now, you rebels. Two things are wrong with it, and both are fatal. The first is the name: rebels. A true word, but God had given no rebuke at all; he had offered water. Moses presents a generous God as a furious one, and the people learn something false about their Maker. The second is the pronoun: shall we bring water, not “shall the LORD”. Somewhere between the tent and the rock, the go-between has put himself where God belongs. Then he strikes the rock twice, in temper, doing what he was not told to do.

Water came out abundantly. Every person and animal in that camp drank through a man who was at that moment sinning against God. God’s kindness to his people is not held back by the state of his servant’s heart, and a church can be fed under a preacher who is in the wrong. That is a mercy for the people and a trap for the servant, because the gushing water felt exactly like approval, and it was not.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Because you did not believe in me, to uphold me as holy in the eyes of the people of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them." These are the waters of Meribah, where the people of Israel quarreled with the LORD, and through them he showed himself holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God bars Moses and Aaron from the land for an unbelief that misrepresented him before the people, and so shows himself holy.

Is it out of proportion? Forty years of bearing this nation, and it ends here. Every honest reader feels the objection: he hit a rock.

Because you did not believe in me. Three things answer it. First, God names the sin, and it is not bad temper but unbelief: Moses did not trust that a spoken word would be enough. Second, the charge is public: in the eyes of the people. Moses was the lens through which the nation saw God, and he smeared it. The higher the platform, the less private the failure, which is why teachers will be judged with greater strictness (James 3:1). Third, Paul tells us what the rock was: they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). At Horeb the Rock was struck once, and life poured out; here he was to be spoken to, because Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many (Hebrews 9:28), is now approached with words, not blows. God’s stated reason is Moses’ unbelief, but many Reformed readers have heard this further note too: Moses took a hammer to that picture in front of the whole nation.

Through them he showed himself holy. God would be shown holy at those waters one way or the other; if his servant would not show it by obeying, God would show it by judging his servant. Yet Moses was not lost. Fourteen centuries later he appears in glory inside the land he was refused, talking with Jesus about Jesus’ coming death (Luke 9:30–31). Moses was kept out of Canaan. He was never kept out of Christ, who upheld his Father as holy at every point where Moses failed.

What it means to uphold God as holy. Here holiness is something shown in the eyes of the people: letting others see God as he really is, not cut down to our size. Moses did not think too little of God that day; he showed him wrongly, lending a generous God his own temper. We do the same whenever our irritation is the face people see when we speak for him. Isaiah said of the LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy (Isaiah 8:13), and Peter sets Christ in that place: in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy (1 Peter 3:15). Jesus never once misrepresented his Father, I have manifested your name (John 17:6), and his faithfulness covers every time we have. So when you next correct a child or answer a doubting friend, ask not only whether your words are true but whether your manner shows what God is like. See Holiness.
verseByVerse.note: “Meribah” means “quarreling” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel asks its brother nation for a peaceful road and, when refused, obeys God by turning away. Moses sends messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom, descended from Esau, Jacob’s twin, recalling Israel’s hardship in Egypt and God’s rescue (vv. 14–16). He asks only to use the King’s Highway, touching no field, vineyard or well (v. 17). Edom refuses and threatens the sword; Israel offers to pay even for water, and Edom comes out with a strong army (vv. 18–20). Since God had forbidden them to fight Edom (Deuteronomy 2:4–5), Israel turns away (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Edom’s refusal continues the long estrangement of Esau’s line from Jacob’s (Gen 25-27; cf. Obadiah), and God teaches Israel to wait on his timing rather than force the road.
verseByVerse.examples: The way forward is sometimes blocked, even by those who should be kin. Secure in what God has promised, we need not repay hostility with hostility (Rom 12:18-19).

verseByVerse.quote: Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom: "Thus says your brother Israel: You know all the hardship that we have met: how our fathers went down to Egypt, and we lived in Egypt a long time. And the Egyptians dealt harshly with us and our fathers. And when we cried to the LORD, he heard our voice and sent an angel and brought us out of Egypt. And here we are in Kadesh, a city on the edge of your territory. Please let us pass through your land. We will not pass through field or vineyard, or drink water from a well. We will go along the King's Highway. We will not turn aside to the right hand or to the left until we have passed through your territory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses appeals to Edom as a brother and asks only to pass along the public road.

Thus says your brother Israel. The phrase is chosen with care. Edom is the nation of Esau; Israel is the nation of his twin, Jacob (Genesis 36:1). The twins fought in the womb, and centuries later their descendants are still on opposite sides of a border. Old family wounds do not heal by being outlived. They get inherited.

When we cried to the LORD, he heard our voice. Moses tells an outsider the gospel of the exodus: slavery, a cry, and a God who heard. Then a painfully modest request: not a field, not a drink from a well, only the King’s Highway, walked straight down the middle. That was the main trade road east of the Dead Sea, running from the Gulf of Aqaba toward Damascus through the heart of Edom.

Why Israel did not fight. A nation with some six hundred thousand fighting men could have taken it. But God had told them not to: Do not contend with them, for I will not give you any of their land, no, not so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession (Deuteronomy 2:5). Esau despised his birthright, and God still kept a promise to him. The God who chooses is not careless of those he did not choose.
verseByVerse.note: The King’s Highway was the main trade road east of the Jordan.

verseByVerse.quote: But Edom said to him, "You shall not pass through, lest I come out with the sword against you." And the people of Israel said to him, "We will go up by the highway, and if we drink of your water, I and my livestock, then I will pay for it. Let me only pass through on foot, nothing more." But he said, "You shall not pass through." And Edom came out against them with a large army and with a strong force. Thus Edom refused to give Israel passage through his territory, so Israel turned away from him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom answers with an army, and Israel, though strong enough to fight, obeys God and turns away, onto a detour God will use.

You shall not pass through. Israel sweetens the offer, and Edom answers with one sentence and an army. The brother came out in force to stop his brother walking down a public road.

So Israel turned away from him. This sentence shows what forty years have produced. They had the numbers and every human reason to force the crossing, and they walked away because God had said the land was Esau’s. That is obedience with nothing in it for the obedient, and it makes no sense unless you believe God decides who has which land.

Where the detour led. Because Edom said no, Israel takes the long road around Seir, and on that road, in the next chapter, God lifts up the bronze serpent that Jesus would claim as a picture of his own cross (John 3:14). Israel could not see the bronze serpent from Kadesh. The detour was not the loss of the plan. It was the plan.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first high priest dies, but the priesthood goes on. At Mount Hor, on Edom’s border, God announces that Aaron will be gathered to his people and will not enter the land, because of Meribah (vv. 22–24). Moses is to take Aaron and his son Eleazar up the mountain, strip Aaron of his priestly garments and put them on Eleazar (vv. 25–26). They climb in the sight of the whole congregation; Aaron dies on the summit, and Moses and Eleazar come down (vv. 27–28). All Israel mourns him for thirty days (v. 29). The man is gone, but the office continues, and it points to a Priest who never dies.
verseByVerse.theology: Aaron dies outside the land, under the same judgment as Moses (v.24), and the office outlives the man. The old priesthood was marked by death, and that weakness makes Christ’s permanent priesthood shine (Hebrews 7:24).
verseByVerse.examples: Grief at a good leader’s death is right, and Israel gave it thirty days. But the Priest who matters most to us will never leave his post.

verseByVerse.quote: And they journeyed from Kadesh, and the people of Israel, the whole congregation, came to Mount Hor. And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron at Mount Hor, on the border of the land of Edom, "Let Aaron be gathered to his people, for he shall not enter the land that I have given to the people of Israel, because you rebelled against my command at the waters of Meribah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aaron will die outside the land, yet God calls it being “gathered to his people”: loss and welcome in one breath.

And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron at Mount Hor. The sentence passed at Meribah is now carried out, and Aaron hears it announced over his own head.

Let Aaron be gathered to his people. Not simply that Aaron shall die, but that he will be gathered. Abraham was gathered to his people (Genesis 25:8), and plainly that means more than burial, because Abraham was buried in a cave in Canaan while his kin lay far away in Ur and Haran. To be gathered is to be brought in to a company already assembled somewhere else. The Old Testament says this quietly, the way a family speaks of someone going home.

Aaron’s silence. No protest is recorded, no plea that forty years had earned a better ending. He is told to climb a mountain he will not come down from, and he climbs it. A man can take God’s hardest word and still walk toward him carrying it, and that, not the golden calf, is the last thing Scripture shows us Aaron doing.

Loss and welcome. The God who shuts the land against Aaron opens something else in the same breath: not a border crossing, but a gathering. That is the shape of a Christian funeral, where loss and welcome are announced together, and why Paul can say that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Take Aaron and Eleazar his son and bring them up to Mount Hor. And strip Aaron of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son. And Aaron shall be gathered to his people and shall die there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aaron’s garments pass to his son, because death ends every earthly priesthood; only Christ’s never ends.

Strip Aaron of his garments. This is one of the most affecting scenes in the Torah. An old man climbs a mountain in the full dress of the high priest: the blue robe with bells and pomegranates round the hem, the breastpiece with the twelve engraved stones over the heart, and on the turban the gold plate that read Holy to the LORD (Exodus 28). For nearly forty years he has carried the names of the tribes over his heart into the holy place before the LORD. At the summit Moses takes it off him piece by piece, until the first high priest of Israel stands on a bare rock with nothing to show for any of it. Then he dies.

And put them on Eleazar his son. The garments go onto Eleazar, and Israel comes down with a high priest. But the man is gone, and that is the limitation Hebrews names: the former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever (Hebrews 7:23–24). There was another hill, and another priest’s garments taken from him, and soldiers who threw dice for them (John 19:23–24). But that Priest had no successor and needed none. He rose and holds his office still.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses did as the LORD commanded. And they went up Mount Hor in the sight of all the congregation. And Moses stripped Aaron of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son. And Aaron died there on the top of the mountain. Then Moses and Eleazar came down from the mountain. And when all the congregation saw that Aaron had perished, all the house of Israel wept for Aaron thirty days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aaron dies before all Israel, and the nation weeps thirty days for a flawed man whom grace had made precious to them.

In the sight of all the congregation. The whole nation watched. Three men went up and two came down, and the second was wearing the robes of the first. Israel read what had happened off the shoulders of the man walking back toward them.

All the house of Israel wept for Aaron. Thirty days of mourning, the same the nation would later give Moses (Deuteronomy 34:8). And look who they were weeping for: the man who made the golden calf and told the feeblest excuse in Scripture, that he threw the gold in the fire and out came this calf (Exodus 32:24), the man who spoke against his own brother (12:1–2). God had not merely tolerated Aaron; he had made him the man Israel could not bear to lose. That is what grace does with a failure who is not thrown away.

A priest who lives forever. The chapter has been an inventory of endings: Miriam buried, Moses barred, Aaron stripped, a road closed by a brother. Hebrews shows what is different now: because our Priest lives forever, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25). The church’s Priest will never be stripped, and she will never gather at the foot of any mountain to weep for him.

Uncertain wording. Deuteronomy 10:6 says Aaron died at Moserah, probably the district in which Mount Hor stood. The mountain itself cannot be identified with certainty: the traditional site near Petra lies inside Edom, while the text places it “on the border of the land of Edom” (v. 23).

keyVerse.quote: Because you did not believe in me, to uphold me as holy in the eyes of the people of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them.
keyVerse.note: God names Moses’ sin at Meribah as unbelief that misrepresented God before the people, and the cost is the land Moses had led Israel toward for forty years. The verse shows how seriously God takes those who speak for him, and that even the greatest servant of the old covenant could not bring God’s people home. Only the faithful Son can.

20.reflection:
The people repeated their parents’ complaints almost word for word (vv. 2–5). What is the difference between lament, which brings our troubles to God, and grumbling, which puts him on trial? How can we turn one into the other?

Moses called the people “rebels” and said “shall we bring water” (v. 10), when God had only offered grace. In what ways can our manner misrepresent God even when our words are true?

Water poured out even though Moses was sinning (v. 11). Why is it dangerous to treat God’s blessing on our work as proof that he approves of our hearts?

Aaron, the high priest, was stripped of his robes and died on Mount Hor (vv. 25–28). How does Christ, who “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25), comfort us when leaders fail and loved ones die?

21.title: The Bronze Serpent: Look and Live
21.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Canaanite, the king of Arad, who lived in the Negeb, heard that Israel was coming by the way of Atharim, he fought against Israel, and took some of them captive.<sup>2</sup>And Israel vowed a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will indeed give this people into my hand, then I will devote their cities to destruction."<sup>3</sup>And the LORD heeded the voice of Israel and gave over the Canaanites, and they devoted them and their cities to destruction. So the name of the place was called Hormah.<sup>4</sup>From Mount Hor they set out by the way to the Red Sea, to go around the land of Edom. And the people became impatient on the way.<sup>5</sup>And the people spoke against God and against Moses, "Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is no food and no water, and we loathe this worthless food."<sup>6</sup>Then the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people, so that many people of Israel died.<sup>7</sup>And the people came to Moses and said, "We have sinned, for we have spoken against the LORD and against you. Pray to the LORD, that he take away the serpents from us." So Moses prayed for the people.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live."<sup>9</sup>So Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a pole. And if a serpent bit anyone, he would look at the bronze serpent and live.<sup>10</sup>And the people of Israel set out and camped in Oboth.<sup>11</sup>And they set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, in the wilderness that is opposite Moab, toward the sunrise.<sup>12</sup>From there they set out and camped in the Valley of Zered.<sup>13</sup>From there they set out and camped on the other side of the Arnon, which is in the wilderness that extends from the border of the Amorites, for the Arnon is the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorites.<sup>14</sup>Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of the LORD, "Waheb in Suphah, and the valleys of the Arnon,<sup>15</sup>and the slope of the valleys that extends to the seat of Ar, and leans to the border of Moab."<sup>16</sup>And from there they continued to Beer; that is the well of which the LORD said to Moses, "Gather the people together, so that I may give them water."<sup>17</sup>Then Israel sang this song: "Spring up, O well!—Sing to it!—<sup>18</sup>the well that the princes made, that the nobles of the people dug, with the scepter and with their staffs." And from the wilderness they went on to Mattanah,<sup>19</sup>and from Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth,<sup>20</sup>and from Bamoth to the valley lying in the region of Moab by the top of Pisgah that looks down on the desert.<sup>21</sup>Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, saying,<sup>22</sup>"Let me pass through your land. We will not turn aside into field or vineyard. We will not drink the water of a well. We will go by the King's Highway until we have passed through your territory."<sup>23</sup>But Sihon would not allow Israel to pass through his territory. He gathered all his people together and went out against Israel to the wilderness and came to Jahaz and fought against Israel.<sup>24</sup>And Israel defeated him with the edge of the sword and took possession of his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, as far as to the Ammonites, for the border of the Ammonites was strong.<sup>25</sup>And Israel took all these cities, and Israel settled in all the cities of the Amorites, in Heshbon, and in all its villages.<sup>26</sup>For Heshbon was the city of Sihon the king of the Amorites, who had fought against the former king of Moab and taken all his land out of his hand, as far as the Arnon.<sup>27</sup>Therefore the ballad singers say, "Come to Heshbon, let it be built; let the city of Sihon be established.<sup>28</sup>For fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the city of Sihon. It devoured Ar of Moab, and swallowed the heights of the Arnon.<sup>29</sup>Woe to you, O Moab! You are undone, O people of Chemosh! He has made his sons fugitives, and his daughters captives, to an Amorite king, Sihon.<sup>30</sup>So we overthrew them; Heshbon, as far as Dibon, perished; and we laid waste as far as Nophah; fire spread as far as Medeba."<sup>31</sup>Thus Israel lived in the land of the Amorites.<sup>32</sup>And Moses sent to spy out Jazer, and they captured its villages and dispossessed the Amorites who were there.<sup>33</sup>Then they turned and went up by the way to Bashan. And Og the king of Bashan came out against them, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei.<sup>34</sup>But the LORD said to Moses, "Do not fear him, for I have given him into your hand, and all his people, and his land. And you shall do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon."<sup>35</sup>So they defeated him and his sons and all his people, until he had no survivor left. And they possessed his land.
21.overview:
Where we are. Miriam and Aaron are dead, Edom has refused Israel its road, and Moses himself has forfeited the land at Meribah (chapter 20). The forty years are nearly over, and this chapter is the turning point: the last great grumbling of the wilderness, the first victories, and the march north at last toward the Jordan.

The message. God deals with his people’s sin and then clears their road. When they despise his bread he sends judgment; when they confess, he does not take the serpents away but lifts up a remedy in the middle of the camp, and whoever looks at it lives. Then the God who healed them goes ahead of them against kings, and against a giant their parents ran from. Life comes by looking to what God has provided, and victory from the God who goes before.

Why it was said. The new generation who heard Numbers on the plains of Moab (see the introduction) had seen Sihon’s land taken with their own eyes. They needed to know that both the healing and the victories were God’s doing, and that the old sin of grumbling still lived in them.

How the chapter makes its case. At Hormah, the place of the old defeat, Israel prays before fighting and wins (vv. 1–3). On the long detour around Edom the people despise the manna, fiery serpents bite them, they confess, and God gives the bronze serpent: look and live (vv. 4–9). The march turns north, and at Beer God gives water before anyone asks, and Israel sings (vv. 10–20). Sihon and Og come out to fight and are defeated, and Israel holds land for the first time (vv. 21–35).

Where it leads. Here the link is not ours to make; Jesus made it: “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15). It is a pattern, and the Lord’s own chosen picture of his cross. He was lifted up bearing the curse that was killing us (Galatians 3:13), and the dying live by looking to him in faith, not by fighting the venom or first making themselves worthy. And the God who walked ahead of Israel against Sihon and Og is the God who in Christ has triumphed over every power ranged against his people (Colossians 2:15).

For us. Notice what you have stopped thanking God for, because daily gifts are the first to be despised. When sin has bitten you, do not stare at the wound or at your own efforts: look to Christ lifted up, and live. And the giants your fears have named are not too big for the God who goes ahead of you.
21.theology:
Look and live. Healing came by looking, not by effort: the purest Old Testament picture of justification by faith, being put right with God simply by trusting Christ (John 3:14–15).

The curse lifted up. The serpent, the sign of the curse since Eden, was raised on a pole. So Christ on the cross bore the curse our sin deserved (Gal 3:13).

Judgment that fits the sin. Venomous words met venomous serpents. God’s judgments often match the sin, yet his mercy provides a remedy in the midst of the curse.
21.examples: You have been bitten by sin and are dying. Do not look to yourself or your worthiness. Look to Christ lifted up, who became the curse for you, and live. The weakest look of faith saves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel learns at Hormah that victory comes from asking God first. The Canaanite king of Arad attacks and takes captives (v. 1). For once trouble drives Israel to prayer rather than complaint: they vow to devote the enemy’s cities to the LORD if he gives them into their hand (v. 2). God hears and gives victory, and the place is named Hormah, “destruction” (v. 3): the very place where, a generation earlier, Israel had been routed after going up without God (14:45). Same ground, same enemy, opposite outcome. It is a first taste of the conquest, granted to dependence.
verseByVerse.theology: Victory comes not by Israel’s might but by the LORD’s gift, sought in prayer and vow (vv.2-3). It is a small first instalment of the conquest, a sign that the God who disciplines his people has not abandoned his promise.
verseByVerse.examples: Our battles are won the same way Israel’s was here, by casting ourselves on God, who “gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57).

verseByVerse.quote: When the Canaanite, the king of Arad, who lived in the Negeb, heard that Israel was coming by the way of Atharim, he fought against Israel, and took some of them captive. And Israel vowed a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will indeed give this people into my hand, then I will devote their cities to destruction." And the LORD heeded the voice of Israel and gave over the Canaanites, and they devoted them and their cities to destruction. So the name of the place was called Hormah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the place of their worst defeat, Israel prays before it fights, and God gives the victory.

Israel vowed a vow to the LORD. The first thing to happen after Aaron’s funeral is a raid, and Israel’s response is the most surprising sentence in the book so far: not a complaint, but prayer. In twenty chapters trouble has rarely driven the people to God, and the change is the point of the verse.

The name of the place was called Hormah. In chapter 14 the people invaded without God, and the enemy “came down and defeated them and pursued them, even to Hormah” (14:45). That defeat was the nation’s lowest point, on the very ground where they now win.

The ground is not the reason. Same place, same enemy, opposite outcome; the one difference is whether God went with them. If there is ground in your own history where you have been beaten a hundred times, a sin or a fear, the ground is not the reason. Israel did not need a different battlefield but a different way of going up: this time they asked first.

Was it just? To “devote to destruction” (Hebrew herem) meant handing a city over wholly to God, usually by destroying it. This was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened over centuries (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4–5), including child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31), and Israel was warned that the land would vomit it out too for the same sins (Leviticus 18:24–28). It was a unique command, carried out through Israel at one moment in redemptive history. It is no pattern for any later war, nation or church: Christ’s kingdom “is not of this world” (John 18:36), and the church’s weapons “are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4).
verseByVerse.note: “Devote to destruction” means to set apart to the LORD for destruction (ESV note); “Hormah” means “destruction” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — The Bronze Serpent: Look and Live
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the last great grumbling of the wilderness with judgment, and then with a remedy anyone can take. On the long detour around Edom the people despise the manna as “worthless food” (vv. 4–5). Fiery serpents bite and many die; the people confess their sin and ask Moses to pray (vv. 6–7). God does not take the serpents away. He has a bronze serpent set on a pole, and whoever is bitten and looks at it lives (vv. 8–9). Jesus took this as the picture of his own cross (John 3:14–15): life for the dying, by looking in faith to what God has lifted up.
verseByVerse.theology: The cure is by looking, not by working, and the thing looked at is an image of what was killing them: a picture of Christ, whom God “made... to be sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21).
verseByVerse.examples: “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth!” (Isaiah 45:22). Salvation is by looking to Christ crucified, not by trying to cure ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: From Mount Hor they set out by the way to the Red Sea, to go around the land of Edom. And the people became impatient on the way. And the people spoke against God and against Moses, "Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? For there is no food and no water, and we loathe this worthless food."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forced south again on a long detour, the people lose patience and despise the very bread God sends them every morning.

The people became impatient on the way. Canaan is north, and they are marching south, back toward the Red Sea, because a brother nation would not let them use its road. The Red Sea here is probably its eastern arm, the Gulf of Aqaba, at the southern end of Edom’s territory (compare Deuteronomy 2:8). They have just buried Aaron. “Impatient” is literally their soul became short: the fraying that comes three-quarters of the way through, when the end should be in sight and the road turns the wrong way.

There is no food and no water. There is no food, and we cannot stand the food: grumbling does not have to be coherent, because the point was never the food.

We loathe this worthless food. The “worthless food” is the manna, the bread God rained down every morning for forty years, which a psalm calls “the grain of heaven” and “the bread of the angels” (Psalm 78:24–25). It is a verdict on God’s goodness from people whose mouths are full of his generosity.

The true bread, despised again. Jesus called himself the true bread from heaven, of which the manna was only a sign (John 6:32–35), and the crowd answered as their fathers had: “the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, ‘I am the bread that came down from heaven’” (John 6:41). The heart that tires of God’s daily gift can tire of his Son.

What have you stopped thanking him for? Anything given daily stops registering as a gift. Ask what you have stopped thanking God for, and you will usually find it is whatever he has been most faithful about. The cure is not to manufacture gratitude but to look again at the Giver.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people, so that many people of Israel died. And the people came to Moses and said, "We have sinned, for we have spoken against the LORD and against you. Pray to the LORD, that he take away the serpents from us." So Moses prayed for the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers venomous words with venomous serpents, and this time the people confess their sin and ask Moses to pray for them.

Fiery serpents. The judgment fits the crime with terrible precision: venomous words are answered by venom. The desert south of Edom is real snake country, and the horror was literal: swelling, burning pain, and hours to live.

We have sinned. Then the second surprise of the chapter. This time the people do not bargain, excuse or blame: “We have sinned, for we have spoken against the LORD and against you.” They name the sin and both parties they wronged, and ask for the one thing they cannot do for themselves: “Pray to the LORD.”

So Moses prayed for the people. This is the man they had just attacked, who one chapter ago lost the land because his patience with them snapped, and he prays. There is a love that rejection does not wear out. It comes from only one place, and Israel is about to be shown a picture of it, hammered out of bronze and lifted on a pole.

Uncertain wording. “Fiery” translates seraphim, “burning ones”, the word used of the seraphim around God’s throne in Isaiah 6 and of a “flying fiery serpent” in Isaiah 14:29 and 30:6. Why the snakes were called burning is not certain: most think of the burning pain of the bite, others of their colour. The likely meaning is simply deadly, venomous snakes.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not take the serpents away; he puts a remedy among them, an image of the very thing that is killing them, and promises life to anyone bitten who looks at it.

The serpents remain. They asked him to “take away the serpents”, and he does not. He leaves the danger in the world and puts a remedy in the middle of it.

When God does not remove it. Paul asked three times for a thorn to be taken out and was told instead, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). That is not a smaller answer, only a harder one: it leaves the sufferer with God himself, not merely with relief.

Everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live. On the pole God puts not a lamb or an angel but a serpent: an image of the very thing killing them, lifted up dead and harmless where every dying man can see it. And the cure is a look. Not a pilgrimage to the pole, not a fee, not a period of improvement first. A man too far gone to stand can still turn his head. God set the price of life at the one thing a dying man is still able to do.

Why does grace offend the self-made? A modern reader’s first reaction is often irritation: surely it cannot be that simple. We trust programmes and effort, and a cure that asks for nothing but a look leaves us nothing to contribute and nothing to boast of; that is exactly why it is the only cure that could work. Yet the look is not easy for a proud man. To lift your eyes to that pole is to admit that you have been bitten, that you are dying, and that the remedy is outside you. Jesus put it with a doctor’s bluntness: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Mark 2:17). Grace is only an insult to people who think they are well. To the dying it is the best news there is.

Was the bronze serpent magic, or an idol? Neither. The image had no power in itself: those who looked were healed because God had promised it, and their look was trust in his word. Nor did it break the second commandment, which forbids making images to worship; God commanded this one as a sign, and when Israel later worshipped it, it was broken up (see the note on v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a pole. And if a serpent bit anyone, he would look at the bronze serpent and live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses does as he is told, and every bitten Israelite who looks lives: the picture Jesus himself chose to explain his cross.

So must the Son of Man be lifted up. When Nicodemus came by night asking about the new birth, Jesus reached for this text: “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14). Of all the pictures available, the lamb, the manna, the mercy seat, this is the one he chose to explain his cross.

Why a serpent. The serpent had stood for the enemy and the curse since Eden (Genesis 3:14–15), and to hang it on a pole was to display it defeated. Paul describes Calvary in the same terms: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us”, for “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” (Galatians 3:13).
