He did not merely deal with the poison. In full public view he took on himself the curse that was killing us, and drew every dying eye to himself.

Nehushtan. Centuries later King Hezekiah “broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until those days the people of Israel had made offerings to it” (2 Kings 18:4). It was called Nehushtan, a name that, as the ESV note explains, sounds like the Hebrew for both bronze and serpent. Anything God gives you to see him through, a church, a teacher, a way of praying, you can turn into something that hides him. The sign is always the same: you begin to love the means more than the Christ it was pointing to.

Look and live. Break the bronze, then, and keep the Christ. There is nothing to do but look: not look and then earn it, not look after cleaning up. The serpent on the pole was only ever an arrow pointing down the centuries to a hill outside Jerusalem, where the Son of God hung in the open air with the whole curse of the world on him, and did not come down, and let the dying look at him. He is what the pole was for. Every eye that has ever turned to him has lived, and not one that turned has been refused.
verseByVerse.note: Centuries later King Hezekiah destroyed the bronze serpent because people were burning incense to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–20 — The Journey and the Song of the Well
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the serpents the road at last runs forward, and Israel sings. The list of camps moves north past Moab to the Arnon (vv. 10–13), with a line from the lost Book of the Wars of the LORD to mark the crossing (vv. 14–15). At Beer God gives water before anyone complains, and the people sing a digging song over the well (vv. 16–18). The march ends on the heights of Pisgah, looking down on the desert that swallowed a generation (vv. 19–20). The section is quiet, but its point is plain: the God who judged and healed is now leading his people home, and complainers are becoming singers.
verseByVerse.theology: The Song of the Well (vv.17-18) is a rare, bright note of grateful worship in a book full of murmuring. The itinerary marks real progress toward the land, and joy over God’s gifts is the fitting response of those being brought home.
verseByVerse.examples: A grumbler and a thankful person often receive the very same gift; they differ in how they take it. The God who brought you through the serpents gives the well too; “give thanks in all circumstances” (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel set out and camped in Oboth. And they set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, in the wilderness that is opposite Moab, toward the sunrise. From there they set out and camped in the Valley of Zered. From there they set out and camped on the other side of the Arnon, which is in the wilderness that extends from the border of the Amorites, for the Arnon is the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the serpents Israel simply travels, and at last the road runs north, up the east side of the Dead Sea toward the Jordan.

Ordinary obedience. After the serpents the text goes quiet: set out and camp, four verses of a nation simply travelling. That is not filler. Most of the Christian life is these verses rather than the ones before them: long stretches of ordinary obedience where nothing happens except that you keep going in the right direction. God records both. The Holy Spirit thought the campsite at Oboth was worth a line in the Bible.

On the other side of the Arnon. The geography is quietly hopeful. The Arnon is the northern border of Moab, so Israel has finally stopped going south. They are moving up the eastern side of the Dead Sea, and every camp from here on is closer to the Jordan than the last.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of the LORD, "Waheb in Suphah, and the valleys of the Arnon, and the slope of the valleys that extends to the seat of Ar, and leans to the border of Moab."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer quotes an old collection of war poems to mark where Israel crossed the Arnon, a reminder that these events happened in real places.

The Book of the Wars of the LORD. Nothing else mentions this book, and no copy survives. It seems to have been a collection of poems on the LORD’s victories, quoted here to fix the crossing of the Arnon. Some think the citation shows that the book was edited after Moses; others, that such a collection was already being made in his day.

Does a lost book mean the Bible is missing something? No. Scripture quotes outside sources fairly often: the Book of Jashar (Joshua 10:13; 2 Samuel 1:18), court annals in Kings, and Greek poets in Paul (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12). Inspiration never meant that every source the writers consulted was inspired; it means that what God caused to be written is true, and what he has given is enough, “able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15). So the lost book is not a hole in the Bible but a footnote in it: evidence that these events happened in a real country with real rivers, and that the writer expected his readers to be able to check.

Uncertain wording. The quotation is a fragment, cut from a longer poem, and its first line has no verb. “Waheb” and “Suphah” are probably place names, though neither is known; “Suphah” could also mean “storm” or “whirlwind”, and some translations supply a verb such as “he took” or “we passed”. The general sense is clear: the poem traces the valleys of the Arnon down to the border of Moab.

verseByVerse.quote: And from there they continued to Beer; that is the well of which the LORD said to Moses, "Gather the people together, so that I may give them water." Then Israel sang this song: "Spring up, O well!—Sing to it!— the well that the princes made, that the nobles of the people dug, with the scepter and with their staffs." And from the wilderness they went on to Mattanah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Beer God gives water before anyone complains, and Israel, for the first time since the Red Sea, sings.

Gather the people together, so that I may give them water. Set this beside the last chapter. At Meribah there was no water, a mob formed, a mediator lost his temper and a rock was struck twice. Here God announces the water before anyone has complained. He gathers them, and gives.

Spring up, O well! And Israel sings over the well. It is a working song, the kind people chant while they dig, with the leaders sharing the work, staffs of office in hand. God provides the water; the nobles dig; the camp sings. Grace and effort stand in one verse, and neither crowds out the other.

From complaint to song. The nation that called God’s bread worthless twelve verses ago is now singing at a hole in the ground. Judgment fell, mercy was lifted up on a pole, and the survivors came out singing. That is what God is doing in the wilderness: making, out of complainers, a people who sing. The same Lord who gives water unasked stood up at a feast in Jerusalem and said, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37).
verseByVerse.note: “Beer” means “well” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: and from Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth, and from Bamoth to the valley lying in the region of Moab by the top of Pisgah that looks down on the desert.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The march ends on the heights of Pisgah, and for the first time Israel looks down on the wilderness from outside it.

The road runs forward. After the long detour, a list of camps that runs steadily forward is itself good news: the road has stopped turning back.

By the top of Pisgah. It ends at the top of Pisgah, the ridge from which Moses will be shown the whole land before he dies (Deuteronomy 34:1), “that looks down on the desert”. For thirty-eight years the wilderness was the horizon in every direction. Now they stand above it. The place that swallowed a generation has become a view from a height. It is not yet the promised land, but it is the first time Israel has seen the wilderness from the outside, and every believer who has come out the far side of a long stretch of God’s discipline knows what that morning felt like.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–35 — Victory over Sihon and Og
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God begins to give his people the land, and the giants their parents feared fall before the children. Israel asks Sihon king of the Amorites for passage; he attacks instead, and loses everything from the Arnon to the Jabbok (vv. 21–24). Israel settles in Heshbon, and an old Amorite taunt-song over Moab is now sung over Sihon’s own ruin (vv. 25–30). Og of Bashan, last of the giants, comes out to battle, and God says, “Do not fear him, for I have given him into your hand” (vv. 31–35). Israel would sing of these victories for centuries as proofs of God’s steadfast love (Psalm 136:17–20).
verseByVerse.theology: The defeat of Sihon and Og is the first great conquest, celebrated for generations (Ps 135:11; 136:19-20). Unbelief had delayed the promise but could not cancel it, and these victories are the down payment on the whole inheritance.
verseByVerse.examples: The God who kept his word to a wandering, faithless people keeps it still; “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, saying, "Let me pass through your land. We will not turn aside into field or vineyard. We will not drink the water of a well. We will go by the King's Highway until we have passed through your territory." But Sihon would not allow Israel to pass through his territory. He gathered all his people together and went out against Israel to the wilderness and came to Jahaz and fought against Israel. And Israel defeated him with the edge of the sword and took possession of his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, as far as to the Ammonites, for the border of the Ammonites was strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sihon refuses Israel’s peaceful request and attacks, and God gives Israel its first land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok.

Let me pass through your land. Israel sends Sihon almost word for word the message she sent Edom, asking only to use the King’s Highway, the main road east of the Jordan. The courtesy has not changed; God’s instruction has. Edom was protected (Deuteronomy 2:5), so Israel turned away from an insult without drawing a sword. Of Sihon God had said, “Behold, I have given into your hand Sihon… Begin to take possession, and contend with him in battle” (Deuteronomy 2:24).

But Sihon would not allow Israel to pass through his territory. Sihon marched out to attack a nation that had asked to use a road. Deuteronomy adds the hardest line: “the LORD your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate” (Deuteronomy 2:30). We should not soften that, nor make it say more than it does. Sihon wanted this war; God did not put into him a desire that was not already there. God gave a man bent on violence over to his own will and used that violence for his own purpose. He rules over human wickedness without ever being its author.

From the Arnon to the Jabbok. The result is the first territory Israel has ever owned, taken by a people whose parents, forty years earlier, had been too frightened to cross a border.

verseByVerse.quote: And Israel took all these cities, and Israel settled in all the cities of the Amorites, in Heshbon, and in all its villages. For Heshbon was the city of Sihon the king of the Amorites, who had fought against the former king of Moab and taken all his land out of his hand, as far as the Arnon. Therefore the ballad singers say, "Come to Heshbon, let it be built; let the city of Sihon be established. For fire came out from Heshbon, flame from the city of Sihon. It devoured Ar of Moab, and swallowed the heights of the Arnon. Woe to you, O Moab! You are undone, O people of Chemosh! He has made his sons fugitives, and his daughters captives, to an Amorite king, Sihon. So we overthrew them; Heshbon, as far as Dibon, perished; and we laid waste as far as Nophah; fire spread as far as Medeba."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel takes Heshbon, and an old Amorite song gloating over Moab’s defeat is now sung over the ruin of the Amorite king himself.

Therefore the ballad singers say. Sihon had taken Heshbon from Moab not long before, and his poets had made a victory ballad about it. That is the song quoted here: the conqueror’s taunt, gloating over Moab’s ruin.

The ballad outlives the empire. Israel, it seems, sings it over the rubble of Heshbon, so that the winner’s taunt-song is chanted at the winner’s funeral. Every empire composes its ballad, and the ballad outlives the empire.

You are undone, O people of Chemosh! Chemosh was Moab’s national god, and the song says he turned his own worshippers into refugees. That is the difference between an idol and God. An idol takes everything you have and then cannot protect the very thing you gave it all to keep. “Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases. Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands” (Psalm 115:3–4).

Uncertain wording. Two things are not certain. Most read the song as an Amorite ballad about Sihon’s conquest of Moab, now turned against him; some think Israel composed it, or added the closing lines (v. 30, “So we overthrew them”). And the last verse is hard to read in Hebrew, so translations differ in its details. The sense is clear on any reading: a trail of fire and ruin from Heshbon to Medeba.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Israel lived in the land of the Amorites. And Moses sent to spy out Jazer, and they captured its villages and dispossessed the Amorites who were there. Then they turned and went up by the way to Bashan. And Og the king of Bashan came out against them, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei. But the LORD said to Moses, "Do not fear him, for I have given him into your hand, and all his people, and his land. And you shall do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon." So they defeated him and his sons and all his people, until he had no survivor left. And they possessed his land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Og, the giant king of the kind their parents feared, comes out to fight; God tells the new generation not to fear him, and they win.

Og the king of Bashan. One more kingdom stands between Israel and the Jordan, and it is the worst. Og was the last of the Rephaim, an ancient race of giants, and his iron bed was over thirteen feet long; you could go and look at it in Rabbah (Deuteronomy 3:11).

Do not fear him. Remember chapter 13: “there we saw the Nephilim… and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers” (13:33), and a generation died in the sand rather than face them. Here is that terror wearing a crown, coming down the road at Edrei. And God says, “Do not fear him, for I have given him into your hand.” The fear that killed the fathers no longer holds the sons.

Remembered in a psalm. Centuries later a psalm sings that day with a refrain on every second line: “to him who struck down great kings, for his steadfast love endures forever… Sihon, king of the Amorites… and Og, king of Bashan, for his steadfast love endures forever” (Psalm 136:17–20). Israel learned to read her military history not as a record of her courage but as a list of God’s mercies.

He does not save halfway. The God who hung a serpent on a pole for a camp of dying grumblers walks in front of them against giants. He deals with the venom, and then he clears the road. So Christ both bears his people’s sin and goes before them to the end, and “in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37).

Was the destruction of Og’s people just? Sihon and Og attacked Israel (vv. 23, 33), and the Amorites’ sin had reached its full measure (Genesis 15:16). It was part of God’s unique judgment on Canaan, not a licence for later wars (see the note on vv. 1–3).
verseByVerse.note: Bashan lay east of the Sea of Galilee, famous for its cattle.

keyVerse.quote: So Moses made a bronze serpent and set it on a pole. And if a serpent bit anyone, he would look at the bronze serpent and live.
keyVerse.note: This is the verse Jesus took up to explain his own cross (John 3:14–15). The dying were not asked to fight the venom or prove themselves worthy, only to look at what God had lifted up, and every one who looked lived.

21.reflection:
The people called God’s daily bread “worthless food” (v. 5). What good gifts of God have become so ordinary to you that you no longer notice or thank him for them?

God did not take the serpents away but gave a remedy in the middle of them (v. 8). How does that shape the way we pray about troubles God has not removed?

Jesus said, “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14). Why is looking such a fitting picture of faith, and why do proud people find it so hard?

The new generation faced the kind of giant their parents had run from, and God said, “Do not fear him” (v. 34). What fear has defeated you before, and what would it look like to face it trusting the God who goes ahead of you?

22.title: Balak and Balaam: The Sovereign God over a Pagan Prophet
22.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the people of Israel set out and camped in the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan at Jericho.<sup>2</sup>And Balak the son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites.<sup>3</sup>And Moab was in great dread of the people, because they were many. Moab was overcome with fear of the people of Israel.<sup>4</sup>And Moab said to the elders of Midian, "This horde will now lick up all that is around us, as the ox licks up the grass of the field." So Balak the son of Zippor, who was king of Moab at that time,<sup>5</sup>sent messengers to Balaam the son of Beor at Pethor, which is near the River in the land of the people of Amaw, to call him, saying, "Behold, a people has come out of Egypt. They cover the face of the earth, and they are dwelling opposite me.<sup>6</sup>Come now, curse this people for me, since they are too mighty for me. Perhaps I shall be able to defeat them and drive them from the land, for I know that he whom you bless is blessed, and he whom you curse is cursed."<sup>7</sup>So the elders of Moab and the elders of Midian departed with the fees for divination in their hand. And they came to Balaam and gave him Balak's message.<sup>8</sup>And he said to them, "Lodge here tonight, and I will bring back word to you, as the LORD speaks to me." So the princes of Moab stayed with Balaam.<sup>9</sup>And God came to Balaam and said, "Who are these men with you?"<sup>10</sup>And Balaam said to God, "Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, has sent to me, saying,<sup>11</sup>'Behold, a people has come out of Egypt, and it covers the face of the earth. Now come, curse them for me. Perhaps I shall be able to fight against them and drive them out.'"<sup>12</sup>God said to Balaam, "You shall not go with them. You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed."<sup>13</sup>So Balaam rose in the morning and said to the princes of Balak, "Go to your own land, for the LORD has refused to let me go with you."<sup>14</sup>So the princes of Moab rose and went to Balak and said, "Balaam refuses to come with us."<sup>15</sup>Once again Balak sent princes, more in number and more honorable than these.<sup>16</sup>And they came to Balaam and said to him, "Thus says Balak the son of Zippor: 'Let nothing hinder you from coming to me,<sup>17</sup>for I will surely do you great honor, and whatever you say to me I will do. Come, curse this people for me.'"<sup>18</sup>But Balaam answered and said to the servants of Balak, "Though Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not go beyond the command of the LORD my God to do less or more.<sup>19</sup>So you, too, please stay here tonight, that I may know what more the LORD will say to me."<sup>20</sup>And God came to Balaam at night and said to him, "If the men have come to call you, rise, go with them; but only do what I tell you."<sup>21</sup>So Balaam rose in the morning and saddled his donkey and went with the princes of Moab.<sup>22</sup>But God's anger was kindled because he went, and the angel of the LORD took his stand in the way as his adversary. Now he was riding on the donkey, and his two servants were with him.<sup>23</sup>And the donkey saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road, with a drawn sword in his hand. And the donkey turned aside out of the road and went into the field. And Balaam struck the donkey, to turn her into the road.<sup>24</sup>Then the angel of the LORD stood in a narrow path between the vineyards, with a wall on either side.<sup>25</sup>And when the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she pushed against the wall and pressed Balaam's foot against the wall. So he struck her again.<sup>26</sup>Then the angel of the LORD went ahead and stood in a narrow place, where there was no way to turn either to the right or to the left.<sup>27</sup>When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she lay down under Balaam. And Balaam's anger was kindled, and he struck the donkey with his staff.<sup>28</sup>Then the LORD opened the mouth of the donkey, and she said to Balaam, "What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times?"<sup>29</sup>And Balaam said to the donkey, "Because you have made a fool of me. I wish I had a sword in my hand, for then I would kill you."<sup>30</sup>And the donkey said to Balaam, "Am I not your donkey, on which you have ridden all your life long to this day? Is it my habit to treat you this way?" And he said, "No."<sup>31</sup>Then the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, with his drawn sword in his hand. So Balaam went on with the princes of Balak.<sup>36</sup>When Balak heard that Balaam had come, he went out to meet him at the city of Moab, on the border formed by the Arnon, at the extremity of the border.<sup>37</sup>And Balak said to Balaam, "Did I not send to you to call you? Why did you not come to me? Am I not able to honor you?"<sup>38</sup>Balaam said to Balak, "Behold, I have come to you! Have I now any power of my own to speak anything? The word that God puts in my mouth, that must I speak."<sup>39</sup>Then Balaam went with Balak, and they came to Kiriath-huzoth.<sup>40</sup>And Balak sacrificed oxen and sheep, and sent for Balaam and for the princes who were with him.<sup>41</sup>And in the morning Balak took Balaam and brought him up to Bamoth-baal, and from there he saw a fraction of the people.
22.overview:
Where we are. Israel has defeated Sihon and Og and now camps on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho, where it will stay to the end of the book. Chapters 22 to 24 pull the camera back to show what Israel cannot see: on the hills above them, a king is paying for their ruin.

The message. No one can curse a people God has blessed. Balak of Moab hires the famous seer Balaam to curse Israel, and God tells Balaam plainly, “You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed” (v. 12). The chapter also exposes Balaam: a man with flawless words about God and a heart for sale, who keeps asking until God lets him go, and who is less able to see God in the road than his own donkey.

Why it was said. The generation about to cross the Jordan needed to know that their safety did not rest on their own strength or goodness (see the introduction). While they slept, enemies plotted, and God had already ruled.

How the chapter makes its case. Balak, terrified by Israel’s victories, sends to the Euphrates for Balaam (vv. 1–6). God forbids him to go or to curse, but when a richer offer comes Balaam asks again, and God lets him go with a warning (vv. 7–20). On the road the angel of the LORD stands against him with a drawn sword; the donkey sees, the seer does not, and only when God opens first her mouth and then his eyes does Balaam fall on his face (vv. 21–35). He reaches Balak declaring that he can speak only God’s word, and is taken up a pagan high place to look down on Israel (vv. 36–41).

Where it leads. By covenant, first: God had promised Abraham to bless those who bless him and curse those who dishonour him (Genesis 12:3), and that blessing comes to its goal in Christ, “so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles” (Galatians 3:14). No accuser can undo it (Romans 8:33). By contrast too: Balaam’s words were true and his heart false, while Christ, tempted with all the kingdoms of the world, had no price at all. And the angel of the LORD who stands in the road to guard God’s people is, in this commentary’s view, the Son himself before his incarnation.

For us. If you are in Christ, the verdict over you is “blessed”, and no plot, curse or accusation can reverse it. But beware Balaam’s sin, the sound words and the divided heart that keeps asking God until the answer improves. And when God narrows your road, look up before you lash out: the obstacle may be your rescue.
22.theology:
Sovereignty over enemies. God so controls the pagan Balaam that he cannot curse the people God has blessed, and no curse can reverse that blessing. If God is for us, who can be against us (Rom 8:31)?

God humbles the proud. The professional seer turns out to be blinder than his donkey, a reminder that all true sight is God’s gift.
22.examples: You may be surrounded by enemies you cannot see, yet God holds their curses in his hand and turns them to blessing. Those whom God has blessed in Christ cannot be cursed. Rest in the sovereign Lord who is for you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A frightened king reaches for a curse against a people he cannot defeat by the sword. Israel camps on the plains of Moab within sight of Jericho (v. 1). Balak has seen Sihon and Og fall, and Moab is sick with dread: this people will lick up everything around them like an ox grazing a field (vv. 2–4). He does not know that God has forbidden Israel to touch Moab. So he sends hundreds of miles to the Euphrates for Balaam, a seer famous for words that work: “he whom you bless is blessed, and he whom you curse is cursed” (vv. 5–6). The stage is set for a contest between pagan ritual and the living God’s blessing.
verseByVerse.theology: Balak’s strategy assumes what the pagan world believed: that a skilled diviner (a reader of omens) could make a god use his power to curse. The whole story will take that belief apart.
verseByVerse.examples: Those who fear God’s people still reach for schemes when force will not work, and the schemes still fail.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Israel set out and camped in the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan at Jericho. And Balak the son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites. And Moab was in great dread of the people, because they were many. Moab was overcome with fear of the people of Israel. And Moab said to the elders of Midian, "This horde will now lick up all that is around us, as the ox licks up the grass of the field." So Balak the son of Zippor, who was king of Moab at that time,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel camps at last within sight of the land, and the king of Moab is overcome with dread at a people God has told not to touch him.

In the plains of Moab. After forty years, this is where they stop: on the flat ground of the east bank, with the river in front of them and Jericho visible across it. Everything from here to the end of the book happens in this one camp, within sight of the land.

As the ox licks up the grass of the field. The first thing that happens is that somebody is terrified. Balak had watched Sihon and Og disappear in a single campaign, and his image is the best line in the chapter: not a battle but a grazing, an animal with its head down working steadily across a meadow, and when it lifts its head the field is gone.

A needless fear. What Balak cannot see is that God had forbidden Israel to touch him: “Do not harass Moab or contend with them in battle, for I will not give you any of their land for a possession” (Deuteronomy 2:9). The king lies awake planning against a nation ordered to leave him alone. That is what fear does when it will not consult God: it manufactures the disaster it was trying to avoid.

verseByVerse.quote: sent messengers to Balaam the son of Beor at Pethor, which is near the River in the land of the people of Amaw, to call him, saying, "Behold, a people has come out of Egypt. They cover the face of the earth, and they are dwelling opposite me. Come now, curse this people for me, since they are too mighty for me. Perhaps I shall be able to defeat them and drive them from the land, for I know that he whom you bless is blessed, and he whom you curse is cursed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balak sends hundreds of miles for a famous seer to curse Israel, believing that blessing and cursing are a skill that can be hired.

Balaam the son of Beor at Pethor. “The River” is the Euphrates, which puts Pethor in upper Mesopotamia, roughly four hundred miles away: the best part of a month’s travel each way, because Balak has heard of a man whose word works. Fear is expensive, and it will pay for anything.

Come now, curse this people for me. Balak wants not an army but a curse. He believes what most of the ancient world believed: that words spoken by the right man with the right ritual have force in themselves. His reason is “he whom you bless is blessed”, and what is missing from it is God.

What these chapters are about. That is why the next three chapters are not really about Balaam. They are about what happens when all the rituals of pagan religion are aimed at a people the living God has already blessed. Balak will build twenty-one altars, offer forty-two animals and climb three mountains, and every time his hired prophet opens his mouth, out will come a blessing.

Uncertain wording. “The land of the people of Amaw” can also be read “the land of the sons of his people”, that is, Balaam’s own homeland. The ESV takes Amaw as the name of a region near the Euphrates. Either way the point stands: Balaam lived far away in the north, and Balak sent a long way for him.
verseByVerse.note: “The River” is the Euphrates (ESV note): Balaam was a well-known diviner from far away.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Balaam plainly that Israel is blessed, and Balaam’s heart is exposed by what he does with that word. The first embassy brings fees for divination, and God answers in the night: do not go, do not curse, “for they are blessed” (vv. 7–12). Balaam sends the men home but passes on only the ban, not the reason (vv. 13–14). Balak, taking the hint, sends a grander delegation and an open offer (vv. 15–17). Balaam protests that a house full of silver and gold could not move him, then asks them to wait while he asks God again; God lets him go, but only to speak what he is told (vv. 18–20).
verseByVerse.theology: God’s first word is unmistakable: Israel “is blessed” (v.12). Balaam’s second inquiry reveals a heart looking for a loophole. God’s permission to go (v.20) is not approval. God is handing a man over to the desire he will not give up, while God stays sovereign over what Balaam may say.
verseByVerse.examples: When we know God’s will but keep asking, hoping he will bless what our hearts are set on, we walk “the way of Balaam.” Beware the prayer that is really a search for permission.

verseByVerse.quote: So the elders of Moab and the elders of Midian departed with the fees for divination in their hand. And they came to Balaam and gave him Balak's message. And he said to them, "Lodge here tonight, and I will bring back word to you, as the LORD speaks to me." So the princes of Moab stayed with Balaam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders bring fees for divination, and the hired seer says he will answer “as the LORD speaks to me”, and the LORD does speak.

The fees for divination. The fee tells us what Balaam is: not a prophet of Israel but a seer for hire; men of his trade blessed and cursed for money. Archaeologists have found his name in a plaster inscription at Deir Alla, in the Jordan valley not far from this camp: “Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods”. It was written about 800 BC, centuries after these events, so a seer of that name was long remembered across the region.

As the LORD speaks to me. This pagan diviner uses Yahweh, the personal name by which God made himself known to Israel, and God actually answers him. That unsettles readers, and it should be faced rather than tidied away.

Speaking through bad men. God is not restricted to speaking through good men. He spoke through Caiaphas, who “did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied” (John 11:51), and through Saul after the Spirit had left him (1 Samuel 19:23–24). A gift from God does not prove the man godly. The New Testament says Balaam “loved gain from wrongdoing” (2 Peter 2:15), yet God will use a hired man’s mouth rather than let one word be spoken against his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And God came to Balaam and said, "Who are these men with you?" And Balaam said to God, "Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, has sent to me, saying, 'Behold, a people has come out of Egypt, and it covers the face of the earth. Now come, curse them for me. Perhaps I shall be able to fight against them and drive them out.'" God said to Balaam, "You shall not go with them. You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God forbids Balaam to go or to curse, and gives the reason that governs the next three chapters: Israel is blessed.

Who are these men with you? God is not gathering information. It is like his question in Eden, “Where are you?”, asked to make a man say aloud what he is doing. Balaam’s summary is accurate as far as it goes, though he leaves out the fee.

For they are blessed. Two sentences, each shutting a door, and the last four words are the foundation of chapters 23 and 24. Not “they are good”, not “they deserve it”: God has spent twenty-one chapters recording their grumbling and rebellion. They are blessed because he blessed them, and for no other reason on earth.

The security of God’s people. That is the security of the people of God, stated to an enemy. The blessing does not rest on Israel’s conduct, so Israel’s conduct cannot cancel it. It rests on a promise made to Abraham centuries before, and the God who made it does not take it back. Paul says where that promise finally lands: Christ redeemed us “so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles” (Galatians 3:14). The blessing Balaam could not touch now rests on everyone who is in Christ, so Paul can pile up every enemy and ask, “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33). A professional curser sat with a purse of gold in the next room, and heaven had already ruled.

verseByVerse.quote: So Balaam rose in the morning and said to the princes of Balak, "Go to your own land, for the LORD has refused to let me go with you." So the princes of Moab rose and went to Balak and said, "Balaam refuses to come with us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam sends the princes home, but passes on only God’s ban on going, not his reason, and so leaves the door open.

The LORD has refused to let me go with you. At first glance Balaam looks obedient. Then compare. God said, “You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed.” Balaam reports only that “the LORD has refused to let me go with you.”

What he left out. The whole heart of the man is in that edit. The reason would have closed the matter for ever; a bare refusal is an invitation to try again. The messengers hear it that way, reporting that “Balaam refuses”, as though the man himself were the obstacle.

Accurate and dishonest. This is how a divided heart talks: nothing technically untrue, and the door left ajar. We all know the answer that is accurate in every particular and dishonest in its whole effect, given so that the thing we still want remains available. When you decline something you would rather have accepted, do you shut the door, or leave it looking as though a better offer might open it?

verseByVerse.quote: Once again Balak sent princes, more in number and more honorable than these. And they came to Balaam and said to him, "Thus says Balak the son of Zippor: 'Let nothing hinder you from coming to me, for I will surely do you great honor, and whatever you say to me I will do. Come, curse this people for me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balak answers Balaam’s half-refusal by raising the price, because he has rightly judged that this man has one.

More in number and more honorable. Balak takes the hint exactly as it was left for him: a bigger delegation, higher-ranking men, and the offer raised in both currencies, honour and a blank cheque. He does not try to persuade Balaam that cursing Israel is right. He simply raises the price. Nobody sends a better offer to someone who has genuinely said no.

Our own price. Here the reader should stop being a spectator. There are things we have refused once and would refuse again at that price, and the honest question is what would have to be added to the offer: a little more money, a little more standing, the one person whose good opinion still governs us. Satan does not give up after one refusal: “when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time” (Luke 4:13).

The one who had no price. That verse is also our hope. The One tempted in the wilderness was offered all the kingdoms of the world and had no price at all, and he refused every offer in our place. His faithfulness is counted to those who have sold out cheaply, and his Spirit now strengthens them to say a cleaner no.

verseByVerse.quote: But Balaam answered and said to the servants of Balak, "Though Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not go beyond the command of the LORD my God to do less or more. So you, too, please stay here tonight, that I may know what more the LORD will say to me." And God came to Balaam at night and said to him, "If the men have come to call you, rise, go with them; but only do what I tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam’s words are flawless and his heart is not: he says nothing could buy him, then asks God again, and God lets him go.

I could not go beyond the command of the LORD. Balaam’s reply is magnificent, and it will be quoted against him for ever after. As a statement about God it is flawless. In his mouth it is also a lie, not in what it asserts but in what it conceals, because the next sentence is “that I may know what more the LORD will say to me.”

What more the LORD will say to me. God had already said it plainly. A man who says he cannot be bought and then asks the buyer to wait overnight while he checks again has told you everything about himself. He wants the money and he wants God to authorise it, and he is prepared to keep asking until the answer improves. Peter names the disease: he “loved gain from wrongdoing” (2 Peter 2:15). His words are sound; his heart is for sale.

Rise, go with them. So God gives him what he keeps asking for, with a leash: “but only do what I tell you.” Has God changed his mind? No. This is permission, and permission is not approval. Israel demanded a king until God gave them one (1 Samuel 8:7–9); of an earlier generation a psalm says, “he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them” (Psalm 106:15). There is a point at which the most frightening thing God can say to a man who will not stop asking is yes. Verse 22 tells us what God thought of the trip.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–35 — The Donkey and the Angel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the road God stands against the man who would not take no for an answer, and a donkey sees what the seer cannot. God is angry that Balaam goes, and the angel of the LORD blocks the way with a drawn sword (vv. 21–23). Three times the donkey turns aside, each time in a narrower place, and three times Balaam beats her (vv. 24–27). God opens her mouth, and her gentle reproach exposes her master (vv. 28–30). Then God opens Balaam’s eyes: the sword was there all along, and the donkey saved his life (vv. 31–33). Balaam’s confession is hedged with excuses, and he is sent on, muzzled, to speak only God’s word (vv. 34–35).
verseByVerse.theology: The talking donkey is God’s gentle mockery of a “seer” who cannot see (vv.23-31). If God can make a donkey speak, he can certainly put his words in Balaam’s mouth. God “catches the wise in their craftiness” (1 Corinthians 3:19) and can use the lowliest instrument to reveal his will.
verseByVerse.examples: God still humbles our pride with unlikely instruments (1 Cor 1:27). Beware being so sure of your own sight that a donkey sees more than you.

verseByVerse.quote: So Balaam rose in the morning and saddled his donkey and went with the princes of Moab. But God's anger was kindled because he went, and the angel of the LORD took his stand in the way as his adversary. Now he was riding on the donkey, and his two servants were with him. And the donkey saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road, with a drawn sword in his hand. And the donkey turned aside out of the road and went into the field. And Balaam struck the donkey, to turn her into the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is angry that Balaam goes, and stands in the road against him with a drawn sword, seen by the donkey and not by the seer.

God’s anger was kindled because he went. The two sentences sit side by side without explanation, and the reader is meant to feel the jolt. He had permission. He went. God was angry. Permission had never meant that God was pleased, and Balaam knew it; he had spent two nights trying to turn the one into the other.

As his adversary. The Hebrew word is satan, in its ordinary sense: one who stands in the road to oppose. Heaven has come out onto the highway with a drawn sword to stop a man going where heaven has just said he may go. That is not a contradiction. It is a kindness to a man God is determined to use, though from the saddle it looks exactly like an obstruction.

The donkey saw the angel of the LORD. And the irony that runs through the chapter begins. A seer whose livelihood rests on seeing what others cannot is sitting on the only creature in the story with functioning eyes, and he beats her for having them.

Where Christians differ: who is the angel of the LORD? He speaks as God himself, “speak only the word that I tell you” (v. 35). Many, especially in the Reformed tradition, see him as the Son of God appearing before his incarnation, as in other appearances of the angel of the LORD; others see a created angel bearing God’s name and authority. This commentary’s view: the angel who speaks and acts as God is best read as the Son. If so, the one standing in the road with a sword to guard his people from a curse is the same Lord who would later stand between them and the curse itself, and take it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel of the LORD stood in a narrow path between the vineyards, with a wall on either side. And when the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she pushed against the wall and pressed Balaam's foot against the wall. So he struck her again. Then the angel of the LORD went ahead and stood in a narrow place, where there was no way to turn either to the right or to the left. When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she lay down under Balaam. And Balaam's anger was kindled, and he struck the donkey with his staff.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The road narrows three times, and three times the donkey saves her master while he beats her for it.

A narrow path between the vineyards. First open country, where the donkey can swing into a field; then a path between vineyard walls, where she crushes his foot against the stone; then a place with no way to turn, where she simply lies down.

How God stops us. Read it as a picture of a man going the wrong way. God does not usually stop us with a wall at the first step. He allows a wide place with a small inconvenience, then a tighter place with a real cost, then no room at all, so that the man might look up before he reaches the sword. Balaam does not look up. He escalates: a blow, a second blow, and finally the staff.

So he struck her again. A man who has decided where he is going cannot tell an obstacle from a rescue, so he attacks whatever slows him down; that is why a man being warned off a course so often turns on the person warning him. Before you next lose your temper with an interruption, ask whether you know what is standing in the road ahead of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD opened the mouth of the donkey, and she said to Balaam, "What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times?" And Balaam said to the donkey, "Because you have made a fool of me. I wish I had a sword in my hand, for then I would kill you." And the donkey said to Balaam, "Am I not your donkey, on which you have ridden all your life long to this day? Is it my habit to treat you this way?" And he said, "No."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God opens the donkey’s mouth, and her gentle question shows up her master’s rage and pride.

Then the LORD opened the mouth of the donkey. Readers are sometimes embarrassed by this verse. We need not be. The text says God did it, and the New Testament treats it as history: “a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet’s madness” (2 Peter 2:16). The God who made throats and language was not stretched by this. The miracle is there to catch our eye, and what it shows is a man behaving as he has behaved all along.

Because you have made a fool of me. His own words are the most revealing he speaks in three chapters. Not that she has hurt him but that she has humiliated him, in front of the princes he is trying to impress. And he wishes for a sword, with no idea that there is one a few feet in front of his face, held by someone who has been considering using it on him.

Am I not your donkey? What she says is quietly devastating. She accuses him of nothing; she appeals to their whole shared life, years of faithful service offered as evidence. And Balaam, who has not noticed he is arguing with a donkey, must give the one-word answer that destroys his own case: “No.”

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, with his drawn sword in his hand. And he bowed down and fell on his face. And the angel of the LORD said to him, "Why have you struck your donkey these three times? Behold, I have come out to oppose you because your way is perverse before me. The donkey saw me and turned aside before me these three times. If she had not turned aside from me, surely just now I would have killed you and let her live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God opens Balaam’s eyes to the sword that was there all along, and the angel tells him the donkey he beat had saved his life.

Then the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam. He had been a few paces from that sword for the whole argument. It did not appear when his eyes were opened; it was there all along, and he was riding straight at it, shouting at his donkey.

Heaven in the road. That is how things stand with a man going his own way who thinks nothing much is happening. Heaven is not idle while we are busy; it is standing in the road. “The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good” (Proverbs 15:3). Balaam’s opened eyes changed nothing about the situation and everything about the man, which is what every genuine awakening does.

Why have you struck your donkey these three times? The angel’s first concern is a detail we might skip. The Lord of hosts, sword drawn, takes time to defend a beaten animal, and tells her owner that she was the one worth sparing. God notices what is done to creatures with no voice.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew verb behind “your way is perverse” is rare, and its exact sense is not certain: suggestions include “reckless”, “headlong” and “contrary”. Whatever the shade, the meaning is clear: Balaam was rushing down a road set against God’s will.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Balaam said to the angel of the LORD, "I have sinned, for I did not know that you stood in the road against me. Now therefore, if it is evil in your sight, I will turn back." And the angel of the LORD said to Balaam, "Go with the men, but speak only the word that I tell you." So Balaam went on with the princes of Balak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam’s confession is hedged with an excuse and an “if”, and he is sent on, muzzled, to speak only the word God gives him.

An excuse inside a confession. “I have sinned” sounds like repentance; read the whole sentence and it falls apart in the hand. First, the excuse is smuggled in: “I have sinned, for I did not know.” If not knowing is the reason, the blame belongs elsewhere, with the angel for being invisible or the donkey for being unclear. Second, and worse, the little word “if”. He has just been told by an armed angel that his way is perverse; there is no “if” left. A man who wanted to turn back would have turned the donkey round. It is the repentance of Pharaoh and of King Saul: sorrow for the sword in the road, not for the road; for the danger, not the sin. Paul draws the line exactly: “godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

The oldest non-apology. Balaam’s sentence would sit comfortably in a modern press release: “mistakes were made”, “I am sorry if anyone was offended”. Each gestures at regret while moving the fault elsewhere. Why is a plain apology so hard? Because if my standing rests on my record, a full confession is a kind of self-destruction. The gospel takes that pressure away at the root. A Christian’s standing rests not on his record but on Christ’s, so he can afford to tell the whole truth about himself, with no “if”. That is why the promise is attached to the bare admission: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). The people most free to say “I was wrong, and there is no excuse” are the people who know they are already forgiven.

Go with the men. The angel’s reply is chilling in its brevity: “Go with the men, but speak only the word that I tell you.” Balaam is sent on, a hired mouth with a sword behind it, all the way to Moab to bless the people he was paid to curse. God has harnessed an unwilling man to his purposes, and that is a terrifying thing to happen to anybody.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hired seer arrives, and the king who bought him finds that he has bought nothing. Balak meets Balaam at the border with wounded pride: why the delay, when he could pay so well (vv. 36–37)? Balaam answers that he has no power of his own and can speak only the word God puts in his mouth (v. 38). Yet he accepts the sacrificial feast and lets Balak lead him up to Bamoth-baal, a high place of Baal, to look down on Israel (vv. 39–41). From there he can see only a fraction of the camp: the enemies of God’s people cannot even take them all in, let alone curse them.
verseByVerse.theology: Balaam’s words at verse 38 set the theme of all that follows: God, not the diviner, controls the outcome. Balak’s careful ritual preparations (v.41) are about to be overturned, proving that no human scheme can reverse the blessing of God.
verseByVerse.examples: “No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD” (Proverbs 21:30). God’s purposes for his people cannot be reversed.

verseByVerse.quote: When Balak heard that Balaam had come, he went out to meet him at the city of Moab, on the border formed by the Arnon, at the extremity of the border. And Balak said to Balaam, "Did I not send to you to call you? Why did you not come to me? Am I not able to honor you?" Balaam said to Balak, "Behold, I have come to you! Have I now any power of my own to speak anything? The word that God puts in my mouth, that must I speak." Then Balaam went with Balak, and they came to Kiriath-huzoth. And Balak sacrificed oxen and sheep, and sent for Balaam and for the princes who were with him. And in the morning Balak took Balaam and brought him up to Bamoth-baal, and from there he saw a fraction of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam reaches Balak declaring that he can speak only God’s word, yet lets the king lead him up a pagan high place to look down on the people he cannot curse.

Am I not able to honor you? Balak rides out to the border to meet him, and his greeting is all wounded vanity. He has staked his kingdom on a superstition and his pride on a purchase, and he is offended that what he paid for was slow to arrive.

The word that God puts in my mouth. Balaam answers with the same flawless orthodoxy, every syllable true. Then he accepts the sacrificial feast and lets Balak walk him up to Bamoth-baal, a name meaning the high places of Baal, to look at the people he has just said he cannot curse. A man can hold a sound doctrine of God in his mouth and be led up a pagan mountain by the elbow.

He saw a fraction of the people. From the highest ground Moab has, the enemies of Israel can take in only a corner of the camp. Balak has spent a fortune and climbed a mountain, and cannot even get the whole nation into his field of view, let alone into his curse. So the chapter closes with a king and a hired seer on a pagan height at dawn, plotting against a people asleep in their tents who know nothing about it, while over their heads the verdict has already been given and cannot be revised: “they are blessed”. Nobody on any mountain in the world can unsay it.

keyVerse.quote: You shall not go with them. You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed.
keyVerse.note: Everything in chapters 22 to 24 turns on these last words. Israel is blessed not because it deserves to be but because God has blessed it, and no hired curse can reverse what God has spoken; in Christ that same blessing rests on all who believe (Galatians 3:14).

22.reflection:
God told Balaam plainly, “You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed” (v. 12), yet Balaam kept asking. In what ways are we tempted to keep asking God until we get the answer we want?

Balaam passed on God’s ban but not God’s reason (vv. 13–14). What does it look like to leave a door “ajar” on a temptation, and how can we shut it properly?

The donkey saw the angel, and the professional seer did not (vv. 22–33). Can you recall an interruption or obstacle that later proved to be God’s protection? How should that change the way we react to the next one?

Balaam’s confession came with an excuse and an “if” (v. 34). Why does knowing that our standing rests on Christ’s record, not ours, free us to confess our sins plainly?

23.title: Balaam's First and Second Oracles: God Is Not Man, That He Should Lie
23.text: <sup>1</sup>And Balaam said to Balak, "Build for me here seven altars, and prepare for me here seven bulls and seven rams."<sup>2</sup>Balak did as Balaam had said. And Balak and Balaam offered on each altar a bull and a ram.<sup>3</sup>And Balaam said to Balak, "Stand beside your burnt offering, and I will go. Perhaps the LORD will come to meet me, and whatever he shows me I will tell you." And he went to a bare height,<sup>4</sup>and God met Balaam. And Balaam said to him, "I have arranged the seven altars and I have offered on each altar a bull and a ram."<sup>5</sup>And the LORD put a word in Balaam's mouth and said, "Return to Balak, and thus you shall speak."<sup>6</sup>And he returned to him, and behold, he and all the princes of Moab were standing beside his burnt offering.<sup>7</sup>And Balaam took up his discourse and said, "From Aram Balak has brought me, the king of Moab from the eastern mountains: 'Come, curse Jacob for me, and come, denounce Israel!'<sup>8</sup>How can I curse whom God has not cursed? How can I denounce whom the LORD has not denounced?<sup>9</sup>For from the top of the crags I see him, from the hills I behold him; behold, a people dwelling alone, and not counting itself among the nations!<sup>10</sup>Who can count the dust of Jacob or number the fourth part of Israel? Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!"<sup>11</sup>And Balak said to Balaam, "What have you done to me? I took you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have done nothing but bless them."<sup>12</sup>And he answered and said, "Must I not take care to speak what the LORD puts in my mouth?"<sup>13</sup>And Balak said to him, "Please come with me to another place, from which you may see them. You shall see only a fraction of them and shall not see them all. Then curse them for me from there."<sup>14</sup>And he took him to the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah, and built seven altars and offered a bull and a ram on each altar.<sup>15</sup>Balaam said to Balak, "Stand here beside your burnt offering, while I meet the LORD over there."<sup>16</sup>And the LORD met Balaam and put a word in his mouth and said, "Return to Balak, and thus shall you speak."<sup>17</sup>And he came to him, and behold, he was standing beside his burnt offering, and the princes of Moab with him. And Balak said to him, "What has the LORD spoken?"<sup>18</sup>And Balaam took up his discourse and said, "Rise, Balak, and hear; give ear to me, O son of Zippor:<sup>19</sup>God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not fulfill it?<sup>20</sup>Behold, I received a command to bless: he has blessed, and I cannot revoke it.<sup>21</sup>He has not beheld misfortune in Jacob, nor has he seen trouble in Israel. The LORD their God is with them, and the shout of a king is among them.<sup>22</sup>God brings them out of Egypt and is for them like the horns of the wild ox.<sup>23</sup>For there is no enchantment against Jacob, no divination against Israel; now it shall be said of Jacob and Israel, 'What has God wrought!'<sup>24</sup>Behold, a people! As a lioness it rises up and as a lion it lifts itself; it does not lie down until it has devoured the prey and drunk the blood of the slain."<sup>25</sup>And Balak said to Balaam, "Do not curse them at all, and do not bless them at all."<sup>26</sup>But Balaam answered Balak, "Did I not tell you, 'All that the LORD says, that I must do'?"<sup>27</sup>And Balak said to Balaam, "Come now, I will take you to another place. Perhaps it will please God that you may curse them for me from there."<sup>28</sup>So Balak took Balaam to the top of Peor, which overlooks the desert.<sup>29</sup>And Balaam said to Balak, "Build for me here seven altars and prepare for me here seven bulls and seven rams."<sup>30</sup>And Balak did as Balaam had said, and offered a bull and a ram on each altar.
23.overview:
Where we are. Balak king of Moab has brought the famous seer Balaam from the Euphrates to curse Israel, and God has warned Balaam to speak only the word he is given (chapter 22). Now, on the heights above the camp, the altars go up and the hired mouth opens.

The message. God’s blessing cannot be bought off, argued down or reversed, because “God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind” (v. 19). Every attempt to curse his people turns into blessing in the cursing mouth. Their safety rests not on their record, which God knows, but on his word, which he will not take back.

Why it was said. Israel, camped below, knew nothing of what was being said about them on the hilltops. The generation about to enter the land needed to hear afterwards that the God who had disciplined them in the wilderness had also, unseen, defended them (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Seven altars are built and the rites performed, and God meets Balaam, not because the ritual worked but because he chose to (vv. 1–6). The first oracle asks, “How can I curse whom God has not cursed?”, marvels at a people set apart and beyond counting, and longs to die as they die (vv. 7–10). Balak protests, and Balaam pleads that he must speak what he is given (vv. 11–12). From Pisgah the second oracle is stronger: God does not lie or change, he has blessed and it cannot be revoked, the LORD is with them as king, and no sorcery can touch them (vv. 13–24). Balak, who wanted a curse, now begs for silence, and fails to get even that (vv. 25–26). Then he tries a third hill, Peor (vv. 27–30).

Where it leads. By God’s character revealed and by promise. The God who cannot lie has made promises that “find their Yes” in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), and the blessing no one could revoke rests on all who are joined to him. Balaam’s question, “How can I curse whom God has not cursed?”, becomes Paul’s: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33). And the lion rising in the camp (v. 24) echoes the promise to Judah that ends in “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5).

For us. Believers do not need to fear curses, accusations or verdicts from any lesser court: the only Judge has already spoken in Christ. Approach God not with a religious technique and a “perhaps” but as children who know their Father keeps his word. And do not imitate Balaam, sound in every word and still for sale.
23.theology:
God's unchanging faithfulness. God is not man, that he should lie or change his mind, so his blessing cannot be revoked.

Sin covered. If verse 21 is read as the older versions read it, God sees no guilt in Jacob, not because they are sinless but because of the grace he has promised them, a faint first sight of the forgiveness Paul describes in Romans 4.

The futility of opposition. Every altar and high place fails to produce a curse. The enemies of God’s people wear themselves out against a decision of God that cannot be changed.
23.examples: The God who cannot lie has spoken his blessing over you in Christ, and it cannot be revoked. Rest in promises that are Yes and Amen in Jesus, sealed by a God who does not change.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hired seer opens his mouth to curse, and God fills it with blessing. Balaam sets up seven altars, the heaviest ritual he knows, and goes off hoping “perhaps” the LORD will meet him (vv. 1–3). God does meet him, on his own terms, and puts a word in his mouth (vv. 4–6). The first oracle states the contract aloud and then confesses that it cannot be done: “How can I curse whom God has not cursed?” Israel is a people set apart and too many to count, and Balaam wishes he could die as they die (vv. 7–10). Balak is outraged, and Balaam can only say that he must speak what the LORD gives (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel’s security rests not on its own merit but on God’s choice of it, and what God has blessed no purchased curse can reach.
verseByVerse.examples: No accusation, curse or scheme can stand against those God has set apart as his own.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balaam said to Balak, "Build for me here seven altars, and prepare for me here seven bulls and seven rams." Balak did as Balaam had said. And Balak and Balaam offered on each altar a bull and a ram. And Balaam said to Balak, "Stand beside your burnt offering, and I will go. Perhaps the LORD will come to meet me, and whatever he shows me I will tell you." And he went to a bare height,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam sets up the most elaborate ritual he knows, and then goes off hoping that “perhaps” the LORD will come.

Build for me here seven altars. Seven altars with a bull and a ram on each is the heaviest ritual apparatus Balaam knows, and he will do it on three summits: twenty-one altars, forty-two animals, a fortune in livestock. In his world the gods responded to correct procedure: get the numbers and the view right, and the power could be tapped and pointed. It is religion as engineering, which is why Balak is paying by the mountain.

Perhaps the LORD will come to meet me. One word gives the enterprise away. After all that expense, the man is not sure anyone is there. Every religion of technique ends in that word, because a god who can be operated cannot be trusted. The believer does not build an altar and hope; he comes to a Father who has already said “Come to me”, and everything needed to bring us to God was done at the cross.

The anxious spirituality of technique. Balaam’s “perhaps” has a modern accent. Much of today’s spirituality is a toolkit: the right ritual, affirmation or visualisation, and the universe is supposed to deliver. The cost is Balaam’s: you are always adjusting the procedure and never at rest. Christianity is not a better technique but the end of technique, because it begins with a God who came to us before we had built anything. The difference shows in how the believer prays: not “perhaps” but “Abba”. “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15). Children need no method to approach their father, only to know that they are his.

verseByVerse.quote: and God met Balaam. And Balaam said to him, "I have arranged the seven altars and I have offered on each altar a bull and a ram." And the LORD put a word in Balaam's mouth and said, "Return to Balak, and thus you shall speak." And he returned to him, and behold, he and all the princes of Moab were standing beside his burnt offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God meets Balaam, not because the altars worked but because he chose to, and puts his own word in the hired man’s mouth.

And God met Balaam. Three words, and they wreck the theory. God came because he had business of his own with this man, and would have come to an empty hillside had he chosen.

I have arranged the seven altars. What Balaam says is quietly damning: no worship, not even a request. He presents his bill: here is what I built, it is all correct, now let us do business. It is the Pharisee in the temple thanking God for his own record (Luke 18:11–12), the oldest religious instinct there is. The honest question is whether the sentence underneath your prayers is ever “Look what I have done” rather than “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13), the prayer of the man Jesus says went home justified.

The LORD put a word in Balaam’s mouth. God does not answer the invoice. The same words describe true prophecy (Deuteronomy 18:18), and here they are deliberately physical. Balaam is not given a vision to interpret. A word is placed in him, and he will carry it down the hill and say it whether he likes it or not. Balak has hired a man; God has taken over his mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balaam took up his discourse and said, "From Aram Balak has brought me, the king of Moab from the eastern mountains: 'Come, curse Jacob for me, and come, denounce Israel!' How can I curse whom God has not cursed? How can I denounce whom the LORD has not denounced?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam’s first oracle announces in front of his client that he cannot curse a people God has not cursed.

Come, curse Jacob for me. The oracle (the message God gives) opens by stating the contract aloud in front of the client: the distance, the commission, the curse that was ordered.

How can I curse whom God has not cursed? Then, instead of the curse, two questions. Not “I will not” but “How can I”: he is not refusing on principle but reporting that it cannot be done, like a man saying he cannot lift a mountain.

The Christian’s security. Everything the New Testament says about a Christian’s security is in the shape of those questions. Paul asks them almost word for word, in the language of a courtroom: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died” (Romans 8:33–34). Somebody has paid a great deal to accuse. But the verdict has already been entered by the only court there is, and there is no higher one to appeal to. A curse has to come from somewhere, and there is nowhere left for this one to come from.

Who has the last word about you? Modern people live in a courtroom that never adjourns: rated, reviewed and appraised, and when the verdicts fall silent the inner critic takes the bench. Ignoring every verdict but your own only makes you judge and defendant at once. Paul’s way out is the one Balaam stumbles on here: there is a court above all the others, and its ruling cannot be appealed. “But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself… It is the Lord who judges me” (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). For those in Christ that Judge has already spoken, before the work of a single day is done. The verdict does not wait on the performance; it sets you free for it.

verseByVerse.quote: For from the top of the crags I see him, from the hills I behold him; behold, a people dwelling alone, and not counting itself among the nations! Who can count the dust of Jacob or number the fourth part of Israel? Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam sees a people set apart by God and beyond counting, and wishes he could die as they die.

A people dwelling alone. Looking down at a camp laid out in a square around a tent, Balaam is struck that they do not blend in. Israel was not distinct because she was better; she was distinct because God had put his name on her. That distinctness continues, “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession” (1 Peter 2:9), though it has never meant retreat from the world. Israel dwelt alone in full view of the nations, so that they would look, and a hired pagan on a hilltop is doing just that.

Who can count the dust of Jacob? God had promised Abraham offspring “as the dust of the earth” (Genesis 13:16), and here a foreign seer, hired to stop that promise, has to count it and cannot.

Let me die the death of the upright. Then the line that ought to stop every reader. He says it on a pagan height, beside smoking altars, in the pay of a king who wants this people destroyed. He wants to die as God’s people die without living as they live: to end up where they end up after a lifetime of going somewhere else. It is the most honest thing he ever says and the most useless, because a man does not get to choose his last hour separately from the years before it. Balaam was killed with the sword among the Midianites, the enemies of the people he had just blessed (31:8): the opposite of what he asked for, chosen one small compromise at a time. Wanting a Christian death is not the same as wanting Christ. But Christ is offered freely to anyone who does want him, and the death of the upright belongs to all who come.

Uncertain wording. “The fourth part of Israel” is an unusual phrase. It may refer to one of the four groups of tribes camped around the tabernacle (chapter 2), so that Balaam cannot count even a quarter of the people; some scholars, comparing a related word in another ancient language, read “the dust cloud of Israel”. Either way the point is the same: the people are past counting.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balak said to Balaam, "What have you done to me? I took you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have done nothing but bless them." And he answered and said, "Must I not take care to speak what the LORD puts in my mouth?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balak protests that he paid for a curse and got a blessing, and Balaam answers correctly but without loyalty: he must say what the LORD gives him.

What have you done to me? Balak has watched his four-hundred-mile investment pronounce a benediction over the people it was hired to destroy, and his cry is pure commercial outrage. Even as he brushes against the will of the Almighty, he can see only a supplier who has failed to deliver.

Must I not take care to speak what the LORD puts in my mouth? Balaam’s reply is correct in every word, and his heart is not in it. Having said it, he will at once agree to try again from a different hill. To say correct things about God is not to be loyal to him; a man can be sound in every word and still be for sale.

Every curse turned to blessing. Underneath the comedy, hold on to the pattern. Every mouth opened against the people of God in these chapters is compelled to bless them. The curse cannot be bought, and no change of hill will produce it. “No weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed, and you shall refute every tongue that rises against you in judgment” (Isaiah 54:17).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A new hilltop brings a stronger blessing and the chapter’s great statement about God. Balak hopes a smaller view of Israel will yield a curse, and repeats the whole ritual on Pisgah (vv. 13–15). The second oracle tells him to his face that God “is not man, that he should lie”: what he has said, he will do (vv. 16–19). He has blessed, and no one can revoke it; the LORD is with his people as their king (vv. 20–21). The God who brought them out of Egypt is their strength, no sorcery can touch them, and they rise like a lion (vv. 22–24). Balak begs for silence, and cannot have even that (vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.theology: Numbers 23:19 is one of the high points of the Bible’s teaching about God: God does not lie or change his mind as men do (cf. 1 Sam 15:29; Mal 3:6), and so his promises to his people are unbreakable (Heb 6:17-18).
verseByVerse.examples: Our hope rests on the same unchanging God, whose promises do not expire.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balak said to him, "Please come with me to another place, from which you may see them. You shall see only a fraction of them and shall not see them all. Then curse them for me from there." And he took him to the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah, and built seven altars and offered a bull and a ram on each altar. Balaam said to Balak, "Stand here beside your burnt offering, while I meet the LORD over there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balak decides the problem was the view, and repeats the whole ritual on another hill, as if God’s verdict depended on the angle.

Please come with me to another place. Balak’s next idea is superstition dressed as strategy: perhaps a smaller view will produce a smaller blessing. He is trying to change God’s verdict by changing the angle, and the whole costly ritual is repeated on the top of Pisgah, on the assumption that the failure was technical.

Looking for another angle. When God has plainly said no, the temptation is not usually to defy him outright but to seek a different vantage point, another counsellor, another passage, another congregation, until the view is narrow enough that the answer we wanted looks defensible. Balak was not a stupid man. He simply could not accept that the obstacle was not the arrangement but the Almighty.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD met Balaam and put a word in his mouth and said, "Return to Balak, and thus shall you speak." And he came to him, and behold, he was standing beside his burnt offering, and the princes of Moab with him. And Balak said to him, "What has the LORD spoken?" And Balaam took up his discourse and said, "Rise, Balak, and hear; give ear to me, O son of Zippor: God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not fulfill it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second oracle tells Balak to his face that God does not lie or change his mind: what he has promised, he will do.

Rise, Balak, and hear. The king of Moab is made to stand beside his own burnt offering and be lectured, and what follows is one of the towering statements about God in the Old Testament, delivered by a man who has been trying to get round it for three days.

God is not man, that he should lie. Two things are denied, and they are the two things men do constantly: we say what is not so, and we say what we mean and then go back on it. God does neither. He is “God, who never lies” (Titus 1:2), and he confirmed his promise with an oath so that “by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement” (Hebrews 6:18). Every one of those promises has its “Yes” in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).

But did God not relent? Scripture also says that God relented, after Moses interceded at Sinai and over Nineveh (Exodus 32:14; Jonah 3:10). Those passages describe something different: God’s unchanging character meeting a changed human situation. He had always been the God who spares the repentant, and Nineveh repented. What this verse denies is that God is fickle, that his word can be renegotiated, or that his promise might quietly lapse. The proof is on the mountain: Balaam has asked twice for a different answer, and God has not moved an inch.

Where Christians differ: does God ever change his mind? Open theists hold that God does not know the future free choices of people and genuinely changes his plans as events unfold, and read the passages where God “relents” in that way. This commentary’s view: God’s purposes and character never change, as this verse says outright; when Scripture says he relented or regretted, it speaks in human terms of his settled response to changed human conduct, a response he purposed all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I received a command to bless: he has blessed, and I cannot revoke it. He has not beheld misfortune in Jacob, nor has he seen trouble in Israel. The LORD their God is with them, and the shout of a king is among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has blessed his people and no one can revoke it, for the LORD himself is with them as their king.

He has blessed, and I cannot revoke it. The blessing is not Balaam’s to give, and so not his to withdraw. Nobody can revoke it, because nobody issued it but God, and the man who most wishes otherwise is the one who says so.

The shout of a king is among them. The camp rings with the acclaim of a king, and the king is the LORD their God (compare Exodus 15:18). Israel has no human king yet; its strength is that God himself reigns in the middle of it.

Where the verse points. On either reading of the first line (see below), the verse points forward. God had spent twenty-two chapters recording what was wrong with this nation. He knew. Yet to an outsider hired to find a fault he could exploit, the answer is that there is nothing there to be used. Behind it stands what Paul makes explicit: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin” (Romans 4:7–8). God saw everything Israel was, set his blessing on them anyway, and would not permit one syllable against them on a foreign mountain. That is not because sin does not matter. It is because God had already determined what he would do about it, on a hill of his own choosing, centuries later.

Uncertain wording. The two Hebrew words in “He has not beheld misfortune in Jacob, nor has he seen trouble in Israel” can mean misfortune and trouble, as the ESV takes them, or iniquity and perverseness, as the King James and other older versions read them. Read the first way, no calamity can overtake this people because the LORD is with them.
