Read the second, God does not look upon iniquity in his covenant people, that is, he does not hold it against them. Godly readers have taken it both ways, and the sentence is genuinely open.

verseByVerse.quote: God brings them out of Egypt and is for them like the horns of the wild ox. For there is no enchantment against Jacob, no divination against Israel; now it shall be said of Jacob and Israel, 'What has God wrought!' Behold, a people! As a lioness it rises up and as a lion it lifts itself; it does not lie down until it has devoured the prey and drunk the blood of the slain."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who brought Israel out of Egypt is their strength; no sorcery can touch them, and they rise like a lion.

Like the horns of the wild ox. The wild ox, the aurochs, the great untamed bull nobody yoked, is a picture not of Israel’s strength but of God’s strength used for Israel. Their power is borrowed, and that is the point.

There is no enchantment against Jacob. Then the flat demolition of Balak’s business plan: the professional diviner announces from his own altars that divination does not work on these people. And so the nations will not ask what Israel has achieved. They will say, “What has God wrought!”, a line so charged that, at the suggestion of a friend’s young daughter, Samuel Morse sent it as the first official message over his telegraph line in 1844.

As a lioness it rises up. The last image is the fiercest. Balak had described Israel as an ox grazing (22:4); God describes them as a lion getting up. It echoes Jacob’s blessing of Judah, “a lion’s cub” (Genesis 49:9), a promise that reaches its end in the last book of the Bible, where the Lion is named at last: “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered” (Revelation 5:5). The strength the nations feared in the camp was never really the camp’s. It was the strength of the One who would one day be born inside it.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew preposition in “no enchantment against Jacob, no divination against Israel” can also mean “in”. Read that way, the line says that Israel does not use sorcery, because God himself tells them what he is doing (compare Deuteronomy 18:10–15). The ESV’s “against” fits Balaam’s situation best: his trade has no power over this people.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balak said to Balaam, "Do not curse them at all, and do not bless them at all." But Balaam answered Balak, "Did I not tell you, 'All that the LORD says, that I must do'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balak, who could not buy a curse, now tries to buy silence, and cannot get that either.

Do not curse them at all, and do not bless them at all. There is genuine comedy here, and Scripture means us to see it: a king with an army and a treasury trying to switch off the word of God like a man slapping a radio, while the blessings keep coming. “He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision” (Psalm 2:4).

All that the LORD says, that I must do. Balaam’s answer is once again perfectly correct, and once again spoken by a man still on the payroll and willing to walk up one more hill. He has told Balak the truth each time, and each time he has stayed for the fee.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–30 — Preparing for a Third Attempt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Balak tries a third time, and the place he chooses is a warning. He takes Balaam to the top of Peor, with the same hopeful “perhaps” and the same seven altars, as if God might at last be persuaded from a different angle (vv. 27–30). His stubbornness is almost pitiable, and it is futile: no curse will come. Yet Peor is the hill below which, two chapters later, Israel will fall into idolatry and immorality, on Balaam’s advice (25:1–9; 31:16). The enemy who cannot curse God’s people can still try to lead them into sin.
verseByVerse.theology: Balak keeps changing locations and rebuilding altars, as if the problem were the setting rather than the sovereign God: stubborn opposition that will not learn and cannot win (Prov 21:30).
verseByVerse.examples: Fighting against God’s settled purpose only wastes the fighter. A God who does not change his mind about blessing us can be trusted when he says no. When we already know the right thing to do (James 4:17), we need not keep looking for a hill from which it might turn out differently.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balak said to Balaam, "Come now, I will take you to another place. Perhaps it will please God that you may curse them for me from there." So Balak took Balaam to the top of Peor, which overlooks the desert. And Balaam said to Balak, "Build for me here seven altars and prepare for me here seven bulls and seven rams." And Balak did as Balaam had said, and offered a bull and a ram on each altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balak tries a third hill, Peor, with the same “perhaps”, unaware that this is the place where Israel will later be harmed, not by a curse but by sin.

Perhaps it will please God. Astonishingly, they go again, and “perhaps” returns, the word Balaam used on the first mountain. Two men who have watched God override them twice are still trying the same door.

The top of Peor. The place should make the reader go cold. In two chapters Israel will be camped below this hill, drawn into the sacrifices of Baal of Peor, and twenty-four thousand will die of a plague (25:3, 9). Everything Balak wanted will happen here, and Balaam will be behind it, because before he goes home he will give one last piece of advice about how to harm a nation you cannot curse (31:16; Revelation 2:14).

Looking the wrong way. So the altars go up a third time on the one hill where the enemy will eventually get what he came for. Balak is standing on the answer to his problem and looking the wrong way, waiting for a curse out of the sky, while the thing that will actually work is in the valley under his feet. The arrangement of these chapters is deliberate: three chapters of God refusing, again and again, to let a word be spoken against his people, and one chapter of what happens next. Whatever Israel had to fear, it was never Balaam’s curse; it was their own hearts.

keyVerse.quote: God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not fulfill it?
keyVerse.note: Spoken by a hired seer to the king who paid him, this is the bedrock of the whole Balaam story: God’s blessing cannot be revoked because God himself does not lie or change. It is the ground of every believer’s confidence, for all God’s promises find their “Yes” in Christ.

23.reflection:
Balaam built altars and then said, “Perhaps the LORD will come to meet me” (v. 3). How is approaching God by technique different from approaching him as a child comes to a father? Where do we slip into the first?

“How can I curse whom God has not cursed?” (v. 8). Whose verdicts on you carry the most weight in your life, and how does God’s verdict in Christ answer them?

“God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind” (v. 19). Which of God’s promises do you find hardest to rely on, and how does this verse speak to that?

Balak kept trying new hills, hoping for a different answer (vv. 13, 27). When God has plainly said no, how do we look for “another angle”, and what would it mean to accept his word instead?

24.title: Balaam's Final Oracles: A Star Shall Come Out of Jacob
24.text: <sup>1</sup>When Balaam saw that it pleased the LORD to bless Israel, he did not go, as at other times, to look for omens, but set his face toward the wilderness.<sup>2</sup>And Balaam lifted up his eyes and saw Israel camping tribe by tribe. And the Spirit of God came upon him,<sup>3</sup>and he took up his discourse and said, "The oracle of Balaam the son of Beor, the oracle of the man whose eye is opened,<sup>4</sup>the oracle of him who hears the words of God, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down with his eyes uncovered:<sup>5</sup>How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, your encampments, O Israel!<sup>6</sup>Like palm groves that stretch afar, like gardens beside a river, like aloes that the LORD has planted, like cedar trees beside the waters.<sup>7</sup>Water shall flow from his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters; his king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted.<sup>8</sup>God brings him out of Egypt and is for him like the horns of the wild ox; he shall eat up the nations, his adversaries, and shall break their bones in pieces and pierce them through with his arrows.<sup>9</sup>He crouched, he lay down like a lion and like a lioness; who will rouse him up? Blessed are those who bless you, and cursed are those who curse you."<sup>10</sup>And Balak's anger was kindled against Balaam, and he struck his hands together. And Balak said to Balaam, "I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed them these three times.<sup>11</sup>Therefore now flee to your own place. I said, 'I will certainly honor you,' but the LORD has held you back from honor."<sup>12</sup>And Balaam said to Balak, "Did I not tell your messengers whom you sent to me,<sup>13</sup>'If Balak should give me his house full of silver and gold, I would not be able to go beyond the word of the LORD, to do either good or bad of my own will. What the LORD speaks, that will I speak'?<sup>14</sup>And now, behold, I am going to my people. Come, I will let you know what this people will do to your people in the latter days."<sup>15</sup>And he took up his discourse and said, "The oracle of Balaam the son of Beor, the oracle of the man whose eye is opened,<sup>16</sup>the oracle of him who hears the words of God, and knows the knowledge of the Most High, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down with his eyes uncovered:<sup>17</sup>I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel; it shall crush the forehead of Moab and break down all the sons of Sheth.<sup>18</sup>Edom shall be dispossessed; Seir also, his enemies, shall be dispossessed. Israel is doing valiantly.<sup>19</sup>And one from Jacob shall exercise dominion and destroy the survivors of cities!"<sup>20</sup>Then he looked on Amalek and took up his discourse and said, "Amalek was the first among the nations, but its end is utter destruction."<sup>21</sup>And he looked on the Kenite, and took up his discourse and said, "Enduring is your dwelling place, and your nest is set in the rock.<sup>22</sup>Nevertheless, Kain shall be burned when Asshur takes you away captive."<sup>23</sup>And he took up his discourse and said, "Alas, who shall live when God does this?<sup>24</sup>But ships shall come from Kittim and shall afflict Asshur and Eber; and he too shall come to utter destruction."<sup>25</sup>Then Balaam rose and went back to his place. And Balak also went his way.
24.overview:
Where we are. Twice Balak has paid for a curse on Israel, and twice Balaam has blessed them instead (chapter 23). Now, on the top of Peor, the story reaches its climax: the last two oracles, the king’s fury, and the seer’s departure.

The message. God not only protects his people; he promises them a King. Balaam gives up his omens, the Spirit of God comes upon him, and he sees Israel as God sees it, planted and lovely, under the promise to Abraham: “Blessed are those who bless you, and cursed are those who curse you” (v. 9). Then, dismissed and unpaid, he sees far off a star coming out of Jacob and a sceptre rising out of Israel, a ruler who will crush the enemies of God’s people (v. 17). And the man who saw all this goes home unchanged.

Why it was said. Israel, about to enter the land without a king, needed to know that their future was not in their own hands but in God’s promise, and that a ruler from Jacob was coming (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The Spirit comes on Balaam, and the third oracle pictures Israel as gardens by a river, with a king greater than Agag, and ends with God’s promise to Abraham turned against the man who paid for a curse (vv. 1–9). Balak, furious, dismisses him without his fee (vv. 10–11). Balaam answers that he can speak only the LORD’s word, and offers one more oracle unpaid (vv. 12–14). The fourth oracle sees a star and a sceptre from Jacob crushing Moab and Edom, and brief oracles follow on Amalek, the Kenites and Asshur, until empires rise and fall before God (vv. 15–24). Then both men go home (v. 25).

Where it leads. By promise, openly. The near fulfilment is David, who subdued Moab and Edom, but the oracle sees further, to “one from Jacob” whose rule has no stated end. Jesus calls himself “the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star” (Revelation 22:16), and wise men from the east, as Balaam was, came looking for the King whose star they had seen (Matthew 2:1–2). The blessing on Abraham’s seed and the King from Jacob meet in Christ.

For us. Look to the Star Balaam saw only at a distance: he has come, and whoever comes to him he will never cast out. Do not mistake spiritual experience or sound words for a changed heart; Balaam had both and went back to his place. And when you have quietly suffered wrong, leave it to God, who settles accounts for his people.
24.theology:
The Star out of Jacob. Balaam prophesies a coming royal King from Israel, fulfilled in Christ, the Star and Scepter.

God's sovereign freedom. God overrules even a pagan, mercenary prophet to proclaim the coming Messiah; he can put the gospel in the mouth of his enemy. The King he announces reigns over every hostile nation.
24.examples: The Star has risen, and the King foretold by a pagan seer reigns. Your security rests not in yourself but in Christ the Scepter of Israel, before whom every enemy will bow and every curse be turned to blessing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit of God comes on the hired seer, and he sees Israel as God sees it. Balaam gives up looking for omens, turns his face to the camp, and the Spirit comes upon him (vv. 1–2). He introduces himself as the man whose eye is opened, flat on his face and wide awake (vv. 3–4). Then he sings of Israel’s tents as palm groves, gardens by a river and trees the LORD has planted (vv. 5–6), of a king greater than Agag and a people strong as a lion (vv. 7–9a). He ends with God’s own promise to Abraham, “Blessed are those who bless you, and cursed are those who curse you”, recited over the king who paid for a curse (v. 9b).
verseByVerse.theology: The third oracle repeats almost word for word God’s covenant promise to Abraham (v.9; cf. Gen 12:3; 27:29). Through a pagan’s mouth God confirms what he swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and pictures Israel’s flourishing as his own planting (v.6).
verseByVerse.examples: The blessing of Abraham still stands over God’s people in Christ, the true offspring of Abraham (Gal 3:16, 29), and no curse can undo it.

verseByVerse.quote: When Balaam saw that it pleased the LORD to bless Israel, he did not go, as at other times, to look for omens, but set his face toward the wilderness. And Balaam lifted up his eyes and saw Israel camping tribe by tribe. And the Spirit of God came upon him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam gives up his omens and simply looks at the camp, and the Spirit of God comes upon him, a gift for a task, not a new heart.

He did not go, as at other times, to look for omens. Three times he has built the altars, and the answer has been the same. He gives up the rituals and simply turns and looks at the camp, laid out “tribe by tribe” around the tabernacle as God had ordered it (chapter 2).

The Spirit upon a man for hire. The Spirit of God, on a man for hire? In the Old Testament the Spirit often comes upon a man to equip him for a task, Samson for strength, Bezalel for craftsmanship, Saul for prophecy after God had rejected him (1 Samuel 19:23–24), and that is not the same thing as a new heart. It can be given to a man who is not saved. What Christians are promised is better: not the Spirit descending on them for a job but taking up residence in them for ever, “the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Romans 8:9), “will be in you” (John 14:17). The Spirit used Balaam but never lived in him, and this chapter shows the difference.

Isn’t spiritual experience the heart of religion? Many now think so: doctrine divides, but a moment of awe on a mountain or in music feels like the real thing. The psychologist William James, in The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), treated religion chiefly as the experiences of individuals in their solitude, and much of our culture has followed him. Balaam is the Bible’s warning: few men had experiences to match his, and none of it changed what he loved. Jesus says that on the last day some will plead their prophecies and hear, “I never knew you” (Matthew 7:23). What saves is not having felt God but being known by him, and that comes through a Person, not a peak: “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

verseByVerse.quote: and he took up his discourse and said, "The oracle of Balaam the son of Beor, the oracle of the man whose eye is opened, the oracle of him who hears the words of God, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down with his eyes uncovered:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam introduces his oracle as a man whose eyes God has opened, lying on the ground and wide awake while God speaks through him.

The man whose eye is opened. Balaam announces who he is, like a professional’s letterhead (repeated at verse 15), and it is full of irony: the man whose eye is opened is the man who two chapters ago could not see an armed angel in front of him while his donkey could. Whatever sight he now has is not his own; God opened his eyes then and is opening them now.

Falling down with his eyes uncovered. This pictures a man flat on the ground and wide awake: not in a trance, not working himself into anything, but prostrate, conscious, and being spoken through. The apparatus of pagan religion has gone; there is only a man on his face and a word he did not choose and cannot stop.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word translated “opened” occurs only here and in verse 15, and its meaning is disputed: some take it as “closed”, that is, shut to the outward world while seeing inwardly. Most modern versions, like the ESV, read “opened”, which suits “his eyes uncovered” in the next line. Either way, Balaam claims to see what God shows him.

verseByVerse.quote: How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, your encampments, O Israel! Like palm groves that stretch afar, like gardens beside a river, like aloes that the LORD has planted, like cedar trees beside the waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Looking down on a tent camp in the desert, Balaam sees what God sees: a lovely people, planted by the LORD like trees by water.

How lovely are your tents, O Jacob. Of all the sentences in Numbers, this is the one the Jewish people have loved most: it opens the morning prayers, and for centuries Jews entering the synagogue have begun with these words. They were composed by a pagan diviner in the pay of a man who wanted the whole camp dead.

Like gardens beside a river. Every picture is wet: palm groves, a river, planted aloes, cedars by the water, and Balaam is looking down at a tent city in a desert where the nation has spent forty years arguing about the next drink. He is describing not what is in front of his eyes but what God sees, and intends to make of them.

Aloes that the LORD has planted. The middle image gives the reason: not a people who turned out well, but trees planted by hand, in ground the gardener chose. Israel’s loveliness is entirely a gift from God, and so is the church’s: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit” (John 15:16). What the enemy saw that morning was not a nation’s achievement. It was God’s gardening, seen from a distance, and it was beautiful.

verseByVerse.quote: Water shall flow from his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters; his king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted. God brings him out of Egypt and is for him like the horns of the wild ox; he shall eat up the nations, his adversaries, and shall break their bones in pieces and pierce them through with his arrows. He crouched, he lay down like a lion and like a lioness; who will rouse him up? Blessed are those who bless you, and cursed are those who curse you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel will have a king greater than its enemies and the strength of a lion, and God’s promise to Abraham stands: those who bless it are blessed, and those who curse it are cursed.

His king shall be higher than Agag. The oracle runs past anything Balaam could have known. Israel will have no king for centuries and is at this moment a refugee column with a tent for a capital. Agag appears to be the royal title of the Amalekites, and the coming king will be greater than he, as happened when Saul and then David broke Amalek (1 Samuel 15).

He lay down like a lion. The strength images intensify. The lion here is not on the hunt but lying down, which is more frightening, because it means the lion is not worried. Israel is asleep in the valley. Nobody is going to wake her.

Blessed are those who bless you. Last comes the most delicious sentence in the Balaam story. It is God’s promise to Abraham, “I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse” (Genesis 12:3), and Balak has paid a fortune to have it reversed. Instead he hears it recited over him by his own employee at his own expense. Nobody outbids God for the last word about his people, and the promise reaches its goal in Christ, Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:14, 16).

Textual note. The Septuagint, the early Greek translation of the Old Testament, reads verse 7 differently: a man will come from his seed and rule many nations, with Gog in place of Agag. It shows that Jews before Christ already heard a coming ruler here.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Balak’s fury ends the contract, but not the word of God. The king claps his hands in contempt, tells Balaam to flee home, and says, truly, that the LORD has kept him from his reward (vv. 10–11). Balaam defends himself by quoting his own fine words: not for a house full of silver and gold could he go beyond the word of the LORD (vv. 12–13). Then, owed nothing and paid nothing, he offers one more oracle about what Israel will do to Moab “in the latter days” (v. 14). The crowning prophecy is about to be given free, because it was never Balaam’s to sell.
verseByVerse.theology: Balak can withhold Balaam’s fee but cannot alter God’s decree. Balaam’s insistence that he can speak only God’s word (vv.12-13), though self-serving, is true, and sets up a word about “the latter days” (v.14) that reaches far beyond Moab to the coming King.
verseByVerse.examples: Those who set themselves against God’s purposes for his people may rage, but they cannot prevail.

verseByVerse.quote: And Balak's anger was kindled against Balaam, and he struck his hands together. And Balak said to Balaam, "I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed them these three times. Therefore now flee to your own place. I said, 'I will certainly honor you,' but the LORD has held you back from honor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balak dismisses Balaam in fury, without his fee, and unwittingly speaks the truth: the LORD has kept him from his reward.

He struck his hands together. A gesture of furious contempt, and all Balak has left: the contract is torn up, and Balaam is dismissed unpaid and told to run.

The LORD has held you back from honor. Balak says one true thing, as an accusation. The silver and the standing at a royal court were within reach, and God stood in the road again, as on the road from Pethor.

The way of Balaam. The man who has just delivered two of the greatest oracles in the Old Testament has lost everything he came for, and Peter tells us he “loved gain from wrongdoing” (2 Peter 2:15). That is what makes what happens next so terrible. Before he leaves the district he will find another way to earn the money, one that does not need God’s permission, and it will kill twenty-four thousand Israelites and eventually him (31:8, 16). A man who wants the wages badly enough will find a way to get them that his conscience will accept. The New Testament calls it “the way of Balaam” (2 Peter 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: And Balaam said to Balak, "Did I not tell your messengers whom you sent to me, 'If Balak should give me his house full of silver and gold, I would not be able to go beyond the word of the LORD, to do either good or bad of my own will. What the LORD speaks, that will I speak'? And now, behold, I am going to my people. Come, I will let you know what this people will do to your people in the latter days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam defends himself with his own correct words, and then, unpaid, offers one more oracle, because God’s word was never his to sell.

Did I not tell your messengers? Balaam defends himself by quoting himself, and once again every word is impeccable, and has never once described his heart. A man can hide a wrong heart behind correct doctrine.

I am going to my people. He does not go; seven chapters later the sword finds him still among the Midianites (31:8). People announce their departure from compromise far more often than they leave it.

Come, I will let you know. Then the greatest thing he ever says, given unpaid: he owes Balak nothing now, and gives the oracle anyway, because it is not his to withhold. The crowning prophecy of the Pentateuch (the five books of Moses) outside Genesis is delivered by a dismissed hireling to a furious pagan king, for no fee at all. God had said he would put a word in this man’s mouth, and it came out whether anyone was paying or not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–25 — The Fourth Oracle: A Star out of Jacob
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last oracle looks down the centuries to a coming King. Balaam sees one “not now… not near”: a star out of Jacob and a sceptre out of Israel, who will crush Moab and dispossess Edom (vv. 15–19). David would fulfil this in part, but “one from Jacob” shall rule beyond him, and the New Testament names him: Jesus, “the bright morning star”. Short oracles follow on Amalek, the Kenites, Asshur and the ships of Kittim, as empires rise and fall at God’s word, until Balaam cries, “Alas, who shall live when God does this?” (vv. 20–24). Then he goes back to his place, unchanged (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophecy is fulfilled in part in David but points ultimately to Christ, “he who has been born king of the Jews” (Matthew 2:2), and the clearest messianic hope in the Pentateuch outside Genesis comes through a hostile prophet.
verseByVerse.examples: The King Balaam saw from afar we know by name: Jesus, reigning forever.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took up his discourse and said, "The oracle of Balaam the son of Beor, the oracle of the man whose eye is opened, the oracle of him who hears the words of God, and knows the knowledge of the Most High, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down with his eyes uncovered: I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel; it shall crush the forehead of Moab and break down all the sons of Sheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam sees, far off, a King from Jacob, a star and a sceptre, who will crush the enemies of God’s people: fulfilled in part in David, and fully in Christ.

I see him, but not now. Take the near horizon first. Centuries later David subdued Moab and garrisoned Edom (2 Samuel 8:2, 14), the two nations named here, and any honest reading has David in view. But the oracle is too large for David alone. “Not now… not near” is a strange way to describe a king in a book that dates events to the month, and verse 19 widens the horizon to a dominion with no stated end. David is the near fulfilment; someone greater stands behind him.

A star shall come out of Jacob. A sceptre is the ruler’s staff, and Jacob had said on his deathbed that “the scepter shall not depart from Judah… and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples” (Genesis 49:10). A star is a king in the language of the ancient East, and it is what Jesus called himself at the end of the Bible: “I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star” (Revelation 22:16). The Star “shall crush the forehead” of the enemy, and many Christians have heard an echo of the first promise, that the seed of the woman would bruise the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). The Hebrew words differ, but the hope is one: a son of the promised line who crushes the enemy of God’s people, and Christ is that Son.

Read of the Messiah. Israel never forgot this verse. The community at Qumran read it of the Messiah; when a rebel leader rose against Rome in AD 132 his followers named him Bar Kokhba, “son of a star”; and readers from the earliest centuries have wondered about the wise men who came “from the east” following a star (Matthew 2:1–2), from the east, as Balaam had come. Matthew does not cite this oracle, and we should not pretend he does. But a seer from the east saw a Star rise out of Jacob and could not say when, and centuries later men from the east saw a star and went to find out.

How Jewish readers take it. Targum Onkelos renders the oracle of a king arising from Jacob and the Messiah anointed from Israel. Maimonides cites it among the Torah’s promises of the King Messiah, applying its lines in turn to David and to the Messiah (Laws of Kings 11:1); others read it of David alone. So Jewish and Christian readers share the conviction that a king from Jacob is in view, and many in both traditions have looked beyond David for him. This commentary sees that King in Jesus, the root and descendant of David (Revelation 22:16).

Uncertain wording. “The sons of Sheth” is obscure. It may name a people otherwise little known, or all humanity as descendants of Seth; but Jeremiah, reworking this oracle against Moab, has “the sons of tumult” (Jeremiah 48:45), and many take it that way: the turbulent peoples around Israel. On any reading the King overthrows those who stand against God’s people.
verseByVerse.note: A star and a sceptre from Israel: understood as a promise of the Messiah, the true King.

verseByVerse.quote: Edom shall be dispossessed; Seir also, his enemies, shall be dispossessed. Israel is doing valiantly. And one from Jacob shall exercise dominion and destroy the survivors of cities!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom, the brother who barred Israel’s road, will be dispossessed, and one ruler from Jacob will reign.

Edom shall be dispossessed. Edom is the brother who slammed the door four chapters ago. Israel asked for a road, was met with an army, and turned away without a fight because God told them to. Now, in an oracle they never heard, God answers Edom for them. Remember that when you have taken an injustice quietly and walked the long way round. Israel’s silence at the border did not end the matter; it handed it to the One better placed to settle it: “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). We can let go of the grievance because the God who has settled our own account will also settle this one.

One from Jacob shall exercise dominion. The last line looks beyond the local map: not Israel collectively, but one from Jacob, a single figure out of this family, ruling. The whole Bible is bending toward a Person here, and a hired diviner in the pay of Moab is announcing it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he looked on Amalek and took up his discourse and said, "Amalek was the first among the nations, but its end is utter destruction." And he looked on the Kenite, and took up his discourse and said, "Enduring is your dwelling place, and your nest is set in the rock. Nevertheless, Kain shall be burned when Asshur takes you away captive." And he took up his discourse and said, "Alas, who shall live when God does this? But ships shall come from Kittim and shall afflict Asshur and Eber; and he too shall come to utter destruction." Then Balaam rose and went back to his place. And Balak also went his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Balaam’s last words see empires rise and fall at God’s command, and then the man who saw the Star goes home unchanged.

Amalek was the first among the nations. Three short oracles close the account, widening until the whole world is in view. Amalek was first because it was the first nation to attack Israel after the exodus, striking at the stragglers (Exodus 17:8; Deuteronomy 25:17–18). Being first to raise a hand against the people of God is a distinction nobody should want.

Your nest is set in the rock. Then the Kenites, the people of Moses’ father-in-law and friends of Israel, whose nest is high and not high enough, for Asshur (Assyria) will carry them off. Then Asshur itself falls to ships from the western coastlands. Balaam is naming the rise and fall of empires he has no earthly means of knowing, and stops to say what a man ought to say from that height: “Alas, who shall live when God does this?”

Then Balaam rose and went back to his place. Verse 25 is the flattest, saddest verse in the story. No repentance, no worship. The man who saw the Star out of Jacob goes home, and on his way out hands Balak the advice that does what three mountains of sorcery could not (31:16). It is possible to see more of God than almost anyone in your generation and be lost, because the eye can be opened while the heart is not. Balaam had the Spirit come upon him, the vision of the Almighty and the Messiah in his mouth, and he went back to his place.

The Star you must come to. The only question at the end of a chapter like this is not what Balaam saw but whether the Star he saw at a distance is the one you have come to. And if you have come, however weakly, you have his own word: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

Uncertain wording. These lines are among the hardest in Numbers. “Kain” is probably the Kenites, with a play on the word for “nest” (qen). Kittim first meant Cyprus, later western seafarers generally (Daniel 11:30 uses it of the Romans). “Eber” may be peoples beyond the Euphrates or the Hebrews themselves, and verse 23 is difficult in Hebrew. The sense is clear: one power after another rises and falls under God’s judgment.

keyVerse.quote: I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel
keyVerse.note: The hired seer who came to curse Israel is made to foresee its King. David fulfilled the oracle in part, but its “one from Jacob” reaches further, to Jesus, “the bright morning star” (Revelation 22:16), whose kingdom has no end.

24.reflection:
The Spirit came upon Balaam, he saw visions and spoke true words about God, yet his heart never changed (vv. 2–4, 25). Why is spiritual experience not the same as knowing Christ, and how can we tell the difference in ourselves?

Balaam saw Israel as “gardens beside a river” and “aloes that the LORD has planted” (v. 6), though it was a grumbling people in a desert. How does it change the way you see your church, or yourself, to know that God sees what he is making of you?

Edom had wronged Israel, and God answered for them (v. 18). Is there an injustice you need to hand over to God rather than settle yourself? What helps you do that?

Balaam saw the Star “not now… not near” (v. 17) and went home unchanged. The wise men saw a star and came to worship. What would it mean for you this week to come to Christ, not just to look at him from a distance?

25.title: Baal of Peor: The Seduction Balaam's Curse Could Not Achieve
25.text: <sup>1</sup>While Israel lived in Shittim, the people began to whore with the daughters of Moab.<sup>2</sup>These invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and bowed down to their gods.<sup>3</sup>So Israel yoked himself to Baal of Peor. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel.<sup>4</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Take all the chiefs of the people and hang them in the sun before the LORD, that the fierce anger of the LORD may turn away from Israel."<sup>5</sup>And Moses said to the judges of Israel, "Each of you kill those of his men who have yoked themselves to Baal of Peor."<sup>6</sup>And behold, one of the people of Israel came and brought a Midianite woman to his family, in the sight of Moses and in the sight of the whole congregation of the people of Israel, while they were weeping in the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>7</sup>When Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose and left the congregation and took a spear in his hand<sup>8</sup>and went after the man of Israel into the chamber and pierced both of them, the man of Israel and the woman through her belly. Thus the plague on the people of Israel was stopped.<sup>9</sup>Nevertheless, those who died by the plague were twenty-four thousand.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD said to Moses,<sup>11</sup>"Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has turned back my wrath from the people of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I did not consume the people of Israel in my jealousy.<sup>12</sup>Therefore say, 'Behold, I give to him my covenant of peace,<sup>13</sup>and it shall be to him and to his descendants after him the covenant of a perpetual priesthood, because he was jealous for his God and made atonement for the people of Israel.'"<sup>14</sup>The name of the slain man of Israel, who was killed with the Midianite woman, was Zimri the son of Salu, chief of a father's house belonging to the Simeonites.<sup>15</sup>And the name of the Midianite woman who was killed was Cozbi the daughter of Zur, who was the tribal head of a father's house in Midian.<sup>16</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>17</sup>"Harass the Midianites and strike them down,<sup>18</sup>for they have harassed you with their wiles, with which they beguiled you in the matter of Peor, and in the matter of Cozbi, the daughter of the chief of Midian, their sister, who was killed on the day of the plague on account of Peor."
25.overview:
Where we are. Israel is camped at Shittim on the plains of Moab, the last stop before the Jordan. King Balak has paid Balaam to curse them, and every curse has turned to blessing (chapters 22 to 24).

The message. What no curse could do from outside, sin did from inside. Israel was drawn by Moabite women to their feasts and from the feasts to bowing before Baal, and the LORD’s anger broke out in a plague. God is jealous for his people as a husband for his wife: he will not share them with another god, and his wrath is turned away only when sin is judged and a priest stands between him and the people.

Why it was said. The new generation stood at the border of a land full of Baal’s shrines and festivals (see the introduction). Their great danger was not the enemy’s sorcery but their own appetites, and the God who had blessed them would not overlook unfaithfulness.

How the chapter makes its case. The fall comes in stages: sexual sin, then the sacrificial meal, then worship, and God’s anger is kindled (vv. 1–3). God orders the guilty leaders executed in public, and Moses passes the order to the judges (vv. 4–5). While the people weep at the tabernacle, a chief of Simeon parades a Midianite woman into his tent; Aaron’s grandson Phinehas alone acts, and the plague stops after twenty-four thousand deaths (vv. 6–9). God declares that Phinehas shared his own jealousy, made atonement and receives a covenant of peace and a lasting priesthood (vv. 10–13). The guilty are named (vv. 14–15), and Midian, who set the trap, is to be treated as an enemy (vv. 16–18).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. A priest who “made atonement” and turned away God’s wrath points to the great Priest, of whom the disciples remembered, “Zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:17). But the pattern is also reversed: Phinehas turned wrath away by the death of the guilty, and Christ by his own death in the place of the guilty. And he is the covenant of peace in person: “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14).

For us. Paul sets this plague before a confident church: “these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction” (1 Corinthians 10:11). Past blessing is no protection against present sin. But Peor is a warning to the careless, not a closed door to the repentant: Christ has turned away the wrath we deserved, and those who flee to him are washed.
25.theology:
Seduction from within. What Balaam's curse could not do, immorality and idolatry accomplished, which is why the greater danger to God's people is usually compromise within rather than attack from without.

Holy jealousy. Phinehas shared God's own jealousy for the purity of his people; his deed was not human cruelty.

Turning away wrath. Phinehas stood between God’s wrath and the people and stopped the plague. He foreshadows Christ, who turns away God’s wrath by dying in his people’s place.
25.examples: The world will try to corrupt by pleasure what it cannot defeat by force. You belong to the Christ who turned God's wrath away forever, so flee sexual immorality and idolatry, walking by the Spirit he has given you (Gal 5:16), and when you fall, run back to him rather than away.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The greatest danger to God’s people was never the enemy’s curse but their own hearts. At Shittim, Israel is drawn by Moabite women into sexual sin, then to the feasts of their gods, and finally to bowing down to Baal of Peor, and the LORD’s anger is kindled (vv. 1–3). Behind it lies Balaam’s advice (31:16): what sorcery could not do, seduction did. God’s answer is swift and public. The leaders who have yoked themselves to Baal are to be executed in the open, and Moses passes the order to Israel’s judges (vv. 4–5), so that the fierce anger of the LORD may turn away from his people.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the dark sequel to Balaam’s blessing, and the enemy is the same one (Num 31:16): only the weapon has changed.
verseByVerse.examples: “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). The enemy’s most effective weapon is not persecution but the slow drift into compromise.

verseByVerse.quote: While Israel lived in Shittim, the people began to whore with the daughters of Moab. These invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and bowed down to their gods. So Israel yoked himself to Baal of Peor. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where Balaam’s curses failed, his advice succeeded: Israel was drawn through sexual sin to the feasts of Moab’s gods, and from the feasts to bowing before Baal, and the LORD’s anger burned.

While Israel lived in Shittim. Read the end of chapter 24 and the start of chapter 25 together, because the connection is the point. Balaam “went back to his place”, and at once “the people began to whore with the daughters of Moab.” Scripture links the two: “Behold, these, on Balaam’s advice, caused the people of Israel to act treacherously against the LORD in the incident of Peor” (31:16), and the risen Christ names “Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and practice sexual immorality” (Revelation 2:14). Shittim (“the acacia meadow”, 33:49) was Israel’s last camp, across the Jordan from Jericho. Peor was a height close by, the very spot from which Balaam had last looked down on the camp (23:28), and Baal of Peor was Baal, the Canaanite god of storm and fertility, worshipped there under a local title.

Balaam’s new weapon. Same campaign, same consultant, new weapon. Three rounds of sorcery produced nothing but blessing, because a people God has blessed cannot be cursed. So Balaam, sacked and unpaid, in effect told Balak: invite them to dinner.

And the people ate. Watch the order of the collapse, because it is the ordinary order: first the women, then the sacrifices, then “the people ate”, and only then they “bowed down to their gods.” To eat a sacrificial meal was to sit at the god’s table and share fellowship with him, which is why Paul warns that those who eat the sacrifices become participants in the altar (1 Corinthians 10:18–21). Nobody got up that morning intending to worship Baal. The idolatry came in last, through the appetite, when the man was already at the table and it would have been awkward to leave. Sin rarely opens by asking for your allegiance. It asks for your evening.

Israel yoked himself to Baal of Peor. Yoked like two oxen, so that neither can turn without the other. Paul uses a similar picture: “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 6:14). And the prophet who looked back on Peor saw what the yoke did: “they came to Baal-peor and consecrated themselves to the thing of shame, and became detestable like the thing they loved” (Hosea 9:10). We become like what we worship.

Why sex was never only private. We like to keep what a man does in bed and what he worships in separate rooms. Peor says they were never separate. Baal’s worship ran on desire, because the gods of fertility and pleasure ask nothing of the heart except its appetite. Our culture has not left that behind so much as renamed it: romance and sexual fulfilment are asked to tell us we are worth something, to rescue us from loneliness, to make us feel fully alive. Whatever carries that weight becomes a god, and no human lover can bear being worshipped. The Bible is not prudish here; it takes sex more seriously than we do (see the note on Song of Songs 8:6–7). And the gospel answers the hunger underneath. There is a Bridegroom who will never tire of his bride, who “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), and only someone already loved like that can receive sex as a gift instead of asking it to be a saviour.
verseByVerse.note: Shittim lay on the plains of Moab across from Jericho.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Take all the chiefs of the people and hang them in the sun before the LORD, that the fierce anger of the LORD may turn away from Israel." And Moses said to the judges of Israel, "Each of you kill those of his men who have yoked themselves to Baal of Peor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God orders the leaders who joined themselves to Baal to be executed in public, and Moses passes the order to the judges: open sin at the top is judged openly, and judgment begins at the top.

Take all the chiefs of the people. Not the young or the weak, but the heads of families. When a nation falls apart at the top, God does not begin his reckoning at the bottom. Verse 5 shows who is meant: “those of his men who have yoked themselves to Baal of Peor.” God is not ordering the innocent to die with the guilty (compare 16:22).

Hang them in the sun before the LORD. The ringleaders are to be put to death in the open, in daylight. The sin was public; the judgment is public, and it is done “that the fierce anger of the LORD may turn away from Israel.”

Moses said to the judges of Israel. This matters for what happens three verses later. There is now a lawful, public, standing order in Israel that the men who have joined themselves to Baal are to be executed. What Phinehas does in verse 8 is not a private outburst. It is the only recorded instance of anyone actually doing what Moses had just told all the judges to do.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew verb behind “hang” is rare; it is used again of the execution of Saul’s sons (2 Samuel 21:6, 9). Its exact meaning is unknown (impaling, hanging, or exposure with limbs broken have all been suggested), but the sense is clear: the guilty are executed and displayed publicly “before the LORD”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s wrath is turned away by a priest who shares his jealousy. While the nation weeps and does nothing, a chief of Simeon brazenly brings a Midianite woman into his tent; Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, alone acts on the sentence already given, and the plague stops (vv. 6–8), though twenty-four thousand have died (v. 9). God declares that Phinehas “was jealous with my jealousy” and “made atonement”, and gives him a covenant of peace and a lasting priesthood (vv. 10–13). The names of the guilty pair, a Simeonite chief and a Midianite princess, show this was a deliberate act of defiance (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Phinehas’s act belongs to a unique moment in Israel’s history and gives no permission for private vengeance; it pictures holy zeal confronting flagrant sin, and points to the greater Priest whose self-offering turns away wrath forever.
verseByVerse.examples: We are called not to the spear but to the same jealousy for God’s honour, beginning with hatred of sin in ourselves, and we rest in the Priest whose blood made the atonement Phinehas only foreshadowed.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, one of the people of Israel came and brought a Midianite woman to his family, in the sight of Moses and in the sight of the whole congregation of the people of Israel, while they were weeping in the entrance of the tent of meeting. When Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose and left the congregation and took a spear in his hand and went after the man of Israel into the chamber and pierced both of them, the man of Israel and the woman through her belly. Thus the plague on the people of Israel was stopped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the nation wept and did nothing, a leading Israelite paraded a Midianite woman into his tent in front of everyone; Phinehas alone carried out the sentence God had given, and the plague stopped.

In the sight of the whole congregation. The scene is staged with terrible care. The congregation is weeping at the tabernacle door, the plague running through the camp, the order to execute the guilty already given. Into that, in broad daylight, a man walks a Midianite woman past a grieving prophet to his tent, while his own people’s funeral goes on around him.

And nobody moves. Not Moses, not the judges who were given the order. Israel stands at the tent door and cries, and every moment of that paralysis means more dead in the camp.

He rose and left the congregation. Then Phinehas, son of the priest Eleazar and grandson of Aaron, rises and takes a spear, and the text says with brutal directness: “Thus the plague on the people of Israel was stopped.”

What it is and what it is not. Modern readers find this passage almost unbearable, and they should not be talked out of that. But be clear. It is not a man taking the law into his own hands: Moses had just ordered the execution of those who joined themselves to Baal, and Phinehas belonged to the priestly house charged with guarding the holiness of the camp. It is not racial: Moses himself had married a Midianite (Exodus 2:21), Israel had welcomed foreigners from the start, and the red heifer’s cleansing was explicitly for “the stranger who sojourns among them” (19:10). It is a lawful death sentence carried out, by the one official in a paralysed nation who was prepared to act, on a man committing the crime in public while the sentence was being announced. Nor is it a pattern for anyone today (see the note on vv. 10–13).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “chamber” occurs only here in the Old Testament. It seems to mean a vaulted tent or an inner part of one; some think it was a shrine tent for Baal’s rites, and the word may play on “belly” in the same verse. The likely sense is simply that Phinehas followed them into the tent and killed them both there.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, those who died by the plague were twenty-four thousand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plague killed twenty-four thousand, the worst single disaster in the book, at the very edge of the land.

Twenty-four thousand. Set that number against the whole book. Nothing in Numbers, not the serpents nor the earth swallowing Korah, killed on this scale in a single episode. And it happened in the last camp, in sight of the river, to the generation that had survived everything else. The enemy that had failed with armies and with sorcery succeeded with hospitality.

Paul’s twenty-three thousand. Paul cites this plague as a warning to a church: “We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day” (1 Corinthians 10:8). The difference deserves a straight answer. Paul says “in a single day”, which Numbers does not; the most natural reading is that twenty-three thousand fell on the worst day, and twenty-four thousand is the total of a plague that plainly ran longer. Both writers also use the round thousands usual in ancient reckoning. Neither figure requires us to think the other writer careless.

Written for our instruction. Paul writes to confident Christians, baptised and sharing the Lord’s Supper, and adds, “these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction” (1 Corinthians 10:11). Past experience of God is no immunity against present sin.

For those who have fallen. The same letter carries the comfort. Of people guilty of exactly these sins Paul writes, “such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11). Peor is a warning to the confident, not a closed door to the repentant.
verseByVerse.note: Paul gives 23,000, perhaps those who died in one day, or a rounded figure.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has turned back my wrath from the people of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I did not consume the people of Israel in my jealousy. Therefore say, 'Behold, I give to him my covenant of peace, and it shall be to him and to his descendants after him the covenant of a perpetual priesthood, because he was jealous for his God and made atonement for the people of Israel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God declares that Phinehas felt his own jealousy for his people, turned back his wrath and made atonement, and rewards him with a covenant of peace and a lasting priesthood. The verdict troubles readers most, and it should be read exactly as it stands.

He was jealous with my jealousy. The word is easily misheard. God’s jealousy is not envy, which wants what belongs to another. Jealousy in Scripture is a husband’s proper refusal to share his wife, the opposite of indifference. God had married this nation at Sinai, and Israel had gone to Baal’s table; his jealousy is not a flaw in his love but the heat of it. Phinehas, alone in the camp, felt what God felt. The commendation is not that he was violent, but that his heart matched God’s when every other heart in Israel had gone numb.

My covenant of peace. Then the startling reward, a covenant of peace for bloodshed that had stopped a slaughter. “Made atonement” is a priest’s word: sin was covered and God’s wrath turned away. Phinehas stood between a holy God and a doomed people, and the wrath stopped at him. The psalm remembers it in the language of the gospel: “Then Phinehas stood up and intervened, and the plague was stayed. And that was counted to him as righteousness” (Psalm 106:30–31), the phrase used of Abraham’s faith (Genesis 15:6). The deed did not earn his acceptance; God declared it the act of a righteous man, faith in action when everyone else had stopped believing God meant what he said.

The Priest who was struck himself. This is why the chapter is in the Bible at all. Phinehas turned away wrath by the death of the guilty. A greater Priest stood in the same place and turned away the same wrath by his own death, having done nothing to deserve it. His covenant of peace was bought with his own body: “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). And his zeal was the same holy jealousy, turned on himself: when he cleared the temple, “his disciples remembered that it was written, ‘Zeal for your house will consume me’” (John 2:17), and that zeal consumed him at the cross. At Peor the priest struck the guilty. At Calvary the Priest was struck himself.

A perpetual priesthood? The high priesthood ran in Phinehas’s line for centuries, through Zadok in Solomon’s day (1 Chronicles 6:4–8), but it ended with the temple. “Perpetual” in the Law means lasting for the whole age of that covenant, and Hebrews shows where it leads: the Levitical priests died one after another, but Christ “holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:24). The promise to Phinehas is not broken; it is taken up into a priesthood that never has to be handed on.

Not a licence today. Phinehas held a priestly office in a nation ruled directly by God’s law, under a standing order through Moses; no Christian holds that office or that order. The church’s zeal is armed differently, for “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4), and when Paul faces sexual sin in the church at Corinth, the remedy he commands is exclusion from the fellowship, not a spear (1 Corinthians 5:1–5). The sword of justice now belongs to the civil ruler (Romans 13:4), never to a private zealot. Zeal for God is still required of us; its instruments have changed entirely.

verseByVerse.quote: The name of the slain man of Israel, who was killed with the Midianite woman, was Zimri the son of Salu, chief of a father's house belonging to the Simeonites. And the name of the Midianite woman who was killed was Cozbi the daughter of Zur, who was the tribal head of a father's house in Midian.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The guilty pair are named, a chief of Simeon and a Midianite princess, which shows this was a deliberate public alliance in defiance of God, not a private lapse.

Zimri and Cozbi. Only now does the text give the names, with full family lines. These were not two young people who lost their heads. Zimri was a clan chief of Simeon; Cozbi was the daughter of a Midianite chief. It looks far more like a deliberate alliance than a romance, two leading families sealing a connection in the most public way available, in open contempt of the God whose plague was running through the camp. Verse 18 confirms it: Cozbi is part of Midian’s “wiles”. Moab and Midian were acting together throughout (22:4, 7), which is why verse 1 speaks of the daughters of Moab and Cozbi is a Midianite. For what may have followed for Simeon, see the note on 26:12–22.

The names are written down. Zimri could have died anonymously, one among twenty-four thousand; instead his name is in the permanent record, attached to the worst thing he ever did. There is a book, and things get written in it, which is why the mercy of Christ is described as a record dealt with: God cancelled “the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands… nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:14).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God holds the tempter to account as well as the tempted. Israel was judged for its own sin, but Midian had planned the seduction, “harassing” Israel not with armies but with “wiles”, and Cozbi, a chief’s daughter, was part of the scheme. So God commands Israel to treat the Midianites as enemies and strike them (vv. 16–18), a reckoning carried out in chapter 31. Read with chapters 22 to 24, the lesson is plain: the people God has blessed cannot be cursed from outside, but they can be lured from within, which is why the church must watch against the devil’s schemes and pray to be kept from the evil one.
verseByVerse.theology: The command against Midian (vv.17-18) is God’s judgment on those who deliberately engineered Israel’s downfall. Peor becomes a byword for turning away from God (Ps 106:28-29; Hos 9:10).
verseByVerse.examples: God still regards with the utmost gravity those who deliberately lead others into sin. “It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck” (Luke 17:2).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Harass the Midianites and strike them down, for they have harassed you with their wiles, with which they beguiled you in the matter of Peor, and in the matter of Cozbi, the daughter of the chief of Midian, their sister, who was killed on the day of the plague on account of Peor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God holds the tempters to account as well as the tempted: Midian, who planned the seduction, is to be treated as an enemy.

Harass the Midianites. The chapter closes with the people who set the trap. First, God does not accept the excuse of the seducer. Israel sinned freely and was judged for it, and those who engineered the temptation are held to account too. Nobody at Peor could plead that they were only tempted, and nobody in Midian that they only offered. Jesus says of the one who causes a little one to stumble, “it would be better for him to have a great millstone fastened around his neck and to be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matthew 18:6). The reckoning comes in chapter 31.

With their wiles. Second, Midian did not defeat Israel; Midian tricked her. Paul uses the same kind of word of the enemy the church faces, “the schemes of the devil” (Ephesians 6:11), and it is the plain lesson of chapters 22 to 25 read as one story. Balak tried a curse and failed, and never dared an army. Then a dinner invitation brought down more of Israel than every enemy in the book combined.

The real danger. The people of God were never in real danger from the curses on the mountain. Twenty-one altars of sorcery produced nothing but blessing. What ruined them walked into the camp smiling and was invited to stay. That is why the Lord Jesus, praying for his own on the last night, did not ask for them to be taken out of the battle. He asked for the one thing Israel lacked at Shittim: “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one” (John 17:15).

keyVerse.quote: it shall be to him and to his descendants after him the covenant of a perpetual priesthood, because he was jealous for his God and made atonement for the people of Israel.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter of shameful collapse, this is God’s own verdict on the one man who stood in the gap. A priest who shared God’s jealousy made atonement and turned back the wrath, and points beyond himself to the Priest whose zeal consumed him, who made atonement by his own death and holds his priesthood for ever.

25.reflection:
Israel’s fall at Peor went in stages: the women, the meal, then worship (vv. 1–2). Why does temptation so often begin with something that seems small or sociable? Where have you seen the same pattern in your own life or in the church?

Chapters 22 to 24 show that no curse could harm Israel, yet chapter 25 shows them ruined from within. What does that teach about where the real dangers to Christians lie today?

God says Phinehas “was jealous with my jealousy” (v. 11). How is God’s jealousy different from human envy, and what would it look like for our hearts to share his zeal without taking up Phinehas’s spear?

Phinehas turned away wrath by the death of the guilty; Christ turned it away by his own death. How does that difference shape the way we respond to our own sin, and to fellow believers who have fallen?

26.title: The Second Census: A New Generation, an Old Faithfulness

These are the clans of Dan according to their clans.<sup>43</sup>All the clans of the Shuhamites, as they were listed, were 64,400.<sup>44</sup>The sons of Asher according to their clans: of Imnah, the clan of the Imnites; of Ishvi, the clan of the Ishvites; of Beriah, the clan of the Beriites.<sup>45</sup>Of the sons of Beriah: of Heber, the clan of the Heberites; of Malchiel, the clan of the Malchielites.<sup>46</sup>And the name of the daughter of Asher was Serah.<sup>47</sup>These are the clans of the sons of Asher as they were listed, 53,400.<sup>48</sup>The sons of Naphtali according to their clans: of Jahzeel, the clan of the Jahzeelites; of Guni, the clan of the Gunites;<sup>49</sup>of Jezer, the clan of the Jezerites; of Shillem, the clan of the Shillemites.<sup>50</sup>These are the clans of Naphtali according to their clans, and those listed were 45,400.<sup>51</sup>This was the list of the people of Israel, 601,730.<sup>52</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>53</sup>"Among these the land shall be divided for inheritance according to the number of names.<sup>54</sup>To a large tribe you shall give a large inheritance, and to a small tribe you shall give a small inheritance; every tribe shall be given its inheritance in proportion to its list.<sup>55</sup>But the land shall be divided by lot. According to the names of the tribes of their fathers they shall inherit.<sup>56</sup>Their inheritance shall be divided according to lot between the larger and the smaller."<sup>57</sup>This was the list of the Levites according to their clans: of Gershon, the clan of the Gershonites; of Kohath, the clan of the Kohathites; of Merari, the clan of the Merarites.<sup>58</sup>These are the clans of Levi: the clan of the Libnites, the clan of the Hebronites, the clan of the Mahlites, the clan of the Mushites, the clan of the Korahites. And Kohath was the father of Amram.<sup>59</sup>The name of Amram's wife was Jochebed the daughter of Levi, who was born to Levi in Egypt. And she bore to Amram Aaron and Moses and Miriam their sister.<sup>60</sup>And to Aaron were born Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.<sup>61</sup>But Nadab and Abihu died when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD.<sup>62</sup>And those listed were 23,000, every male from a month old and upward. For they were not listed among the people of Israel, because there was no inheritance given to them among the people of Israel.<sup>63</sup>These were those listed by Moses and Eleazar the priest, who listed the people of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.<sup>64</sup>But among these there was not one of those listed by Moses and Aaron the priest, who had listed the people of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai.<sup>65</sup>For the LORD had said of them, "They shall die in the wilderness." Not one of them was left, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun.
26.overview:
Where we are. The plague at Peor has just ended (chapter 25), and with it the last of the generation that refused the land at Kadesh. Israel is camped on the plains of Moab across the Jordan from Jericho, and here the third part of the book begins.

The message. God has kept his word of judgment to the last man, and he has kept his word of promise just as exactly. The generation counted at Sinai is gone, except Caleb and Joshua, yet a new generation of almost the same size stands at the border, counted name by name for the inheritance God swore to Abraham. Unbelief cannot enter, but God’s promise outlives the unbelievers.

Why it was said. The children of the wilderness had grown up beside their parents’ graves (see the introduction). Before they crossed the Jordan they needed to know that God had not given up on Israel, that each of them was known to him, and that the land would be shared fairly and by his own hand.

How the chapter makes its case. “After the plague” God orders a new count of fighting men (vv. 1–4). Tribe by tribe the list runs from Reuben to Naphtali, pausing over Dathan and Abiram and the surviving sons of Korah, over Judah’s lost sons, and over five daughters with no brother (vv. 5–51); the total, 601,730, is almost the same as at Sinai. The land is to be shared by size and placed by lot (vv. 52–56). The Levites are counted apart, because the LORD is their inheritance (vv. 57–62). Then the two lists are compared, and only Caleb and Joshua appear on both (vv. 63–65).

Where it leads. By covenant faithfulness and by pattern. The God who kept every word to Israel kept his promise to Judah’s line, and the King came from it. The chapter also exposes a need: a whole generation fell in the wilderness “because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:19), and only those who trusted God’s word entered. The new generation is led in by Joshua, whose name in Greek is Jesus, and believers are given “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4) by the greater Joshua, who knows his own by name.

For us. No one is lost in the crowd of God’s people: he counts and names his own. His warnings are as sure as his promises, so do not presume on his patience; and his promises are as sure as his warnings, so do not despair of his faithfulness to the next generation.
26.theology:
God's faithfulness across generations. The covenant did not die with the unbelieving generation. God raised up a new people and kept his promise.

Severity and kindness. Judgment is carried out in full on the rebels, and kindness is shown to their children, neither cancelling the other (Rom 11:22).

Grace in unexpected places. The sons of Korah did not die; the rebel's line was preserved to sing God's praises.
26.examples: God's promises outlive every failure and span every generation. The inheritance is sure because it rests on his faithfulness, not yours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–51 — The Census of the New Generation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is starting again with a new generation, and the long lists are a monument to his faithfulness. Over the graves of Peor he orders a second count of the men able to go to war (vv. 1–4), not of those counted in chapter 1, who have died in the wilderness, but of their children. Tribe by tribe the names run on, and the list keeps stopping to remember: Dathan and Abiram swallowed up, yet the sons of Korah spared (vv. 5–11); Simeon shrunk and Judah the strongest (vv. 12–22); five daughters named who should not be on a soldiers’ roll (v. 33). The total, 601,730, is almost the same as forty years before (v. 51).
verseByVerse.theology: The fathers died, but the promise endured. Even the roll-call of tribes preaches that God keeps covenant to a thousand generations (Deut 7:9).
verseByVerse.examples: Where one generation fails, God raises up another; his promise never dies with those who forfeit it (Ps 145:4).

verseByVerse.quote: After the plague, the LORD said to Moses and to Eleazar the son of Aaron, the priest, "Take a census of all the congregation of the people of Israel, from twenty years old and upward, by their fathers' houses, all in Israel who are able to go to war." And Moses and Eleazar the priest spoke with them in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying, "Take a census of the people, from twenty years old and upward," as the LORD commanded Moses. The people of Israel who came out of the land of Egypt were:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Over the graves of Peor, God orders a new count: he is starting again with the next generation.

After the plague. The saddest and most hopeful words in the chapter: the counting begins over twenty-four thousand fresh graves.

Able to go to war. The purpose is stated twice: those “able to go to war”, and in verse 53 the land “divided for inheritance”. The document is both an army list and a land register, and it is the same list, because in God’s arrangement the people who receive the inheritance are the people who go in to take it.

A second census. It has been done before. Chapter 1 counted a nation for a march that should have taken eleven days (Deuteronomy 1:2) and collapsed at Kadesh. This is the same procedure with an entirely different set of men, every one of the first list now dead except two. God is not repeating himself. He is starting again, with the sons of the people who would not go, and this time they will cross.
verseByVerse.note: The first census, of the generation now dead, is in chapter 1.

verseByVerse.quote: Reuben, the firstborn of Israel; the sons of Reuben: of Hanoch, the clan of the Hanochites; of Pallu, the clan of the Palluites; of Hezron, the clan of the Hezronites; of Carmi, the clan of the Carmites. These are the clans of the Reubenites, and those listed were 43,730. And the sons of Pallu: Eliab. The sons of Eliab: Nemuel, Dathan, and Abiram. These are the Dathan and Abiram, chosen from the congregation, who contended against Moses and Aaron in the company of Korah, when they contended against the LORD and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up together with Korah, when that company died, when the fire devoured 250 men, and they became a warning. But the sons of Korah did not die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The roll of Reuben remembers the rebels the earth swallowed, and records that Korah’s sons were spared: a warning and a mercy.

Reuben, the firstborn of Israel. The register opens with Reuben and almost at once stops being a list, pausing to retell the story of Dathan and Abiram and the earth that swallowed them (vv. 9–10; chapter 16). A roll of the covenant people is also a memorial, and God writes into it both the mercy and the warning.

But the sons of Korah did not die. Eight words that change everything. Korah went down into the ground, and his sons were not in the pit. The text does not explain how; it records the survival, and Scripture spends centuries showing what God did with it. “Of the Sons of Korah” stands over eleven psalms, among them the one every homesick believer knows: “As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God” (Psalm 42:1), and “How lovely is your dwelling place, O LORD of hosts!” (Psalm 84:1). The descendants of the man who resented Aaron’s priesthood became the temple singers who served beside it and taught Israel to long for God.

A family name redeemed. That is the gospel written into a genealogy. The rebel’s sin did not settle his children’s destiny, for “the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father” (Ezekiel 18:20), and God did not merely spare that family; he gave it the music. If you carry a family name or a history you would rather not have, this verse is for you. The sons of Korah did not die. They sang.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Simeon according to their clans: of Nemuel, the clan of the Nemuelites; of Jamin, the clan of the Jaminites; of Jachin, the clan of the Jachinites; of Zerah, the clan of the Zerahites; of Shaul, the clan of the Shaulites. These are the clans of the Simeonites, 22,200. The sons of Gad according to their clans: of Zephon, the clan of the Zephonites; of Haggi, the clan of the Haggites; of Shuni, the clan of the Shunites; of Ozni, the clan of the Oznites; of Eri, the clan of the Erites; of Arod, the clan of the Arodites; of Areli, the clan of the Arelites. These are the clans of the sons of Gad as they were listed, 40,500. The sons of Judah were Er and Onan; and Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. And the sons of Judah according to their clans were: of Shelah, the clan of the Shelanites; of Perez, the clan of the Perezites; of Zerah, the clan of the Zerahites. And the sons of Perez were: of Hezron, the clan of the Hezronites; of Hamul, the clan of the Hamulites. These are the clans of Judah as they were listed, 76,500.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two figures tell a story: Simeon, whose chief led the way at Peor, has shrunk by nearly two thirds, while Judah, the tribe of the King, is the strongest.

The clans of the Simeonites. Simeon has collapsed: 59,300 fighting men at Sinai (1:23), here 22,200, though several tribes grew. And the man who paraded a Midianite woman past a weeping nation was “chief of a father’s house belonging to the Simeonites” (25:14). Scripture does not say the two facts are connected, and we should not be more certain than it is. But the plague may well have fallen heaviest on the tribe whose chief led the way into it, and the ruin of a people can begin with one man of standing who decides the rules are for other people.

The clans of Judah. Judah is the largest tribe at 76,500, as in chapter 1. Jacob had said, “The scepter shall not depart from Judah… and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples” (Genesis 49:10). Through Perez, Tamar’s son, would come David (Ruth 4:18–22). Centuries before Bethlehem, the tribe that will carry the King is quietly the strongest name on the list, and nobody counting that morning knew why.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Issachar according to their clans: of Tola, the clan of the Tolaites; of Puvah, the clan of the Punites; of Jashub, the clan of the Jashubites; of Shimron, the clan of the Shimronites. These are the clans of Issachar as they were listed, 64,300. The sons of Zebulun, according to their clans: of Sered, the clan of the Seredites; of Elon, the clan of the Elonites; of Jahleel, the clan of the Jahleelites. These are the clans of the Zebulunites as they were listed, 60,500. The sons of Joseph according to their clans: Manasseh and Ephraim. The sons of Manasseh: of Machir, the clan of the Machirites; and Machir was the father of Gilead; of Gilead, the clan of the Gileadites. These are the sons of Gilead: of Iezer, the clan of the Iezerites; of Helek, the clan of the Helekites; and of Asriel, the clan of the Asrielites; and of Shechem, the clan of the Shechemites; and of Shemida, the clan of the Shemidaites; and of Hepher, the clan of the Hepherites. Now Zelophehad the son of Hepher had no sons, but daughters. And the names of the daughters of Zelophehad were Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. These are the clans of Manasseh, and those listed were 52,700.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a soldiers’ roll God has five women named, preparing for their request in the next chapter.

The daughters of Zelophehad. At verse 33 a military register does what no ancient muster roll does, and names five women: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah.

Names that should not be there. This is a list of men who can fight, kept for dividing land among men. These five cannot fight and, by the customs of the ancient world, cannot inherit; their father is dead and his line has run out. By the logic of the document they should not appear in it, yet God has their names written down in full, one chapter before they walk up to Moses and ask for what nobody thought they could have (27:1–11). The next chapter has been prepared for here, by a God who counted them before they asked.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of Ephraim according to their clans: of Shuthelah, the clan of the Shuthelahites; of Becher, the clan of the Becherites; of Tahan, the clan of the Tahanites. And these are the sons of Shuthelah: of Eran, the clan of the Eranites. These are the clans of the sons of Ephraim as they were listed, 32,500. These are the sons of Joseph according to their clans. The sons of Benjamin according to their clans: of Bela, the clan of the Belaites; of Ashbel, the clan of the Ashbelites; of Ahiram, the clan of the Ahiramites; of Shephupham, the clan of the Shuphamites; of Hupham, the clan of the Huphamites. And the sons of Bela were Ard and Naaman: of Ard, the clan of the Ardites; of Naaman, the clan of the Naamites. These are the sons of Benjamin according to their clans, and those listed were 45,600. These are the sons of Dan according to their clans: of Shuham, the clan of the Shuhamites. These are the clans of Dan according to their clans. All the clans of the Shuhamites, as they were listed, were 64,400. The sons of Asher according to their clans: of Imnah, the clan of the Imnites; of Ishvi, the clan of the Ishvites; of Beriah, the clan of the Beriites.
