Of the sons of Beriah: of Heber, the clan of the Heberites; of Malchiel, the clan of the Malchielites. And the name of the daughter of Asher was Serah. These are the clans of the sons of Asher as they were listed, 53,400.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Clan after clan is counted in the same words, because God misses nobody among his people.

According to their clans. Modern readers skim these paragraphs. Ask why God did not.

Why God counts. A census is an act of ownership; nobody counts carefully what they do not intend to keep. The repetition that makes the chapter tedious is the point: God goes through this nation clan by clan and misses nobody. He had done it at Sinai, and every man on that list was now dead; he does it again, unhurried, as though the losses had changed nothing about his method.

He calls his own sheep by name. So the Lord Jesus describes his care: “he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out… I know my own and my own know me” (John 10:3, 14). There is no such thing, in Scripture, as being lost in the crowd of the redeemed.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Naphtali according to their clans: of Jahzeel, the clan of the Jahzeelites; of Guni, the clan of the Gunites; of Jezer, the clan of the Jezerites; of Shillem, the clan of the Shillemites. These are the clans of Naphtali according to their clans, and those listed were 45,400. This was the list of the people of Israel, 601,730.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The total is almost exactly Sinai’s: God buried a generation for its unbelief, yet his promise lost nothing.

601,730. Set the total beside Sinai’s 603,550. The difference is 1,820 men. In between, an entire adult generation died under a sentence of judgment, and the nation arriving at the Jordan is very nearly the size of the one that left the mountain.

The promise lost nothing. God carried the most severe judgment in the book through to the last man over thirty-eight years, and at the end his promise to Abraham stood exactly where it had stood. He buried a generation and replaced it, almost one for one. The numbers show what Paul says: “Note then the kindness and the severity of God” (Romans 11:22). Both, neither cancelling the other, printed in the same column of a census.

Are the numbers literal? Two million people in the wilderness? Some take the word for “thousand” as a clan or military unit, which would make the army a few thousand. But the totals add up as thousands, and the census silver of Exodus 38:25–26 matches 603,550 men exactly. This commentary takes the numbers as written, while acknowledging that others who hold Scripture just as high read the word as a unit, and that the question is still debated (see the introduction). On the plain reading, the wilderness did not feed them; God did, with manna for forty years.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 52–56 — The Land Divided by Lot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The land is God’s gift, shared fairly and placed by his hand. Each tribe’s portion is to match its size, measured by the count just taken, so that the large receive more and the small less (vv. 52–54). But where each tribe will live is decided by lot (vv. 55–56), and in Israel the lot was God’s decision, not chance. Fairness and God’s sovereign choice work together, so that no tribe could grab the best land and none could be cheated. The New Testament uses the same picture for the believer’s inheritance in Christ, measured and placed by the Father.
verseByVerse.theology: The inheritance is proportioned by size but distributed by lot (vv.54-56), and “the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). The inheritance is a gift received by God’s appointment, a foretaste of the one “kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4).
verseByVerse.examples: Our inheritance too is God’s gift, assigned by his hand and not earned by our merit, so there is room neither for boasting nor for envy.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Among these the land shall be divided for inheritance according to the number of names. To a large tribe you shall give a large inheritance, and to a small tribe you shall give a small inheritance; every tribe shall be given its inheritance in proportion to its list. But the land shall be divided by lot. According to the names of the tribes of their fathers they shall inherit. Their inheritance shall be divided according to lot between the larger and the smaller."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each tribe’s share matches its size, but where it lies is decided by lot, that is, by God.

According to the number of names. Two principles are held together. The size of each portion is decided by the census, fair and proportionate, so that no family is crowded or given more than it can work.

But the land shall be divided by lot. The location is decided by the lot, that is, by God: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). Counting settles how much; God’s choice settles where. Nobody lobbied for the good valleys, and nobody was cheated of acreage.

Our inheritance in Christ. That combination runs into the New Testament as a great comfort: “In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Ephesians 1:11), and the word Paul uses carries the idea of a share given by lot (see inheritance). Your portion is not a leftover, not drawn by chance, and not awarded for your performance. It was measured out by a Father who knows the size of you, and placed by a hand that never slips.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should decide things by casting lots. Its last use in Scripture came before the Spirit was poured out (Acts 1:26); we seek God’s will through his word, prayer and wise counsel.
verseByVerse.note: The total was 601,730 men (v. 51), almost the same as forty years before.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 57–65 — The Levites, and the Old Generation Gone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word comes exactly true, in judgment as in mercy. The Levites are counted separately, from a month old, because they receive no land: the LORD himself is their inheritance (vv. 57–62). Their list pauses over the family of Moses, Aaron and Miriam, and over Nadab and Abihu, who died for offering unauthorised fire. Then the chapter closes by comparing the two counts. Of all the men listed at Sinai, not one is left, except Caleb and Joshua (vv. 63–65): God’s sentence at Kadesh has been carried out to the last man, and his promise to the two who trusted him has been kept just as exactly.
verseByVerse.theology: The end of the old generation fulfils God’s word of judgment to the letter (14:29-30), and the two men who believed him are spared, living proof that “whoever does the will of God abides forever” (1 John 2:17).
verseByVerse.examples: God’s warnings are as certain as his promises (Heb 3:16-19). Faith is the difference between those who fall in the wilderness and those who enter the rest (Heb 4:1-2), and it rests not on our strength but on the God who keeps his word to the last letter.

verseByVerse.quote: This was the list of the Levites according to their clans: of Gershon, the clan of the Gershonites; of Kohath, the clan of the Kohathites; of Merari, the clan of the Merarites. These are the clans of Levi: the clan of the Libnites, the clan of the Hebronites, the clan of the Mahlites, the clan of the Mushites, the clan of the Korahites. And Kohath was the father of Amram. The name of Amram's wife was Jochebed the daughter of Levi, who was born to Levi in Egypt. And she bore to Amram Aaron and Moses and Miriam their sister. And to Aaron were born Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. But Nadab and Abihu died when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD. And those listed were 23,000, every male from a month old and upward. For they were not listed among the people of Israel, because there was no inheritance given to them among the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites are counted apart because they receive no land: the LORD himself is their inheritance.

The list of the Levites. The Levites are counted from “a month old”, babies included, because this tribe is not mustered for war. And they are kept off the main roll “because there was no inheritance given to them”.

Counted most, given least. The tribe counted most carefully receives least. Twelve names on the list are attached to territory; Levi’s is attached to a tent. God had explained the exchange to Aaron: “I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel” (18:20), and here it is on paper, a separate list and no land at the end. The other tribes are listed by what they can do, because they will fight for land. Levi is listed by who they are.

Amram’s family. The list also pauses over Amram’s family, Aaron, Moses and Miriam, and over Nadab and Abihu, who “died when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD” (Leviticus 10:1–2). Even the priestly genealogy carries its graves. The tribe nearest the holiness of God had learned most painfully what that nearness costs.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of “who was born to Levi in Egypt” is compressed and does not name the mother. “Daughter of Levi” may mean a descendant, since family lines often skip generations, which would fit the long stay in Egypt. Either way, Moses, Aaron and Miriam came from Levi’s line.

verseByVerse.quote: These were those listed by Moses and Eleazar the priest, who listed the people of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho. But among these there was not one of those listed by Moses and Aaron the priest, who had listed the people of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai. For the LORD had said of them, "They shall die in the wilderness." Not one of them was left, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only Caleb and Joshua appear on both counts: God’s sentence and God’s promise both came true to the letter.

Not one of them was left. The chapter ends by checking one list against the other, and the result is devastating. Two lists taken forty years apart, six hundred thousand men on each, and the overlap is two names. God had said, “They shall die in the wilderness” at Kadesh, and he meant it. Every word came true, one funeral at a time, over thirty-eight years.

Except Caleb and Joshua. But read the exception, because the same faithfulness is in it. Caleb and Joshua had stood before a nation that wanted to stone them and said, “the LORD is with us; do not fear them” (14:9), and God had promised those two men they would go in. Four decades later, with everyone they had known buried behind them, they are standing on the plains of Moab being counted. The God who is exact about his warnings is exact about his promises, and it is the same exactness. “The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever” (Isaiah 40:8), and a chapter of names and numbers turns out to be the proof of it.

The greater Joshua. Joshua is about to lead the new generation in (27:18–23), and in Greek his name is Jesus. Our Joshua trusted his Father perfectly where we did not, and brings all his people home.

keyVerse.quote: For the LORD had said of them, ‘They shall die in the wilderness.’ Not one of them was left, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun.
keyVerse.note: After hundreds of names, the chapter’s point comes in one verse. God’s sentence on unbelief was carried out to the last man, and his promise to the two who trusted him was kept just as exactly: his warnings and his promises are equally sure.

26.reflection:
The new count begins “after the plague” (v. 1), with a whole generation buried behind it. What does it tell us about God that he starts again with the children of those who failed? Where do you need that hope, for yourself or for the next generation?

The list pauses to remember Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Korah who did not die, and five daughters with no brother (vv. 9–11, 33). Why do you think God has these stories written into a census? What does it say about how he sees individuals in a crowd?

The land was shared by size but placed by lot (vv. 52–56). How does knowing that our inheritance in Christ is measured and placed by God (Ephesians 1:11) help with contentment, comparison and envy?

Only Caleb and Joshua appear on both lists (v. 65). What does this chapter teach about taking both God’s warnings and God’s promises seriously?

27.title: The Daughters of Zelophehad; Joshua Commissioned
27.text: <sup>1</sup>Then drew near the daughters of Zelophehad the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, from the clans of Manasseh the son of Joseph. The names of his daughters were: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.<sup>2</sup>And they stood before Moses and before Eleazar the priest and before the chiefs and all the congregation, at the entrance of the tent of meeting, saying,<sup>3</sup>"Our father died in the wilderness. He was not among the company of those who gathered themselves together against the LORD in the company of Korah, but died for his own sin. And he had no sons.<sup>4</sup>Why should the name of our father be taken away from his clan because he had no son? Give to us a possession among our father's brothers."<sup>5</sup>Moses brought their case before the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD said to Moses,<sup>7</sup>"The daughters of Zelophehad are right. You shall give them possession of an inheritance among their father's brothers and transfer the inheritance of their father to them.<sup>8</sup>And you shall speak to the people of Israel, saying, 'If a man dies and has no son, then you shall transfer his inheritance to his daughter.<sup>9</sup>And if he has no daughter, then you shall give his inheritance to his brothers.<sup>10</sup>And if he has no brothers, then you shall give his inheritance to his father's brothers.<sup>11</sup>And if his father has no brothers, then you shall give his inheritance to the nearest kinsman of his clan, and he shall possess it. And it shall be for the people of Israel a statute and rule, as the LORD commanded Moses.'"<sup>12</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Go up into this mountain of Abarim and see the land that I have given to the people of Israel.<sup>13</sup>When you have seen it, you also shall be gathered to your people, as your brother Aaron was,<sup>14</sup>because you rebelled against my word in the wilderness of Zin when the congregation quarreled, failing to uphold me as holy at the waters before their eyes." (These are the waters of Meribah of Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin.)<sup>15</sup>Moses spoke to the LORD, saying,<sup>16</sup>"Let the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation<sup>17</sup>who shall go out before them and come in before them, who shall lead them out and bring them in, that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd."<sup>18</sup>So the LORD said to Moses, "Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him.<sup>19</sup>Make him stand before Eleazar the priest and all the congregation, and you shall commission him in their sight.<sup>20</sup>You shall invest him with some of your authority, that all the congregation of the people of Israel may obey.<sup>21</sup>And he shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before the LORD. At his word they shall go out, and at his word they shall come in, both he and all the people of Israel with him, the whole congregation."<sup>22</sup>And Moses did as the LORD commanded him. He took Joshua and made him stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation,<sup>23</sup>and he laid his hands on him and commissioned him as the LORD directed through Moses.
27.overview:
Where we are. The new generation has just been counted for the land (chapter 26), and five daughters were named in the list who had no brother to inherit. Israel waits on the plains of Moab, and two questions hang over the camp: who will inherit, and who will lead when Moses is gone?

The message. God provides for his people’s future, both their inheritance and their shepherd. He hears five women with no standing and declares, “The daughters of Zelophehad are right”, making their case a law for every family. And when Moses must die outside the land, God answers his prayer for a shepherd by appointing Joshua, a man in whom is the Spirit. No one’s place among God’s people is forgotten, and no flock of his is left without a shepherd.

Why it was said. A generation about to enter Canaan needed to know that the land would be held fairly, family by family, and that the leadership God had given through Moses would not die with him (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The five sisters come forward before the whole assembly and ask for their father’s portion so that his name will not vanish (vv. 1–4). Moses takes the case to the LORD, who rules in their favour (vv. 5–7) and sets a full order of inheritance for Israel (vv. 8–11). Then God tells Moses to view the land he will not enter because of Meribah (vv. 12–14). Moses asks for a shepherd for the people (vv. 15–17), and God names Joshua, who is commissioned publicly with Moses’ hands on him and placed beside the priest (vv. 18–23).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Moses’ prayer that Israel “may not be as sheep that have no shepherd” is answered for a generation by Joshua, and for ever by Jesus, who saw the crowds “like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36) and laid down his life for them. Joshua bears Jesus’ own name, yet he receives only “some” of Moses’ authority and has to ask the priest for God’s will; the offices are divided until one comes who is Prophet, Priest and King at once. And the “nearest kinsman” who keeps a family’s inheritance points, many Christians have seen, to the Son of God who became our brother to restore what we had lost.

For us. Come boldly to God with what you need, as the daughters did, trusting his promise. Leaders should take hard questions to God rather than pretend to know. And when God says no, as he did to Moses, his no is never his last word to those who are his.
27.theology:
God hears the faithful appeal. The daughters of Zelophehad, bold in faith, are declared right by God himself, who honors the overlooked.

The limit of the law. Moses sees the land but cannot enter it. Moses, who gave the law, cannot bring the people into rest. That points beyond him to a greater Leader.

The greater Joshua. Spirit-filled Joshua leads Israel into the land, foreshadowing Jesus, who leads his people into eternal rest (Heb 4:8–9).
27.examples: God hears the bold faith of the overlooked and secures your inheritance in Christ. The greater Joshua leads you into the rest the law could never give, and you will never be left as sheep without a shepherd.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God hears those with no standing, and makes their case a law for all. Five sisters whose father died without sons come forward before Moses, the priest and the whole congregation, and ask for a share of the land so that their father’s name will not be lost from his clan (vv. 1–4). Moses does not improvise but brings their case before the LORD, who answers, “The daughters of Zelophehad are right” (vv. 5–7). Then God turns one family’s request into a statute for every family: an order of inheritance through daughters, brothers, uncles and the nearest kinsman, so that no household’s portion in the land is lost (vv. 8–11).
verseByVerse.theology: God’s ruling (v.7) establishes a lasting statute protecting daughters’ inheritance where there is no son, a striking dignity in the ancient world. God’s justice hears the voiceless (cf. Ps 68:5), and Moses’ habit of bringing hard cases “before the LORD” (v.5) models leadership that seeks God’s will.
verseByVerse.examples: God still hears the appeal of those the world overlooks, so bring your hard cases before the LORD, as these sisters and Moses did.

verseByVerse.quote: Then drew near the daughters of Zelophehad the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, from the clans of Manasseh the son of Joseph. The names of his daughters were: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. And they stood before Moses and before Eleazar the priest and before the chiefs and all the congregation, at the entrance of the tent of meeting, saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five women with no one to speak for them come to the front of the whole assembly to make their case.

Then drew near. Stage the scene properly, because everything depends on it. The whole nation is assembled, the leadership drawn up at the tabernacle door: Moses, the high priest, the tribal chiefs. Every person with standing is a man. And out of the crowd walk five unmarried women with no father, no brothers, no one to speak for them and no earlier case to appeal to, and they keep walking until they are at the front. They “drew near”, the word Numbers uses for approaching God at the tent. They did not ask an uncle to plead for them in private.

The names of his daughters. The text names them twice, here and in the census (26:33): Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, Tirzah, listed as carefully as any chief in the muster roll.

verseByVerse.quote: "Our father died in the wilderness. He was not among the company of those who gathered themselves together against the LORD in the company of Korah, but died for his own sin. And he had no sons. Why should the name of our father be taken away from his clan because he had no son? Give to us a possession among our father's brothers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sisters argue carefully that their father died under the common sentence, not in Korah’s rebellion, and ask that his name not be lost for want of a son.

Our father died in the wilderness. Their reasoning is careful, plainly long thought out. Their father died under the general sentence at Kadesh, no better and no worse than six hundred thousand others. He was not with Korah, whose rebels probably forfeited their land, so they rule out the one ground on which the claim could be refused. And he left no sons, which by the custom of every nation around them meant the family was finished.

Why should the name of our father be taken away? Then the plea, not what a modern reader expects. Not “this is unfair to us”, but “Why should the name of our father be taken away from his clan because he had no son?” In Israel a family’s land and its name went together. To hold no portion was to have no place in the covenant people and, after a generation, no memory. They are fighting for a dead man’s place among the people of God.

Faith that makes arrangements. Nobody in that assembly has crossed the Jordan. These women are pressing a claim to a field in a country nobody has set foot in, because they believe God will give it. That is faith of a practical kind, the sort that makes arrangements, and it rests not on their strength but on his promise. Set your own praying beside it. Do you ask God for things you have already begun to plan for, or only for things you would be quietly unsurprised not to receive?

Uncertain wording. “Died for his own sin” is brief. Most take it to mean that he died for the sin his whole generation shared at Kadesh, not for a special rebellion that would cost his family its land.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses brought their case before the LORD. And the LORD said to Moses, "The daughters of Zelophehad are right. You shall give them possession of an inheritance among their father's brothers and transfer the inheritance of their father to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses does not know the answer, so he takes the case to God, and God rules that the daughters are right.

Moses brought their case before the LORD. Moses is the lawgiver of Israel, who has spoken with God face to face, the most competent man alive on what the law requires, and he does not know the answer. He does not improvise a ruling to protect his authority. He takes their case to God. Anyone who leads anything should read that verse twice. The temptation for a leader is to appear to know when he does not; the greatest leader in the Old Testament admitted it and went to God.

The daughters of Zelophehad are right. Then the verdict, startling in its bluntness: “right”. God does not merely make a compassionate exception; he says their reading of what the covenant required was correct, and the leadership had not thought it through. Five women with no standing understood the mind of God on a point of law better than the chiefs of the twelve tribes. It will not be the last time in Scripture that the people with no standing turn out to have seen furthest: “God chose what is low and despised in the world… so that no human being might boast in the presence of God” (1 Corinthians 1:28–29).

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall speak to the people of Israel, saying, 'If a man dies and has no son, then you shall transfer his inheritance to his daughter. And if he has no daughter, then you shall give his inheritance to his brothers. And if he has no brothers, then you shall give his inheritance to his father's brothers. And if his father has no brothers, then you shall give his inheritance to the nearest kinsman of his clan, and he shall possess it. And it shall be for the people of Israel a statute and rule, as the LORD commanded Moses.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God turns one family’s request into a law for every family: an order of inheritance that keeps each household’s land within the clan, ending with the nearest kinsman.

A statute and rule. Instead of granting the petition and moving on, God gives a complete order of succession, daughter, brothers, uncles, nearest kinsman, “a statute and rule” for the nation. One family’s grievance becomes permanent law. Because five women were brave enough to walk to the front, every daughter in Israel for a thousand years had a right she would not otherwise have had. God did not make them a special case; he made their case the reason for a law. That is like him. He does not merely relieve the person in front of him; he alters the arrangements so that the next person never has to ask.

What it does not mean. The ruling covered daughters where there was no son, and chapter 36 adds that such heiresses marry within their tribe, so that the land stays where God placed it. It did not make sons and daughters equal heirs, but in its world it was a real protection.

The nearest kinsman. The chain ends with “the nearest kinsman”: a relative close enough and willing enough to keep a lost family’s portion in the family. That is the custom, the kinsman-redeemer, that saves a widow in Bethlehem when Boaz buys back the family’s land and marries Ruth (Ruth 4:1–10). Many Christians have seen in it a picture of what the Son of God did about the inheritance we had forfeited: “he had to be made like his brothers in every respect” (Hebrews 2:17). A kinsman was needed. He became one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–23 — Joshua Appointed to Succeed Moses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God provides a shepherd for his people when their great leader must die. Moses is told to climb the Abarim range, see the land he will not enter because he failed to honour God at Meribah, and be gathered to his people (vv. 12–14). His only concern is for the flock: he asks the God who knows every spirit to appoint a man who will go before them, so that they are not “as sheep that have no shepherd” (vv. 15–17). God names Joshua, “a man in whom is the Spirit”. Moses lays his hands on him before the priest and the people, gives him some of his authority, and obeys without a word of complaint (vv. 18–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Moses’ last concern is for the flock, and God’s answer is Joshua: the work of God is bigger than any one servant, and he provides for it beyond each servant’s lifetime.
verseByVerse.examples: When a pastor or leader we have leaned on is taken from us, the loss is real; but the flock was never his to keep, and the Shepherd who never dies goes on leading his people all the way into the promised rest.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Go up into this mountain of Abarim and see the land that I have given to the people of Israel. When you have seen it, you also shall be gathered to your people, as your brother Aaron was, because you rebelled against my word in the wilderness of Zin when the congregation quarreled, failing to uphold me as holy at the waters before their eyes." (These are the waters of Meribah of Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Moses to climb the mountain, see the land he may not enter because he failed to honour God at Meribah, and then die: real severity, and real tenderness.

Go up into this mountain of Abarim. The writer has put these paragraphs side by side deliberately. Moses has just settled the inheritance law of a land he will never own a foot of, and the moment the case is closed, God tells him to climb a hill, look at it, and die. The Abarim are the highlands of Moab rising above the plains where Israel was camped; Deuteronomy names the peak, Mount Nebo, the top of Pisgah (Deuteronomy 32:49; 34:1).

Failing to uphold me as holy. The severity is unsoftened. One episode at Meribah (20:2–13), decades of faithfulness either side of it, and the sentence stands. God is not sentimental about his own glory, least of all when his friends obscure it.

See the land. But look at what he gives. Not simply “you shall die”, but “see the land”. Moses is shown the whole of it, Gilead, Dan, Judah, the Negeb, right to the sea (Deuteronomy 34:1–3). He is refused the possession and granted the view, and then “gathered to your people”, Scripture’s quiet word for a homecoming.

Inside the land at last. Centuries later Peter, James and John look up on a mountain and there he is, inside the land at last, in glory, talking with Jesus about his departure (Luke 9:30–31). God’s no to Moses was real, and it was not the last word he spoke to him.
verseByVerse.note: Abarim was the mountain range of Moab; its peak Nebo overlooks Jericho.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke to the LORD, saying, "Let the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation who shall go out before them and come in before them, who shall lead them out and bring them in, that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Told he is about to die, Moses asks nothing for himself, only that God would give the people a shepherd who goes before them.

Moses spoke to the LORD. A man has just been told that he is about to die. Read what he says next. Not one word about himself: no appeal against the sentence, no request that his own sons be considered, and they never are. His whole concern is that this exasperating nation, which broke his heart for forty years and cost him the land, should not be left without someone to walk in front of them. That is the measure of the man, and why God trusted him with them.

The God of the spirits of all flesh. He calls on the only one who knows what is inside every human being, because no man can see far enough into another to make this appointment safely. And he asks for a leader who will “go out before them”, whose place is in front, taking first whatever is coming.

As sheep that have no shepherd. The phrase does not stay in Numbers. It becomes the prophets’ charge against Israel’s failed leaders (Ezekiel 34:5). Then Jesus goes through Galilee and sees the crowds, and “he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36). God answered Moses’ prayer for one generation with Joshua, and finally, for every generation, in the one who said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Moses asked for a man who would go out before the flock. God sent a Shepherd who went out before them all the way to a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD said to Moses, "Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Make him stand before Eleazar the priest and all the congregation, and you shall commission him in their sight. You shall invest him with some of your authority, that all the congregation of the people of Israel may obey. And he shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before the LORD. At his word they shall go out, and at his word they shall come in, both he and all the people of Israel with him, the whole congregation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God chooses Joshua because the Spirit is in him, and has him commissioned in public, receiving some of Moses’ authority and seeking God’s will through the priest.

A man in whom is the Spirit. The qualification named is not experience or courage, though Joshua had both, but that the Spirit is in him. Every servant of God since has been equipped the same way, and the Spirit is now given to all who belong to Christ. The ceremony is public, “in their sight”, with Moses’ hand laid on him, the pattern the church still follows in setting people apart (Acts 6:6; 1 Timothy 4:14).

Some of your authority. Some, not all. Moses spoke with God “face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (Exodus 33:11); Joshua must stand before the priest, who will inquire for him “by the judgment of the Urim”, kept in the high priest’s breastpiece, by which Israel sought God’s answer on great national decisions.

Prophet and priest divided. So the authority Moses held alone is deliberately split between leader and priest, and never again given whole to one man in Israel. The gap was left open on purpose. For centuries no one man both spoke God’s word and stood in God’s presence for the people. Then a man walked out of the Jordan who was Prophet, Priest and King at once. He needed nobody to inquire for him, because the word he spoke was his own.

The name Joshua. Joshua is Yehoshua, “the LORD saves”, the same name, in its later form Jesus, that an angel would give to Mary’s child. Hebrews makes the comparison and leaves it deliberately unfinished: “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on” (Hebrews 4:8). One Joshua took them into Canaan. The other takes his people into rest.

Uncertain wording. No one knows exactly what the Urim (with the Thummim, Exodus 28:30) were or how they worked. The most common view is that they were sacred lots giving a yes or no answer before the LORD (compare 1 Samuel 14:41). Either way, Joshua was to lead under God’s word, not his own judgment.
verseByVerse.note: The Urim was used by the priest to learn God’s will (see Exod 28:30).

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses did as the LORD commanded him. He took Joshua and made him stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation, and he laid his hands on him and commissioned him as the LORD directed through Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses obeys to the letter, handing his life’s work to another with his own hands and without a word of complaint.

Moses did as the LORD commanded him. Consider what that obedience cost. A dying man publicly hands his work over, with his own hands, to the one who will do what he himself has longed to do for forty years and been refused. Scripture records not a syllable of reluctance, no wistful speech, no attempt to keep a little authority back.

Given and withheld. Two parties are handed something in this chapter they were not entitled to: five women who should have inherited nothing, and an assistant with no claim to succeed Moses. And the same chapter takes from the greatest man in Israel the one thing he most wanted. God gives to those with no claim and withholds from the man with every claim, and in both directions he is entirely good. Moses, who failed once at Meribah, did not enter Canaan; he entered glory, because his standing rested on the God who forgives and not on his record. And he never lost the flock. He handed them to a Joshua, and God would one day hand them to another, who never failed at any rock.

keyVerse.quote: Let the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation who shall go out before them and come in before them, who shall lead them out and bring them in, that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd.
keyVerse.note: A dying man’s only prayer is for the flock he must leave. God answered it with Joshua, and finally with Jesus, who saw the crowds “like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36) and laid down his life for the sheep.

27.reflection:
The daughters of Zelophehad came to the front of the whole assembly to ask for a share in a land no one had yet entered (vv. 1–4). What does their boldness teach us about faith and about prayer? Is there something you have stopped asking God for?

Moses did not know the answer, so he took the case to the LORD (v. 5). Why is it hard for leaders, parents or anyone with responsibility to admit they do not know? What would it look like to follow Moses’ example?

Told he would die outside the land, Moses asked only for a shepherd for the people (vv. 15–17). How does his prayer point to Jesus, the good shepherd? How does it challenge the way we think about our own plans and legacy?

God said no to Moses’ great desire, yet Moses later stood in the land with Jesus (Luke 9:30–31). How might that help us when God says no to something we long for?

28.title: The Continual Offerings: The Rhythm of Worship
28.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Command the people of Israel and say to them, 'My offering, my food for my food offerings, my pleasing aroma, you shall be careful to offer to me at its appointed time.'<sup>3</sup>And you shall say to them, This is the food offering that you shall offer to the LORD: two male lambs a year old without blemish, day by day, as a regular offering.<sup>4</sup>The one lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the other lamb you shall offer at twilight;<sup>5</sup>also a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with a quarter of a hin of beaten oil.<sup>6</sup>It is a regular burnt offering, which was ordained at Mount Sinai for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>Its drink offering shall be a quarter of a hin for each lamb. In the Holy Place you shall pour out a drink offering of strong drink to the LORD.<sup>8</sup>The other lamb you shall offer at twilight. Like the grain offering of the morning, and like its drink offering, you shall offer it as a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>9</sup>"On the Sabbath day, two male lambs a year old without blemish, and two tenths of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, and its drink offering:<sup>10</sup>this is the burnt offering of every Sabbath, besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.<sup>11</sup>"At the beginnings of your months, you shall offer a burnt offering to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish;<sup>12</sup>also three tenths of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, for each bull, and two tenths of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, for the one ram;<sup>13</sup>and a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering for every lamb; for a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>14</sup>Their drink offerings shall be half a hin of wine for a bull, a third of a hin for a ram, and a quarter of a hin for a lamb. This is the burnt offering of each month throughout the months of the year.<sup>15</sup>Also one male goat for a sin offering to the LORD; it shall be offered besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.<sup>16</sup>"On the fourteenth day of the first month is the LORD's Passover,<sup>17</sup>and on the fifteenth day of this month is a feast. Seven days shall unleavened bread be eaten.<sup>18</sup>On the first day there shall be a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work,<sup>19</sup>but offer a food offering, a burnt offering to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old; see that they are without blemish;<sup>20</sup>also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil; three tenths of an ephah shall you offer for a bull, and two tenths for a ram;<sup>21</sup>a tenth shall you offer for each of the seven lambs;<sup>22</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, to make atonement for you.<sup>23</sup>You shall offer these besides the burnt offering of the morning, which is for a regular burnt offering.<sup>24</sup>In the same way you shall offer daily, for seven days, the food of a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. It shall be offered besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.<sup>25</sup>And on the seventh day you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work.<sup>26</sup>"On the day of the firstfruits, when you offer a grain offering of new grain to the LORD at your Feast of Weeks, you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work,<sup>27</sup>but offer a burnt offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old;<sup>28</sup>also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for each bull, two tenths for one ram,<sup>29</sup>a tenth for each of the seven lambs;<sup>30</sup>with one male goat, to make atonement for you.<sup>31</sup>Besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, you shall offer them and their drink offering. See that they are without blemish.
28.overview:
Where we are. The new generation has been counted (chapter 26) and Joshua appointed to lead it in (chapter 27). Before Israel crosses the Jordan, God sets out the offerings of the whole year, in this chapter and the next, for life in the land.

The message. God claims all of his people’s time as his own, and he keeps them near him by sacrifice. Every day begins and ends with a lamb on the altar; on that daily foundation the Sabbath, the new moon and the great feasts are added, until no day, week, month or season is left out. What looks like a timetable is a picture of a redeemed people living their whole life before God, and always by way of an offering he provides.

Why it was said. The generation about to settle in Canaan would soon be busy with fields, harvests and wars, surrounded by the festivals of Baal (see the introduction). They needed a calendar that kept the LORD at the centre of ordinary time, and that remembered each year that they were a people saved by the blood of a lamb.

How the chapter makes its case. God calls the offerings “my food” and “my pleasing aroma”, and requires them “at its appointed time” (vv. 1–2). The base is the regular burnt offering, a lamb at morning and at twilight with grain and drink (vv. 3–8). On the Sabbath it is doubled (vv. 9–10), and each new moon brings a larger burnt offering with a goat for a sin offering (vv. 11–15). Then the year: Passover and the seven days of Unleavened Bread (vv. 16–25), and the firstfruits at the Feast of Weeks (vv. 26–31), each with its sin offering and each “besides the regular burnt offering”.

Where it leads. By pattern, confirmed by the New Testament. The lambs that never stopped dying show that none of them could finish the work, and Christ did: “when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down” (Hebrews 10:12). “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7); he rose as “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20); and at Pentecost the Spirit came. He is the Lamb without blemish the whole calendar was waiting for.

For us. Our place with God does not depend on keeping a rhythm, for the one sacrifice is finished and Christ always lives to intercede for us. But God still wants all our time, and steady habits of prayer, Scripture and gathering with his people keep us near him on the ordinary days when we feel nothing at all.
28.theology:
Continual worship. Fellowship with God was meant to be constant, not occasional. The special days were always added to the daily offering and never replaced it.

The continual intercession of Christ. The unbroken offering foreshadows our Great High Priest, who never stops asking the Father to accept us for the sake of his finished sacrifice.

Time made holy. Day, week, month and season are all given to God, a pattern Isaiah carries forward to the worship of the new creation (Isa. 66:23).
28.examples:
Then: Israel offered the continual morning and evening sacrifice, with added offerings for Sabbaths, new moons and feasts, so that worship filled the whole calendar.

Now: The endless offerings that could never finish dealing with sin are fulfilled in Christ’s one finished sacrifice and his unceasing intercession. Day and night your Mediator pleads for you, and his Spirit in you is what turns a distracted day into an offering. Your worship will never be as constant as the old altar was meant to be; his intercession is, and that is what keeps you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before any festival, there is a steady heartbeat of approach to God. The LORD begins by calling the offerings “my food” and “my pleasing aroma”, to be offered at their appointed times (vv. 1–2): worship is first giving God what is his. Then comes the foundation of the whole calendar, the regular offering, a male lamb without blemish every morning and another at twilight, with flour, oil and a drink offering (vv. 3–8). Whatever else happened in Israel, the lamb at dawn and dusk never stopped, a daily reminder that sinners come near to God only through a sacrifice, and a pattern fulfilled when Christ offered himself once for all.
verseByVerse.theology: The tamid, the continual daily offering (vv. 3–6), frames all of Israel’s worship. Before any feast comes the unbroken approach to God morning and evening, a pattern the godly kept in their own prayers (Ps 55:17; Dan 6:10). Because Christ’s one offering is always sufficient, we may now draw near to God at any hour (Heb 10:19–22).
verseByVerse.examples: In Israel no morning or evening passed without a lamb on the altar. For the Christian, worship belongs to Monday as much as to Sunday. A short prayer at the start and end of the day is a small echo of the old rhythm, offered not to bring God near but because, through the Lamb, he already is (Heb 10:22).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Command the people of Israel and say to them, 'My offering, my food for my food offerings, my pleasing aroma, you shall be careful to offer to me at its appointed time.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The offerings are God’s, given at his appointed times: worship is first giving God what belongs to him.

My offering, my food. Before a single animal is named, God says again and again in one sentence whose these offerings are: “My offering, my food for my food offerings, my pleasing aroma”. That is the frame for the next two chapters, and without it the calendar reads as religious bookkeeping. This is not Israel arranging her devotional life; it is a covenant Lord telling the people he redeemed what belongs to him.

What “my food” means. The phrase needs explaining, because Israel’s neighbours meant it literally: their gods were fed by sacrifice. Scripture flatly denies that: “If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine” (Psalm 50:12). God keeps the word and its warmth but removes the pagan idea: the rising smoke does not feed him, it pleases him.

A pleasing aroma. Paul applies the phrase to the cross, where Christ “gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (Ephesians 5:2), and then, astonishingly, to a gift sent to a missionary in prison, “a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God” (Philippians 4:18).

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall say to them, This is the food offering that you shall offer to the LORD: two male lambs a year old without blemish, day by day, as a regular offering. The one lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the other lamb you shall offer at twilight; also a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with a quarter of a hin of beaten oil. It is a regular burnt offering, which was ordained at Mount Sinai for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. Its drink offering shall be a quarter of a hin for each lamb. In the Holy Place you shall pour out a drink offering of strong drink to the LORD. The other lamb you shall offer at twilight. Like the grain offering of the morning, and like its drink offering, you shall offer it as a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s worship rests on a lamb offered every morning and evening without fail, a sacrifice that could never finish its work, until Christ’s one offering did.

A regular offering. The foundation of the whole calendar is its smallest item. “Regular” translates tamid, “continual”: whatever else was happening in Israel (harvest, war, plague, a good king or a bad one), a lamb died at dawn and a lamb died at dusk, and the smoke went up from that altar for the best part of a thousand years. Every feast in the chapter is offered “besides the regular burnt offering”; the special days are added on top and never replace it.

Worship for the land. The calendar is restated on the edge of Canaan because it assumes life in the land: flour, oil and wine in these quantities (a tenth of an ephah, a quarter of a hin) belong to a farming people, worshipping with harvests not yet reaped (compare 15:2).

The cost. Two things follow. First, the cost: seven hundred and thirty lambs a year, for centuries, and none of them ever finally dealt with sin, which is the argument of Hebrews. “Every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down” (Hebrews 10:11–12). The old priests never sat down because the work was never done.

Assurance. Second, assurance. Israel lived each ordinary hour under a sacrifice at each end of the day; nobody had to wonder at three in the afternoon whether God had been approached. Christians have that assurance permanently, not because we keep the rhythm, but because “he always lives to make intercession” for us (Hebrews 7:25). The tamid was silenced more than once by exile and war (Daniel 8:11). His intercession has never stopped, and never will.

Why repetition is not hypocrisy. Many assume worship is only real when it is spontaneous, and that the same prayer every morning is going through the motions. Israel’s calendar disagrees, and so does the rest of life. Nobody thinks a pianist’s scales are insincere, or that a marriage is fake because a husband kisses his wife goodbye every morning whether or not he feels like it. Routines are how love lasts once feelings come and go. C. S. Lewis, in his Letters to Malcolm, observed that a familiar form of worship serves us best when we no longer have to think about it, so that our attention is free for God. The lamb at dawn and dusk was not Israel performing for God. It was God keeping Israel near him on the days nobody felt anything at all. That is still what our habits are for: not to earn a place with him, which the Lamb has done once for all, but to keep turning up to receive what he gives.

Uncertain wording. “At twilight” is literally “between the two evenings”: either between sunset and dark, or (as later Jewish practice took it) the afternoon before sunset. “Strong drink” (v. 7) usually means beer or other fermented drink, but verse 14 names wine, so it may mean wine here. “In the Holy Place” probably means the sanctuary area, at the altar, not inside the tent.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Sabbath and New Moon Offerings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God claims the week and the month as well as the day. On the Sabbath the daily offering is doubled, so that the day of rest becomes a day of fuller worship (vv. 9–10). At the start of each month a larger burnt offering of bulls, a ram and seven lambs is offered, with grain and wine in fixed measure (vv. 11–14), and a male goat as a sin offering (v. 15). So every new month in Israel began by naming sin again and bringing God the provision he had appointed for it, and every special offering was added “besides” the regular one, never in place of it.
verseByVerse.theology: The Sabbath and new-moon offerings (vv. 9–15) train God’s people to receive each week and month from his hand: My times are in your hand (Ps 31:15).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the start of each month was marked with fuller sacrifices, so that Israel never drifted through the calendar without remembering whose it was.

Now: the Lord’s Day and the turning of the seasons can serve the same purpose: a deliberate pause to hand the coming week or month back to God, and to confess what the last one held.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the Sabbath day, two male lambs a year old without blemish, and two tenths of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, and its drink offering: this is the burnt offering of every Sabbath, besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering. "At the beginnings of your months, you shall offer a burnt offering to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish; also three tenths of an ephah of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, for each bull, and two tenths of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, for the one ram; and a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering for every lamb; for a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. Their drink offerings shall be half a hin of wine for a bull, a third of a hin for a ram, and a quarter of a hin for a lamb. This is the burnt offering of each month throughout the months of the year. Also one male goat for a sin offering to the LORD; it shall be offered besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sabbath doubles the daily offering and each new month begins with a greater one and a sin offering: God claims the week and the month as well as the day.

On the Sabbath day. On the Sabbath the offering is doubled: the day of rest is the day worship increases, not slackens. Stopping work cleared the day, so that a nation could turn to God without the plough in the way.

At the beginnings of your months. Then the months, marked by the new moon. God claims the day at dawn and dusk, the week at its seventh day, the month at its first, and in the next chapter the year at its climax, until no part of time is left ungiven to him. Isaiah carries the same two markers forward to the end of all things: “From new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath, all flesh shall come to worship before me, declares the LORD” (Isaiah 66:23).

One male goat for a sin offering. Every month, as Israel marked the turning of the season, sin was named again. The calendar of a redeemed people had a sin offering built into it, because God knew what a month does to his people and made provision in advance.

Where Christians differ: does the Sabbath bind Christians today? It was the sign of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 31:13), and the New Testament calls Sabbaths “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16–17). Many godly Reformed Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, binding by the fourth commandment, and this commentary honours them; Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), so no day binds the conscience (Romans 14:5); rest and gathering for worship on the Lord’s Day remain good gifts, gladly taken up out of joy and wisdom rather than as a law. Faithful Christians differ on this, and should differ charitably.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–31 — Passover, Unleavened Bread, and Firstfruits
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s year retells the story of salvation, and Christ fulfils it. The year begins with Passover, remembering the lamb whose blood saved Israel in Egypt, followed by seven days of Unleavened Bread with holy gatherings, rest from work and daily offerings, including a goat “to make atonement for you” (vv. 16–25). Then comes the day of firstfruits at the Feast of Weeks, when the first of the new grain was offered (vv. 26–31). The New Testament names Christ our Passover lamb and the firstfruits of the resurrection, and it was at the Feast of Weeks, Pentecost, that the Spirit was poured out.
verseByVerse.theology: The feasts are a calendar that points forward to Christ (cf. Lev 23). Passover proclaims redemption by the lamb’s blood; Unleavened Bread calls for a life swept clean of the old leaven, the yeast that pictures sin (1 Cor 5:8); the Feast of Weeks becomes Pentecost, the first harvest of the Spirit (Acts 2). The offerings surround each feast with worship, but the deepest meaning of the feasts is the rescue they act out, now accomplished in Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples: Year by year Israel retold the story of her rescue and thanked God for the harvest. The church does the same at the Lord’s Supper, where she remembers the Lamb who was sacrificed for her, and every new believer gathered in is part of the harvest that began at Pentecost.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the fourteenth day of the first month is the LORD's Passover, and on the fifteenth day of this month is a feast. Seven days shall unleavened bread be eaten. On the first day there shall be a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work, but offer a food offering, a burnt offering to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old; see that they are without blemish; also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil; three tenths of an ephah shall you offer for a bull, and two tenths for a ram; a tenth shall you offer for each of the seven lambs; also one male goat for a sin offering, to make atonement for you. You shall offer these besides the burnt offering of the morning, which is for a regular burnt offering. In the same way you shall offer daily, for seven days, the food of a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. It shall be offered besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering. And on the seventh day you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The year opens with Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, remembering the night God saved Israel by the blood of a lamb; Christ is our Passover lamb.

The LORD’s Passover. The year opens where the nation opened: with the night in Egypt when the blood was on the doorposts. Israel’s calendar is built to make her remember. Every feast retells a saving act. The New Testament applies both halves of this spring feast, Passover and Unleavened Bread, in a single verse: “Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump… For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

First the lamb, then the leaven. The order must not be reversed. The sacrifice is not the reward for the housecleaning; it is the reason for it. Israel did not earn Passover by removing the yeast; she removed the yeast because the lamb had died and she was leaving Egypt in the morning. A Christian who thinks he must clean up before the sacrifice can be his has misread the feast, and will spend his life sweeping.

Must Christians keep these feasts? They were shadows fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and the Lord’s Supper has taken the Passover’s place. Keeping them is a matter of freedom, not obligation (Romans 14:5–6), and never a condition of standing with God (Galatians 4:10–11).

verseByVerse.quote: "On the day of the firstfruits, when you offer a grain offering of new grain to the LORD at your Feast of Weeks, you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work, but offer a burnt offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old; also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for each bull, two tenths for one ram, a tenth for each of the seven lambs; with one male goat, to make atonement for you. Besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, you shall offer them and their drink offering. See that they are without blemish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the Feast of Weeks the first of the new grain is offered, a pledge of the harvest to come; Christ rose as the firstfruits, and at this feast the Spirit was poured out.

The day of the firstfruits. This is the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, when the first of the wheat was offered before any new grain was eaten. The meaning of firstfruits is one of the loveliest in the Old Testament. A farmer brings the first sheaf, not the last, before the harvest is safely in: a pledge that the rest is coming. The first barley sheaf had already been waved during Unleavened Bread, on “the day after the Sabbath” (Leviticus 23:10–11), and many have noticed that in the year Jesus died this was the very day he rose. Paul uses the picture for the empty tomb: “Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). The resurrection of Jesus is the first sheaf of a harvest, carried into the presence of God as the guarantee that every believer’s body will rise after him.

Pentecost. Fifty days after the Passover at which Jesus died, at the feast where Israel had brought her first grain for centuries, the Spirit fell and three thousand were gathered in (Acts 2:41; see Pentecost). Israel kept harvesting a field. God was keeping an appointment.

Without blemish. The chapter ends where it began, with the regular offering and animals “without blemish”. For a thousand years Israel searched her flocks for something perfect enough to offer, and never once found anything better than a lamb. Then John the Baptist stood by a river, looked at Jesus walking toward him, and said the sentence the whole calendar had been waiting for: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29).

keyVerse.quote: This is the food offering that you shall offer to the LORD: two male lambs a year old without blemish, day by day, as a regular offering.
keyVerse.note: The whole calendar rests on this daily lamb, offered morning and evening without a break. Its endless repetition showed that no lamb could finish the work, and pointed to the Lamb of God, whose single sacrifice is complete and who always lives to intercede for us.

28.reflection:
God calls the offerings “my food” and “my pleasing aroma” (v. 2). How does it change worship to see it first as giving God what is his rather than expressing what we feel?

A lamb was offered every morning and evening for centuries, yet none of them could take away sin (Hebrews 10:11–12). How does Christ’s finished sacrifice give assurance on the days you feel far from God?

Israel’s calendar claimed every day, week, month and season for God. What habits of prayer, Scripture and worship help you live all your time before him, and how do you keep them from becoming a way of earning his favour?

Passover, firstfruits and the Feast of Weeks are all fulfilled in Christ’s death, resurrection and gift of the Spirit. Which of these fulfilments most encourages you, and why?

29.title: The Feasts of the Seventh Month: The Climax of the Worship Year
29.text: <sup>1</sup>"On the first day of the seventh month you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work. It is a day for you to blow the trumpets,<sup>2</sup>and you shall offer a burnt offering, for a pleasing aroma to the LORD: one bull from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish;<sup>3</sup>also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for the bull, two tenths for the ram,<sup>4</sup>and one tenth for each of the seven lambs;<sup>5</sup>with one male goat for a sin offering, to make atonement for you;<sup>6</sup>besides the burnt offering of the new moon, and its grain offering, and the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offering, according to the rule for them, for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>"On the tenth day of this seventh month you shall have a holy convocation and afflict yourselves. You shall do no work,<sup>8</sup>but you shall offer a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma: one bull from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old: see that they are without blemish.<sup>9</sup>And their grain offering shall be of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for the bull, two tenths for the one ram,<sup>10</sup>a tenth for each of the seven lambs:<sup>11</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the sin offering of atonement, and the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offerings.<sup>12</sup>"On the fifteenth day of the seventh month you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work, and you shall keep a feast to the LORD seven days.<sup>13</sup>And you shall offer a burnt offering, a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD, thirteen bulls from the herd, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old; they shall be without blemish;<sup>14</sup>and their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for each of the thirteen bulls, two tenths for each of the two rams,<sup>15</sup>and a tenth for each of the fourteen lambs;<sup>16</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>17</sup>"On the second day twelve bulls from the herd, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>18</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>19</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offerings.<sup>20</sup>"On the third day eleven bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>21</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>22</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>23</sup>"On the fourth day ten bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>24</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>25</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>26</sup>"On the fifth day nine bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>27</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>28</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>29</sup>"On the sixth day eight bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>30</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>31</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offerings.<sup>32</sup>"On the seventh day seven bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>33</sup>with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>34</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offering.<sup>35</sup>"On the eighth day you shall have a solemn assembly. You shall not do any ordinary work,<sup>36</sup>but you shall offer a burnt offering, a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD: one bull, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish,<sup>37</sup>and the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bull, for the ram, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities;<sup>38</sup>also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering.<sup>39</sup>"These you shall offer to the LORD at your appointed feasts, in addition to your vow offerings and your freewill offerings, for your burnt offerings, and for your grain offerings, and for your drink offerings, and for your peace offerings."<sup>40</sup>So Moses told the people of Israel everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
29.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 28 set out the daily, weekly and monthly offerings and the spring feasts. Chapter 29 completes Israel’s worship calendar with the seventh month, the holiest and fullest of the year, given to the new generation on the plains of Moab before they enter the land.

The message. God’s year for his people climbs to a peak of joy, and the road to that joy runs through atonement. The trumpet calls the nation to attention, the Day of Atonement cleanses it, and then comes the most lavish week of the year, when a forgiven people rejoices in all that God has given. Worship that begins with God’s call and rests on his cleansing ends in overflowing gladness.

Why it was said. The generation about to settle in Canaan would soon have houses, vineyards and harvests, and with them the temptation to forget the God who had carried them through the wilderness and to copy the harvest festivals of Baal (see the introduction). The seventh month fixed in their year a reminder that they were sinners who needed atonement and pilgrims who had once lived in tents.

How the chapter makes its case. The month opens with a day of trumpets and its own offerings (vv. 1–6). Ten days later comes the Day of Atonement, a day of fasting and rest (vv. 7–11). Then the Feast of Booths: seven days of burnt offerings, beginning with thirteen bulls and counting down to seven, seventy in all, more than any other feast (vv. 12–34), and an eighth day of solemn assembly (vv. 35–38). The calendar closes by leaving room for vow and freewill offerings, and Moses tells the people everything the LORD commanded (vv. 39–40).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern, as Hebrews and John read it. The Day of Atonement, when one high priest entered once a year with blood, gives way to Christ, who “entered once for all into the holy places … by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12). On the last great day of Booths, Jesus stood up and offered himself as the living water the feast had prayed for (John 7:37–38). And the trumpet that opened the month still sounds ahead of us: “the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable” (1 Corinthians 15:52).

For us. Our joy before God rests not on our offerings but on the one sacrifice that has opened the way in. Because the atonement is finished, Christian worship can be both costly and glad, and we live as pilgrims, forgiven, giving freely, and waiting for the last trumpet and the feast that will never end.
29.theology:
The lavishness of worship. The abundance of offerings in the seventh month proclaims that God’s redemption deserves extravagant, joyful worship.

Atonement at the centre. The Day of Atonement points to Christ, who secured with his own blood the eternal redemption the annual day could only foreshadow (Heb 9:12).

A rehearsal for eternity. The month’s pattern of call, cleansing and harvest is the pattern of the last day: the last trumpet, the finished work of Christ, and the nations gathered home.
29.examples:
Then: Israel’s holiest month overflowed with worship, as trumpets sounded, atonement was made for the nation, and the Feast of Booths recalled the wilderness years and gave thanks for the harvest.

Now: every feast of that month was a rehearsal for a joy that is already yours in Christ and still to be completed when he comes. Worship him with the gladness the seventh month was meant to teach.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Trumpets and the Day of Atonement
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The seventh month begins with a summons and reaches its depth in cleansing. On the first day trumpets sound over the camp, a holy day with no ordinary work, and a burnt offering of a bull, a ram and seven lambs, with a goat for a sin offering, is added to the new moon and daily offerings (vv. 1–6). On the tenth day comes the Day of Atonement, the only fast the law commands: the people humble themselves and rest while the same offerings are brought, besides the sin offering of atonement itself (vv. 7–11). God first calls his people to attention, then deals with their sin, and only then leads them into the feast.
verseByVerse.theology: The trumpet blast (v. 1) summons God’s people to holy attention, a call that sounds again at the last day (1 Cor 15:52; 1 Thess 4:16). The Day of Atonement (vv. 7–11), with its fasting and its sin offering, is the yearly cleansing of the nation (Lev 16), fulfilled once for all when Christ entered… by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption (Heb 9:12). The extra offerings here surround with worship what the blood accomplishes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the trumpet woke the nation to worship, and the Day of Atonement humbled and cleansed them before God.

Now: the cleansing is finished, and the trumpet is still to come. We live between the two, forgiven and waiting.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the first day of the seventh month you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work. It is a day for you to blow the trumpets, and you shall offer a burnt offering, for a pleasing aroma to the LORD: one bull from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish; also their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for the bull, two tenths for the ram, and one tenth for each of the seven lambs; with one male goat for a sin offering, to make atonement for you; besides the burnt offering of the new moon, and its grain offering, and the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offering, according to the rule for them, for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The holiest month opens with a trumpet blast that calls the whole nation to stop and attend to God.

It is a day for you to blow the trumpets. The seventh month is to Israel’s year what the seventh day is to her week, and it opens with noise. Trumpets summon the congregation, sound the alarm in war, and are blown over the sacrifices as “a reminder of you before your God” (10:9–10). A trumpet is not music but an interruption: something has begun, and you must come (see Feast of Trumpets). Even this day of celebration has its sin offering “to make atonement for you” (v. 5): Israel never came before God, even to rejoice, except through a sacrifice.

The last trumpet. The trumpet keeps that meaning to the end of the Bible: “at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable” (1 Corinthians 15:52; compare 1 Thessalonians 4:16). Every autumn Israel heard a blast over the camp and stopped. One day a blast will go out over the whole earth, and everyone who ever lived will stop; for those who trust the one who comes, it will be the sound of homecoming.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the tenth day of this seventh month you shall have a holy convocation and afflict yourselves. You shall do no work, but you shall offer a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma: one bull from the herd, one ram, seven male lambs a year old: see that they are without blemish. And their grain offering shall be of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for the bull, two tenths for the one ram, a tenth for each of the seven lambs: also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the sin offering of atonement, and the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once a year the whole nation stopped eating and working and humbled itself while atonement was made for its sins.

Afflict yourselves. The usual phrase for fasting and self-humbling (Psalm 35:13), and the only fast the law of Moses commanded. While the people fasted, the high priest went behind the curtain with blood. Leviticus 16 describes the Day of Atonement itself (“the sin offering of atonement”, v. 11); Numbers adds only the offerings that surround it.

Once a year. Hebrews builds its central argument on this day: into the Most Holy Place “only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood” (Hebrews 9:7). One man, one day, one room, and a curtain still in the way. Then the contrast: “we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:19–20).

Both commands changed in Christ. The day had two commands, to afflict yourselves and to do no work, and Christ has changed both. The mourning is answered, for the sin mourned every autumn has been dealt with once for all. The rest is deepened, for the Christian rests for good from working to earn God’s favour (Hebrews 4:10). Believers still fast and grieve over sin (Matthew 6:16–18), but as people already forgiven, never to win forgiveness.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Five days after the fast comes the greatest celebration of the year. The Feast of Booths opens with thirteen bulls, two rams and fourteen lambs (vv. 12–16), and on each following day one bull fewer, until seventy bulls have been offered in the week (vv. 17–34). An eighth day of solemn assembly closes it more quietly, with a single bull (vv. 35–38). These offerings are the floor, not the ceiling: vow and freewill offerings may be brought besides, and Moses passes on every word (vv. 39–40). The costliest week of the year was also the most joyful, for a people forgiven and provided for had every reason to give lavishly.
verseByVerse.theology: Booths (Tabernacles) celebrated both the gathering in of the harvest and God’s faithful care in the wilderness (Lev 23:42–43). Its lavish offerings express overflowing gratitude. It looked forward to the final gathering in of God’s people; Jesus chose its last great day to offer himself as the true water (see vv. 35–38); and it anticipates the day when God will live among his people for ever, when the harvest is home and the journey is over.
verseByVerse.examples: For seven days Israel lived in booths. We are still pilgrims in temporary tents (2 Cor 5:1), giving thanks for what God has given and longing for the day when he will wipe away every tear (Rev 21:4). The great feast is still ahead.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work, and you shall keep a feast to the LORD seven days.
