And you shall offer a burnt offering, a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD, thirteen bulls from the herd, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old; they shall be without blemish; and their grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths of an ephah for each of the thirteen bulls, two tenths for each of the two rams, and a tenth for each of the fourteen lambs; also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five days after the fast, a forgiven people kept the greatest feast of the year, living in shelters to remember how God had carried them through the wilderness.

Keep a feast to the LORD seven days. The Feast of Booths, the harvest-home of the year (Deuteronomy 16:13), opens with the largest single day of sacrifice in the calendar. Leviticus gives the command that names it: “You shall dwell in booths for seven days … that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 23:42–43).

Why they camped out. A generation on the edge of a land full of houses they did not build (Deuteronomy 6:10–11) is told to camp out once a year, for ever. God knew what prosperity does to memory. One week a year a wealthy farmer slept under leaves and remembered that his family once had nothing and was carried by God. The Lord’s Supper works the same way: a small, physical, repeated act that keeps a people from forgetting what saved them.

Pilgrims still. Abraham lived that way all his life, “living in tents with Isaac and Jacob … For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:9–10). That is what Israel still was, and what the church has never stopped being. And when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), John’s verb means to pitch a tent: in Jesus, God came to camp among his people.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the second day twelve bulls from the herd, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering, and their drink offerings. "On the third day eleven bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering. "On the fourth day ten bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering, besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering and its drink offering. "On the fifth day nine bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering. "On the sixth day eight bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offerings. "On the seventh day seven bulls, two rams, fourteen male lambs a year old without blemish, with the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Day by day the bulls count down from thirteen to seven, seventy in all, in the costliest and happiest week of Israel’s year.

Seventy bulls. Eighteen verses in which almost nothing changes except one thing, deliberately: the bulls count down, and the week’s total is exactly seventy. Jewish interpreters connected this with the seventy nations of Genesis 10, reading the week as Israel offering on behalf of the world. Numbers does not say so, and no honest reader should claim more than the text gives. But the thought fits Scripture, for this is the feast the prophet Zechariah says the nations will one day keep: “Then everyone who survives of all the nations that have come against Jerusalem shall go up year after year to worship the King, the LORD of hosts, and to keep the Feast of Booths” (Zechariah 14:16).

Costly and glad. This was the most expensive week of the year, a herd of cattle burned in seven days at the busiest point of harvest, and the week of greatest joy (Deuteronomy 16:14–15). Costly worship and glad worship are not opposites here; they are the same week.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the eighth day you shall have a solemn assembly. You shall not do any ordinary work, but you shall offer a burnt offering, a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the LORD: one bull, one ram, seven male lambs a year old without blemish, and the grain offering and the drink offerings for the bull, for the ram, and for the lambs, in the prescribed quantities; also one male goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering and its grain offering and its drink offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A quieter eighth day closes the feast, and on the last day of this feast Jesus stood up and offered himself as living water.

On the eighth day. One bull instead of thirteen: a final gathering before everyone goes home.

The water ceremony. By Jesus’ time the feast had gained a ceremony not in the law, described in the Mishnah (the early Jewish law code). Each morning of the feast a priest filled a golden pitcher at the pool of Siloam and poured it out at the altar, a rite long linked with “With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation” (Isaiah 12:3). It was a prayer for rain, and many think it also recalled the water from the rock (20:11).

On the last day of the feast. John records what happened one year at that moment: “On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink’” (John 7:37). Interpreters differ on whether this “last day” is the seventh day or the eighth; either way it was the feast’s climax. Soon afterwards, with the great lamps of the feast still in memory, he said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12).

He answered it out loud. Generations of pouring out water at the foot of an altar, and then a carpenter from Nazareth stood up in the middle of it and offered himself to anyone in the crowd who was thirsty. Every autumn the feast had been a prayer for water. He answered it out loud.

Uncertain wording. “Solemn assembly” (ʿatsereth) comes from a root meaning to hold back. It may mean a closing assembly, or a day when the people were held back from work and kept together before the LORD; it is also used of the last day of Unleavened Bread (Deuteronomy 16:8). Either way it is a final, sacred gathering.

verseByVerse.quote: "These you shall offer to the LORD at your appointed feasts, in addition to your vow offerings and your freewill offerings, for your burnt offerings, and for your grain offerings, and for your drink offerings, and for your peace offerings." So Moses told the people of Israel everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fixed offerings are the least God asks, and he leaves room for all that a grateful heart wants to bring besides.

Your vow offerings and your freewill offerings. This clause keeps the calendar from becoming a cage. Chapters 28 and 29 are the floor, not the ceiling: God specifies what is due, then makes room for whatever a grateful Israelite might bring beyond it. A freewill offering is what its name says: nobody commanded it and nobody counted it.

Keeping the balance. That balance is easy to lose either way. A believer can reduce his life with God to the appointed times and never come to him uninvited, or despise the appointed times as routine and worship only when he feels like it. Israel was given both in the same sentence. The freewill offering grew from a redeemed people’s gratitude, and the Spirit now stirs that gladness beyond duty in believers (2 Corinthians 9:7).

Everything just as the LORD had commanded. An old man near the end of his life read out every bull, every ram, every tenth of an ephah, exactly as given. Israel’s whole calendar reached the people because Moses refused to shorten what God had said.

keyVerse.quote: On the tenth day of this seventh month you shall have a holy convocation and afflict yourselves.
keyVerse.note: The Day of Atonement stands at the heart of the holiest month, between the trumpet that calls the people and the feast that celebrates God’s goodness. Israel could rejoice at Booths only because its sins had first been dealt with, and the yearly fast pointed to the one sacrifice by which Christ secured an eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12).

29.reflection:
The seventh month moves from a trumpet call (v. 1), to a day of fasting and atonement (v. 7), to a week of feasting (v. 12). Why do you think God put atonement before celebration? What happens to our joy when we try to skip the middle step?

Only the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, once a year, with blood (Hebrews 9:7). How does Hebrews 10:19–22 change the way you come to God in prayer and worship?

Israel, about to live in houses, was told to live in booths for a week each year to remember the wilderness. What habits help you remember that you are a pilgrim whom God has carried, especially when life is comfortable?

The Feast of Booths was both the costliest and the most joyful week of the year, and it left room for freewill offerings beyond what was required (v. 39). Where might God be inviting you to give gladly beyond the minimum?

30.title: Vows: The Integrity of the Word
30.text: <sup>1</sup>Moses spoke to the heads of the tribes of the people of Israel, saying, "This is what the LORD has commanded.<sup>2</sup>If a man vows a vow to the LORD, or swears an oath to bind himself by a pledge, he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.<sup>3</sup>"If a woman vows a vow to the LORD and binds herself by a pledge, while within her father's house in her youth,<sup>4</sup>and her father hears of her vow and of her pledge by which she has bound herself and says nothing to her, then all her vows shall stand, and every pledge by which she has bound herself shall stand.<sup>5</sup>But if her father opposes her on the day that he hears of it, no vow of hers, no pledge by which she has bound herself shall stand. And the LORD will forgive her, because her father opposed her.<sup>6</sup>"If she marries a husband, while under her vows or any thoughtless utterance of her lips by which she has bound herself,<sup>7</sup>and her husband hears of it and says nothing to her on the day that he hears, then her vows shall stand, and her pledges by which she has bound herself shall stand.<sup>8</sup>But if, on the day that her husband comes to hear of it, he opposes her, then he makes void her vow that was on her, and the thoughtless utterance of her lips by which she bound herself. And the LORD will forgive her.<sup>9</sup>(But any vow of a widow or of a divorced woman, anything by which she has bound herself, shall stand against her.)<sup>10</sup>And if she vowed in her husband's house or bound herself by a pledge with an oath,<sup>11</sup>and her husband heard of it and said nothing to her and did not oppose her, then all her vows shall stand, and every pledge by which she bound herself shall stand.<sup>12</sup>But if her husband makes them null and void on the day that he hears them, then whatever proceeds out of her lips concerning her vows or concerning her pledge of herself shall not stand. Her husband has made them void, and the LORD will forgive her.<sup>13</sup>Any vow and any binding oath to afflict herself, her husband may establish, or her husband may make void.<sup>14</sup>But if her husband says nothing to her from day to day, then he establishes all her vows or all her pledges that are upon her. He has established them, because he said nothing to her on the day that he heard of them.<sup>15</sup>But if he makes them null and void after he has heard of them, then he shall bear her iniquity."<sup>16</sup>These are the statutes that the LORD commanded Moses about a man and his wife and about a father and his daughter while she is in her youth within her father's house.
30.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 29 closed Israel’s calendar with “your vow offerings and your freewill offerings” (29:39). Chapter 30 turns to vows themselves, the promises Israelites made to God, often in trouble, and paid at the sanctuary afterwards. Moses gives these rules to the heads of the tribes, the men answerable for their households.

The message. God keeps his word, so his people must keep theirs: a promise made to him binds. Yet the God who holds his people to their word is not trying to trap them in their worst moments. He provides a merciful release for rash vows made by those who depend on others, limits that power to a single day, and holds the man who misuses it answerable to him.

Why it was said. In Israel a household lived from one shared store of land, flocks and labour. A daughter or wife who vowed goods, or a long fast, could bind the whole family to what was not hers alone to give. On the edge of settled life in the land, Israel needed to know which promises stood.

How the chapter makes its case. First the principle: a man who vows must do all that he said (vv. 1–2). Then three cases in which a woman’s vow may be cancelled on the day it is heard: a young woman in her father’s house (vv. 3–5), a woman who marries with a vow already on her (vv. 6–8), and a wife in her husband’s house (vv. 10–13). A widow or divorced woman, like a man, is bound by her own word (v. 9). Silence confirms a vow, and a husband who cancels one too late carries the guilt himself (vv. 14–16).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God and by the need the chapter exposes. God is the God whose word never fails, and “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). And the chapter ends with a husband who “shall bear her iniquity” (v. 15). That is not a prophecy, but it points beyond itself to a greater Husband who freely took on himself the guilt of a bride who could not pay what she owed (Isaiah 53:6; Ephesians 5:25).

For us. Be slow to promise and faithful to keep what you have promised, for God hears. Do not try to buy his favour with vows of self-punishment; he never asked for them. And where you have broken your word, confess it and put it right where you can, resting not on your own faithfulness but on Christ’s.
30.theology:
The sanctity of speech. A vow to God binds. Because God is a God of his word, his people are to be people of their word; to break a vow to him is to lie before the One who is Truth itself. And he has kept his own word in the fullest way: all the promises of God find their Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Plain truthfulness. Jesus calls his people to such transparent integrity that their plain word is as trustworthy as any oath (see vv. 1–2), for they serve the God who cannot lie.
30.examples:
Then: Israel was bound to keep every vow made to the LORD, with the household head able to confirm or annul vows made by dependents, guarding against rash pledges.

Now: Your word is sacred because you serve the God whose word never fails, and his Spirit in you is the Spirit of truth, who makes a truthful tongue possible. Let your yes be yes. And when you find you have broken your word, confess it and make it right where you can: Christ kept every word he spoke in your place, and his faithfulness, not yours, is your standing with God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Words spoken to God bind, and God himself guards how they bind. A man’s vow must be kept to the letter (vv. 1–2). A young woman in her father’s house, a bride who brings a vow into marriage and a wife in her husband’s house may each have a rash vow cancelled by father or husband, but only on the day he hears of it, and then the LORD forgives her (vv. 3–8, 10–13). A widow or divorced woman answers to God for her own word, as a man does (v. 9). Silence confirms a vow, and a husband who cancels one later carries the guilt himself (vv. 14–16). The power is narrow, protective and answerable to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
He shall not break his word (v. 2): a vow to God is a serious, binding thing (cf. Deut 23:21–23; Eccl 5:4–5). A promise made in God’s hearing is not to be treated lightly. The provisions for cancelling a woman’s vow within the household reflect the ordered authority of that society, yet the governing principle, keep your word to God, is timeless, and Jesus deepens it until among truthful people vows become almost unnecessary.

Does a Christian husband hold this power today? No. The annulment procedure belonged to Israel’s household law, and the New Testament does not carry it into the church. A believing wife answers to the Lord for her own promises. Headship, where Scripture speaks of it, is Christ’s kind of self-giving love, never control; a man who uses religion to dominate or harm his wife has abandoned it, and abuse is never to be tolerated.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a vow to God was no light matter; the one who made it was bound to keep it.

Now: God still weighs our words. Be slow to promise and faithful to perform, for “it is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay” (Ecclesiastes 5:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke to the heads of the tribes of the people of Israel, saying, "This is what the LORD has commanded. If a man vows a vow to the LORD, or swears an oath to bind himself by a pledge, he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A promise made to God must be kept, every word of it. For a man there is no release clause.

He shall not break his word. Everything else in the chapter is measured against this. No father can annul a man’s vow, no elder review it, no circumstance end it: he said it, so he does it. The chapter so often read as a restriction on women opens by binding men absolutely. The subject follows from 29:39: an Israelite in trouble would often promise God a sacrifice or gift if he delivered him, and pay it at the sanctuary afterwards, as Hannah did (1 Samuel 1:11, 24; Psalm 66:13–14).

Why vows bind. Because God keeps his word. A vow was made “to the LORD”, and breaking it implied that the God who hears lets things slide: a lie about his character told with your life.

Rash vows. Scripture shows what the absence of a release clause could mean. Jephthah made a rash vow and destroyed his own daughter with it (Judges 11:30–39). Herod made a rash promise at a birthday party and beheaded John the Baptist rather than look weak before his guests (Mark 6:23–26). Both should have broken their word: a promise to do evil binds nobody, and the sin lay in making it. There is a pride that dresses up as integrity, and it is most dangerous when it will not admit it should never have spoken.

Where Christians differ: may Christians make vows and take oaths? Quakers and many Anabaptists refuse all oaths, reading “Do not take an oath at all” (Matthew 5:34) as absolute. Most churches, with the Westminster Confession (chapter 22), hold that Jesus forbids casual and evasive swearing, not solemn promises before God. This commentary’s view: lawful oaths and vows are permitted: marriage vows, oaths in court, ordination vows. God himself swore an oath (Hebrews 6:17), and Paul called God to witness (2 Corinthians 1:23). Jesus’ point is that a Christian’s plain word should be as good as any oath: “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). What a Christian promises, he must keep.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a woman vows a vow to the LORD and binds herself by a pledge, while within her father's house in her youth, and her father hears of her vow and of her pledge by which she has bound herself and says nothing to her, then all her vows shall stand, and every pledge by which she has bound herself shall stand. But if her father opposes her on the day that he hears of it, no vow of hers, no pledge by which she has bound herself shall stand. And the LORD will forgive her, because her father opposed her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A father may cancel his young daughter’s vow, but only on the day he hears of it, and then God freely releases her.

If her father opposes her. These cases are often misread, and four things govern them, every one of which limits the father rather than the daughter. First, the window is a single day; after that the vow is fixed and he has no power over it. Second, it applies only to an unmarried girl still in her father’s household (v. 16), who in that economy had no property of her own and might have pledged goods or labour that were not hers to pledge. Third, he can only annul; he can never impose a vow. Fourth, the release is not grudging: “the LORD will forgive her.” God will not hold a woman liable for a promise she has been prevented from keeping.

A protection. Read plainly, this is household law for a society in which the family was one economic unit, not a verdict on the worth of women. It comes three chapters after five women with no legal standing walked to the front of the assembly and God said, “The daughters of Zelophehad are right” (27:7), and changed Israel’s inheritance law because of them. Same book, same Lawgiver, same season on the plains of Moab. Whatever chapter 30 is doing, it cannot be read as contempt for women.

verseByVerse.quote: "If she marries a husband, while under her vows or any thoughtless utterance of her lips by which she has bound herself, and her husband hears of it and says nothing to her on the day that he hears, then her vows shall stand, and her pledges by which she has bound herself shall stand. But if, on the day that her husband comes to hear of it, he opposes her, then he makes void her vow that was on her, and the thoughtless utterance of her lips by which she bound herself. And the LORD will forgive her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A rash vow that a woman brings into her marriage can be lifted by her husband on the day he hears of it, and God stands behind the release.

Any thoughtless utterance of her lips. The second case has the same single day, the same limited power and the same gracious clause, and names the kind of vow in view: a word blurted out before the cost was counted. Things get promised at gravesides and in hospital corridors on the worst night of a person’s life: “If you will only do this, I will never again…” Such a vow can be sincere, godly in motive and completely unpayable.

Mercy in the statute book. The law neither mocks such promises nor treats them as unbreakable chains. Someone who loves her and stands outside the emotion of the moment may say within a day: this must not bind you for forty years. And God himself stands behind the release. That is not a loophole but mercy written into the law, and it shows us the God who wrote it. He is not looking for ways to hold his people to their worst moments.

Uncertain wording. “Thoughtless utterance” translates a rare Hebrew noun found only here (vv. 6, 8). Its verb means to speak rashly or blurt out (Leviticus 5:4; Psalm 106:33), so the sense is clear enough: a vow spoken hastily, without weighing what it would cost.

verseByVerse.quote: (But any vow of a widow or of a divorced woman, anything by which she has bound herself, shall stand against her.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A widow or a divorced woman answers to God for her own word, just as a man does.

A widow or a divorced woman. This bracketed verse carries more than it looks. She has no father over her and no husband beside her; nobody can annul what she says. Her word goes straight to God and binds her exactly as a man’s does.

Full standing, and exposed. Both sides of that are true. It is a statement of full standing: whatever the surrounding cultures thought of a woman alone, Israel’s law treats her promises as those of an adult who answers to God directly. It also leaves her exposed, with nobody to catch a rash word before it hardens.

God’s particular concern. Which is why Scripture insists that God watches over such people himself: “Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation” (Psalm 68:5). The woman with no one standing over her in this chapter is the woman God repeatedly names as his own particular concern. She is not less protected. Her protection has been taken up by someone higher than a household.

verseByVerse.quote: And if she vowed in her husband's house or bound herself by a pledge with an oath, and her husband heard of it and said nothing to her and did not oppose her, then all her vows shall stand, and every pledge by which she bound herself shall stand. But if her husband makes them null and void on the day that he hears them, then whatever proceeds out of her lips concerning her vows or concerning her pledge of herself shall not stand. Her husband has made them void, and the LORD will forgive her. Any vow and any binding oath to afflict herself, her husband may establish, or her husband may make void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A husband may confirm or cancel his wife’s vow, above all a vow to afflict herself, so the power chiefly protects her from punishing herself.

In her husband’s house. The third case is a wife who vows while married. The pattern holds, and verse 13 names the kind of vow chiefly in view: vows “to afflict herself”.

Any binding oath to afflict herself. That changes the picture. The vows the law is most concerned about are vows of self-denial: fasting, abstaining, going without. So the authority here is mainly a power to stop someone hurting herself, not to stop her serving God. A wife who in grief or guilt pledges to fast for a year, or to give away what the household needs to live on, can be relieved of it. It is a brake on self-punishment.

Still needed. That guard is still needed. Religious people try to settle their account with God by taking something from themselves, and the more ashamed they are, the heavier the pledge. The gospel has no place for it: such rules have “an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh” (Colossians 2:23). God never made self-punishment the price of forgiveness; Christ paid it.

verseByVerse.quote: But if her husband says nothing to her from day to day, then he establishes all her vows or all her pledges that are upon her. He has established them, because he said nothing to her on the day that he heard of them. But if he makes them null and void after he has heard of them, then he shall bear her iniquity." These are the statutes that the LORD commanded Moses about a man and his wife and about a father and his daughter while she is in her youth within her father's house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A husband who stays silent confirms his wife’s vows, and one who cancels them too late carries her guilt himself.

If her husband says nothing. Silence is not neutrality. A husband who says nothing “establishes all her vows”. A man who declines to engage with what is happening in his household has not avoided responsibility for it; he has taken it on by default.

He shall bear her iniquity. The chapter turns on this. If he lets the vow stand and later prevents her keeping it, the guilt passes to him. That rules out any idea of unchecked male authority. The power is bounded by a day, can only release and never impose, and its misuse is charged to the man’s account before God. That is the biblical shape of headship wherever it appears: never permission to do as he likes, always a responsibility he must answer for, measured by “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25).

Another Husband carried her guilt. Here a husband carries his wife’s guilt through his own failure. The verse is not a prophecy of Christ, but Christians can hardly miss the likeness. Another Husband carried his bride’s guilt by deliberate choice. He heard what she had bound herself to and could not pay, and he did not cancel it but took it on himself: “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). Israel could be released from a rash vow by a word from a man who loved her. The church was released from an unpayable debt by a Man who took it on himself and carried it away.

What it does not mean. Not that a Christian husband may overrule his wife’s promises to God (see the section introduction above), and never a licence for control: abuse is never to be tolerated.

keyVerse.quote: If a man vows a vow to the LORD, or swears an oath to bind himself by a pledge, he shall not break his word. He shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth.
keyVerse.note: This is the principle every case in the chapter is measured against: a word spoken to God binds, because God keeps his own. The rest of the chapter adds mercy for the rash and the dependent, but never weakens this. It is fulfilled in Christ, who kept every word, and it calls his people to be as good as their word.

30.reflection:
Verse 2 gives a man no way out of his vow. Why does God take our words so seriously? Where are you most tempted to promise lightly, to God or to other people?

Jephthah and Herod kept promises they should never have made. How can we tell the difference between faithfulness to our word and a pride that will not admit we promised wrongly?

Verse 13 lets a husband cancel a vow “to afflict herself”. Why are people drawn to punishing themselves to settle their account with God, and how does the gospel answer that?

The chapter ends with a husband bearing his wife’s iniquity (v. 15). How does this help you see what Christ has done with the promises you have broken?

31.title: War Against Midian: Holy War and the Seriousness of Sin
31.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Avenge the people of Israel on the Midianites. Afterward you shall be gathered to your people."<sup>3</sup>So Moses spoke to the people, saying, "Arm men from among you for the war, that they may go against Midian to execute the LORD's vengeance on Midian.<sup>4</sup>You shall send a thousand from each of the tribes of Israel to the war."<sup>5</sup>So there were provided, out of the thousands of Israel, a thousand from each tribe, twelve thousand armed for war.<sup>6</sup>And Moses sent them to the war, a thousand from each tribe, together with Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, with the vessels of the sanctuary and the trumpets for the alarm in his hand.<sup>7</sup>They warred against Midian, as the LORD commanded Moses, and killed every male.<sup>8</sup>They killed the kings of Midian with the rest of their slain, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, the five kings of Midian. And they also killed Balaam the son of Beor with the sword.<sup>9</sup>And the people of Israel took captive the women of Midian and their little ones, and they took as plunder all their cattle, their flocks, and all their goods.<sup>10</sup>All their cities in the places where they lived, and all their encampments, they burned with fire,<sup>11</sup>and took all the spoil and all the plunder, both of man and of beast.<sup>12</sup>Then they brought the captives and the plunder and the spoil to Moses, and to Eleazar the priest, and to the congregation of the people of Israel, at the camp on the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.<sup>13</sup>Moses and Eleazar the priest and all the chiefs of the congregation went to meet them outside the camp.<sup>14</sup>And Moses was angry with the officers of the army, the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, who had come from service in the war.<sup>15</sup>Moses said to them, "Have you let all the women live?<sup>16</sup>Behold, these, on Balaam's advice, caused the people of Israel to act treacherously against the LORD in the incident of Peor, and so the plague came among the congregation of the LORD.<sup>17</sup>Now therefore, kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman who has known man by lying with him.<sup>18</sup>But all the young girls who have not known man by lying with him keep alive for yourselves.<sup>19</sup>Encamp outside the camp seven days. Whoever of you has killed any person and whoever has touched any slain, purify yourselves and your captives on the third day and on the seventh day.<sup>20</sup>You shall purify every garment, every article of skin, all work of goats' hair, and every article of wood."<sup>21</sup>Then Eleazar the priest said to the men in the army who had gone to battle: "This is the statute of the law that the LORD has commanded Moses:<sup>22</sup>only the gold, the silver, the bronze, the iron, the tin, and the lead,<sup>23</sup>everything that can stand the fire, you shall pass through the fire, and it shall be clean. Nevertheless, it shall also be purified with the water for impurity. And whatever cannot stand the fire, you shall pass through the water.<sup>24</sup>You must wash your clothes on the seventh day, and you shall be clean. And afterward you may come into the camp."<sup>25</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>26</sup>"Take the count of the plunder that was taken, both of man and of beast, you and Eleazar the priest and the heads of the fathers' houses of the congregation,<sup>27</sup>and divide the plunder into two parts between the warriors who went out to battle and all the congregation.<sup>28</sup>And levy for the LORD a tribute from the men of war who went out to battle, one out of five hundred, of the people and of the oxen and of the donkeys and of the flocks.<sup>29</sup>Take it from their half and give it to Eleazar the priest as a contribution to the LORD.<sup>30</sup>And from the people of Israel's half you shall take one drawn out of every fifty, of the people, of the oxen, of the donkeys, and of the flocks, of all the cattle, and give them to the Levites who keep guard over the tabernacle of the LORD."<sup>31</sup>And Moses and Eleazar the priest did as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>32</sup>Now the plunder remaining of the spoil that the army took was 675,000 sheep,<sup>33</sup>72,000 cattle,<sup>34</sup>61,000 donkeys,<sup>35</sup>and 32,000 persons in all, women who had not known man by lying with him.<sup>36</sup>And the half, the portion of those who had gone out in the army, numbered 337,500 sheep,<sup>37</sup>and the LORD's tribute of sheep was 675.<sup>38</sup>The cattle were 36,000, of which the LORD's tribute was 72.<sup>39</sup>The donkeys were 30,500, of which the LORD's tribute was 61.<sup>40</sup>The persons were 16,000, of which the LORD's tribute was 32 persons.<sup>41</sup>And Moses gave the tribute, which was the contribution for the LORD, to Eleazar the priest, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>42</sup>From the people of Israel's half, which Moses separated from that of the men who had served in the army—<sup>43</sup>now the congregation's half was 337,500 sheep,<sup>44</sup>36,000 cattle,<sup>45</sup>and 30,500 donkeys,<sup>46</sup>and 16,000 persons—<sup>47</sup>from the people of Israel's half Moses took one of every 50, both of persons and of beasts, and gave them to the Levites who kept guard over the tabernacle of the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>48</sup>Then the officers who were over the thousands of the army, the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, came near to Moses<sup>49</sup>and said to Moses, "Your servants have counted the men of war who are under our command, and there is not a man missing from us.<sup>50</sup>And we have brought the LORD's offering, what each man found, articles of gold, armlets and bracelets, signet rings, earrings, and beads, to make atonement for ourselves before the LORD."<sup>51</sup>And Moses and Eleazar the priest received from them the gold, all crafted articles.<sup>52</sup>And all the gold of the contribution that they presented to the LORD, from the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, was 16,750 shekels.<sup>53</sup>(The men in the army had each taken plunder for himself.)<sup>54</sup>And Moses and Eleazar the priest received the gold from the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and brought it into the tent of meeting, as a memorial for the people of Israel before the LORD.
31.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 25 told how Israel, drawn in by Moabite and Midianite women at Peor, fell into idolatry and immorality, and God commanded, “Harass the Midianites and strike them down” (25:17). Now, with the new generation counted and Moses about to die, that sentence is carried out. It is his last task before he is “gathered to your people” (v. 2).

The message. God judges those who deliberately set out to destroy his people by leading them into sin, and he does it precisely, through the instrument he chooses, at the time he sets. Yet the chapter cares as much about what follows the battle: soldiers who obeyed God come home unclean, and officers who lost not one man bring their gold as an offering. Judgment is real, death defiles, and survival is mercy.

Why it was said. The new generation was about to enter a land whose religion offered the same mixture of sex and idolatry that had nearly destroyed them at Peor (see the introduction). They had to learn that God takes such corruption with deadly seriousness, and that even a war he commands is no occasion for pride.

How the chapter makes its case. God commands vengeance on Midian, and a force of twelve thousand goes out with Phinehas the priest (vv. 1–6). They kill the five kings and Balaam, and bring back captives and plunder (vv. 7–12). Moses, angry that the women who carried out Balaam’s plan have been spared, gives the hardest command in the book (vv. 13–18). The army stays outside the camp seven days to be purified, with all it brought back (vv. 19–24). The spoil is divided between fighters and congregation, with a share for the LORD and the Levites (vv. 25–47), and the officers, having lost no one, bring gold to the tent of meeting as a memorial (vv. 48–54).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by the character of God and the need the chapter exposes. It shows a God whose judgments are terrible, and leaves every reader asking how anyone can stand before him. The answer is the cross, where the Judge of all the earth bore his own judgment: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). And the water that cleansed the soldiers from death (chapter 19) points to “the blood of Christ” that will “purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Hebrews 9:14).

For us. This chapter is never a charter for violence, for Christ’s kingdom does not advance by the sword (John 18:36). It calls us to take sin seriously, above all sin that corrupts others, and to come home from every battle as those officers did, knowing we have been spared by mercy.
31.theology:
The seriousness of sin. The judgment on Midian answers a calculated seduction that nearly destroyed Israel. Sin is graver than we dare imagine; the wonder is God’s patience with it.

Death defiles. Even soldiers who had obeyed God had to be purified before they could worship, a picture of the deeper cleansing of Christ’s blood (vv. 19–24).

The corrupter judged. Balaam, who could not curse Israel but taught her enemies how to seduce her, dies in the judgment (v. 8).
31.examples: Read this trembling text in its setting, never as a charter for violence. Let it show you how seriously God takes the corruption of his people, and let it drive you to the cross, where the judgment your sin deserved fell on Christ so that you might be spared and cleansed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s sentence on Midian from chapter 25 is carried out as Moses’ last commission. The war is the LORD’s vengeance, not Israel’s: a fixed force of a thousand from each tribe goes out with Phinehas the priest, carrying the holy vessels and the trumpets (vv. 1–6). They kill every man of these Midianite clans, the five kings, and Balaam, who had counselled Midian’s plan, then burn their towns and bring the captives and plunder to Moses and Eleazar on the plains of Moab (vv. 7–12). The judgment falls where the guilt lay, and Balaam meets the end his love of gain prepared.
verseByVerse.theology: The Midian war is judgment on those who engineered Israel’s fall at Peor (25:16–18; 31:16), and Balaam’s death (v. 8) closes his story. These judgments belong to a unique, unrepeatable moment in Israel’s history and must not be made a pattern for the church, whose weapons… are not of the flesh (2 Cor 10:4); yet they reveal the real severity of God against those who deliberately lead his people into sin (Luke 17:1–2).
verseByVerse.examples: We fight not with swords but against sin and the schemes that corrupt, in the strength of the Spirit Christ has given, not our own. Yet the warning stands: God takes with deadly seriousness those who lead his people astray, and the love of money can ruin even a gifted soul.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Avenge the people of Israel on the Midianites. Afterward you shall be gathered to your people." So Moses spoke to the people, saying, "Arm men from among you for the war, that they may go against Midian to execute the LORD's vengeance on Midian. You shall send a thousand from each of the tribes of Israel to the war." So there were provided, out of the thousands of Israel, a thousand from each tribe, twelve thousand armed for war. And Moses sent them to the war, a thousand from each tribe, together with Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, with the vessels of the sanctuary and the trumpets for the alarm in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends a small force, led by a priest, to carry out his own sentence on Midian, as Moses’ last task.

Avenge the people of Israel on the Midianites. Moses passes the command on not as “avenge yourselves” but “to execute the LORD’s vengeance on Midian” (v. 3). It is not tribal payback but a judicial sentence, and the judge is God.

A thousand from each tribe. The size of the force says the same: twelve thousand out of a nation that had just counted 601,730 fighting men (26:51). Two per cent. Nobody conquers a country with two per cent of an army. This is a punitive expedition of fixed size against a fixed target, and a priest goes with it carrying holy things. Israel is not being turned loose. Phinehas goes rather than his father, probably because the high priest was not to defile himself by going near the dead (Leviticus 21:10–11), and fittingly, since Phinehas had stood against Midian’s scheme at Peor (25:7–8).

A precise target. Moab began the seduction at Shittim (25:1) and is not touched, because God had forbidden it: “Do not harass Moab or contend with them in battle” (Deuteronomy 2:9). Midian, which worked with Balaam to engineer the whole thing, is judged. God’s judgments land where the guilt is, and stop.

verseByVerse.quote: They warred against Midian, as the LORD commanded Moses, and killed every male. They killed the kings of Midian with the rest of their slain, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, the five kings of Midian. And they also killed Balaam the son of Beor with the sword. And the people of Israel took captive the women of Midian and their little ones, and they took as plunder all their cattle, their flocks, and all their goods. All their cities in the places where they lived, and all their encampments, they burned with fire, and took all the spoil and all the plunder, both of man and of beast. Then they brought the captives and the plunder and the spoil to Moses, and to Eleazar the priest, and to the congregation of the people of Israel, at the camp on the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgment falls on Midian’s kings and on Balaam, the prophet who sold his counsel to destroy the people he had blessed.

The five kings of Midian. The battle is told in a sentence, and the text pauses over the five kings. One is familiar: Zur, the father of Cozbi, the woman Phinehas killed in the tent (25:15). The men at the top of Midian had put their own daughters into the plan.

Balaam the son of Beor. Then, almost in passing, Balaam. This is the man who stood on a mountain with the Spirit of God upon him and said, “Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!” (23:10). He set off home (24:25), yet when the sword came he was among the enemies of the nation he had blessed four times. He could not sell Balak a curse, so he sold Midian a plan instead (v. 16), and the fee cost him his life.

The money. The New Testament never mentions him without the money: he “loved gain from wrongdoing” (2 Peter 2:15); men “abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error” (Jude 11); the risen Christ names “the teaching of Balaam” as a live danger in a congregation (Revelation 2:14). A man may hold flawless doctrine and receive real revelation and still be lost, because none of that is the same as loving God more than what God’s enemies offer to pay.

If every male was killed, how is Midian strong again in Judges 6? Because this war touched only part of Midian. These were the Midianite clans near Moab, under five kings; Midian was a widespread desert people, and “every male” is the language of decisive victory over this group, not of the whole nation. Judges 6 comes perhaps two centuries later.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The returning army meets anger and then cleansing. Moses rebukes the officers for sparing the women through whom Balaam’s plan at Peor had been carried out (vv. 13–16), and orders that the boys and the women who had lain with men be put to death, while the young girls are kept alive (vv. 17–18). Then every soldier who has killed or touched the dead, with the captives and everything brought back, must stay outside the camp seven days and be purified, metal by fire and water, everything else by water (vv. 19–24). Even a war God commanded left its fighters unclean: nothing touched by death comes casually into his presence.
verseByVerse.theology: Even a war God commanded left a defilement that had to be cleansed (vv. 19–24; cf. Num 19). Death is the enemy and the wage of sin (Romans 6:23), never something God’s people handle lightly.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians too sometimes have to confront sin and death at close quarters: in church discipline, in hard pastoral work, in the aftermath of evil done to others. We do not come away untouched, and we need not stay soiled. Whoever has touched what defiles may come back and be cleansed (1 John 1:7–9).

verseByVerse.quote: Moses and Eleazar the priest and all the chiefs of the congregation went to meet them outside the camp. And Moses was angry with the officers of the army, the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, who had come from service in the war. Moses said to them, "Have you let all the women live? Behold, these, on Balaam's advice, caused the people of Israel to act treacherously against the LORD in the incident of Peor, and so the plague came among the congregation of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is angry because the women who had been spared were the very ones through whom Balaam’s plan at Peor had been carried out. Verse 16 is the hinge of the chapter and must be read before the next two verses.

On Balaam’s advice. This finally tells us what happened at Shittim. It was no accident of two peoples camped close together; it was planned. Balaam had learned on three mountains that no fee could buy a curse on Israel, so he drew a conclusion: a people who cannot be cursed can be tempted into sin, and then God himself will judge them. Midian carried out the plan with its own women, a chief’s daughter among them, and twenty-four thousand Israelites died (25:9). The women before Moses are, in the text’s own account, the people through whom that plan was carried out. That does not make what follows easy. It does mean that a reader who treats this as an unprovoked massacre of bystanders has not read verse 16.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore, kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman who has known man by lying with him. But all the young girls who have not known man by lying with him keep alive for yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s judgment falls on the Midianite boys and on the women who had lain with men: a unique sentence on the clans that plotted Israel’s ruin, and never a pattern for anyone. These are the two hardest verses in Numbers.

No comfortable reading. There is no honest way to make them comfortable: if they appal you, you are reading them correctly. Scripture does not ask anyone to feel nothing here, and to hurry past them or pretend the words say something gentler would not be honest. So let us say what can be said, and then say plainly what cannot.

The devoted judgment of God. First, what the passage is: God’s judgment (akin to what the Old Testament elsewhere calls herem, handing something wholly over to God, here for destruction) on a particular people, at a particular moment, by a specific command, in the unrepeatable period when God ruled one nation directly as its king. It is dated, bounded and explicitly commanded, and Scripture never generalises it. Moses treats the married women as those through whom the plan of verse 16 was carried out; the text does not sort them one by one, and we should not pretend it does. The command is given to a force drafted for the task with a priest, not a mob, and it is over within days.

Not a model for anyone. Second, what the passage is not, and this cannot be said too strongly: a model for anyone, anywhere, ever again. No church, nation, movement or individual has the authority Israel had here, and the New Testament closes the door: “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting” (John 18:36); “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4). Every Christian who has reached for this chapter to justify violence has read it against the plain teaching of his own Lord.

Keep alive for yourselves. Third, the girls who were spared. The phrase reads horribly in English and needs its legal setting. The law for a woman taken captive in war is Deuteronomy 21:10–14, unlike anything else in the ancient world: she is given a full month to mourn her father and mother, may then be married, not used, and if the man no longer wants her she must go free; he may never sell her or treat her as a slave, “since you have humiliated her”. It is not our world and not painless, but it is far from what a modern reader assumes.

But why the boys? This is the part that stays with every honest reader, and Scripture does not give a full reason. The likeliest is that in the ancient world a clan’s sons carried on its name and its feuds, and God was ending the line of the Midianite houses that had set out to destroy Israel; the same reasoning lies behind the judgment on Amalek in 1 Samuel 15. This commentary will not invent more than that. What can be said is that no child who died that day passed out of the hands of the Judge of all the earth, and Christians have long confessed that little ones who die are not beyond his mercy in Christ (the Westminster Confession 10.3 speaks of elect infants dying in infancy being saved by Christ).

The question underneath. Fourth, what troubles us is really not Israel but God. Does God have the right to end human lives? He does, and exercises it in every generation; everyone who dies, dies at a time he appointed: “See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god beside me; I kill and I make alive” (Deuteronomy 32:39). What is unusual in Numbers 31 is not that God judges, but that he does it visibly, through a named instrument, where we can watch.

Where an honest reader is left. Abraham’s question stands, asked in trust and not as an accusation: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25). We are not given a full account of this chapter. We are given something better: proof of what kind of God is judging. He did not settle the question of his justice by explaining Numbers 31. He settled it by coming himself, standing under the judgment his justice required, and dying of it: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). A reader who cannot see to the bottom of this chapter is asked to trust the character of the One who bled at Calvary. That is not evasion. It is the only ground on which anyone has been able to look at the severity of God without despair.

Where Christians differ: how should such commands be read? Some have treated them as allegory, or as Israel’s mistaken idea of what God wanted, so that God never really commanded them. Some evangelical scholars hold that Old Testament war reports, like others of their time, often use sweeping language for decisive victory. Most Reformed and evangelical interpreters take the command as truly given by God. This commentary’s view: the command was truly God’s, a just and unrepeatable judgment on persistent and deliberate wickedness, never a pattern or licence for violence today. To say God never gave it sets us against the text; and this chapter itself records a limited judgment on particular clans (see the note on vv. 7–12).

verseByVerse.quote: Encamp outside the camp seven days. Whoever of you has killed any person and whoever has touched any slain, purify yourselves and your captives on the third day and on the seventh day. You shall purify every garment, every article of skin, all work of goats' hair, and every article of wood." Then Eleazar the priest said to the men in the army who had gone to battle: "This is the statute of the law that the LORD has commanded Moses: only the gold, the silver, the bronze, the iron, the tin, and the lead, everything that can stand the fire, you shall pass through the fire, and it shall be clean. Nevertheless, it shall also be purified with the water for impurity. And whatever cannot stand the fire, you shall pass through the water. You must wash your clothes on the seventh day, and you shall be clean. And afterward you may come into the camp."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soldiers who had obeyed God still came home unclean, and had to be cleansed before they could worship.

Encamp outside the camp seven days. What comes next is easy to miss and morally enormous. The army has carried out a judgment God commanded, and God does not send them home as heroes. He sends them outside the camp for seven days, to be cleansed with the water made from the ashes of the red heifer (chapter 19), the provision for defilement by death. Hebrews names this rite as a picture of Christ: if the ashes of a heifer made the defiled outwardly clean, how much more will the blood of Christ purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:13–14).

Unclean, not guilty. Israel’s soldiers came back from obeying God unclean. Not guilty; unclean. There is no garland, no parade, no suggestion that killing at God’s command left a man untouched. He had handled death, and had to be washed before he could worship. A religion that sends its soldiers to a week outside the camp and a sprinkling of water is not a religion that glories in blood.

Everything that can stand the fire. Eleazar the priest adds the rule for the plunder: what can stand the fire goes through the fire, everything else through the water. Nothing comes into the camp unpurified, and each thing is cleansed by the strongest means it can survive. Paul uses a similar image for the day every Christian’s work is examined: “it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done” (1 Corinthians 3:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Victory is met with fairness and worship. God has the plunder counted in public and divided in two, half for the twelve thousand who fought and half for the congregation who stayed home (vv. 25–27). A share goes to the LORD from each half, one in five hundred from the fighters and one in fifty from the people, given to the priest and the Levites (vv. 28–47). Then the officers, finding that not one man is missing, bring the gold they had picked up as an offering to make atonement for themselves, and it is laid up in the tent of meeting as a memorial (vv. 48–54). Spared by mercy, they give back to God.
verseByVerse.theology: A portion of everything is set apart as a contribution to the LORD (vv. 28–29): even the spoils of war belong first to God, who gave the victory. Victory is received as grace and returned in worship.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: not a single Israelite soldier had fallen, and the officers, knowing they had been spared by mercy, brought their gold to the LORD.

Now: every safe deliverance calls for worship. What we receive from God’s hand we return to him, knowing it was his before it was ours: all things come from you, and of your own have we given you (1 Chr 29:14).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Take the count of the plunder that was taken, both of man and of beast, you and Eleazar the priest and the heads of the fathers' houses of the congregation, and divide the plunder into two parts between the warriors who went out to battle and all the congregation. And levy for the LORD a tribute from the men of war who went out to battle, one out of five hundred, of the people and of the oxen and of the donkeys and of the flocks. Take it from their half and give it to Eleazar the priest as a contribution to the LORD. And from the people of Israel's half you shall take one drawn out of every fifty, of the people, of the oxen, of the donkeys, and of the flocks, of all the cattle, and give them to the Levites who keep guard over the tabernacle of the LORD." And Moses and Eleazar the priest did as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God divides the spoil fairly between those who fought and those who stayed home, and asks least of those who had risked most.

Half to those who stayed. Half goes to the twelve thousand who fought and half to the congregation who stayed home. David will make the same ruling centuries later: “as his share is who goes down into the battle, so shall his share be who stays by the baggage. They shall share alike” (1 Samuel 30:24). God’s people share the outcome of a work only some of them could do.

One out of five hundred. The tribute is levied unequally, in the direction nobody would expect: the fighters give one in five hundred, the congregation one in fifty, ten times as much. The fighters had risked their lives, so less is asked of them. God takes account of what a gift cost the giver, as Jesus did watching a widow’s two coins: “they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had” (Mark 12:44).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the plunder remaining of the spoil that the army took was 675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, 61,000 donkeys, and 32,000 persons in all, women who had not known man by lying with him. And the half, the portion of those who had gone out in the army, numbered 337,500 sheep, and the LORD's tribute of sheep was 675. The cattle were 36,000, of which the LORD's tribute was 72. The donkeys were 30,500, of which the LORD's tribute was 61. The persons were 16,000, of which the LORD's tribute was 32 persons. And Moses gave the tribute, which was the contribution for the LORD, to Eleazar the priest, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The spoil is counted to the last animal, in public, and God’s share is handed to the priest.

Who does the counting. Modern readers skim the accounts. Notice instead who does the counting: Moses, Eleazar and the heads of the fathers’ houses together (v. 26), with the figures written down to the last animal. No single man handles it and nothing is taken on trust. The LORD’s share, thirty-two persons among it, goes to Eleazar for the service of the sanctuary. The figures are very large, and, as with the census totals, some careful scholars think ancient ways of counting may be at work (see the introduction); either way the point is precision in the open.

Honourable in the sight of man. That is Paul’s standard with the church’s money: “We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man” (2 Corinthians 8:20–21). Wherever God’s people handle money, the books should be open. Keeping honest accounts is part of godliness.

verseByVerse.quote: From the people of Israel's half, which Moses separated from that of the men who had served in the army— now the congregation's half was 337,500 sheep, 36,000 cattle, and 30,500 donkeys, and 16,000 persons— from the people of Israel's half Moses took one of every 50, both of persons and of beasts, and gave them to the Levites who kept guard over the tabernacle of the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites, who had not fought and owned no land, receive a fixed share of the people’s half.

One of every 50. Out of a war they took no part in, the Levites are given a portion. The tribe with no inheritance is provided for out of everyone else’s, so that its men can serve at the tabernacle full time. The arrangement of chapter 18 does not lapse because the nation is at war. God’s provision for those who serve at his tent is not suspended by circumstances, and it is not funded out of what is left over; it is a fixed share, set aside first.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the officers who were over the thousands of the army, the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, came near to Moses and said to Moses, "Your servants have counted the men of war who are under our command, and there is not a man missing from us. And we have brought the LORD's offering, what each man found, articles of gold, armlets and bracelets, signet rings, earrings, and beads, to make atonement for ourselves before the LORD." And Moses and Eleazar the priest received from them the gold, all crafted articles. And all the gold of the contribution that they presented to the LORD, from the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, was 16,750 shekels. (The men in the army had each taken plunder for himself.) And Moses and Eleazar the priest received the gold from the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and brought it into the tent of meeting, as a memorial for the people of Israel before the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Officers who had not lost a single man brought their gold to God, knowing they had been spared by mercy.

Not a man missing from us. Twelve thousand men went out against five kings and twelve thousand came back. In an ancient war that is not luck, and they did not think it was.

To make atonement for ourselves. Then the surprising part. Not thanksgiving, atonement. They had lost nobody, and their instinct was that they needed covering. They had counted the men (v. 49), and at a census every Israelite gave “a ransom for his life to the LORD” (Exodus 30:12), for every life belongs to God. These men had spent a week outside the camp being sprinkled and had understood: coming home alive does not prove that you deserved to. Twenty-four thousand had died at Peor and these had not, and the difference was mercy and nothing else. So they gave away the gold they had picked up on the battlefield, 16,750 shekels of it.

As a memorial. The gold was laid up in the tent of meeting as a memorial, not spent. So the last act of the last war Moses ordered was a pile of enemy jewellery in the tabernacle, put there by soldiers who came home whole and could say nothing except that they had been spared and had not earned it. There is no better posture for anyone who has come through something they did not deserve to come through.

Uncertain wording. “Beads” translates a rare word found only here and in Exodus 35:22. It was some kind of gold ornament, but whether beads, a pendant or a necklace is not known; translations differ.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, these, on Balaam’s advice, caused the people of Israel to act treacherously against the LORD in the incident of Peor, and so the plague came among the congregation of the LORD.
keyVerse.note: This verse explains the whole chapter. Midian’s judgment answers a deliberate plan, devised by Balaam, to destroy Israel by leading it into sin, and it shows how seriously God takes those who corrupt his people. It also shows Balaam’s strategy, which has never gone away: a people who cannot be cursed can still be tempted.

31.reflection:
Verse 16 shows that Balaam, unable to curse Israel, found another way: leading the people into sin. Where do you see the same strategy at work against God’s people today, and how can we guard one another?

Verses 17–18 are deeply troubling. How does it help to see both what the passage is and what it is not? How does the cross help you trust God where you cannot see the whole answer?

Soldiers who had obeyed God still had to be cleansed before coming back into the camp (vv. 19–24). What does that teach about contact with death and evil, and where do you need Christ’s cleansing after hard things you have been through?

The officers who lost no one brought their gold “to make atonement for ourselves” (v. 50). What have you come through that you did not deserve to, and how might you give thanks for it?

32.title: The Tribes East of Jordan: The Danger of Settling for Less
32.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the people of Reuben and the people of Gad had a very great number of livestock. And they saw the land of Jazer and the land of Gilead, and behold, the place was a place for livestock.<sup>2</sup>So the people of Gad and the people of Reuben came and said to Moses and to Eleazar the priest and to the chiefs of the congregation,<sup>3</sup>"Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sebam, Nebo, and Beon,<sup>4</sup>the land that the LORD struck down before the congregation of Israel, is a land for livestock, and your servants have livestock."<sup>5</sup>And they said, "If we have found favor in your sight, let this land be given to your servants for a possession. Do not take us across the Jordan."<sup>6</sup>But Moses said to the people of Gad and to the people of Reuben, "Shall your brothers go to the war while you sit here?<sup>7</sup>Why will you discourage the heart of the people of Israel from going over into the land that the LORD has given them?<sup>8</sup>Your fathers did this, when I sent them from Kadesh-barnea to see the land.<sup>9</sup>For when they went up to the Valley of Eshcol and saw the land, they discouraged the heart of the people of Israel from going into the land that the LORD had given them.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD's anger was kindled on that day, and he swore, saying,<sup>11</sup>'Surely none of the men who came up out of Egypt, from twenty years old and upward, shall see the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, because they have not wholly followed me,<sup>12</sup>none except Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite and Joshua the son of Nun, for they have wholly followed the LORD.'<sup>13</sup>And the LORD's anger was kindled against Israel, and he made them wander in the wilderness forty years, until all the generation that had done evil in the sight of the LORD was gone.<sup>14</sup>And behold, you have risen in your fathers' place, a brood of sinful men, to increase still more the fierce anger of the LORD against Israel!<sup>15</sup>For if you turn away from following him, he will again abandon them in the wilderness, and you will destroy all this people."<sup>16</sup>Then they came near to him and said, "We will build sheepfolds here for our livestock, and cities for our little ones,<sup>17</sup>but we will take up arms, ready to go before the people of Israel, until we have brought them to their place. And our little ones shall live in the fortified cities because of the inhabitants of the land.<sup>18</sup>We will not return to our homes until each of the people of Israel has gained his inheritance.<sup>19</sup>For we will not inherit with them on the other side of the Jordan and beyond, because our inheritance has come to us on this side of the Jordan to the east."<sup>20</sup>So Moses said to them, "If you will do this, if you will take up arms to go before the LORD for the war,<sup>21</sup>and every armed man of you will pass over the Jordan before the LORD, until he has driven out his enemies from before him<sup>22</sup>and the land is subdued before the LORD; then after that you shall return and be free of obligation to the LORD and to Israel, and this land shall be your possession before the LORD.<sup>23</sup>But if you will not do so, behold, you have sinned against the LORD, and be sure your sin will find you out.<sup>24</sup>Build cities for your little ones and folds for your sheep, and do what you have promised."<sup>25</sup>And the people of Gad and the people of Reuben said to Moses, "Your servants will do as my lord commands.<sup>26</sup>Our little ones, our wives, our livestock, and all our cattle shall remain there in the cities of Gilead,<sup>27</sup>but your servants will pass over, every man who is armed for war, before the LORD to battle, as my lord orders."<sup>28</sup>So Moses gave command concerning them to Eleazar the priest and to Joshua the son of Nun and to the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel.<sup>29</sup>And Moses said to them, "If the people of Gad and the people of Reuben, every man who is armed to battle before the LORD, will pass with you over the Jordan and the land shall be subdued before you, then you shall give them the land of Gilead for a possession.<sup>30</sup>However, if they will not pass over with you armed, they shall have possessions among you in the land of Canaan."<sup>31</sup>And the people of Gad and the people of Reuben answered, "What the LORD has said to your servants, we will do.<sup>32</sup>We will pass over armed before the LORD into the land of Canaan, and the possession of our inheritance shall remain with us beyond the Jordan."<sup>33</sup>And Moses gave to them, to the people of Gad and to the people of Reuben and to the half-tribe of Manasseh the son of Joseph, the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites and the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, the land and its cities with their territories, the cities of the land throughout the country.<sup>34</sup>And the people of Gad built Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer,<sup>35</sup>Atroth-shophan, Jazer, Jogbehah,<sup>36</sup>Beth-nimrah and Beth-haran, fortified cities, and folds for sheep.<sup>37</sup>And the people of Reuben built Heshbon, Elealeh, Kiriathaim,<sup>38</sup>Nebo, and Baal-meon (their names were changed), and Sibmah. And they gave other names to the cities that they built.<sup>39</sup>And the sons of Machir the son of Manasseh went to Gilead and captured it, and dispossessed the Amorites who were in it.<sup>40</sup>And Moses gave Gilead to Machir the son of Manasseh, and he settled in it.<sup>41</sup>And Jair the son of Manasseh went and captured their villages, and called them Havvoth-jair.<sup>42</sup>And Nobah went and captured Kenath and its villages, and called it Nobah, after his own name.
32.overview:
Where we are. Israel is camped on the plains of Moab. The kingdoms of Sihon and Og are already conquered (chapter 21), Midian has been judged (chapter 31), and only the Jordan lies between the people and Canaan. Then two tribes ask not to cross.

The message. God’s people must not settle for less than he has promised, and none of them may rest while their brothers still fight. The request of Reuben and Gad sounds like the unbelief of Kadesh all over again, but when Moses confronts them they promise to cross and fight in front until every tribe has its inheritance, and Moses binds them to that promise before God: “be sure your sin will find you out” (v. 23).

Why it was said. This was the generation whose fathers had died in the wilderness for refusing to enter at Kadesh-barnea (chapters 13–14). Moses, about to die without crossing himself, feared above all that they would lose heart at the same border (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Reuben and Gad, rich in cattle, ask for the grazing land east of the Jordan: “Do not take us across the Jordan” (vv. 1–5). Moses hears Kadesh in it and warns that they will discourage the nation and bring God’s anger again (vv. 6–15). They answer that they will build homes for their families and then go armed ahead of their brothers until all Israel is settled (vv. 16–19). Moses accepts on those terms, with a solemn warning (vv. 20–24); they agree, and he commits the bargain to Eleazar, Joshua and the heads of the tribes (vv. 25–32). The land is given to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, and they build and take their towns (vv. 33–42).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need it exposes. Reuben and Gad already had their land, yet crossed the river to win an inheritance for their brothers that would never be theirs. That is a small picture of the elder Brother who had everything, left it, and fought for brothers whose inheritance he did not need, and who will not count the work finished until every one of them is home: “I go to prepare a place for you” (John 14:2). And the sin that doomed the last generation, not wholly following the LORD (v. 11), is answered only by the one Son who followed his Father all the way.

For us. Beware of a comfort that stops short of what God calls you to, and of a faith so private that your brothers and sisters fight alone. Keep the promises you make before God, and where you have broken them, do not wait for your sin to find you: bring it into the light, where Christ has already borne it.
32.theology:
The danger of settling for less. We are tempted to be content with a lesser good rather than press into the fullness God promises in Christ.

Solidarity in the battle. No tribe may enjoy its rest while its brothers still fight. The people of God advance together, keeping faith with one another until the whole work is done.

Sin as a pursuer. A broken vow before God is never left behind; it follows the one who broke it until it is confessed (see v. 23).
32.examples:
Then: Reuben and Gad sought to settle east of the Jordan but were bound by covenant to fight alongside their brothers until all Israel received its inheritance.

Now: The inheritance across the river is already secured for you by Christ, who did not stop short for his own comfort; that is why you need not settle on the near bank. His Spirit is given to carry you on and to keep you faithful to your brothers and sisters in the battle. And where you have stopped short or broken your word, the sin that pursues you has a place to stop: it was laid on him, and it is answered by confession, not by hiding.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Request of Reuben and Gad
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Settling short of God’s promise looks like unbelief, and it endangers everyone. Reuben and Gad, with great herds, see the rich grazing east of the Jordan and ask to stay there: “Do not take us across the Jordan” (vv. 1–5). Moses asks whether their brothers are to fight while they sit, and warns that they will discourage the whole nation, as the spies did at Kadesh-barnea (vv. 6–9). Then he retells God’s oath against the generation that did not wholly follow him, sparing only Caleb and Joshua, and charges these men with risking the same anger again (vv. 10–15). No choice about obeying God is purely private.
verseByVerse.theology: Moses’ alarm (vv. 6–15) is that settling short of the promise, and leaving the brothers to fight alone, would discourage the whole people as the spies once did. The passage warns against contentment with a lesser inheritance and against a self-interest that leaves the family of God to struggle alone.
verseByVerse.examples: Beware a comfort that leaves your brothers and sisters to carry the battle alone. Christ bore your burden first, and so his people bear one another’s burdens (Galatians 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the people of Reuben and the people of Gad had a very great number of livestock. And they saw the land of Jazer and the land of Gilead, and behold, the place was a place for livestock. So the people of Gad and the people of Reuben came and said to Moses and to Eleazar the priest and to the chiefs of the congregation, "Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sebam, Nebo, and Beon, the land that the LORD struck down before the congregation of Israel, is a land for livestock, and your servants have livestock." And they said, "If we have found favor in your sight, let this land be given to your servants for a possession. Do not take us across the Jordan."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reuben and Gad look at their herds and at the grass, and ask to stop short of the promised land.

A place for livestock. The order of the sentences shows what has gone wrong: the possessions come first, then the looking, then the wanting, then the request. Their case names nine towns and adds “your servants have livestock”, without a word about the promise to Abraham, their brothers or the crossing. Their whole case is a list of what they own. Then the words that alarm Moses: “Do not take us across the Jordan.”

Not forbidden land. Be fair to them. This land was not forbidden; God had given it to Israel in chapter 21, and Moses will grant the request. Their situation was real: enormous herds and enormous grass. But something has quietly reversed. They had walked forty years toward a promise, and within sight of it asked to stop. The danger to a believer is seldom a decision to abandon God. It is finding somewhere comfortable a few miles short, and slowly turning a stopping place into a home.
verseByVerse.note: Gilead lay east of the Jordan; Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh settled there.

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to the people of Gad and to the people of Reuben, "Shall your brothers go to the war while you sit here? Why will you discourage the heart of the people of Israel from going over into the land that the LORD has given them? Your fathers did this, when I sent them from Kadesh-barnea to see the land. For when they went up to the Valley of Eshcol and saw the land, they discouraged the heart of the people of Israel from going into the land that the LORD had given them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses warns that if two tribes sit out the war, they will discourage the whole nation, as the spies did at Kadesh.

Shall your brothers go to the war while you sit here? Moses’ question has been quoted in every generation since. He begins not with their motives but with the other tribes, who would cross into fortified cities with the same fighting spread over fewer shoulders.
