Your fathers did this. His real fear comes next: if two tribes may stay behind, everyone else will conclude that crossing is optional, and lose heart. Then he names the precedent, Kadesh-barnea. Ten spies did not force anyone to do anything. They spoke their reluctance out loud, with conviction, and a nation went to pieces, at the cost of forty years and a generation of graves. Nobody in the church makes a purely private decision about how much of God’s call to obey. Somebody is always watching, taking the measure of what is apparently allowed.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD's anger was kindled on that day, and he swore, saying, 'Surely none of the men who came up out of Egypt, from twenty years old and upward, shall see the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, because they have not wholly followed me, none except Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite and Joshua the son of Nun, for they have wholly followed the LORD.' And the LORD's anger was kindled against Israel, and he made them wander in the wilderness forty years, until all the generation that had done evil in the sight of the LORD was gone. And behold, you have risen in your fathers' place, a brood of sinful men, to increase still more the fierce anger of the LORD against Israel! For if you turn away from following him, he will again abandon them in the wilderness, and you will destroy all this people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God condemned the last generation because they did not follow him all the way, and Moses fears these men will do the same and drag the whole nation down with them.

They have not wholly followed me. Moses retells the Kadesh story to men who were children when it happened and have lived under its sentence ever since. The reason God gave is stated once of the many and once of the two: the many “have not wholly followed me”, while Caleb and Joshua “have wholly followed the LORD”. The Hebrew means to fill up after him, to follow all the way. The condemned generation had not renounced God; they followed partially and stopped where it got frightening. Now two tribes propose to follow as far as the river.

A brood of sinful men. These are the sharpest words in the chapter, and not measured diplomacy. Moses, nearly a hundred and twenty, has buried a generation and cannot bear to watch it begin again. His charge, “you will destroy all this people”, holds two tribes responsible for what their choice would do to the rest. There is no private discipleship in Scripture: “If one member suffers, all suffer together” (1 Corinthians 12:26); “none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself” (Romans 14:7).

Isn’t my faith my own business? Most of us were raised to think so: belief is private, and what I do with God is between him and me. Alexis de Tocqueville, watching the young American democracy in the 1830s, described the quiet temptation of a free and prosperous people: each man draws back into the little circle of his family and friends and gladly leaves the wider society to look after itself. That is very nearly what Reuben and Gad proposed: folds for the flocks, houses for the children, and the war across the river somebody else’s affair. It felt reasonable. But a faith kept private is usually a faith kept under my own control, adjusted to my comfort and answerable to no one. The gospel will not leave it there. You were never your own project: you were bought, and bought into a family, with brothers and sisters you did not choose: “he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen” (1 John 4:20). God does not adopt only children.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tribes answer the charge by promising more than was asked. They will build pens and towns for their families, then go armed before their brothers and not come home until every Israelite has his inheritance (vv. 16–19). Moses accepts on those terms, and warns that if they fail, “be sure your sin will find you out” (vv. 20–24). They agree, now naming their families first (vv. 25–27), and Moses commits the agreement to Eleazar, Joshua and the heads of the tribes so that it will outlive him (vv. 28–30). Before them all, the two tribes take Moses’ terms as the LORD’s word and promise to keep it (vv. 31–32).
verseByVerse.theology: The tribes’ pledge to fight before they rest resolves Moses’ concern: they will not abandon the family of God. His warning in verse 23 is not mainly that hidden sin will be exposed, but that a broken promise to God becomes a pursuer that overtakes the one who broke it. Solidarity with the brothers and faithfulness to one’s word are the conditions of the blessing.
verseByVerse.examples: God sees the vow we keep and the one we break. But the sin that would find us out can also be brought into the light by us, and there it meets mercy (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Then they came near to him and said, "We will build sheepfolds here for our livestock, and cities for our little ones, but we will take up arms, ready to go before the people of Israel, until we have brought them to their place. And our little ones shall live in the fortified cities because of the inhabitants of the land. We will not return to our homes until each of the people of Israel has gained his inheritance. For we will not inherit with them on the other side of the Jordan and beyond, because our inheritance has come to us on this side of the Jordan to the east."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rebuked, the two tribes promise to march in front of their brothers and to stay until every Israelite has his land.

We will take up arms. Their reply is one of the best moments in the book. They do not argue, or defend themselves against the charge of being “a brood of sinful men”. They come nearer and improve the request: they will go not merely with their brothers but before them, in the front rank, and not return until every Israelite has his inheritance.

The measure of it. They already have their land; nothing on the far bank will ever be theirs. They commit themselves to years of war for the sole purpose of getting other families into fields they will never set foot in. Some seven years later Joshua sends them home with these words: “You have not forsaken your brothers these many days, down to this day, but have been careful to keep the charge of the LORD your God” (Joshua 22:3).

For the interests of others. That is what a Christian is called into: not securing his own standing and watching from the east bank, but crossing over for people whose inheritance will never be his. “Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others” (Philippians 2:4), and Paul points at once to Christ, who did exactly that for us.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses said to them, "If you will do this, if you will take up arms to go before the LORD for the war, and every armed man of you will pass over the Jordan before the LORD, until he has driven out his enemies from before him and the land is subdued before the LORD; then after that you shall return and be free of obligation to the LORD and to Israel, and this land shall be your possession before the LORD. But if you will not do so, behold, you have sinned against the LORD, and be sure your sin will find you out. Build cities for your little ones and folds for your sheep, and do what you have promised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses accepts their promise, and warns that if they break it their sin will hunt them down.

If you will do this. Moses spells out the terms with a lawyer’s precision, then gives the warning that has passed into the language and is usually quoted wrongly: “be sure your sin will find you out.”

Be sure your sin will find you out. It is often heard as “your secret sins will come to light”, which the Bible says elsewhere (Luke 12:2), but not here. Here the sin is a pursuer. A broken promise will hunt down the man who broke it: not a stain waiting to be discovered but a creditor on the road behind you who knows your name. “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Galatians 6:7). For the Christian there is one place where that pursuer is stopped: the cross, where Christ, who kept every word, took the debt of those who had not. A believer outruns his sin not by speed but by turning round and confessing it.

Build cities for your little ones. Then a small, easily missed correction. They had said sheepfolds first, then cities for the children. Moses gives them back their own sentence with the children put first: “Build cities for your little ones and folds for your sheep.” Not a syllable of rebuke, just the words rearranged, and any man who has let his work take precedence over his family knows what has been done to him in that verse.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Gad and the people of Reuben said to Moses, "Your servants will do as my lord commands. Our little ones, our wives, our livestock, and all our cattle shall remain there in the cities of Gilead, but your servants will pass over, every man who is armed for war, before the LORD to battle, as my lord orders."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reuben and Gad accept Moses’ terms without bargaining, and now name their families before their flocks.

Your servants will do as my lord commands. They speak as servants, and listen to the order of their answer: “our little ones, our wives” come first and the livestock after them. They have taken Moses’ quiet correction to heart (see the note on vv. 20–24).

Before the LORD to battle. The phrase is repeated through these verses (vv. 20–22, 27, 29, 32). This is the LORD’s war, fought with the ark going ahead of the people (10:35; Joshua 4:11–13), and the two tribes are not merely doing their brothers a favour but serving under God. “Every man who is armed for war” probably means the fighting men chosen and equipped for the campaign rather than every adult male: Joshua 4:13 counts about forty thousand who crossed, fewer than the men of Reuben and Gad numbered in 26:7, 18, so some must have stayed to guard the towns and families.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses gave command concerning them to Eleazar the priest and to Joshua the son of Nun and to the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel. And Moses said to them, "If the people of Gad and the people of Reuben, every man who is armed to battle before the LORD, will pass with you over the Jordan and the land shall be subdued before you, then you shall give them the land of Gilead for a possession. However, if they will not pass over with you armed, they shall have possessions among you in the land of Canaan."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses makes the agreement public and binding, so that it will be enforced after his death.

Moses gave command concerning them. The agreement is not left as a handshake. Moses commits it to Eleazar, Joshua and the tribal heads, restates the terms before them, and defines the penalty: if they do not cross armed, they forfeit the east bank and take their chances with everyone else in Canaan. It is witnessed, binding, and enforceable after Moses is dead.

Realism about memory. That is not cynicism about their sincerity but realism about human memory. Good intentions formed in a moment of conviction thin out over seven years of war with your family on the other side of a river. Reuben and Gad were helped by having their promise put beyond the reach of their own later feelings, which is why God gives his people vows, covenants and public ceremonies rather than leaving everything to the state of the heart on the day.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Gad and the people of Reuben answered, "What the LORD has said to your servants, we will do. We will pass over armed before the LORD into the land of Canaan, and the possession of our inheritance shall remain with us beyond the Jordan."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two tribes take Moses’ terms as the word of the LORD and pledge before everyone to keep them.

What the LORD has said to your servants, we will do. At first they said “as my lord commands” (v. 25); now, before Eleazar, Joshua and the heads of the tribes, they say “what the LORD has said”. They recognise Moses’ terms as God’s word, so their promise is made to God himself, the kind of promise Moses has just warned them not to break (v. 23). Years later they will say almost the same to Joshua: “All that you have commanded us we will do” (Joshua 1:16).

The possession of our inheritance shall remain with us. Their last words still look east, and Moses grants the land at once (v. 33). The pledge and the request stand side by side: they may have their inheritance beyond the Jordan, but only as men who first cross it for their brothers. Joshua 22:1–4 records that they kept every word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 33–42 — The Settlement of the Transjordan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The agreement is carried out: blessing received, duty still owed. Moses gives the kingdoms of Sihon and Og to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh (v. 33). Gad and Reuben build and fortify their towns and sheepfolds, renaming cities that bore the names of other gods (vv. 34–38). Clans of Manasseh, led by Machir, Jair and Nobah, capture Gilead and its villages and settle there (vv. 39–42). The eastern tribes now have homes, but their word still binds them to cross the river with their brothers, and the book of Joshua records that they kept it.
verseByVerse.theology: The settlement (vv. 33–42) carries out the agreement: land granted and cities built, on the understanding that the pledge will be honoured. God makes room for the real circumstances of his people while holding them to their commitments.
verseByVerse.examples: Blessing received does not release us from promised duty. The eastern tribes built their homes knowing that their word still bound them to the far bank, and faithfulness follows us into our rest as well.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses gave to them, to the people of Gad and to the people of Reuben and to the half-tribe of Manasseh the son of Joseph, the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites and the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, the land and its cities with their territories, the cities of the land throughout the country. And the people of Gad built Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer, Atroth-shophan, Jazer, Jogbehah, Beth-nimrah and Beth-haran, fortified cities, and folds for sheep. And the people of Reuben built Heshbon, Elealeh, Kiriathaim, Nebo, and Baal-meon (their names were changed), and Sibmah. And they gave other names to the cities that they built.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses gives the conquered kingdoms east of the Jordan to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, and they rebuild their towns, renaming those that carried other gods’ names.

Their names were changed. An easily missed detail: they rebuild Nebo and Baal-meon, “their names were changed”, and give other names to the cities they built. Most likely the old names were the problem. Nebo probably carried the name of the Babylonian god Nabu, and Baal-meon carried Baal’s. These families had just watched twenty-four thousand die over Baal of Peor, and would not raise their children under that name. God had said, “make no mention of the names of other gods, nor let it be heard on your lips” (Exodus 23:13), and they took him seriously enough to repaint the signposts.

In everyday life. Taking possession of anything for God involves that kind of renaming. A believer inherits a family, a business, a set of habits, and finds somebody else’s name over the door. Leaving it up because it was there first is how a place quietly stays what it always was.

Why is half of Manasseh here? Machir’s clan had already taken Gilead (vv. 39–42), and Moses gave it to them; the rest of Manasseh settled west of the Jordan (Joshua 17).

Uncertain wording. The bracketed “their names were changed” is a compressed note, and its exact sense is uncertain. Most take it to record that the settlers renamed these towns; some think it tells readers not to speak the gods’ names aloud. The old names survived in common use (Jeremiah 48:22; Ezekiel 25:9).

verseByVerse.quote: And the sons of Machir the son of Manasseh went to Gilead and captured it, and dispossessed the Amorites who were in it. And Moses gave Gilead to Machir the son of Manasseh, and he settled in it. And Jair the son of Manasseh went and captured their villages, and called them Havvoth-jair. And Nobah went and captured Kenath and its villages, and called it Nobah, after his own name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Clans of Manasseh take Gilead, and the tribes east of the Jordan are home, though Scripture leaves their choice open to reflection.

Was it a mistake? Scripture does not say so, and we should not say more than Scripture. Moses granted it, God permitted it, and Joshua later commended these men warmly for keeping every word of the bargain (Joshua 22:2–4). But the later history is sober reading. The eastern tribes had no river between them and their enemies, as everybody else had. They stood first in the path of every invasion from the east, and when the Assyrian came it was Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh who went into exile first (1 Chronicles 5:26). Good grass, and no river in front of it. There is nothing here to condemn and a great deal to think about, and the chapter leaves it exactly there.

The promise kept. What it does not leave in doubt is the promise they made and kept. They crossed a river they did not need to cross, fought a war they had nothing to gain from, and stayed until every family in Israel stood on its own ground. Only then did they go home. That is a small picture of something far greater. There is an elder Brother who already possessed everything and left it to fight for brothers whose inheritance he had no need of (Philippians 2:6–8; Hebrews 2:10–11). He has won it, and says what he is doing now: “I go to prepare a place for you … I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also” (John 14:2–3). He will not count the work finished until every one of his brothers is standing on his inheritance.
verseByVerse.note: “Havvoth-jair” means “the villages of Jair” (ESV note).

keyVerse.quote: But if you will not do so, behold, you have sinned against the LORD, and be sure your sin will find you out.
keyVerse.note: The chapter turns on a promise made before God, and this warning seals it. Sin here is not a secret waiting to be exposed but a pursuer that hunts down the one who broke his word. The only place it is stopped is the cross, where Christ, who kept every word, bore the debt of those who had not.

32.reflection:
The request of Reuben and Gad begins with what they owned (vv. 1–4). Where might comfort or possessions be quietly turning a stopping place into a home in your life?

Moses asks, “Shall your brothers go to the war while you sit here?” (v. 6). Who in your church is carrying a load you could share, and what keeps you on the east bank?

The two tribes crossed a river they did not need to cross, for an inheritance that would never be theirs (vv. 16–19). How does Christ’s doing far more than this for us shape the way we serve one another?

Verse 23 says, “be sure your sin will find you out.” What difference does it make to think of sin as a pursuer rather than a secret, and what does it look like to turn and confess it rather than run?

33.title: The Stages of the Journey: Every Step Known to God
33.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the stages of the people of Israel, when they went out of the land of Egypt by their companies under the leadership of Moses and Aaron.<sup>2</sup>Moses wrote down their starting places, stage by stage, by command of the LORD, and these are their stages according to their starting places.<sup>3</sup>They set out from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month. On the day after the Passover, the people of Israel went out triumphantly in the sight of all the Egyptians,<sup>4</sup>while the Egyptians were burying all their firstborn, whom the LORD had struck down among them. On their gods also the LORD executed judgments.<sup>5</sup>So the people of Israel set out from Rameses and camped at Succoth.<sup>6</sup>And they set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, which is on camped at Hor-haggidgad.<sup>33</sup>And they set out from Hor-haggidgad and camped at Jotbathah.<sup>34</sup>And they set out from Jotbathah and camped at Abronah.<sup>35</sup>And they set out from Abronah and camped at Ezion-geber.<sup>36</sup>And they set out from Ezion-geber and camped in the wilderness of Zin (that is, Kadesh).<sup>37</sup>And they set out from Kadesh and camped at Mount Hor, on the edge of the land of Edom.<sup>38</sup>And Aaron the priest went up Mount Hor at the command of the LORD and died there, in the fortieth year after the people of Israel had come out of the Punon.<sup>43</sup>And they set out from Punon and camped at Oboth.<sup>44</sup>And they set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, in the territory of Moab.<sup>45</sup>And they set out from Iyim and camped at Dibon-gad.<sup>46</sup>And they set out from Dibon-gad and camped at Almon-diblathaim.<sup>47</sup>And they set out from Almon-diblathaim and camped in the mountains of Abarim, before Nebo.<sup>48</sup>And they set out from the mountains of Abarim and camped in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho;<sup>49</sup>they camped by the Jordan from Beth-jeshimoth as far as Abel-shittim in the plains of Moab.<sup>50</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying,<sup>51</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you pass over the Jordan into the land of Canaan,<sup>52</sup>then you shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you and destroy all their figured stones and destroy all their metal images and demolish all their high places.<sup>53</sup>And you shall take possession of the land and settle in it, for I have given the land to you to possess it.<sup>54</sup>You shall inherit the land by lot according to your clans. To a large tribe you shall give a large inheritance, and to a small tribe you shall give a small inheritance. Wherever the lot falls for anyone, that shall be his. According to the tribes of your fathers you shall inherit.<sup>55</sup>But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you, then those of them whom you let remain shall be as barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides, and they shall trouble you in the land where you dwell.<sup>56</sup>And I will do to you as I thought to do to them."
33.overview:
Where we are. Israel is camped on the plains of Moab, with the new generation counted (chapter 26), Joshua commissioned (chapter 27) and the eastern tribes settled (chapter 32). Before the crossing, Moses writes down every camp from Egypt to the Jordan, and God gives his orders for the land ahead.

The message. The God who led his people every step of the way, through deliverance and disaster and the long stretches where nothing seemed to happen, has kept the record himself, and he has brought them to the edge of his promise. Because the land is his gift, they must take it wholeheartedly: leave no idol standing and make no terms with the sin that ruined the nations before them, or it will ruin them too.

Why it was said. Most of those listening had been children in the wilderness or were born there (see the introduction). Before they crossed, they needed to own the whole story, failures included, as God’s leading, and to hear that the religion of Canaan was the same danger that Peor had just shown them (chapter 25).

How the chapter makes its case. The record is written at God’s command and begins with the Passover and Egypt’s judgment (vv. 1–4). The early stages pass the sea, Marah and Elim on the way to Sinai (vv. 5–15); then comes a run of mostly forgotten names, with a few that recall failure, as far as Kadesh (vv. 16–37); then Aaron’s death on Mount Hor and the last stages to the plains of Moab (vv. 38–49). Finally God commands Israel to drive out the inhabitants, destroy their idols and divide the land by lot, warning that whatever they spare will torment them, and that he will treat Israel as he meant to treat Canaan (vv. 50–56).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. The journey began with the blood of the Passover lamb, and “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The wilderness road becomes the pattern of the Christian life between redemption and home (1 Corinthians 10:1–11; Hebrews 3–4), and Jesus has gone ahead through the last river as our forerunner (Hebrews 6:20). And Israel’s failure to finish the task (Judges 1–2) exposes our need of one who never made terms with sin.

For us. Every stage of your life, bitter, sweet or simply uneventful, is written in God’s record, and the first entry is redemption by the Lamb’s blood. So keep setting out, and do not make peace with the idols he has told you to tear down: a tolerated sin never stays small.
33.theology:
Every stage known to God. Not one mile of the pilgrimage is lost or forgotten, the uneventful years included.

The redeemed are pilgrims. The rhythm of setting out and camping marks a people always on the move, led by God from redemption to inheritance.

Wholehearted obedience. Idols left standing become thorns, and sin tolerated becomes a snare, so God’s people are called to put to death the sins they are tempted to spare.
33.examples: Your life has its own list of stages: green pastures and dark valleys, joys and failures, and long stretches in which nothing seemed to happen. All of it is known to God and held in his care. You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle. Are they not in your book? (Psalm 56:8). He is leading you, stage by stage, home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–49 — The Stages of the Journey
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses writes down, at God’s command, the whole journey from Rameses to the plains of Moab. It opens with the exodus, Israel marching out the day after the Passover while Egypt buries its firstborn (vv. 1–4). The early stages run past the sea, Marah’s bitter water and Elim’s springs to Sinai (vv. 5–15). Then come long lines of names, most unknown elsewhere, broken by places that recall failure, such as Kibroth-hattaavah and Kadesh (vv. 16–37). The list pauses only for Aaron’s death on Mount Hor before it ends on the plains of Moab (vv. 38–49). Every stage, eventful or not, was God’s leading, and every one is kept in his record.
verseByVerse.theology: The recorded itinerary (vv. 1–49) is a memorial of God’s faithful leading through good camps and bitter ones alike, as Moses would later urge: remember the whole way that the LORD your God has led you (Deut 8:2). None of it was aimless; the God who led by cloud and fire (9:15–23) was writing a purposeful story all the way home.
verseByVerse.examples: Looking back over your own road, the bitter waters as well as the shade, is itself an act of faith. It is how a believer learns that none of it was wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the stages of the people of Israel, when they went out of the land of Egypt by their companies under the leadership of Moses and Aaron. Moses wrote down their starting places, stage by stage, by command of the LORD, and these are their stages according to their starting places. They set out from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month. On the day after the Passover, the people of Israel went out triumphantly in the sight of all the Egyptians, while the Egyptians were burying all their firstborn, whom the LORD had struck down among them. On their gods also the LORD executed judgments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God had every stage of the journey written down, and the record begins with redemption: Israel marching out of a judged Egypt the morning after the Passover.

By command of the LORD. Before a single place-name, the chapter says who commissioned the list. This is not a diary Moses kept for himself. An old man on the plains of Moab had a record of every place his people had pitched a tent, including the places of failure and the years when nothing happened, and God said: put it all in. Nothing was too tedious or too shameful to keep.

Went out triumphantly. The record starts not in the wilderness but at a funeral in Egypt. Israel went out “triumphantly” (literally, “with a high hand”) while the Egyptians buried their firstborn and the LORD judged their gods. The first line of the itinerary is redemption by the blood of a lamb. Every stage that follows is the journey of a people bought out of slavery. So is every stage of a Christian’s life: whatever else is on the list, the first entry is redemption by the blood of the Lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).

verseByVerse.quote: So the people of Israel set out from Rameses and camped at Succoth. And they set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, which is on the edge of the wilderness. And they set out from Etham and turned back to Pi-hahiroth, which is east of Baal-zephon, and they camped before Migdol. And they set out from before Hahiroth and passed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness, and they went a three days' journey in the wilderness of Etham and camped at Marah. And they set out from Marah and came to Elim; at Elim there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there. And they set out from Elim and camped by the Red Sea. And they set out from the Red Sea and camped in the wilderness of Sin. And they set out from the wilderness of Sin and camped at Dophkah. And they set out from Dophkah and camped at Alush. And they set out from Alush and camped at Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink. And they set out from Rephidim and camped in the wilderness of Sinai.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The early stages record the greatest miracle and the bitterest water in the same plain tone, and after each, bitter or sweet, Israel set out again.

Through the midst of the sea. One of the greatest miracles of the Old Testament is entered between two campsites in the same tone as everything else, as if it were an ordinary day.

Marah and Elim. Then Marah, where the water was bitter (Exodus 15:23), and Elim, with “twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees”, one of the very few descriptive details in the chapter, and a green one. Forty years later a man writing an itinerary still remembered the shade at Elim.

And they set out. The bitter and the sweet came one after the other, as in a believer’s life they always do. God does not run his people through Marah because he has nothing better, nor park them at Elim because the journey is over. The line under each entry is the same: “and they set out”. Nobody stays at Elim. Nobody stays at Marah either.

verseByVerse.quote: And they set out from the wilderness of Sinai and camped at Kibroth-hattaavah. And they set out from Kibroth-hattaavah and camped at Hazeroth. And they set out from Hazeroth and camped at Rithmah. And they set out from Rithmah and camped at Rimmon-perez. And they set out from Rimmon-perez and camped at Libnah. And they set out from Libnah and camped at Rissah. And they set out from Rissah and camped at Kehelathah. And they set out from Kehelathah and camped at Mount Shepher. And they set out from Mount Shepher and camped at Haradah. And they set out from Haradah and camped at Makheloth. And they set out from Makheloth and camped at Tahath. And they set out from Tahath and camped at Terah. And they set out from Terah and camped at Mithkah. And they set out from Mithkah and camped at Hashmonah. And they set out from Hashmonah and camped at Moseroth. And they set out from Moseroth and camped at Bene-jaakan. And they set out from Bene-jaakan and camped at Hor-haggidgad. And they set out from Hor-haggidgad and camped at Jotbathah. And they set out from Jotbathah and camped at Abronah. And they set out from Abronah and camped at Ezion-geber. And they set out from Ezion-geber and camped in the wilderness of Zin (that is, Kadesh). And they set out from Kadesh and camped at Mount Hor, on the edge of the land of Edom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Most of the wilderness years left nothing behind but a name, and God had every one of those camps written into his record.

Name after name. Twenty-two verses pass in which almost nothing is said: most of these names appear nowhere else in the Bible and cannot be placed on any map we have. This is what the wilderness years actually consisted of.

Kibroth-hattaavah. A few names still carry their stories. Kibroth-hattaavah means “graves of craving”, where the people demanded meat and those who craved it were buried (11:34). Hazeroth is where Miriam and Aaron turned on Moses (12:1). Verse 36 reaches Kadesh, where the whole thing went wrong (chapters 13–14).

The value of the ordinary. But most of the list is unremarkable, and that is its value. Between the disasters and the deliverances lay years of ordinary marching that produced no story. There is a strange comfort in a page of forgotten place-names: the stretches of a life in which nothing happens are not gaps in the record. They are the record. He was there at Rithmah too.

verseByVerse.quote: And Aaron the priest went up Mount Hor at the command of the LORD and died there, in the fortieth year after the people of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt, on the first day of the fifth month. And Aaron was 123 years old when he died on Mount Hor. And the Canaanite, the king of Arad, who lived in the Negeb in the land of Canaan, heard of the coming of the people of Israel. And they set out from Mount Hor and camped at Zalmonah. And they set out from Zalmonah and camped at Punon. And they set out from Punon and camped at Oboth. And they set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim, in the territory of Moab. And they set out from Iyim and camped at Dibon-gad. And they set out from Dibon-gad and camped at Almon-diblathaim. And they set out from Almon-diblathaim and camped in the mountains of Abarim, before Nebo. And they set out from the mountains of Abarim and camped in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho; they camped by the Jordan from Beth-jeshimoth as far as Abel-shittim in the plains of Moab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list stops only once, for Aaron’s death, and then runs on to the plains of Moab, where the reader is standing: in sight of the land but not yet in it.

Aaron the priest went up Mount Hor. Only here does the itinerary halt, for a death: Aaron’s, dated to the day, with his age. The record of a whole nation stops for one man. God counts the stages, and he also counts those who do not finish them.

Aaron was 123 years old. His age fits Exodus 7:7, which makes him eighty-three when he first stood before Pharaoh. Deuteronomy 10:6 says Aaron died at Moserah: Moseroth was a camp nearby (v. 30), and Mount Hor rose in that region, so Deuteronomy names the area and Numbers the mountain.

In the plains of Moab. From Mount Hor the road turns toward the river, and the list ends exactly where the reader is standing. It ends on the wrong side of the water: forty years, and the final camp within sight of the land and not in it, where Numbers closes and Moses will die.

From afar. Hebrews reads the Old Testament this way: “These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13). Every believer’s list ends at a riverbank of some sort, and no believer stands there alone: Jesus has gone ahead as forerunner (Hebrews 6:20), through death and out the other side. The question is not whether you get all the way in during this life, but whether God’s record shows somebody who went out from Egypt and kept setting out.
verseByVerse.note: Aaron died aged 123, in the fortieth year.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the plains of Moab God turns from the road behind to the land ahead. When Israel crosses the Jordan it must drive out the inhabitants, destroy their carved stones, cast images and high places, and settle the land as his gift, dividing it by lot, larger shares to larger tribes (vv. 50–54). Then the warning: whatever they spare will become “barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides”, and if Israel takes up the sins of Canaan, God will do to Israel what he meant to do to Canaan (vv. 55–56). The gift calls for wholehearted obedience, and God’s own people have no immunity.
verseByVerse.theology: The command to dispossess the Canaanites and destroy their idols (vv. 51–53) guards Israel from the idolatry that would later ruin her, and the warning of verse 55 proved tragically true in Judges. Tolerated sin does not stay contained; it festers and wounds, a lesson the New Testament applies to the sin we must put to death in ourselves (see vv. 50–56).
verseByVerse.examples: The sin we spare in ourselves does not stay quiet. But the call to deal with it comes to people already raised with Christ, and they do not fight alone: the Spirit who lives in them gives the strength.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you pass over the Jordan into the land of Canaan, then you shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you and destroy all their figured stones and destroy all their metal images and demolish all their high places. And you shall take possession of the land and settle in it, for I have given the land to you to possess it. You shall inherit the land by lot according to your clans. To a large tribe you shall give a large inheritance, and to a small tribe you shall give a small inheritance. Wherever the lot falls for anyone, that shall be his. According to the tribes of your fathers you shall inherit. But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you, then those of them whom you let remain shall be as barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides, and they shall trouble you in the land where you dwell. And I will do to you as I thought to do to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must drive out Canaan’s peoples and destroy every shrine, for whatever it spares will torment it, and if it takes up Canaan’s sins it will share Canaan’s judgment.

Drive out all the inhabitants. The chapter turns from history to command, and the command is total: not coexist with, but destroy. Israel had just watched twenty-four thousand of its own die because they accepted an invitation to the sacrificial feasts of Moab’s gods (25:2, 9). God will not leave the shrines standing.

Figured stones, metal images, high places. Figured stones were probably carved stones set up for worship, metal images were cast idols, and high places were local open-air shrines, often on hilltops, with an altar and standing stones. The high places outlasted the conquest by centuries, and even good kings of Judah failed to remove them (1 Kings 15:14).

By lot. The land was divided by lot, larger shares to larger tribes, so that no one could accuse Moses or Joshua of favouritism; God decided (Proverbs 16:33). The apostles’ use of the lot (Acts 1:26) came before the Spirit was given, and Christians now seek God’s will through Scripture, prayer and wise counsel.

As barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides. Then the warning, in two images chosen with care. A barb in the eye: small, permanently painful, ruining your sight. A thorn in the side: out of reach, catching every time you move. Neither is fatal, both are unbearable, and neither goes away on its own: that is what a tolerated sin does to a believer. Judges 1 and 2 record Israel doing exactly what it was warned of, and Judges 2:3 turns this verse back on it.

I will do to you as I thought to do to them. The last line is the most sobering. Israel had no immunity: if it took up the Canaanites’ sins it would be judged for them, and the exile proved it. Belonging to God’s covenant people was never a licence to sin but a calling to holiness.

The one who never spared sin. Israel’s failure to finish the job, repeated in every believer, is why the gospel is good news. Christ fought sin to the end and never once made terms with it, and his obedience is counted to those who confess they have spared what they should have slain.

Put it to death. So Paul tells Christians, “Put to death therefore what is earthly in you” (Colossians 3:5): not manage it, kill it. But he says it to people whose life “is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3), who do it “by the Spirit” (Romans 8:13).

Was it just? This was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened over centuries (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4–5), including child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31), and Israel was warned that the land would vomit it out too for the same sins (Leviticus 18:24–28). It was a unique command for one moment in redemptive history, and no pattern for any later war, nation or church: Christ’s kingdom is “not of this world” (John 18:36), and the weapons of the church’s warfare “are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4).

Uncertain wording. “Figured stones” translates a rare Hebrew word (maskit) used of carved or pictured work (compare Leviticus 26:1). It was an object of worship, probably a stone carved with images or symbols, but exactly what it looked like is not known.

keyVerse.quote: Moses wrote down their starting places, stage by stage, by command of the LORD, and these are their stages according to their starting places.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter hangs on this verse: the list exists because God wanted it kept. Every camp of forty years, the miracles, the failures and the forgotten places alike, mattered to him, and the generation about to cross was to know its story as his leading. The same God keeps the record of every stage of his people’s lives.

33.reflection:
Moses wrote down every stage “by command of the LORD” (v. 2), including the places of failure. Why might God want his people to remember the whole story and not just the highlights? What would your own list of stages include?

Marah and Elim come one after the other (vv. 8–9). How have you known both the bitter and the sweet in your walk with God, and what does “and they set out” say to you in your present season?

Most of the names in verses 16–37 record nothing at all. How does it change the ordinary, uneventful stretches of life to know that God was there too?

God warned that whatever Israel spared would become “barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides” (v. 55). Is there a sin you have been tolerating rather than putting to death, and how does Christ’s victory give you hope to fight it?

34.title: The Boundaries of Canaan: The Specificity of God's Promise
34.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Command the people of Israel, and say to them, When you enter the land of Canaan (this is the land that shall fall to you for an inheritance, the land of Canaan as defined by its borders),<sup>3</sup>your south side shall be from the wilderness of Zin alongside Edom, and your southern border shall run from the end of the Salt Sea on the east.<sup>4</sup>And your border shall turn south of the ascent of Akrabbim, and cross to Zin, and its limit shall be south of Kadesh-barnea. Then it shall go on to Hazar-addar, and pass along to Azmon.<sup>5</sup>And the border shall turn from Azmon to the Brook of Egypt, and its limit shall be at the sea.<sup>6</sup>"For the western border, you shall have the Great Sea and its coast. This shall be your western border.<sup>7</sup>"This shall be your northern border: from the Great Sea you shall draw a line to Mount Hor.<sup>8</sup>From Mount Hor you shall draw a line to Lebo-hamath, and the limit of the border shall be at Zedad.<sup>9</sup>Then the border shall extend to Ziphron, and its limit shall be at Hazar-enan. This shall be your northern border.<sup>10</sup>"You shall draw a line for your eastern border from Hazar-enan to Shepham.<sup>11</sup>And the border shall go down from Shepham to Riblah on the east side of Ain. And the border shall go down and reach to the shoulder of the Sea of Chinnereth on the east.<sup>12</sup>And the border shall go down to the Jordan, and its limit shall be at the Salt Sea. This shall be your land as defined by its borders all around."<sup>13</sup>Moses commanded the people of Israel, saying, "This is the land that you shall inherit by lot, which the LORD has commanded to give to the nine tribes and to the half-tribe.<sup>14</sup>For the tribe of the people of Reuben by fathers' houses and the tribe of the people of Gad by their fathers' houses have received their inheritance, and also the half-tribe of Manasseh.<sup>15</sup>The two tribes and the half-tribe have received their inheritance beyond the Jordan east of Jericho, toward the sunrise."<sup>16</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>17</sup>"These are the names of the men who shall divide the land to you for inheritance: Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun.<sup>18</sup>You shall take one chief from every tribe to divide the land for inheritance.<sup>19</sup>These are the names of the men: Of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh.<sup>20</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Simeon, Shemuel the son of Ammihud.<sup>21</sup>Of the tribe of Benjamin, Elidad the son of Chislon.<sup>22</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Dan a chief, Bukki the son of Jogli.<sup>23</sup>Of the people of Joseph: of the tribe of the people of Manasseh a chief, Hanniel the son of Ephod.<sup>24</sup>And of the tribe of the people of Ephraim a chief, Kemuel the son of Shiphtan.<sup>25</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Zebulun a chief, Elizaphan the son of Parnach.<sup>26</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Issachar a chief, Paltiel the son of Azzan.<sup>27</sup>And of the tribe of the people of Asher a chief, Ahihud the son of Shelomi.<sup>28</sup>Of the tribe of the people of Naphtali a chief, Pedahel the son of Ammihud."<sup>29</sup>These are the men whom the LORD commanded to divide the inheritance for the people of Israel in the land of Canaan.
34.overview:
Where we are. The journey has been recorded and the command to take the land given (chapter 33). Now, with Israel still on the plains of Moab and not one tribe holding a field west of the Jordan, God draws the land’s borders, south, west, north and east, and names the men who will divide it.

The message. God’s promise is not vague but definite. He speaks of the land as already settled, “the land that shall fall to you for an inheritance”, and marks it out as a man walks the bounds of a property he is about to hand over; then he names the accountable men who will share it out. The borders are drawn in advance because the gift is sure.

Why it was said. A generation that had watched its parents die in the wilderness, and that faced walled cities across the river, needed to know that the promise was not a mood but a deed with its corners named (see the introduction). It also needed the division to be orderly and fair, so that no tribe or family could be cheated.

How the chapter makes its case. God traces the southern border from the Salt Sea past Kadesh-barnea to the Brook of Egypt (vv. 1–5), the sea on the west (v. 6), the northern line to Lebo-hamath (vv. 7–9) and the eastern line down by the Sea of Chinnereth and the Jordan (vv. 10–12). Moses notes that two and a half tribes already have their land east of the Jordan (vv. 13–15). Then God names Eleazar, Joshua and a chief from each of the ten remaining tribes to divide the land, among them Caleb, who had waited forty years for this (vv. 16–29).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise. Joshua could bring Israel into Canaan, but not into God’s final rest (Hebrews 4:8). The New Testament widens the land promise: Abraham was to be “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), the meek “shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5), and those who belong to Christ, Abraham’s true offspring, are heirs with him (Galatians 3:29). Jesus has gone to prepare a place for his people (John 14:2), as definite as any surveyed country.

For us. Christians often hold heaven loosely, as a vague hope. This chapter says God’s promises have borders: your inheritance in Christ is “kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4), so you can live, give and suffer now as someone whose deed is already signed.
34.theology:
A definite promise. God draws the borders before Israel enters: his promises are definite, not vague.

A reserved inheritance. The bounded land points to the inheritance kept in heaven for God’s people (1 Peter 1:4; see vv. 6–12), as real as the land and far more secure.

God shares out the land. The land is divided by lot and by appointed leaders, so that each tribe’s portion comes from God’s own hand.
34.examples: Your inheritance in Christ is not a vague hope. You may not be able to picture it, any more than a slave born in Egypt could picture the hills of Canaan, but its borders are drawn and it is being kept for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Boundaries of the Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God traces the borders of Canaan before Israel has set foot in it. The southern line runs from the end of the Salt Sea past Kadesh-barnea to the Brook of Egypt (vv. 1–5); the Great Sea forms the west (v. 6); the northern line runs from the sea to Mount Hor and Lebo-hamath (vv. 7–9); the eastern line comes down past the Sea of Chinnereth to the Jordan and the Salt Sea (vv. 10–12). Moses adds that Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh already have their inheritance east of the Jordan (vv. 13–15). The promise is not vague but a real, bounded gift, mapped in advance because it is sure.
verseByVerse.theology: God defines the land’s boundaries in detail (vv. 1–12): what he promises, he specifies. The earthly inheritance, carefully bounded, points to the sure inheritance God has prepared for his people in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: before Israel crossed over, God had already drawn the borders of their home.

Now: our home is just as certainly prepared: I go to prepare a place for you (John 14:2). God promises a real place, not merely a comforting feeling.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Command the people of Israel, and say to them, When you enter the land of Canaan (this is the land that shall fall to you for an inheritance, the land of Canaan as defined by its borders), your south side shall be from the wilderness of Zin alongside Edom, and your southern border shall run from the end of the Salt Sea on the east. And your border shall turn south of the ascent of Akrabbim, and cross to Zin, and its limit shall be south of Kadesh-barnea. Then it shall go on to Hazar-addar, and pass along to Azmon. And the border shall turn from Azmon to the Brook of Egypt, and its limit shall be at the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Israel owns a single field, God speaks of the land as theirs and marks its southern border point by point: a promise he means to keep has edges.

The land that shall fall to you. Two things are remarkable here, and neither is the geography. The first is the tense. Israel has a river in front of it and walled cities beyond, yet God speaks of the land as settled and does what a man does when a property is already his: he walks the boundary and names the corners.

As defined by its borders. The second is the precision: not a land but a surveyed one, its southern border traced from the Salt Sea (the Dead Sea) past Kadesh-barnea to the Brook of Egypt, with its turning points named. Vagueness is the mark of promises nobody intends to keep. A man who is actually going to hand over a field tells you where the fence runs.

Smaller than the promise. These borders are smaller than the promise of Genesis 15:18, from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates, which the rule of David and Solomon reached (1 Kings 4:21). Israel never fully occupied even these (Judges 1), through its own failure, not God’s.

Where Christians differ: does the land promise still belong to the Jewish people and modern Israel? Dispensationalists hold that it does: God’s promise to Abraham’s physical descendants remains literal, with its borders, and awaits fulfilment. Others note that Joshua says “Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed” (Joshua 21:45), and that the New Testament widens the promise: Abraham was to be “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), and the patriarchs looked for “a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16). This commentary’s view: the land is fulfilled in Christ and in the new creation his people will inherit (Matthew 5:5), because the New Testament itself widens it. This commentary honours brothers who hold that the land promise still stands, and gladly agrees with the many, Reformed believers among them, who expect a great future turning of the Jewish people to their Messiah (Romans 11:25–26).

verseByVerse.quote: "For the western border, you shall have the Great Sea and its coast. This shall be your western border. "This shall be your northern border: from the Great Sea you shall draw a line to Mount Hor. From Mount Hor you shall draw a line to Lebo-hamath, and the limit of the border shall be at Zedad. Then the border shall extend to Ziphron, and its limit shall be at Hazar-enan. This shall be your northern border. "You shall draw a line for your eastern border from Hazar-enan to Shepham. And the border shall go down from Shepham to Riblah on the east side of Ain. And the border shall go down and reach to the shoulder of the Sea of Chinnereth on the east. And the border shall go down to the Jordan, and its limit shall be at the Salt Sea. This shall be your land as defined by its borders all around."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The western, northern and eastern borders close the circle: the land is defined on every side, with nothing left open.

All around. Many of these places cannot now be located with confidence, but they could be then. This is a legal description of real estate, drawn before possession, and closed “all around”: there is no open side.

Our inheritance. That is the certainty the New Testament gives a Christian’s inheritance. Peter, writing to people who owned little and were about to lose that, calls it “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4). Kept, reserved, already under guard. Heaven is not a mood or a vague idea; it is as definite as a surveyed coastline, and much of its comfort lies in this, that God speaks of it the way a man speaks of a deed he has already signed.

Uncertain wording. “Lebo-hamath” may be a town (often identified with modern Lebweh in Lebanon) or may mean the entrance of Hamath, the approach to Hamath’s territory; translations differ. The Mount Hor of verse 7 is not the one where Aaron died (33:38) but an unidentified northern peak.
verseByVerse.note: The Great Sea is the Mediterranean; the Sea of Chinnereth is the Sea of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses commanded the people of Israel, saying, "This is the land that you shall inherit by lot, which the LORD has commanded to give to the nine tribes and to the half-tribe. For the tribe of the people of Reuben by fathers' houses and the tribe of the people of Gad by their fathers' houses have received their inheritance, and also the half-tribe of Manasseh. The two tribes and the half-tribe have received their inheritance beyond the Jordan east of Jericho, toward the sunrise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two and a half tribes east of the Jordan keep their place in Israel, though their land lies outside the borders just drawn.

The two tribes and the half-tribe. The eastern tribes are not written out of Israel; their portion is recorded as already settled, and the map is drawn for everyone else. Two chapters ago they made an agreement with Moses (chapter 32), and here it is in the title deeds. God keeps the arrangements his people make before him.

Toward the sunrise. Yet there is a wistful note. The land surveyed here is “the land of Canaan”, the promise proper, and the eastern portion is described only by where it lies in relation to somewhere else: “beyond the Jordan”, “toward the sunrise”. Their inheritance is real, granted by God. It is simply not inside these borders. Scripture does not moralise about it, and neither should we.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–29 — The Leaders Who Will Divide the Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God names the men who will divide the land: Eleazar the priest, Joshua the son of Nun, and one chief from each of the ten tribes still to receive land west of the Jordan (vv. 16–18). Each chief is named with his father and his tribe, beginning with Caleb of Judah (vv. 19–29). The inheritance will be shared out not by an anonymous committee but by named, accountable men, so that the gift is distributed rightly. And at the head of the list stands the one spy of Judah who believed God forty years earlier and has waited ever since to see him keep his word.
verseByVerse.theology: God appoints named, accountable leaders, a priest, a commander and a representative from each tribe, to divide the inheritance (vv. 17–29). The orderly sharing out under appointed authority reflects a God who is not a God of confusion but of peace (1 Cor 14:33).
verseByVerse.examples: The land was divided not by a free-for-all but by named men who answered for their work. God still loves that kind of order in his church: things done decently and in order (1 Cor 14:40), by leaders who can be held to account.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "These are the names of the men who shall divide the land to you for inheritance: Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun. You shall take one chief from every tribe to divide the land for inheritance. These are the names of the men: Of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh. Of the tribe of the people of Simeon, Shemuel the son of Ammihud. Of the tribe of Benjamin, Elidad the son of Chislon. Of the tribe of the people of Dan a chief, Bukki the son of Jogli. Of the people of Joseph: of the tribe of the people of Manasseh a chief, Hanniel the son of Ephod. And of the tribe of the people of Ephraim a chief, Kemuel the son of Shiphtan. Of the tribe of the people of Zebulun a chief, Elizaphan the son of Parnach. Of the tribe of the people of Issachar a chief, Paltiel the son of Azzan. And of the tribe of the people of Asher a chief, Ahihud the son of Shelomi. Of the tribe of the people of Naphtali a chief, Pedahel the son of Ammihud." These are the men whom the LORD commanded to divide the inheritance for the people of Israel in the land of Canaan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God names every man who will divide the land, so that his gift is shared out openly by accountable leaders, and among them is Caleb, whose forty-year wait is about to end.

These are the names of the men. God will not have the inheritance divided by an anonymous committee. Eleazar the priest and Joshua lead, and every man who will hold a measuring line over somebody else’s future is named, with the tribe he answers to. None could take a bribe or favour his clan without the whole nation knowing who did it. Being answerable for God’s work is not a modern management idea; it is written into the arrangements from the start.

Caleb the son of Jephunneh. Look at the first name. Nearly forty years earlier Caleb walked into this land as a spy and told a terrified nation, “Let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it” (13:30), and they talked of stoning him (14:10). He watched every man who disagreed with him die in the desert, one funeral at a time. Now, nearly eighty (Joshua 14:7, 10), he sits on the commission that will hand out the fields.

The promise paid. God had promised him this land when nobody else believed a word of it (14:24), and here the promise begins to be paid, in a list of surveyors. He is faithful to nations and to maps, and to old men who were right and had to wait four decades to be shown it.

A greater Joshua. Joshua shared out the land but could not give God’s final rest (Hebrews 4:8). His name is the Hebrew form of “Jesus”, and it points to the one who does.

keyVerse.quote: Command the people of Israel, and say to them, When you enter the land of Canaan (this is the land that shall fall to you for an inheritance, the land of Canaan as defined by its borders),
keyVerse.note: This verse sets the tone of the chapter. God speaks of a land Israel does not yet hold as already given, and defines it by its borders, because a gift he truly means to give has edges. Every line of the survey that follows is the promise made concrete.

34.reflection:
God speaks of the land as “the land that shall fall to you” before Israel owns any of it (v. 2). Which of God’s promises do you find hardest to treat as settled, and why?

Peter calls our inheritance “kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4). How would treating heaven as definite rather than vague change the way you spend your money, time and hope this week?

God named every man who would divide the land (vv. 16–29). What does this teach about honesty and accountability in church leadership and in our own work?

Caleb waited almost forty years to see God keep his word (v. 19). What have you been waiting on God for, and what helps you keep trusting while you wait?

35.title: Cities of Refuge: A Place to Flee, a Death That Frees
35.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Command the people of Israel to give to the Levites some of the inheritance of their possession as cities for them to dwell in. And you shall give to the Levites pasturelands around the cities.<sup>3</sup>The cities shall be theirs to dwell in, and their pasturelands shall be for their cattle and for their livestock and for all their beasts.<sup>4</sup>The pasturelands of the cities, which you shall give to the Levites, shall reach from the wall of the city outward a thousand cubits all around.<sup>5</sup>And you shall measure, outside the city, on the east side two thousand cubits, and on the south side two thousand cubits, and on the west side two thousand cubits, and on the north side two thousand cubits, the city being in the middle. This shall belong to them as pastureland for their cities.<sup>6</sup>"The cities that you give to the Levites shall be the six cities of refuge, where you shall permit the manslayer to flee, and in addition to them you shall give forty-two cities.<sup>7</sup>All the cities that you give to the Levites shall be forty-eight, with their pasturelands.<sup>8</sup>And as for the cities that you shall give from the possession of the people of Israel, from the larger tribes you shall take many, and from the smaller tribes you shall take few; each, in proportion to the inheritance that it inherits, shall give of its cities to the Levites."<sup>9</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you cross the Jordan into the land of Canaan,<sup>11</sup>then you shall select cities to be cities of refuge for you, that the manslayer who kills any person without intent may flee there.<sup>12</sup>The cities shall be for you a refuge from the avenger, that the manslayer may not die until he stands before the congregation for judgment.<sup>13</sup>And the cities that you give shall be your six cities of refuge.<sup>14</sup>You shall give three cities beyond the Jordan, and three cities in the land of Canaan, to be cities of refuge.<sup>15</sup>These six cities shall be for refuge for the people of Israel, and for the stranger and for the sojourner among them, that anyone who kills any person without intent may flee there.<sup>16</sup>"But if he struck him down with an iron object, so that he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death.<sup>17</sup>And if he struck him down with a stone tool that could cause death, and he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death.<sup>18</sup>Or if he struck him down with a wooden tool that could cause death, and he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death.<sup>19</sup>The avenger of blood shall himself put the murderer to death; when he meets him, he shall put him to death.<sup>20</sup>And if he pushed him out of hatred or hurled something at him, lying in wait, so that he died,<sup>21</sup>or in enmity struck him down with his hand, so that he died, then he who struck the blow shall be put to death. He is a murderer. The avenger of blood shall put the murderer to death when he meets him.<sup>22</sup>"But if he pushed him suddenly without enmity, or hurled anything on him without lying in wait<sup>23</sup>or used a stone that could cause death, and without seeing him dropped it on him, so that he died, though he was not his enemy and did not seek his harm,<sup>24</sup>then the congregation shall judge between the manslayer and the avenger of blood, in accordance with these rules.<sup>25</sup>And the congregation shall rescue the manslayer from the hand of the avenger of blood, and the congregation shall restore him to his city of refuge to which he had fled, and he shall live in it until the death of the high priest who was anointed with the holy oil.<sup>26</sup>But if the manslayer shall at any time go beyond the boundaries of his city of refuge to which he fled,<sup>27</sup>and the avenger of blood finds him outside the boundaries of his city of refuge, and the avenger of blood kills the manslayer, he shall not be guilty of blood.<sup>28</sup>For he must remain in his city of refuge until the death of the high priest, but after the death of the high priest the manslayer may return to the land of his possession.<sup>29</sup>And these things shall be for a statute and rule for you throughout your generations in all your dwelling places.<sup>30</sup>"If anyone kills a person, the murderer shall be put to death on the evidence of witnesses. But no person shall be put to death on the testimony of one witness.<sup>31</sup>Moreover, you shall accept no ransom for the life of a murderer, who is guilty of death, but he shall be put to death.<sup>32</sup>And you shall accept no ransom for him who has fled to his city of refuge, that he may return to dwell in the land before the death of the high priest.<sup>33</sup>You shall not pollute the land in which you live, for blood pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it.<sup>34</sup>You shall not defile the land in which you live, in the midst of which I dwell, for I the LORD dwell in the midst of the people of Israel."
35.overview:
Where we are. The land has been mapped and its dividers named (chapter 34). Now God provides for two groups: the Levites, who receive no territory of their own, and anyone who kills another person by accident. The two provisions belong together, for the cities of refuge are Levite towns.

The message. God’s justice and his mercy meet in the cities of refuge. Life is so sacred to him that no murderer can buy his way out and shed blood pollutes the land he lives in; yet he will not let a man die for an accident before anyone has heard the facts. The refuge is open to Israelite and foreigner alike, and the one who flees there goes free only when the high priest dies.

Why it was said. In the ancient world, with no police or public prosecutor, a slain man’s blood was avenged by his nearest kinsman, and grief does not weigh evidence. Israel was about to settle a land whose former peoples had filled it with bloodshed (see the introduction), and God was going to dwell in the middle of it.

How the chapter makes its case. The tribes give the Levites forty-eight cities with pastureland, scattered through the land, each tribe in proportion to its size (vv. 1–8). Six become cities of refuge, three on each side of the Jordan, for anyone who kills without intent (vv. 9–15). The law defines murder by the weapon and the heart (vv. 16–21) and accidental killing by the absence of enmity (vv. 22–24). The congregation judges, and the manslayer lives in the city until the high priest dies (vv. 25–29). Two witnesses are required, no ransom may be taken for either murderer or manslayer, and the chapter ends by saying why: blood pollutes the land, and the LORD dwells there (vv. 30–34).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. Hebrews describes believers as those “who have fled for refuge” (Hebrews 6:18), and the freedom that came by the high priest’s death is fulfilled in our High Priest, who died on purpose and lives for ever. The chapter also lays bare our need: no ransom can be paid for a life, and only blood answers blood. Christ gave “his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), and his blood “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24).

For us. There is complete safety in Christ and none anywhere else, so stay within the walls. And this law gives hope to anyone who carries a death they never intended: God distinguishes accident from murder, and so should we.
35.theology:
Justice and mercy meet. The cities shelter the unintentional killer without sparing the murderer: God provides safety without denying justice.

Christ our refuge. Christ is the city to which the guilty flee from the just sentence of the law (Heb 6:18).

Freed by the high priest’s death. The refugee’s release came through the death of the high priest, and ours through the death of our High Priest.
35.examples: If your conscience accuses you, do not try to outrun it or argue with it; run to Christ. The door of the refuge stands open, and inside it no accuser can reach you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levites have no territory, for the LORD is their portion (18:20–24), so the other tribes give them cities to live in, with pastureland measured around each for their flocks and herds (vv. 1–5). There are forty-eight in all, six of which will be cities of refuge (vv. 6–7), and each tribe gives in proportion to its size, many cities from the large tribes and few from the small (v. 8). The result is that the men who taught God’s law lived scattered throughout Israel, within reach of every family, and that the places of refuge were the towns of those whose business was the holiness and mercy of God.
verseByVerse.theology: The Levites, having no land-inheritance because “the LORD is their portion” (18:20), are given forty-eight cities distributed among all the tribes (vv. 7–8). The scattering had a purpose: those set apart for God’s service lived within reach of every Israelite, so that teaching in God’s law reached the whole nation. It pictures how God means the knowledge of himself to saturate the life of his people, never confined to one corner (cf. Mal 2:7, the priest’s lips guarding knowledge).
verseByVerse.examples: The tribe devoted to God was spread through all the others, so no Israelite lived far from the ministry of the Word. God’s servants are still scattered, as salt and light, through the whole of life (Matt 5:13–14).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, saying, "Command the people of Israel to give to the Levites some of the inheritance of their possession as cities for them to dwell in. And you shall give to the Levites pasturelands around the cities. The cities shall be theirs to dwell in, and their pasturelands shall be for their cattle and for their livestock and for all their beasts. The pasturelands of the cities, which you shall give to the Levites, shall reach from the wall of the city outward a thousand cubits all around. And you shall measure, outside the city, on the east side two thousand cubits, and on the south side two thousand cubits, and on the west side two thousand cubits, and on the north side two thousand cubits, the city being in the middle. This shall belong to them as pastureland for their cities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites receive no territory of their own, but God gives them towns to live in, with pastureland, throughout the other tribes’ land.

Cities for them to dwell in. The Levites get no tribal region, for the LORD is their portion (18:20–24), but God does not leave them homeless: they receive towns inside everyone else’s territory, with pastureland measured round each for their animals.

Scattered in Israel. Look at what the arrangement does. Levi is not settled in a block but distributed, so that families throughout the nation lived within reach of someone whose life was the law of God (Deuteronomy 33:10). Jacob had said on his deathbed what sounded like a curse: “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis 49:7). The scattering came, and in God’s hands the punishment became the means by which a nation was taught. He does not always remove what he has pronounced; sometimes he turns it round and uses it for good.

Uncertain wording. Verse 4 says the pastureland reaches “outward a thousand cubits all around” from the wall, and verse 5 measures two thousand cubits on each side. The usual explanation is that verse 4 measures outward from the wall and verse 5 gives the length of each side of the resulting square, but the exact layout is uncertain and other arrangements have been proposed. A thousand cubits is roughly 450 metres.

verseByVerse.quote: "The cities that you give to the Levites shall be the six cities of refuge, where you shall permit the manslayer to flee, and in addition to them you shall give forty-two cities. All the cities that you give to the Levites shall be forty-eight, with their pasturelands. And as for the cities that you shall give from the possession of the people of Israel, from the larger tribes you shall take many, and from the smaller tribes you shall take few; each, in proportion to the inheritance that it inherits, shall give of its cities to the Levites."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six of the Levites’ forty-eight cities are to be cities of refuge, and every tribe gives cities in proportion to its size.

The six cities of refuge. Named first, the cities where a man could run for his life were Levites’ towns. The fugitive arrived not at a garrison but among men whose business was the mercy and holiness of God. Sanctuary and instruction were put in the same place: a man running for his life would end up living among those best equipped to tell him why he was still alive.

In proportion. The cost is shared by a rule that runs through Scripture: many cities from the larger tribes, few from the smaller, each according to its size. The New Testament applies the same rule to Christian giving: “if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have” (2 Corinthians 8:12).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six Levite cities become cities of refuge, three on each side of the Jordan, open to Israelite and foreigner alike, where anyone who kills without intent is safe from the avenger of blood until the congregation hears the case (vv. 9–15). The law distinguishes murder, shown by the weapon and by hatred (vv. 16–21), from accidental killing (vv. 22–24). The manslayer must stay in the city until the high priest dies (vv. 25–29). Two witnesses are required, and no ransom is accepted for murderer or manslayer (vv. 30–32), because blood pollutes the land where the LORD dwells (vv. 33–34). Justice and mercy meet, and life is sacred to God.
verseByVerse.theology: The cities of refuge picture the gospel: a God-appointed place where one who has shed blood, but is not condemned to die, is safe from the avenger. The manslayer goes home only at the death of the high priest (vv. 25, 28), and so the death of our great High Priest sets us free (Heb 9:15). And the insistence that blood pollutes the land until the murderer himself is put to death (vv. 33–34) upholds the sanctity of life and the justice of God, justice fully satisfied at the cross, where the High Priest was himself the sacrifice.
verseByVerse.examples: Inside the city the manslayer could sleep at night. That is what it means to belong to Christ: not that the past is unreal, but that it can no longer reach you to destroy you.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When you cross the Jordan into the land of Canaan, then you shall select cities to be cities of refuge for you, that the manslayer who kills any person without intent may flee there. The cities shall be for you a refuge from the avenger, that the manslayer may not die until he stands before the congregation for judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sets apart cities of refuge so that someone who has killed without intent cannot be put to death by the avenger before the congregation has heard the case.

The avenger. The institution needs its background. In a society with no police and no public prosecutor, pursuing a killer fell to the dead man’s nearest relative, “the avenger of blood” (go’el haddam). That was not lawlessness but the only enforcement there was; without it a man could be killed and nothing would happen. The same word go’el names the kinsman-redeemer who buys back a relative’s land (Leviticus 25:25; Ruth 4:1–6).

The weakness. But it had a terrible weakness. A grieving brother riding out on the day of the funeral is in no condition to tell murder from accident. Between the death and the vengeance there was nothing: no hearing, no evidence, no delay.

Until he stands before the congregation for judgment. So God puts something in the gap. More than three thousand years ago, he legislated a right to a hearing before execution. The whole purpose is to slow a killing down long enough for the facts to be established. This is not indifference to blood (the verses that follow are fierce about it) but an absolute refusal to let a man die before anybody has found out what he did.
verseByVerse.note: The six cities are named in Joshua 20:7–8: Kedesh, Shechem and Hebron west of the Jordan; Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead and Golan to the east.

verseByVerse.quote: And the cities that you give shall be your six cities of refuge. You shall give three cities beyond the Jordan, and three cities in the land of Canaan, to be cities of refuge. These six cities shall be for refuge for the people of Israel, and for the stranger and for the sojourner among them, that anyone who kills any person without intent may flee there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The six cities are spread on both sides of the Jordan, within reach of anyone, and they protect the foreigner as fully as the Israelite.

Three cities beyond the Jordan. Three cities on each side of the river, spread so that a man could reach one in time: God arranged the map around the speed of a frightened human being. Deuteronomy adds that the distances were to be measured, or perhaps the roads prepared (Deuteronomy 19:3), and later Jewish tradition says the roads were kept clear and signposted.

For the stranger and for the sojourner. Then a clause this book keeps repeating: the cities are for Israel “and for the stranger and for the sojourner among them”. The foreigner gets the same protection on the same terms. The water of cleansing was for “the stranger who sojourns among them” (19:10); the offerings were “one statute for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you” (15:15); now the refuge. Long before any Gentile had heard of him, the God of Israel wrote the outsider into the emergency provisions of his law.
