When Paul writes that Christ “has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14), it is not a change of mind but the finishing of something begun here.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if he struck him down with an iron object, so that he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death. And if he struck him down with a stone tool that could cause death, and he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death. Or if he struck him down with a wooden tool that could cause death, and he died, he is a murderer. The murderer shall be put to death. The avenger of blood shall himself put the murderer to death; when he meets him, he shall put him to death. And if he pushed him out of hatred or hurled something at him, lying in wait, so that he died, or in enmity struck him down with his hand, so that he died, then he who struck the blow shall be put to death. He is a murderer. The avenger of blood shall put the murderer to death when he meets him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Murder is identified by two tests, the weapon used and the hatred behind it, and the murderer must be put to death.

He is a murderer. Before mercy is extended, murder is defined with care. The first test is the instrument: iron, stone or wood “that could cause death”. A man who swings an iron bar at somebody’s head has told you what he intended, whatever he says afterwards.

Out of hatred. The second test is the heart, stated three ways in two verses: hatred, lying in wait, enmity. God’s law is not content to establish that a death occurred; it goes after what the man wanted and how long he had wanted it.

The avenger of blood shall himself put the murderer to death. Once murder is established, the avenger carries out a lawful sentence, not a private feud: the elders of the killer’s own town hand him over (Deuteronomy 19:11–12).

Murder and manslaughter. The distinction between murder and manslaughter, on which Western law still turns, is not obvious, and few ancient codes drew it so carefully. It is here because the God who gave the law reads motives. And he takes it further, where no court can reach: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). A court in Israel could punish only what the hand had done. Jesus went after the hatred that puts the weapon in the hand (Matthew 5:21–22), and then bore on the cross the guilt of every heart he exposed.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if he pushed him suddenly without enmity, or hurled anything on him without lying in wait or used a stone that could cause death, and without seeing him dropped it on him, so that he died, though he was not his enemy and did not seek his harm, then the congregation shall judge between the manslayer and the avenger of blood, in accordance with these rules.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A death caused without hatred or intent is not murder, and the congregation, not either grieving or frightened party, must judge between the manslayer and the avenger.

Without enmity. The other case is written with unusual tenderness. Three tests, each looking inside the man rather than at the corpse: no enmity, no lying in wait, no desire for his harm. And the picture in the middle is utterly ordinary: a man with a stone in his hands and somebody below he never saw. It took a second, and a man is dead.

The congregation shall judge. And who decides? Not the frightened man, who would always plead accident, nor the grieving one, who would always call it murder, but God’s assembly, hearing both, at a distance from the grave. Mercy in Scripture is never a failure to look at the facts. It is what the facts turn out to allow, once somebody has heard them.

For anyone who has caused a death. This is the passage for anyone who has caused a death: the driver at the junction, the doctor who missed it, the parent who looked away for the length of a phone call. People carry these for decades under the same accusation: you are a killer. God’s law had a different category for them. It did not pretend nothing had happened: a life was gone, and the man went into exile for years. But it said: this is not murder, you are not a murderer, and there is a place for you where the accuser cannot reach you. If that weight has become crushing, talk to a pastor or biblical counsellor, and see your doctor too; getting help is no failure of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: And the congregation shall rescue the manslayer from the hand of the avenger of blood, and the congregation shall restore him to his city of refuge to which he had fled, and he shall live in it until the death of the high priest who was anointed with the holy oil. But if the manslayer shall at any time go beyond the boundaries of his city of refuge to which he fled, and the avenger of blood finds him outside the boundaries of his city of refuge, and the avenger of blood kills the manslayer, he shall not be guilty of blood. For he must remain in his city of refuge until the death of the high priest, but after the death of the high priest the manslayer may return to the land of his possession.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The manslayer is safe inside the city of refuge, but only there, and he goes free only when the high priest dies.

Until the death of the high priest. The sentence is like nothing else in the law. No fine, no fixed term, no labour: he lives in the city “until the death of the high priest”, whether next week or in forty years, and nothing he does affects it. The reason is not arbitrary. The high priest stood for the whole nation before God, bearing the tribes’ names over his heart and making atonement for the people. When he died an era closed, and, as the law itself implies, the outstanding blood-guilt died with him. It took a death to release the man: not his own, not the victim’s, but the priest’s.

Beyond the boundaries. The warning attached is severe: a manslayer who goes beyond the city’s boundaries may be killed, and the avenger “shall not be guilty of blood”. Inside the wall, untouchable; one step outside, unprotected.

Ours died on purpose. Christians have long seen Christ here, rightly. “We who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us” (Hebrews 6:18) is written in the language of this chapter, by a man whose whole letter is about a High Priest. Ours has died, and everyone who has run to him is free, not by serving out a term or by improving, but because the sentence went into the ground with him. And here Christ far surpasses the picture. The manslayer’s release came by an accident of timing, from a priest who never knew his name and did not die for him. Ours died on purpose, knowing exactly who we were and what we had done, and calling it love. And unlike every priest of Aaron’s line, he did not stay dead: he holds his priesthood permanently and always lives to intercede for those who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:24–25), so the release can never be undone.

Abide in me. That is the gospel’s comfort and its seriousness together: complete safety in Christ and none anywhere else. The man who wanders out to see whether the old country is still there has left the only place where he cannot be reached. “Abide in me, and I in you” (John 15:4).
verseByVerse.note: Joshua 20:6 specifies the high priest in office at the time.

verseByVerse.quote: And these things shall be for a statute and rule for you throughout your generations in all your dwelling places. "If anyone kills a person, the murderer shall be put to death on the evidence of witnesses. But no person shall be put to death on the testimony of one witness. Moreover, you shall accept no ransom for the life of a murderer, who is guilty of death, but he shall be put to death. And you shall accept no ransom for him who has fled to his city of refuge, that he may return to dwell in the land before the death of the high priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one may be executed on one witness, and no payment can buy off a murderer’s death or the manslayer’s early return, because a human life cannot be priced.

On the evidence of witnesses. No one may be condemned on the word of one witness (v. 30). The two-witness rule protects against false accusation, and the New Testament applies it to church discipline (2 Corinthians 13:1; 1 Timothy 5:19).

No ransom for the life of a murderer. In much of the ancient world a killing could be settled by payment, and a rich man could afford a death. Israel forbade it, because of what a human being is: “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image” (Genesis 9:6). The law will not put a price on the image of God at any figure. Nor may the manslayer pay to go home early. The system cannot be bought at either end.

A ransom for many. Hold those two verses and then read this: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). God had declared in his own law that for a life like ours no ransom would be accepted. Then the only ransom he would ever take, he provided himself, at the price of his own Son. “You were ransomed … not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). No amount of money could have bought a single one of us out. It was never going to be money.

Where Christians differ: does the death penalty for murder still apply? Israel’s civil law ended when Israel ceased to be a nation ruled directly by God, and some Christians hold that the death penalty has no place in a modern state, out of mercy and because of the risk of error; faithful believers differ here. This commentary’s view: the command to punish murder came earlier, to all mankind (Genesis 9:6), and Paul says the ruler “does not bear the sword in vain” (Romans 13:4), so the state retains the right to take the life of a murderer, with due process and certain guilt; whether it does so is for just rulers to decide.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not pollute the land in which you live, for blood pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it. You shall not defile the land in which you live, in the midst of which I dwell, for I the LORD dwell in the midst of the people of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shed blood pollutes the land and can be answered only by blood, and the land must be kept clean because the LORD himself lives among his people.

Blood pollutes the land. The chapter ends by saying why all this mattered. Blood soaks into the ground and stays: “no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it”. Ceremony, payment and time cannot wash it out. So it has been since the first murder: “The voice of your brother’s blood is crying to me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10). Shed blood has a voice, and it does not stop.

I the LORD dwell in the midst. And the reason the land must be kept clean is the reason for everything in the book: “I the LORD dwell in the midst of the people of Israel.” Not visits; dwells. The camp arranged around a tent, the Levites ringing it, the cleansing of the death-defiled, the refuge cities, the boundaries: all exist for that clause. A God who lives among people has views about the ground they live on.

A better word. So the book that opened by arranging a camp around God’s dwelling closes its law with blood crying out of the ground, and Scripture answers that voice in one place. The church has come “to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). Abel’s blood cried for justice and could not be quieted. Christ’s blood was poured out on the same cursed ground and cries louder, and what it says is not “avenge” but “forgive”. The avenger has been met. The Priest has died. The refuge is open, and its door is a Person.

Why can’t we just move on? We tend to treat guilt as a feeling to be managed: give it time, forgive yourself, move on. Numbers will not allow it. Here the stain is in the ground, not merely in the mind, and the clock does not wash it out. Our greatest writers side with Numbers rather than with our self-help. Shakespeare’s Lady Macbeth tells her husband on the night of the murder that a little water will clear them of the deed. By the end of the play she is walking in her sleep, rubbing at a spot no one else can see, and saying that all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten her little hand. Every audience knows she is right. A wrong done to someone made in God’s image does not evaporate because we have stopped looking at it; it waits. That would be unbearable news if guilt could only be forgotten or endured. But it can be answered, by the better word of Christ’s blood.

keyVerse.quote: And the congregation shall rescue the manslayer from the hand of the avenger of blood, and the congregation shall restore him to his city of refuge to which he had fled, and he shall live in it until the death of the high priest who was anointed with the holy oil.
keyVerse.note: Here justice and mercy meet: the manslayer is rescued, but he must live within the refuge, and his freedom waits on the death of the anointed high priest. Hebrews takes up exactly this language for those who have fled to Christ, our High Priest, whose death sets us free and whose endless life keeps us safe.

35.reflection:
God would not let anyone be executed before the congregation had heard the case (v. 12). What does that teach about how we should respond when someone is accused, whether in the news, at church or in our own family?

The cities of refuge were for “the stranger and for the sojourner” as well as for Israel (v. 15). Who are the outsiders in your community, and how does the gospel’s welcome shape the way you treat them?

The manslayer went free only “after the death of the high priest” (v. 28), and was safe only inside the city (vv. 26–27). What does it mean for you to have fled to Christ for refuge and to stay within his protection?

The chapter says that shed blood pollutes the land and cannot simply be forgotten (v. 33). Why can’t guilt just be “moved on” from, and how does the blood of Christ answer it?

36.title: The Inheritance Preserved: God's Faithfulness to the Last Detail
36.text: <sup>1</sup>The heads of the fathers' houses of the clan of the people of Gilead the son of Machir, son of Manasseh, from the clans of the people of Joseph, came near and spoke before Moses and before the chiefs, the heads of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel.<sup>2</sup>They said, "The LORD commanded my lord to give the land for inheritance by lot to the people of Israel, and my lord was commanded by the LORD to give the inheritance of Zelophehad our brother to his daughters.<sup>3</sup>But if they are married to any of the sons of the other tribes of the people of Israel, then their inheritance will be taken from the inheritance of our fathers and added to the inheritance of the tribe into which they marry. So it will be taken away from the lot of our inheritance.<sup>4</sup>And when the jubilee of the people of Israel comes, then their inheritance will be added to the inheritance of the tribe into which they marry, and their inheritance will be taken from the inheritance of the tribe of our fathers."<sup>5</sup>And Moses commanded the people of Israel according to the word of the LORD, saying, "The tribe of the people of Joseph is right.<sup>6</sup>This is what the LORD commands concerning the daughters of Zelophehad: 'Let them marry whom they think best, only they shall marry within the clan of the tribe of their father.<sup>7</sup>The inheritance of the people of Israel shall not be transferred from one tribe to another, for every one of the people of Israel shall hold on to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers.<sup>8</sup>And every daughter who possesses an inheritance in any tribe of the people of Israel shall be wife to one of the clan of the tribe of her father, so that every one of the people of Israel may possess the inheritance of his fathers.<sup>9</sup>So no inheritance shall be transferred from one tribe to another, for each of the tribes of the people of Israel shall hold on to its own inheritance.'"<sup>10</sup>The daughters of Zelophehad did as the LORD commanded Moses,<sup>11</sup>for Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah, the daughters of Zelophehad, were married to sons of their father's brothers.<sup>12</sup>They were married into the clans of the people of Manasseh the son of Joseph, and their inheritance remained in the tribe of their father's clan.<sup>13</sup>These are the commandments and the rules that the LORD commanded through Moses to the people of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.
36.overview:
Where we are. Numbers ends on the plains of Moab with a sequel to chapter 27, where the daughters of Zelophehad won the right to inherit their father’s land. Now the leaders of their clan raise the consequence: if the daughters marry into another tribe, the land will go with them.

The message. God keeps every portion of his people’s inheritance safe. In one ruling he upholds the daughters’ right and protects the tribe’s land, and the book that recorded so much failure ends with not one promise lost: the people are on the riverbank, the land is mapped, and even one family’s fields are secure.

Why it was said. Each family’s land was meant to stay in the family for ever, guarded by the jubilee, because the land was God’s gift held in trust from him (Leviticus 25:23; see the introduction). The tribes needed to know that a just ruling for five women would not quietly unravel the inheritance of others.

How the chapter makes its case. The heads of Gilead’s clan come before Moses and point out the problem, which even the jubilee would make permanent (vv. 1–4). Moses, at the LORD’s word, declares them right: the daughters may marry whom they choose, within their father’s tribe, so that no inheritance passes from one tribe to another (vv. 5–9). The daughters obey, marrying their cousins, and their inheritance stays in the tribe (vv. 10–12). A closing line sets the seal on the laws given on the plains of Moab (v. 13).

Where it leads. To Christ through the character of God, the same in both Testaments. The God who will not let one family’s portion slip away is the Father whose will, Jesus says, is “that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me” (John 6:39). In Christ believers have an inheritance kept in heaven, and are themselves guarded by God’s power until they receive it (1 Peter 1:4–5). Numbers leaves Israel short of the land; the faithful Son brings his people all the way home.

For us. God cares about the small, legal, unglamorous details of his people’s lives, and he is not careless with what he has given you. Like these five sisters, contend boldly for what God has promised, and then accept humbly the way he arranges it.
36.theology:
Faithfulness in the smallest detail. No part of God’s promise is too small for his care.

The inheritance preserved. God secures the allotment so that not one portion is lost, a picture of the inheritance kept in heaven for those who are guarded by his power through faith (1 Pet 1:4–5).

Faithful obedience. The book ends with the daughters ordering their lives by God’s word.
36.examples: The God who made sure no tribe lost its portion guards your inheritance in Christ. Not one of his promises will fail, and he will bring his pilgrim people home, losing none.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Keeping the Inheritance in the Tribe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zelophehad’s daughters had won the right to inherit (chapter 27), but the leaders of their clan see a problem: if the women marry outside the tribe, the land will pass to another tribe, and the jubilee will make the loss permanent (vv. 1–4). God, through Moses, declares the clan right and gives a ruling that costs neither side: the daughters may marry whom they think best, within their father’s tribe, and no inheritance is to pass between tribes (vv. 5–9). The five sisters obey, marrying their cousins, and their inheritance remains (vv. 10–12). The book closes on the plains of Moab with the land guarded, ready to be received (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The final chapter guards the inheritance so that no portion passes from one tribe to another (v. 9). That Numbers, a book of wandering and failure, ends fixed on a secure inheritance testifies to God’s faithfulness: despite forty years of rebellion, the promise stands, mapped, apportioned and protected, waiting for the new generation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the book of wandering ends not in the desert but with every tribe’s portion guarded.

Now: despite all our wandering, our inheritance is guarded by God himself, kept in heaven for you (1 Pet 1:4), and the land is ahead.

verseByVerse.quote: The heads of the fathers' houses of the clan of the people of Gilead the son of Machir, son of Manasseh, from the clans of the people of Joseph, came near and spoke before Moses and before the chiefs, the heads of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel. They said, "The LORD commanded my lord to give the land for inheritance by lot to the people of Israel, and my lord was commanded by the LORD to give the inheritance of Zelophehad our brother to his daughters. But if they are married to any of the sons of the other tribes of the people of Israel, then their inheritance will be taken from the inheritance of our fathers and added to the inheritance of the tribe into which they marry. So it will be taken away from the lot of our inheritance. And when the jubilee of the people of Israel comes, then their inheritance will be added to the inheritance of the tribe into which they marry, and their inheritance will be taken from the inheritance of the tribe of our fathers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders of Zelophehad’s clan raise an honest question: if his daughters marry outside the tribe, their land will be lost to the tribe for ever.

The heads of the fathers’ houses. The book closes with a legal question, raised with scrupulous care. The heads of Gilead’s clan come openly before Moses and the chiefs, and they begin by reciting the earlier ruling, correctly, as the word of the LORD.

When the jubilee comes. Their difficulty is real. If the daughters marry outside the tribe, the land goes with them. The jubilee returned every sold field to its family, but this land would not have been sold; it would have passed by inheritance to the husband’s tribe. So the jubilee, designed to keep land in the clan for ever, would here lock the loss in.

Honest disagreement. They bring it to the leadership rather than to the women, and they do not object that the daughters got too much; they ask only how to keep the ruling from unravelling something else. That is what honest disagreement among God’s people looks like: a question asked openly, to the right people, about the consequences of a decision rather than the decision itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses commanded the people of Israel according to the word of the LORD, saying, "The tribe of the people of Joseph is right. This is what the LORD commands concerning the daughters of Zelophehad: 'Let them marry whom they think best, only they shall marry within the clan of the tribe of their father. The inheritance of the people of Israel shall not be transferred from one tribe to another, for every one of the people of Israel shall hold on to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers. And every daughter who possesses an inheritance in any tribe of the people of Israel shall be wife to one of the clan of the tribe of her father, so that every one of the people of Israel may possess the inheritance of his fathers. So no inheritance shall be transferred from one tribe to another, for each of the tribes of the people of Israel shall hold on to its own inheritance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God declares the clan right and keeps both the daughters’ inheritance and the tribe’s land whole: they may marry whom they choose, within their father’s tribe.

The tribe of the people of Joseph is right. These are almost the words God used of the daughters themselves nine chapters earlier: “The daughters of Zelophehad are right” (27:7). The same verdict, to the other side. God had not made a mistake in chapter 27; he had made a ruling that raised a second question, and now he answers that too.

Let them marry whom they think best. The answer costs neither party anything. The freedom comes first and the limit second: “whom they think best”, more choice than most women in the ancient world had, and then one boundary around it. The daughters keep the land and the choice; Manasseh keeps its allotment.

Two legitimate claims. God is not obliged to settle every dispute by finding one party at fault. Sometimes two legitimate claims collide, and the answer is not a compromise in which everyone loses a little but a provision neither side had thought of. He can uphold the rights of five orphaned women and keep a tribe’s land whole at the same time, without taking anything from either.

What it does not mean. This was a rule for heiresses of land in Israel, not a law about whom believers may marry today. The New Testament’s boundary for a Christian’s marriage is that it be “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39).

verseByVerse.quote: The daughters of Zelophehad did as the LORD commanded Moses, for Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah, the daughters of Zelophehad, were married to sons of their father's brothers. They were married into the clans of the people of Manasseh the son of Joseph, and their inheritance remained in the tribe of their father's clan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The five daughters obey, marrying their cousins within Manasseh, and their father’s inheritance stays in his clan.

The daughters of Zelophehad did as the LORD commanded. The last thing this book records about Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah and Noah is obedience. The women who walked to the front of a national assembly and pressed a claim nobody had ever granted now accept a limit on whom they may marry, without a word of protest, marrying “sons of their father’s brothers”, their cousins.

Courage and submission. Both belong to the same character. It takes courage to tell Moses and the chiefs that the law as it stands is not right, and something as rare to hear God narrow your options afterward and comply. Real faith does both: it contends for what God has promised, and then bows to the way God arranges it. A person who can only do the first is not brave, only wilful; one who can only do the second is not humble, only passive.

Their inheritance remained. And they did not get less than they asked: “their inheritance remained”. Their father’s name was not taken away from his clan (27:4). Because five women asked, a man who had died in the wilderness still had a place among the people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the commandments and the rules that the LORD commanded through Moses to the people of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book ends quietly on the plains of Moab, with Israel on the near bank and every promise of God intact.

In the plains of Moab. The last verse of Numbers has no fanfare: no oration, no crossing. Just a closing line for the laws and a map reference: “by the Jordan at Jericho”. On the wrong bank, in sight of the walls.

How the book began. Consider how the book began: a census at Sinai, a nation drawn up in order around the tent of God, about to march eleven days to the promise. Then the quail and the graves of craving, ten spies and a night of weeping, forty years, Korah, the rock struck twice, Miriam buried, Aaron stripped of his priestly robes on a mountain, the serpents, Peor, Moses told he may look and not enter. Numbers records a generation that could not be got into a land eleven days away.

What stands on the riverbank. Yet look at what stands on that riverbank: a nation as large as the one that left Sinai; a high priest in office and a commissioned leader with the Spirit in him; a calendar of worship, a law of refuge, a map with borders drawn, and five women whose title deeds are in order. Everything Israel deserved was a wilderness. Everything Israel has is a gift.

He remains faithful. The book with the most human failure in the Pentateuch ends with not one promise of God cancelled by that failure. “If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13). The reader is left on the near bank with the land in view, where every believer stands, facing the character of the God who brought them that far. He did not bring them through the wilderness to leave them at the water. Behind them the graves; in front of them the Jordan; over them the same pillar of cloud that had never once failed to move on ahead.

The one who brings us over. Moses could bring Israel to the river but not across it. Christ takes his people the rest of the way: “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9).

keyVerse.quote: The inheritance of the people of Israel shall not be transferred from one tribe to another, for every one of the people of Israel shall hold on to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers.
keyVerse.note: The whole ruling turns on this principle: each family’s share in the land is God’s gift, to be held and not lost. It shows a God who guards even the smallest portion of his people’s inheritance, and it points to the inheritance in Christ that can never pass out of the hands of those to whom it is given.

36.reflection:
The clan leaders raised their concern openly and respectfully, to the right people (vv. 1–4). What can we learn from them about handling disagreement in a church or family?

God found a ruling that honoured both the daughters and the tribe (vv. 5–9). Where are you tempted to assume that one side must lose for the other to win?

The daughters pressed their claim boldly (chapter 27) and then accepted God’s limit humbly (vv. 10–12). Which of these comes harder to you, and why?

Numbers ends with Israel on the riverbank, every promise intact despite forty years of failure (v. 13). How does God’s faithfulness to them encourage you about his faithfulness to you in Christ?
